News.title: ‘Much-loved’ dad who died after SUV smashed into busy Lidl supermarket is pictured as driver released
News.content:
CRASH TRAGEDY ‘Much-loved’ dad who died after SUV smashed into busy Lidl supermarket is pictured as driver released







Next

A DAD tragically died after a woman driving car suffered a “medical incident” at the wheel and crashed into a Lidl supermarket.

James Singh Jagpal, 39 from Wolverhampton, was pronounced dead at the scene after the car smashed into the building in Finchfield Hill, Wolverhampton, on Friday (23 October) at 6pm.



James had been inside the store when the blue Renault Zoe tore through the glass doors.

Emergency services rushed to the supermarket, with three people rushed to hospital, including two shoppers and the driver who is in her 70s.



Mr Jagpal’s family today issued a statement which said: “A much-loved son and brother, devoted partner of over 20 years and loving father to two wonderful daughters.

“Known for his kindness, generosity and wonderful sense of humour, James was loved by so many and will be deeply missed by all who knew him.



“James was the absolute centre of our world, and it is unimaginable how we will navigate life without him by our side.

“We would like to express our sincere gratitude to the staff, customers and emergency services who immediately came to James’s aid at the scene.”

The family continue to be supported by specially-trained officers and have asked people to stop sharing distressing footage of the crash’s aftermath online.

West Midlands Police are continuing to probe the collision to understand the circumstances.



They have urged anyone who was driving in the are between 5pm and 6pm on Friday to get in contact.

Cops are also keen to hear from people who have any dashcam footage which might show the SUV.

You can get in touch by calling 101 and quoting log 4069 of 23 October.

More to follow… For the latest news on this story keep checking back at The Sun Online

News.title: Chancellor admits he can’t protect families from cost crisis as Budget to offer limited help on rising bills
News.content:
Next

JOHN Healey will admit he cannot protect families entirely from global cost of living shocks despite promising “breathing space” at today’s Budget.

He will use his first financial package to offer Brits limited help with everyday costs funded by pushing up the tax burden to a peacetime record.



But the Chancellor, who was out jogging on Tuesday morning, was accused of running away from the tough decisions on welfare spending and eye-watering debt.

Mr Healey is expected to mount a raid on the banks, betting firms and online retailers while also hitting workers with sneaky “stealth” taxes.



He is also expected to add 2p to the cost of a pint by increasing beer duty – despite campaigners begging for relief for struggling pubs which are closing down at a rate of one a day.

Mr Healey will lower his £24billion financial buffer to foot cost of living help for families impacted by higher prices triggered by the Iran War.

He will say he wants to give families “breathing space” with everyday costs, especially soaring food and energy bills.

The Chancellor said: “We can’t stop these shocks that hit Britain, but we can make Britain more resilient when they do.”

He added: “The world’s a highly uncertain place.

“Conflicts abroad are pushing up energy prices, and the cost of living here at home – piling pressure on the families, on businesses, and on our public finances.”



It will include a 16th consecutive fuel duty freeze and targeted help for vulnerable households, which will be funded by hiking taxes on banks.

Mr Healey is prevented from doing anything substantial on bills by the inheritance left by his predecessor Rachel Reeves.

He cannot raise significant taxes, he cannot borrow more, and he is unable to make serious welfare cuts without squaring Labour MPs.



This fiscal prison created by the previous manifesto is why many people think Mr Burnham could call a general election sooner rather than later.

Shocking figures show Britain’s debt mountain stands at more than £3trillion.

A staggering £1 in every £13 is currently being spent on debt interest.

Mr Healey has faced repeated demands to cut spending by targeting the welfare bill that is set to hit £400billion by the turn of the next decade.

The Tories are calling on the Chancellor not to turn a blind eye to the major issues facing Britain – saying a “do-nothing” Budget will not make people feel more safe.



Healey resigned from government earlier this year in protest at Labour’s failure to spend 3 per cent of GDP on the military.

Shadow Treasury Minister Richard Fuller said: “Britain’s public finances are on a cliff edge.

A ‘do-nothing’ Budget will not solve the problems staring us in the face: a spiraling welfare bill, a crippling tax burden, mounting debt and rising global threats.



“When we see the Budget, we must ask: is it fair to take more and more money from hard-pressed working families just to spend it on more benefits?

“Will more tax hikes and more borrowing make us better off? And is it right to leave our Armed Forces under-resourced?

“Labour are running scared of the big decisions necessary to get our country back on track. Burnham must not bottle it.”



Reform spokesman Robert Jenrick added: “John Healey can’t keep fiddling while the economy burns.

“Borrowing costs are soaring, national debt has surpassed £3trillion, and the tax burden is at a record high.

“We need a break-glass Budget that finally puts the economy back on track.”

Shadow Chancellor Andrew Griffith tonight said warned Labour to stop “maxing out” the nation’s credit card.

He said: “Our public finances are on a cliff edge. John Healey must use his Budget to take tough decisions, instead of continuing to kick the can down the road.



“He must stop maxing out the nation’s credit card, tackle the out-of-control welfare bill and address rising global threats.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“If Healey fudges defence spending rather than properly funding 3% by 2030 in his Budget, he must resign.

“Defence is the first duty of any government, and we cannot leave our armed forces waiting any longer.”

News.title: Chancellor’s Budget MUST cut taxes, go for growth, and make work pay – but will he deliver ANY of it?
News.content:
Time to deliver







Next

TODAY John Healey delivers his maiden Budget — and hard-working Brits will be watching closely.

This is the first real road test, not just for the new Chancellor, but for Andy Burnham’s government.



What Sun readers want is a big dollop of common sense.

What they dread is a continued fixation with the failed tax-and-spend ideology that has plunged this country into a financial mess.



Healey faces a nightmare economic landscape, with Britain buried under a £3trillion debt mountain, the economy flatlining and inflation creeping up.

Yet despite this bleak horizon, the path back to sanity is blindingly clear.



Firstly, tough, uncompromising action is needed to slash the biggest drain on taxpayers’ money — the hugely bloated £334billion welfare bill.

We simply cannot afford to pile on more debt to fund further welfare dependency.

Finally getting tough would send a powerful message to the jittery markets that Britain is serious about living within our means.

Next, the tax burden — already the highest in peacetime — must be slashed.



This should start with hacking back punitive business taxes that are strangling firms, stifling growth, and locking nearly a million under-25s out of jobs.

Urgent relief is also needed — for firms and families — from sky-high energy prices.

That means cutting wasteful green subsidies before household energy bills hurtle towards £2,200 in the spring.

The blueprint for Britain’s recovery is obvious: cut taxes, go for growth, and make work pay.

Will the Chancellor deliver ANY of it?



Or will the day end with debt up, the welfare bill up, and more job-crushing tax rises on business?

The stakes could not be higher.

Prepare for war

THE Chancellor knows better than most the terrifying danger of starving our brave Armed Forces of cash.

After all, he quit as Defence Secretary when former PM Sir Keir Starmer refused to take the threat posed by Vladimir Putin seriously enough.

Now he has been given advice by Volodymyr Zelensky, whose heroic nation has been at war with Russia for four long years.



In an exclusive interview with The Sun, Ukraine’s leader warns rearming should be a top priority and pleads: “Don’t delay.”

It is hoped that John Healey will heed his advice when he delivers his Budget this afternoon.

Yet he is expected to announce only a “down payment” on meeting Nato commitments.

Worse still, former Tory defence supremo Sir Ben Wallace claims that Labour is cooking the books — falsely inflating spending figures by sneakily counting cash meant for spy agencies MI5, MI6, and GCHQ.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

The message is staring Labour in the face: If you want peace, prepare for war.



It is time to back our boys and fund our Forces — before it is too late.

News.title: As John Healey tries to balance books, union chiefs in a parallel universe want more pay for less work
News.content:
Next

THE Chancellor will today attempt the almost impossible task of balancing spending demands while keeping the bond market vigilantes from Britain’s door.

But there is a parallel universe where there are no such pressures on public spending, where everyone can be paid as much money as they like — while working fewer hours.



That is the fantasy universe of the public sector trade unions.

Was anyone surprised to hear that the British Medical Association has announced a two-day strike next month by NHS consultants?



NHS strikes have become like Halloween or Guy Fawkes Night: A fixed part of the calendar.

The BMA — a grubby trade union like all the others, in spite of its pretensions to be a professional association — has not only demanded a fat pay rise but also a cut in their standard weekly working hours from 40 to 35.



The strike will mean yet more operations and procedures being postponed, at a time when there is a backlog of six million people awaiting treatment.

A backlog that has been made much worse by repeated strikes by doctors’ and nurses’ unions over the past three years.

Health Secretary Yvette Cooper has feebly called the BMA’s actions “disappointing” and “irresponsible”.

Sorry, but the government in which she has served for the past two years shares a big part of the blame.



Trade unions will always push for higher pay for their members, as well as shorter working hours.

They don’t care about the country’s dire fiscal situation.

But it is the Government’s job to resist unreasonable demands and make sure the country doesn’t go bust.

Instead, what did Labour do as soon as it returned to power in 2024?

It awarded fat pay rises to the public sector unions, without any requirement for workers to improve their lamentably poor productivity by adopting better working practices.



Bizarrely, former Chancellor Rachel Reeves complained that the Tories had left behind a £22billion “black hole” in the public finances — when £9billion of that was down to the pay rises she and her colleagues had just splashed on the public sector.

Last week, the Office for National Statistics revealed that in the past 12 months, public sector workers have received average, inflation-busting pay rises of 6.3 per cent, more than twice the three per cent awarded to private sector workers.

And what have the trade unions done to thank the Government for its largesse (or rather, its generosity with taxpayers’ money)? Why, call even more strikes.



The unions think they can get away with it because they see the Government as a pushover, and ministers have done everything they can to encourage that opinion.

One of the most foolish acts of Keir Starmer as Prime Minister was one of his very first: To repeal Rishi Sunak’s law demanding minimum service levels on strike days in the public services.

It meant a return to the bad old days when the unions thought they could hold the country to ransom.

He followed it up with the Employment Rights Act, which demands, among other things, that employers send their employees a letter pretty well encouraging them to join a union.

Andy Burnham was installed at No10 as the unions’ patsy, and he has done everything he can to repay them.



One of his first actions was to award train drivers on Avanti West Coast services a basic pay rise of 3.6 per cent, plus time and a half for working on a Sunday as well as a £720 bonus merely for turning up to work five days a week.

Maybe he was worried that a strike would stop him getting to his new No10 North in his beloved Manchester, but there was no justification in the pay award whatsoever.

How ridiculous that train drivers are now one of the highest-paid occupations in Britain, with average earnings of over £76,000 a year, more than lawyers and senior police officers.

This, for a job which in many cases should not even exist: There is tried and tested technology for automating trains.

And guess what: Since the Avanti train drivers were given their pay award, ­drivers on the TransPennine and Chiltern lines have called strikes for higher pay, too.



The Labour Party doesn’t like it when people describe trade unions as their paymasters, but sorry, that is exactly what they are.

They fill the Labour Party coffers, and in return they get almost everything they ask for.

They get fat pay rises, as well as laws making it easier for them to go on strike and demand even more.

Even more outrageously, taxpayers are funding their activities.

In 2023/24, taxpayers spent nearly £100million on trade union “facility time” — where officials are allowed to carry out union activity in their paid hours.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

No matter how hard John Healey tries to balance the books today, you can be sure his efforts will be undermined by yet more unreasonable demands from the unions.

There will have to be a very big change in culture within the Labour Party before it is any different.

News.title: Missing Capybara Samba is spotted for the first time in months as net closes in on at-large rodent
News.content:
Next

SAMBA the runaway capybara has been spotted on cameras more than six months after escaping from a Hampshire zoo as the net finally closes in on her.

The furry fugitive broke out of Marwell Zoo on March 17 with her sister Tango while being moved into a temporary enclosure.



Now in an update from Marwell Zoo, the youngster has been spotted on wildlife cameras and plans are being drawn up to catch her for good.

Tango, her sister, was quickly recovered after the great escape and she was found in some bushes close to the zoo.



The “more adventurous” Samba, however, has been in hiding ever since.

A dog walker first spotted the large rodent sitting on the river bank in the days following her escape, but the capybara was spooked by a dog barking and jumped into the water.



Thermal drones and sniffer dogs were regularly deployed to try and track her down with no luck.

But the implementation of regular feeding spots seems to have done the trick.



The zoo has said the chase is far from over, however, as Samba still needs to be captured.

A spokesperson for Marwell Zoo said: “Recovering Samba is a gradual and carefully managed process. Although we know the area she is in, it isn’t simply a case of being able to approach and collect her.

“It’s vital that we keep any stress to an absolute minimum, as frightening or disturbing her could cause her to move away from the area and make her safe recovery more difficult.

“Over recent weeks, we have installed additional wildlife cameras, which have provided further photographic evidence of Samba.

“We have also been establishing a feeding area, encouraging her to become familiar with the location and return regularly. This is an important step in our plans to safely recover her.



“As Samba is currently on private land, and to avoid disturbing her or disrupting our ongoing efforts, we are keeping details of her exact location confidential.”

In July the Zoo announced the arrival of seven-year-old Ripple the capybara.

He was brought in to live alongside Tango and ensure her “continued welfare by providing her with appropriate companionship”.

They emphasised the introduction of Ripple would not detract from the efforts to find Samba.

News.title: Zelensky’s stark warning to UK ahead of Healey’s Budget as he tells The Sun: ‘Spend on defence NOW before it’s too late’
News.content:
Next

VOLODYMYR Zelensky today urges Chancellor John Healey to put his money where his mouth is and make defence spending his top priority — before it is too late.

In an exclusive interview ahead of today’s Budget, the wartime leader called on him to stick to his word and put Britain on a war footing.



The Ukraine president said: “Can the United Kingdom trust Russia or not? If not, defence needs to be 100 per cent the priority.

“My advice to John is don’t delay. Sorry John . . . but it’s important to be direct.”





Referring to Russian tyrant Vladimir Putin, he adds: “He’s testing everything and testing everybody.

“The danger of Russia is bigger than Ukraine. Much bigger.”

Mr Healey, who quit as Defence Secretary over Sir Keir Starmer’s failure to increase military spending as a proportion of GDP, is set to promise “a down-payment” on hitting three per cent by 2030.

No10 has delayed setting out a detailed spending plan for meeting its Nato commitment to increase defence funding until next autumn.



Critics fear it will leave Britain exposed and unprepared amid Putin’s ongoing hybrid war.

Mr Zelensky said: “You need to build your military and tactical facilities and rebuild a lot of different things. Air defence is weak in Europe, not only in the UK.

“We have to understand and respect today’s situation. I don’t know all the problems but I think Russian policy is very dangerous.”



An ally of Mr Healey told The Sun last night: “John’s going to fund the Defence Investment Plan in full today, which is critical for protecting us and Ukraine.”

In a candid interview from his fortified Kyiv HQ, Mr Zelensky said Donald Trump must stop sucking up to war criminal Putin.

He urged PM Andy Burnham and other world leaders to find their voice, stand up to the US President and call out his blatant betrayal.

Mr Zelensky told me: “This is one of our weapons — to speak honestly, to be open and to be clear.

“There’s a lot of pressure on Ukraine at this moment, of course, and I have to be louder and I will be.



“I’m very thankful to Andy, personally, because after all these things, these challenges, difficult nights, very tough nights for our people, he reacted very quickly. But can they be more direct? Yes.”

Mr Zelensky said he had not spoken to Mr Trump since the US President had told reporters last week: “Russia, frankly, has been fine on Ukraine. They haven’t been doing much.”

Hours earlier, one-year-old Angelina Mariukhna was killed when a drone hit her pushchair at a park in Ukraine’s second city of Kharkiv.



Her mum, Inna, 28, also died.

Mr Trump’s special envoy Steve Witkoff fanned the flames when he addressed Putin as “Sir” during peace talks in St Petersburg and described him as “a humanitarian”.

Ukraine’s use of tycoon Elon Musk’s Starlink system was then restricted with no warning, which saw thousands of drones used to defend Ukraine fall from the sky.

Mr Zelensky contrasted Trump’s desire to end the war with his cosying up to Putin.

He also told how Washington derailed talks in Brussels on Monday to focus on the Middle East.



The Kyiv leader, who has vowed not to be pushed into a peace deal, told me: “Everything in this war depends on the will of different countries or leaders.

“What do we need? Not to make pauses. If your will is really to push Russians to ceasefire, you don’t need pauses. You make steps.

“Yes? Each day, each two days, meetings, decisions, technical groups, decisions.



“We decided to have a meeting in Brussels. The Americans invited us. They invited. Now they postponed it.

“Why? Because there are some tensions around the Middle East.” Asked if he felt supported by Mr Trump, he replied: “We are on the same side when we speak about the terms of ending this war.

“But we need more support — there is no pressure (on Russia).

WE SEE VLAD LIES UKRAINE can see through Vladimir Putin’s lies because many of its citizens were born in the USSR, President Zelensky has told The Sun. Survivors of Soviet-era oppression understand the tyrant’s mind games “more clearly” than Americans, he said. In a warning aimed squarely at US President Donald Trump and his golf-buddy envoy Steve Witkoff, Zelensky said: “When Putin’s lying, we see it, feel it. “I think that we understand Russians more clearly than the United States.” Witkoff sparked fury among Ukraine’s allies by hailing Putin a “humanitarian” last week, while Trump has previously dubbed him a “genius”. But speaking exclusively to The Sun, Zelensky said: “Putin is a deeply Soviet person. His reality, his mentality, we understand it because my generation were in the Soviet Union, in Ukraine, [in] the period of USSR.” And he added: “Putin’s personal attitude to Ukraine is that he hates us. “He thinks that all our territory is his territory and his personal goal is to occupy it and to destroy it.”

“No strong signals from the United States mean that Putin is doing well. We don’t hear condemnation of aggression. We need it.”

He urged the US to adopt a neutral position to broker a peace deal.



Mr Zelensky continued: “If the United States, our strong partner, understands that Putin’s goal is to occupy us and to destroy us, they can’t be on Putin’s side.”

He is careful not to cause a deeper split with the US, but when asked if Trump is on Putin’s side he replies: “I don’t know.”

He ends by telling me he draws strength from the resilience of his people.

Hours later, Sun photographer Ian Whittaker and I headed to a basement bomb shelter as 16 hypersonic ballistic missiles and drones rocked Kyiv.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

The blitz on the capital and its energy infrastructure has been almost non-stop for weeks as the Kremlin seeks to impose the harshest of winters on Ukraine.

News.title: US diplomat flown out of UK after ‘swapping sick abuse images with brother’ named and pictured
News.content:
EMBASSY 'PAEDO' US diplomat flown out of UK after ‘swapping sick abuse images with brother’ named and pictured







Next

THE US diplomat who is alleged to have swapped sick child abuse images with his brother has been named as Lieutenant Colonel Michael Morris.

The 39-year-old US Air Force Lieutenant Colonel worked as an assistant military attaché at the embassy in south-west London.



He is understood to have been flown out of the United Kingdom on a cargo plane before he could be questioned by British police.

The controversial operation saw the man seized from the US embassy in London and taken back to a military base in the States instead of being place in custody.



The US Air Force told the BBC it was pursuing a criminal prosecution against Lt Col Morris, and charges will be assessed to decide if he is tried by court-martial.

The Met Police said it is “liaising regularly with the US authorities”.

The dawn raid in August, which The Sun on Sunday exclusively revealed, came after his brother Benjamin Morris was arrested in a sting, in June.

Benjamin, 33, is facing a trial in Illinois for 30 counts of making and sending abuse images of children under 13.

He denies the charges.

The charges relate to a period between March and April of this year.



Prosecutors have accused the pair of “exchanging back and forth” more than 75 child abuse images of under-13s on messaging service Telegram.

News.title: Chris Mason: Budget needs to go some way towards delivering PM's promises
News.content:
Two quotes from the chancellor and the prime minister get to the heart of this Budget.

"The money New Labour had in the 90s is simply not there nowâ¦.Britain has it harder now," Chancellor John Healey said last month.

And from Andy Burnham, days before he became prime minister: "This change...is the most significant change moment in our politics for 40 years."

So what happens when the economic realities confront the political ambitions of this new government?

As Helen Miller, director of the Institute for Fiscal Studies (IFS), puts it, external: "We have a relatively new government with seemingly big ambitions but facing a long list of constraints.

"Some of those constraintsâ¦are self imposed, others are being worsened by global events, most noticeably war in the Middle East."

Let's be clear, plenty in Westminster in all parties will say that the amount of money around isn't everything â how well taxpayers' money is spent and where it is spent matters too.

And spending less and taxing less, plenty argue, should be a priority.

But in the bones of many in the Labour Party is an instinct that the government, the state, can and should be a vital agent in driving change and improvements in people's lives â a world-view grounded in a sense that governments should proudly step in, rather than one that believes they should get out of the way.

And how do you deliver a proudly proactive state, delivering for people in a noticeable way, when the tax burden is generationally high, the national debt is sky high, energy bills are rising and inflation is higher than expected?

In short: it is not easy.

News.title: Minimum wage set to rise but 18-20 year-olds will not get bigger increase
News.content:
The rise in the minimum wage is expected to be announced in the Budget, but 18-to-20 year-olds are set to see lower increases than in previous years, the BBC understands.

Pay for younger workers will rise in line with the increase in minimum pay for employees aged 21 years and over.

However, the increase for younger workers is lower than that seen in the previous two years, when Labour raised the rate to meet a manifesto promise that it would remove "discriminatory age bands" with all adults entitled to the same minimum wage.

Chancellor John Healey is also announcing measures to give families what he is calling "breathing space" with the cost of living.

"The manifesto pledge on equalisation still applies but we were always clear it could happen over time," Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds told the BBC:

"Of course, you want not just good wages but good work, " he added. "It is a balance of making sure the pressures on the labour market are taken into account."

The Times reported that the National Minimum Wage for 18-to-20 year-olds is likely to rise by 3.9% from Â£10.85 an hour to around Â£11.27.

That is a smaller rise than the 26% increase the Labour government has put in place for younger workers since returning to power in 2024.

Even after the reported rise, the rate remains below the National Living Wage for older workers, which is currently Â£12.71 an hour. It is set to rise by 3.9% to Â£13.20, the Times said.

Andrea Egan, general secretary of the union Unison, said it was "deeply unfair" to keep paying different rates for the same job.

"Twenty year-old care workers, teaching assistants and security guards do the same work as their older colleagues," she said. "They don't pay less in the supermarket or at the petrol pump. They must be paid equally."

News.title: Two in court over alleged Iran-linked plot at RAF Fairford
News.content:
Two British nationals have appeared in court in connection with an alleged Iran-linked plot at RAF Fairford last month.

Mohmed Abdulkarim, 24, from Westminster, London, has been charged with assisting a foreign intelligence service, which police earlier said they believed to be Iran.

Nouman Essghir, also 24 and from Westminster, has been charged with entering a prohibited place for a purpose prejudicial to the UK on 22 August - weeks before he was arrested near the airbase in Gloucestershire alongside four other men.

The pair appeared at Westminster Magistrates' Court on Tuesday.

A major incident was declared after three suspicious vans were seen near the US-operated airbase on 27 September.

Dozens of residents were evacuated and a large cordon was put up in the area around the base. No explosive materials were found in the vans by police but a quantity of petrol was seized.

The court heard vans bearing the logo "Fuel2You" were spotted close to the base.

In the early hours, the vans came across a Ministry of Defence Police cordon and re-routed to another location.

Police arrived and arrested five men. They later revealed that one had called 999 and reported what was going on.

During the hearing at Westminster Magistrates' Court, Essghir stood in the dock wearing a grey sweatshirt and confirmed his name and address.

His charge relates to an alleged "reconnaissance mission" on 22 August, around a month before the Fairford incident.

Abdulkarim is charged with helping with the plot.

He appeared in court in a wheelchair wearing a checked shirt, jeans and a baseball cap. He confirmed his name and address.

Both men are charged under the 2023 National Security Act.

Essghir has been remanded in custody, while Abdulkarim has been granted bail with conditions including the surrender of his passport.

The case will be next heard at the Old Bailey on 20 November.

News.title: King acknowledges 'suffering of the past' as Caribbean tour begins
News.content:
King Charles has arrived in the Bahamas for a nine-day tour of the Caribbean - the first time he has visited the region as monarch.

The King, wearing sunglasses and a grey suit, was given a ceremonial welcome at the airport before attending a youth rally.

Prior to the trip, Buckingham Palace said the King would not shy away from "colonial legacy" and the impact of the slave trade during the visit but, in line with the UK government position, he will not apologise for Britain's role in the slave trade or offer reparations.

Appearing at his first engagement, he told young people it is "only right" to "acknowledge the great suffering and injustices of the past".

Upon arriving on the island, he met island's Governor General Dame Cynthia A. Pratt and its Prime Minister Philip Edward, before speaking with members of the Royal Bahamas Defence Force as he inspected a guard of honour on the runway.

The King was then met with cheers as he arrived for his first engagement at a youth rally at Clifford Park - where he attended the island's independence celebrations as Prince of Wales in 1973.

During his speech, the King acknowledged his 50-year-long commitment to fighting climate change and highlighted the challenges faced by low-lying Caribbean islands, saying that "our world cries out for healing".

He went on to call on the young people at the rally to "take up the sacred task to play your part" as "in years to come, this will be surely be the measure of every person - how they answered the call to care for planet earth - the source of our life, our prosperity and our security".

News.title: Men abused woman after her husband drugged and advertised her online, court told
News.content:
Four men sexually assaulted a woman after her then-husband drugged her and advertised her on Craigslist, Grindr and swinging websites, a court has been told.

Norman Macksoni, 48, Richard Wilkins, 62, Connor Sanderson-Doyle, 32, and Mohammed Hassan, 38, are on trial at Winchester Crown Court after pleading not guilty to sexual offences against Joanne Young.

They are charged jointly with her ex-husband Philip Young, 50, a former Conservative councillor, who has admitted to drugging and raping her over 13 years.

As the trial began, prosecutor Sarah Jones KC told the jury: "This case is about whether it is ever reasonable to have sex with an unknown woman without checking with her first."

Warning: This story contains distressing details

Joanne Young, who has waived her right to anonymity, told police that to her knowledge she had a "fairly normal" and "always monogamous" sex life with her husband.

But on one occasion in 2023, she said she had woken up with restraints and a blindfold on while a man was carrying out a sexual act on her.

Jones told the jury Joanne had believed her husband was performing the sexual act on her when in reality he was "stage managing another unknown person" who was "taking his place without her knowledge".

Jones told the jury Young had advertised Joanne online, seeking "strangers to come and sleep with his wife".

"He presented it as a kink for both of them, but there was no information from Joanne herself to support this and the photos he posted of her to advertise his offer showed her inanimate and tied to the bed blindfolded," Jones told the court.

"The nightcap they shared, it appeared, would be used to plunge her into a state where anything could be done to her by whoever answered and she would be unaware or unable to remember."

News.title: Landline switchover could cut people off in emergency, minister warned
News.content:
Plans to switch off the UK's traditional landline phone network could leave people in remote areas unable to contact help in an emergency, MPs have warned.

Landline operators aim to complete the switch to an internet-based network instead of copper-wire cables by the end of January next year.

The government and operators say the move to digital landlines will offer a more reliable service.

But MPs representing remote areas of the UK urged security minister Dan Jarvis to ensure that scrapping the copper-wire network did not make their communities more vulnerable in a storm or other emergency.

Unlike digital services, the traditional landline network does not rely on mains electricity and continues to work in a power cut.

Labour MP Torcuil Crichton, who represents the Western Isles constituency of Na h-Eileanan an Iar, said: "Resilience is inbuilt in the islands but we have major problems with connectivity because of this move from analogue to digital phone lines."

He said that "when the power goes out people don't have the phone, they don't have the internet and often they don't have a mobile signal either".

Retail service providers have been giving back-up battery packs to vulnerable customers, which can keep landline phones operating for an hour or more.

But Crichton said this was "simply not adequate" and that mobile phone providers "simply don't have the means to maintain or keep their signal going during storms".

He urged the minister to get telecoms firms to "up their digital game" to protect places "on the edge where people are vulnerable, isolated from their neighbours, where the ambulance is an hour away and the storm is 70 miles an hour".

Similar concerns were raised by MPs from the West Country and the Lake District.

Markus Campbell-Savours, Labour MP for Penrith and Solway, said: "I ask the minister to imagine an elderly constituent living alone in an isolated Lake District valley where copper phone lines have been replaced by fibre.

"A storm takes out the power to their router in the night and by the time they wake, the modest battery back up has failed, as has the mobile mast, does the minister share my concerns that they would have no way to raise an alarm in an emergency and agree that we need a new technological solution to protect the elderly?"

News.title: Trump vs Obama - which president has the star power to get out the vote?
News.content:
As President Donald Trump and former President Barack Obama hit the campaign trail for Republican and Democratic candidates, both parties are hoping their star power can boost turnout in a critical midterm election. The BBC's Sarah Smith attended rallies featuring both men to ask attendees which president they think can still get voters to the polls.

Read more here for a simple guide to the US midterm elections.

News.title: I'm a single mum and limit my weekly shop to £40 - here's what I want from the Budget
News.content:
Chloe Chin-Saad's husband passed away four years ago and her biggest worry is the cost of living.

She's very grateful that the rent she pays on her south London maisonette is set below the market rate as it is housing association accommodation, but says life was easier when she shared the bills. "Two incomes make a massive difference."

She lives with her 16-year-old son, and says her energy bill has risen sharply over the past year and she now pays about Â£200 a month on gas and electricity.

"We try to be more aware, we think more about how long we run the hot water when we do the dishes."

Chloe, 40, and her son have cut back on luxuries like going to M&S and the cinema, and she now tries to limit the weekly food shop to Â£40.

But she can't do anything to reduce her Â£200 council tax bill, the Â£250 a month she pays on car finance, or the amount she spends on medicines for her various health conditions, including rheumatoid arthritis.

Two mobile phone bills, and food and pet insurance for her dog also add to her costs. She says the amount she has left over at the end of each month varies, and sometimes she is left with as little as Â£50.

Chloe wants to see more help for single-parent families.

"I don't access benefits but I work full-time and it's hard. Can the government do anything else to help? Something on our tax bill perhaps."

News.title: Russell Brand told police he never had non-consensual sex
News.content:
Warning - this report contains graphic content

Russell Brand told police in interviews in response to allegations of rape and sexual assault that he had been "very promiscuous" in the past, but had never engaged in "non-consensual sexual activity", a court has heard.

Brand, 51, was interviewed four times between 2023 and 2025 by officers.

The TV and media personality is currently on trial at Southwark Crown Court in London on three counts of rape and other offences. He denies all the charges.

Jurors heard on Tuesday that he gave a prepared statement in each of the police interviews. In November 2023, he said: "I have repeatedly stated publicly and written extensively that I led a very promiscuous life, that I have spent years openly denouncing. I have never engaged in non-consensual activity."

News.title: UK and EU officials to discuss freedom of movement
News.content:
Speaking to BBC Radio 4's Today programme, Reynolds said current discussions ahead of the summit are around food and drink, electricity and emissions trading.

He said: "What the prime minister has also said, quite rightly, is we face a series of policy changes on the European side that will affect us.

"We need to get as little uncertainty as possible, we need to have a way to resolve what our long-term relationship will be and he is going to set that out after the summit.

"He is going to be frank with the British people about what the trade-offs are but no assumptions have been made on that."

Pressed on whether UK officials are talking to the EU about freedom of movement Reynolds said: "They will be talking to them about what the future options for our relationship might be.

"But here and now, the focus should be on the summit and the tangible difference improvements we're going to make."

A government spokesperson stressed there were no current discussions on freedom of movement.

"We are working with the EU on the areas set out and agreed ahead of the UK-EU Summit and within the manifesto red lines," the spokesperson added.

Burnham is far more willing to have a public conversation around Brexit than his predecessor Sir Keir Starmer, whose government was nervous about reopening a debate that proved so contentious in the past.

Some people within the Labour Party had been urging Sir Keir to go further and there is a widely held view that Burnham's comments are likely to go down well with voters tempted by the Liberal Democrats and Greens.

But there is nervousness among Labour MPs with small majorities in Brexit-supporting, Reform-facing constituencies.

Labour MP Melanie Onn, whose constituency Great Grimsby and Cleethorpes backed leaving the EU, told the Today programme Burnham risked losing trust by talking about going beyond the 2024 manifesto at a future election.

"I don't think that the scars have healed for many people around the country so I do think this is an unnecessary conversation to be having at this time," she said.

Onn, who lost her seat in 2019 to the Conservatives but won it back in 2024, warned against re-opening the conversation, saying: "Trust is incredibly important, it's hard-earned and easily lost, and on this matter I think that we should tread incredibly carefully."

Speaking to BBC Wales, Labour MP Ruth Jones said: "We need to be very careful here. We must respect the Brexit referendum result."

Asked if a referendum on freedom of movement was something she would support, the MP for Newport West and Islwyn said: "We're a long way from that. Andy Burnham is floating the idea, and it's great to float ideas, but let's talk it through and see what does it mean, because another referendum at this particular time would be divisive."

Reform UK leader Nigel Farage told BBC Breakfast that "Andy Burnham has no mandate to be in Brussels, to be negotiating any of this" and called for the prime minister to put his ideas to the public in a general election.

On Monday, Burnham left the door open to a potential referendum on freedom of movement with the EU.

The prime minister caused some confusion when he told broadcasters that he would not reintroduce free movement without a referendum, but Downing Street later said no decisions had been made on whether a public vote would be needed.

Housing Secretary Angela Rayner told the BBC on Sunday that no options for the UK's future relationship could be taken off the table.

But Burnham did appear to draw some red lines of his own when he told the Sunday Times, external that he would not be in favour of the UK joining the euro or the border-free Schengen zone.

The fact the prime minister has not been willing to say the same thing about free movement is being seen in Westminster as evidence that he believes it is a genuine option.

News.title: Chancellor to promise £15m to tackle misogyny in Budget
News.content:
The "misogyny prevention fund" is expected to be confirmed in the Budget and is intended to support the work of a national taskforce established last month, external and chaired by Women and Equalities Minister Bridget Phillipson.

Healey said the money will support "practical action to tackle misogyny head-on" and he hopes it will attract additional funding from businesses and philanthropists to increase its reach.

Phillipson said daily incidents of misogyny, including sexist slurs and workplace discrimination, have "no place in modern Britain".

She said: "This funding is a critical step as we work to confine misogyny to the history books, where it belongs."

Phillipson added that "everyone, from big business to members of the public, can do their bit to stamp out misogyny and improve the lives of women and girls everywhere".

When launching the taskforce chaired by Phillipson, the government said last month that it would aim to ensure government policy is "shaped by those most affected by misogyny".

It added its first meeting would focus on young people and later look at "workplaces, digital spaces and social cohesion".

Statistics published by the Office for National Statistics this month showed an estimated 12.8% of females aged 16 and over in England and Wales - around 3.2m - experienced at least one of domestic abuse, sexual victimisation or stalking in the year to March 2026.

The figure was an estimated 8.9% for males - around 2.1m.

For the Conservatives, Morrissey cited the estimates for women and girls as she criticised the announcement.

She said: "Labour simply aren't serious about tackling the crisis of violence against women and girls.

"This week it seems they will get the hard-pressed British taxpayer to fork out Â£15m to fund projects to tackle the 'manosphere'."

News.title: Parents who killed their baby have sentences increased
News.content:
A couple who "fatally battered" their three-month-old son have had their "unduly lenient" sentences for murder increased.

Klevi Pirjani, 38, and 35-year-old Nivalda Pirjani, from Wirral, Merseyside, were sentenced in April to a minimum of 19 years and 15 years in April over the death of their son, 13-week-old Miguel.

The Court of Appeal has now increased Klevi Pirjani's sentence to 21 years and six months, while Nivalda Pirjani will have to serve 17 years and nine months.

Miguel was taken to Alder Hey children's hospital in November 2024. He had severe head injuries and died five days after being admitted.

Miguel was found to have suffered 41 separate bone fractures in at least four separate incidents.

The Attorney General, Ellie Reeves, referred their sentences to the Court of Appeal, with barristers for the government arguing that the original sentences did not "meet the justice of this terrible case".

News.title: Boy who stabbed girl at school was radicalised online, says father
News.content:
Warning: The following report contains details that some may find distressing

The father of a teenager who tried to kill a fellow pupil in a school knife attack has described his devastation and belief that his son was "radicalised" by extreme material online.

The boy, now 16, was found guilty of attempted murder last week after a trial heard how he harboured a hatred of women, had a fascination with serial killers and had planned to target others in the attack at Thorpe St Andrew School, near Norwich.

Speaking exclusively to the BBC and calling for tighter controls, the boy's father said he did not want to "absolve" his son but suggested online material and "a culture of violence and horror" had influenced him.

The government said it was committed to ensuring all children were safe from radicalisation and threats online, pointing to its Prevent anti-terrorism scheme and the Online Safety Act, which compels social media platforms to remove and prevent the spread of illegal content.

The boy cannot be identified due to his age, and nor can witnesses and the victim in the case.

His father, who we are calling John, apologised to the 15-year-old girl injured in the attack on 11 March, saying: "We're so very sorry for what happened."

John spoke of his fears that young men were being radicalised towards violence and hatred.

"You can think... it can never happen to my family or my son couldn't be involved, but that's what we thought and that wasn't the case," he said.

News.title: Unnamed celebrity accused of 'inappropriate sexual activities', court hears
News.content:
A celebrity has asked the High Court to prevent two news organisations from publishing his identity and allegations that he abused his status for many years to engage, or attempt to engage, in "inappropriate sexual activities with a large number of girls and young women".

The unnamed celebrity is seeking an injunction, and his legal team told the first day of a trial on Tuesday that any publication would be "highly likely" to lead him to kill himself.

They told the court that his drastic reaction was not because of any wrongdoing, but because of the fear of "trial by media".

The man denies abusing "his power and position as a celebrity to contact and forge relationships with young women and teenagers to try to have sex with them", the court heard.

The legal team for ITN and Guardian News and Media (GNM) told the court that the celebrity's "suicide risk" could be mitigated and there was no proper basis "to restrain the publication of public interest journalism".

A medical report carried out for the court said inpatient treatment could provide "significant, but not complete mitigation of the risk", but that treatment, perhaps for months, had "a realistic potential to reduce the risk".

The judge, Mr Justice Nicklin, said there was "significant public interest" in the proceedings and that "this is a difficult and important case".

He added: "The court must determine it fairly, on the evidence and legal submissions."

News.title: Police failings in friends' death on mountain ridge could risk lives, coroner warns
News.content:
More people could die on remote mountains unless police do a better job in responding to dropped 999 calls, a coroner has warned.

The bodies of friends Eddie Hill, 20, and Jayden Long, 19, both from Dereham, Norfolk, were found on a mountain ridge in Eryri, also known as Snowdonia, on 19 February, a day after a call from Long to North Wales Police was disconnected.

Officers did try unsuccessfully to call him back, but then made "limited" efforts to find out who owned the phone and took more than three hours to alert mountain rescue, assistant coroner Sarah Riley said.

North Wales Police said it had taken steps to strengthen its policies and procedures.

Hill and Long died in extreme winter conditions on Crib y Ddysgl, a ridge that peaks at 1,065m (3,494ft), less than a mile north of Yr Wyddfa's summit and linking it to the notoriously narrow ridge of Crib Goch.

A Prevention of Future Deaths, external report said police received a discontinued call from Long's mobile phone at 16:27 GMT on 18 February.

A playback captured him saying "hello" and "can you hear me?" before the call was lost.

News.title: More high winds hit parts of UK as Storm Boelo clean-up continues
News.content:
Strong winds are expected to continue across Scotland and parts of Northern Ireland on Tuesday, after Storm Boelo brought flooding and power cuts to thousands over the weekend.

While conditions are set to improve for much of the UK after a wet and windy morning, clean-up efforts could be hampered elsewhere - including in Scotland, where a third of a month's rain fell during the storm.

The Energy Networks Association (ENA) said almost 8,000 people were still without power after more than 800,000 experienced cuts.

Two men were killed by falling trees during the storm on Sunday - a man in his 20s whose car was hit in north London and a 60-year-old man in Dumfries and Galloway identified as Richard Baines, the long-serving curator of Logan Botanic Garden.

A deep area of low pressure, while not severe enough to be a named storm, still brought strong winds with gusts of 65-80mph to parts of western England and Wales in the early hours of Tuesday morning.

Through the rest of Tuesday, the strongest winds will be across Scotland and the northern coast of Northern Ireland, where a Met Office yellow warning is due to be in place until 21:00 GMT.

Gusts will continue to reach 50-60mph, possibly up to 70mph in the most exposed parts of northwest and northern Scotland.

That is is likely to bring further travel disruption and more power cuts in places.

Elsewhere across the UK, Tuesday will be a blustery day, but the wind is not likely to cause any major impacts.

Strong winds and heavy rain will ease off later on Tuesday, with the rest of the week looking much calmer across the UK.

Boelo is the second storm to have hit parts of the UK in recent days, following Storm Austen.

Leo Slade, CEO of the ENA said it had been "a tough weekend" and that efforts to reconnect some properties were being hampered by the weather, with sustained winds of 50-85mph across parts of Scotland and northern England.

"Until that weather system passes, we can't safely get engineers out to replace poles, to get wires back up, so today is going to be a hive of activity in getting engineers out into the field," he told the BBC.

He stressed that the UK's power network was very resilient and money was spent to prepare for these sorts of scenarios, but said a debate was needed over how much more investment was required to mitigate for further storms brought by climate change.

The Met Office has warned about the possibility of further power cuts and people should make sure they have essentials prepared, including torches and batteries.

News.title: Vivek Ramaswamy’s former teacher slams him over controversial ad: ‘I taught you better’
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

A former teacher of embattled Vivek Ramaswamy scolded the Republican over a controversial attack ad he ran about his Democratic opponent, Amy Acton, in the Ohio governor’s race.

Retired teacher Michael Pogue turned up at one of Ramaswamy’s campaign events in Cincinnati on October 24 in protest, holding a banner that said, “Shame on you, Vivek! I taught you better.”

Pogue taught Ramaswamy when he was in eighth grade at Princeton Junior High School, according to the Cincinnati Enquirer, and called on his former pupil to issue a “full retraction and sincere apology” to Acton.

The attack ad received bipartisan backlash after it featured Acton’s estranged mother, Donna Arthur, who lost custody of her children after her late husband was indicted for raping Acton when she was a child. Arthur called her daughter a “liar” in the 30-second ad. He was never prosecuted on that charge before the couple fled the state.

“This latest attack on Dr. Acton hits home,” Pogue told the Enquirer. “I had too many students who were raped.”

open image in gallery A former teacher of embattled Vivek Ramaswamy scolded the Republican for a controversial attack ad he ran about his Ohio Democratic opponent, Amy Acton ( Reuters )

The Enquirer reports that Pogue was the only person in opposition to the ad at the campaign event, with other attendees telling the outlet they were more concerned about immigration and jobs.

Not all of Ramaswamy’s former teachers agree with Pogue.

On the same day as Pogue’s protest, Ramaswamy posted on X that he had been reunited with his first-grade teacher at a campaign stop. “Saw my first-grade teacher Mrs. Hendel at our stop at Shooters Sports Grill in Hamilton today,” he said. We’re going to fight for our kids to get the best education they can, starting at a young age.”

Hendel gave Ramaswamy a certificate last year that touted him as the “future governor of Ohio,” which he shared on social media. “I always knew you would become the super successful person you are today,” Hendel wrote. “I will always be in your court.”

The Independent has contacted Ramaswamy’s campaign for comment.

Ramaswamy’s attack ad and his refusal to back down have resulted in the loss of big endorsements and venue cancellations.

The MAGA loyalist has defended the ad as “legitimate,” with President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance also rallying to his defense. The controversy comes as polls show a tight race in Ohio, with one week until Election Day.

open image in gallery Anti-Ramaswamy demonstrators hold up signs as his campaign bus goes by. At another event, retired teacher Michael Pogue went to protest against his former student and held up a sign that said, ‘I taught you better’ ( Reuters )

But several Republicans, including Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine, have denounced the ad and called for it to be taken down.

Over the weekend, Ohio’s largest newspaper, The Plain Dealer, broke with its policy against endorsing candidates in major races to back Acton for governor.

“Vivek Ramaswamy, seeking the highest office in this state, has produced a campaign  that weaponizes the sexual abuse his opponent, Amy Acton, suffered as a child,” the paper’s editorial board wrote.

“There are moments when a community must decide what it stands for, when its institutions have a duty to speak and when silence itself becomes a statement,” it added.

Ramaswamy has acknowledged that his campaign released the ad, which went viral on social media, and continued to defend it.

“It is an ad from our campaign, and the thing that I want to say is that I would love for this race and this election to be about the substantive issues that impact Ohioans, and unfortunately, Amy Acton has been hiding from those issues,” he told reporters last week.

Brendan Rascius contributed reporting

News.title: Fleetwood v Arsenal LIVE: Minnows beat champions in Carabao Cup’s greatest ever shock
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Jay Lynch of Fleetwood Town celebrates saving Arsenal's fourth penalty taken by Bruno Guimaraes ( Getty )

Fleetwood Town produced the biggest shock in Carabao Cup history as they defeated Premier League champions Arsenal in a penalty shoot-out to reach the quarter-finals.

The Cod Army, who lie 18th in League Two and some 84 places below the Gunners in the English football pyramid, converted all five of their penalties in the shoot-out, with goalkeeper Jay Lynch saving from Bruno Guimaraes and Conor Haughey scoring the winning kick after a 1-1 draw.

Fleetwood had dared to dream when they took a stunning lead in the 21st minute as Aaron Loupalo-Bi fired low into the net to give the lowest-ranked team in the competition a first-half advantage against a much-changed Arsenal side who struggled to find any sharpness.

A frustrated Mikel Arteta responded by sending on Martin Odegaard at half-time and Viktor Gyokeres levelled soon after, but they could not get a winner. Fleetwood survived constant pressure, with goalkeeper Lynch making a brilliant save to deny Ben White and get the minnows through to penalties.

Arsenal’s frustration boiled over when 16-year-old wonderkid Max Dowman was sent off for kicking out an opponent, having been on the receiving end of a heavy challenge before then.

News.title: Canelo vs Mbilli: Start time, undercard and how to watch fight this weekend
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Canelo Alvarez will return to the ring this weekend, challenging Christian Mbilli for the WBC super-middleweight title in Riyadh.

Although the Saudi city has been the target of deadly attacks in recent weeks, Canelo has arrived ahead of his first fight in 13 months, after he was outpointed by fellow great Terence Crawford in Las Vegas.

Against Mbilli, the 36-year-old Canelo faces a stern task; the Cameroonian is the younger man, at 31, and he enters his first title defence with an unbeaten record.

open image in gallery Canelo Alvarez (right) at the weigh-in for his fight with Terence Crawford ( Getty )

Last time out, on the Canelo vs Crawford undercard, Mbilli fought Lester Martinez to a brutal draw to retain the interim WBC title, but he was later upgraded to regular champion when Crawford retired.

Can Canelo prove that he is still among the best in the world? Or, as he returns from elbow surgery, will he show himself to be in the twilight of his great career? Here’s all you need to know.

When is the fight?

Canelo vs Mbilli will take place on Saturday 31 October at the ANB Arena in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia. The main card is expected to begin at 6pm GMT (11am PT / 1pm CT / 2pm ET), with main-event ring walks following at 8.30pm GMT (1.30pm PT / 3.30pm CT / 4.30pm ET).

How can I watch it?

The event will stream live exclusively on DAZN pay-per-view at a cost of £24.99 ($79.99 in the US), and on DAZN Ultimate Tier – which is priced at £24.99 per month. You can purchase the fight or an Ultimate Tier subscription here.

Will the event go ahead, and why is this a question?

The organisation of the fight card has been the subject of intense speculation in recent weeks, due to numerous deadly attacks on Riyadh’s airports. Per Saudi authorities, more than 300 people have been left injured and at least 21 dead, due to strikes by the Yemen-aligned Houthis.

The international airport has reopened, but the US Department of State has urged citizens to “reconsider travel to Saudi Arabia due to risk of drone and missile targeting", while areas near the Yemen border have been listed as such: “do not travel due to terrorism”.

News.title: Mom arrested for leaving four kids at home while she went to Vegas
News.content:
A Florida woman was arrested for leaving her four kids at home while she went to Las Vegas.

The Osceola County Sheriff’s Office received a 911 call from one of the children that a dumbbell fell on her nine-year-old brother’s head on October 21. No adult was present when officers arrived.

The injured child was taken to the hospital and later released.

Fifty-year-old Irene Miller told police over the phone that she was in Vegas for work.

Miller was arrested at the airport after she returned. She faces four counts of child neglect.

News.title: Xabi Alonso’s return to Liverpool felt inevitable – behind the scenes, the reality was always different
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

A wonderful long passer and a midfielder with the capacity to score from the halfway line, Xabi Alonso always seemed to have the ability to plot the way to a far-off target with expert precision. For years, the theory was that it would transport the former Liverpool midfielder to the dugouts at Anfield. When it has, though, it has been the opposition technical area: first with Bayer Leverkusen, then Real Madrid, the other club with whom he won the Champions League, now with Chelsea, the club beaten on Merseyside in two Champions League semi-finals two decades ago.

A man who created many a Liverpool goal has promised he will celebrate “for sure” if Chelsea score at Anfield on Wednesday; he had nothing to celebrate in 2024, however, when his Leverkusen were walloped 4-0, or last year, when his Real lost 1-0.

open image in gallery Alonso has returned to Anfield with Bayer Leverkusen and Real Madrid but coming back with Chelsea for the Carabao Cup fourth round will bring a different atmosphere ( Getty )

The chant in Alonso’s playing days, when Liverpool represented the ancien regime and Chelsea the nouveau riche, was that the Londoners “ain’t got no history”. Liverpool and Alonso have plenty; he scored their first goal against AC Milan in “the miracle of Istanbul”, and they spiralled into decline after his 2009 sale to Real. When he took Leverkusen to an unbeaten double, he looked a Liverpool manager in waiting. Now the wait may be never-ending.

When Jurgen Klopp announced in January 2024 that he would stand down, Alonso seemed the best candidate. Including, it soon transpired, to Klopp himself, who appeared to give the Basque his blessing as his successor. Describing managers of his vintage as dinosaurs, the German said: “The next generation is already there and I would say Xabi is standout.”

Whether or not the Liverpool hierarchy at the time concurred, they were soon deterred. While Bayern Munich mounted a public chase of Alonso, Liverpool did not. “At that time, I was at Leverkusen and I was aware of the situation but I decided to stay,” he said. He never spoke to Liverpool.

The greater surprise, perhaps, was that he did not in 2026, either. Two years ago, after Ruben Amorim was wrongly described as the frontrunner, Arne Slot was instead appointed. Slot won a Premier League title while Madrid, the third superclub Alonso represented, hired him a year later.

Yet his sacking by Real in January felt like a case of bad timing for an increasingly beleaguered Slot. Alonso’s sudden availability made him the obvious alternative, the king over the water. The idea of Alonso was seductive to many a Liverpool fan, if not to their hierarchy. They did not intervene when Chelsea made their move for a man who once had his ankle broken by Frank Lampard in one of the many flashpoints of a rivalry that had a bitterness when Rafa Benitez and Jose Mourinho patrolled the technical areas.

open image in gallery Alonso became a great at Anfield while Liverpool’s rivalry with Chelsea peaked on the pitch ( Getty )

When Liverpool eventually did sack Slot, they instead opted for an outsider, but one who they felt represented an identity adopted after Alonso left. If his coaching career has been influenced by Carlo Ancelotti and Pep Guardiola, and while he also played for Mourinho, some might say Benitez’s more structured tactics are reflected in his teams. Andoni Iraola’s high-energy approach is more reminiscent of Klopp, a kind of chaos theory designed to galvanise Anfield.

Iraola, hired by former Liverpool sporting director Richard Hughes for Bournemouth, was the stealth candidate hiding in plain sight. That Alonso and Iraola share an agent may mean the new Chelsea manager was always aware of Liverpool’s thinking. They have shared a friendship since boyhood, since they played for Antiguoko in San Sebastian.

“We were close friends, we grew up together, we played in the same team, we played as football players against each other, we played together in the national team with Spain and in the Basque country, but now he is the opposition and we want to beat him and the same way he will do with us,” said Iraola.

open image in gallery Iraola, a close friend of Alonso’s from the Basque country, has now won four games in a row at Liverpool ( Reuters )

They have been on different sides of a divide before – Athletic Bilbao and Real Sociedad – and their relationship has been put on hold for now. It is a familiar theme for Iraola, in part because of the extraordinary depth of coaching talent in the Basque country. He faced his former assistant at Rayo Vallecano, Inigo Perez, when Villarreal visited Anfield last week, while it is another Antiguoko alumnus, Arsenal’s Mikel Arteta, on Sunday.

There are other reunions. A reason to think Liverpool might have turned to Alonso earlier this year was his success with two of their 2025 recruits; Florian Wirtz was named the Bundesliga’s player of the season when Alonso’s unbeaten Leverkusen became champions, while Jeremie Frimpong was also pivotal. Given the latter’s erratic form with Liverpool, it can feel like an even greater achievement.

Alonso credited Wirtz, in particular, with facilitating his progress. “For sure, one of the main reasons for me being here is the time that I spent with him in Leverkusen,” he said. “He was a special player. He helped me so much.”

If a season is an examination of whether Iraola can get the same excellence from Wirtz as Alonso did, a Carabao Cup tie offers an early comparison. Alonso has a trophy-winning pedigree as both player and manager that Iraola lacks. He has his Liverpool past, but Liverpool decided Iraola was their future.
