News.title: Healey vows to give Britons ‘fresh hope for future’ in first Budget
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

John Healey has moved to reassure voters and nervous financial markets ahead of his first Budget as chancellor with an eve-of-statement video promising “hope for the future”.

At the chancellor prepares to unveil his Budget in the Commons on Wednesday, he is hoping to continue with prime minister Andy Burnham’s feelgood approach with retail offerings on the cost of living.

But the City is already concerned about a planned raid on bank profits to help Mr Healey fill a black hole in public spending and provide much-needed financial headroom in anticipation of more financial shocks in 2027.

There are threats that the current tax situation means that banks are considering moving headquarters out of London to European rivals, including Hamburg and Paris.

open image in gallery Chancellor John Healey will deliver his autumn Budget statement on Wednesday ( PA )

But Mr Healey aimed to assure them that he is providing financial stability and security while also telling voters who are still uncertain about Labour that he will provide help for them with rising costs.

In his eve-of-Budget video, Mr Healey said: “Breathing space for today and fresh hope for the future. That's what today's Budget will deliver.

“The world’s a highly uncertain place. Conflicts abroad are pushing up energy prices, and the cost of living here at home – piling pressure on the families, on businesses, and on our public finances.

“But Britain's economy is showing real signs of resilience: investments up, productivity is growing, and we had the joint fastest growth in the G7 in the first half of this year.”

It is understood that Mr Healey wants to find money to help the poorest households with energy bills as well as freeze fuel duty again.

He is under pressure to properly fund pay rises in the public sector with unions threatening strike action next year but he acknowledged that the international situation will make things difficult.

Referring to the continuing wars in the Middle East and Ukraine which are driving up inflation and hitting interest rates on people’s mortgages, the chancellor admitted: “We can't stop these shocks that hit Britain, but we can make Britain more resilient when they do.

open image in gallery John Healey prepares for his first Budget as chancellor ( Lauren Hurley/No 10 Downing Street )

“So, this Budget is designed to give households breathing space from some of the everyday costs, provide targeted support for businesses and self-employed people, and to start the long-term action needed to get energy costs down for good.”

However, he insisted that despite claims Labour has become “anti-business”, he does want to back them, even though he is set to add to cost pressures by agreeing to a 4 per cent rise in the minimum wage.

He said: “Breathing space today must go hand-in-hand with building for the future.

So, we'll back British businesses and entrepreneurs, we'll invest in the technologies that drive future growth, and we'll build more homes, shift power out of Whitehall, so that leaders locally can drive growth in every postcode.”

In an interview with ITV, Wes Streeting, the defence secretary, confirmed that his department will see extra funding in the Budget as Labour aims towards meeting the 3 per cent of GDP on defence and security by 2030, after repeated pressure to do so from Donald Trump.

Mr Healey resigned as Sir Keir Starmer’s defence secretary, triggering the events which saw Mr Burnham replace him as prime minister because of a failure by the previous government to find the military funding needed.

open image in gallery Streeting has confirmed that defence is getting more money ( AFP/Getty )

In his video, he insisted that he would come good on his promise to find the cash for defence.

Mr Healey said: “In an uncertain world, we will strengthen national security and our defences, as well as our support for Ukraine.”

But he insisted that the government will not take risks with the country’s finances.

“We'll do all of this responsibly, sticking within tight fiscal rules, and make sure every pound is well invested,” he insisted.

“Because this Budget is about getting through this difficult moment. But it's also about putting Britain on a future path, a better future path. Breathing space today, and fresh hope for the future.”

News.title: Healey: ‘Breathing space’ Budget will move toward lowering energy costs for good
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

John Healey has promised to use his first Budget to give households and businesses “breathing space today” from everyday costs while taking action to bring down energy bills for good in the future.

The Chancellor is expected to announce a freeze in fuel duty as well as plans for longer-term reforms as he seeks to make Britain “more resilient” from global shocks.

In a video message before he delivers the autumn statement on Wednesday, Mr Healey insisted the Government would move to ease the cost of living “responsibly” by sticking to Labour’s self-imposed fiscal rules.

The Chancellor is facing an uncertain economic backdrop ahead of his first Budget in the role, amid a challenging remit to balance the country’s finances while supporting Britons facing cost-of-living pressures.

He said: “Breathing space for today and fresh hope for the future. That’s what today’s Budget will deliver.

“The world’s a highly uncertain place. Conflicts abroad are pushing up energy prices, and the cost of living here at home – piling pressure on families, on businesses, and on our public finances.

“But Britain’s economy is showing real signs of resilience: investments up, productivity is growing, and we had the joint fastest growth in the G7 in the first half of this year.”

Mr Healey added: “This Budget is designed to give households breathing space from some of the everyday costs, provide targeted support for businesses and self-employed people, and to start the long-term action needed to get energy costs down for good.”

The Chancellor will have limited scope for big giveaways because of the stretched public finances, made worse by international market turmoil caused by the Iran war, and little has been leaked ahead of his statement on Wednesday.

He is sticking with the rules set by predecessor Rachel Reeves, requiring day-to-day spending to be financed by taxes rather than borrowing by 2029/30 and that public debt as a share of the economy should fall in the same year.

open image in gallery Prime Minister Andy Burnham has asked ministers to look at energy costs (Carlos Jasso/PA) ( PA Wire )

But changes aimed at easing the cost of living are set to feature heavily, with Mr Healey expected to cancel January’s planned increase in fuel duty, keeping the rate of the levy frozen for the 16th year at 52p per litre, as first reported by The Sun.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham has also ordered the Chancellor and Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh to examine scrapping standing charges from gas bills.

He wants to break the link to stop the price of wholesale gas setting electricity bills too, even though the fossil fuel only makes up a small percentage of total generation.

The Chancellor is also expected to end the Carers’ Allowance cliff edge which has penalised unpaid carers for going over their earnings limit, even by as little as a few pence per week.

As part of a series of measures billed as “everyday fixes,” ministers have announced plans to make a higher tax-free mileage allowance of 55p permanent, and to slash tariffs on a range of popular foods, including chocolate, beans and gherkins, to make them cheaper for shoppers.

open image in gallery The last budget was delivered by Rachel Reeves (PA) ( PA Archive )

The Chancellor is also set to announce a rise in the minimum wage by nearly 4%, while ending the trend of hiking the national minimum wage for those aged 18 to 20 by more than the rate for older workers, raising it instead roughly in line with the rate for over 21-year-olds, according to reports.

Opposition critics have pressured the Chancellor to use the Budget to set out a clear path for defence spending to hit 3% of national income by 2030, but he looks set to wait until next year’s spending review before announcing this road map.

In his message ahead of Wednesday, Mr Healey insisted that “in an uncertain world, we will strengthen national security and our defences, as well as our support for Ukraine”.

He said: “We’ll back British businesses and entrepreneurs, we’ll invest in the technologies that drive future growth, and we’ll build more homes, shift power out of Whitehall, so that leaders locally can drive growth in every postcode.

“We’ll do all of this responsibly, sticking within tight fiscal rules, and make sure every pound is well invested.

“Because this Budget is about getting through this difficult moment. But it’s also about putting Britain on a future path, a better future path.”

The Tories said Mr Healey was set to “shy away” from the difficult decisions, including bringing down the welfare bill, which the Prime Minister has said he does not want to do through “crude cuts”.

Shadow chancellor Andrew Griffith said: “Our public finances are on a cliff edge. John Healey must use his Budget to take tough decisions, instead of continuing to kick the can down the road. He must stop maxing out the nation’s credit card, tackle the out-of-control welfare bill and address rising global threats.

“If Healey fudges defence spending rather than properly funding 3% by 2030 in his Budget, he must resign. Defence is the first duty of any government, and we cannot leave our armed forces waiting any longer.

“The Conservatives are the only party with a plan to back hard work, cut spending, cut taxes and get Britain working again.”

open image in gallery Richard Fuller, shadow chief secretary to the Treasury, said Labour is ‘running scared of the big decisions necessary to get our country back on track’ (Jacob King/PA) ( PA Wire )

The Liberal Democrats warned against a “steady as she goes” Budget and urged the Chancellor to go further by cutting fuel duty and other costs.

“Families are being squeezed from all sides, businesses face mounting costs, and for many it feels like even the basic joys in life have become unaffordable,” deputy leader Daisy Cooper said.

“That has to end. Today the Chancellor must cut energy bills, slash fuel duty and reduce VAT on our treasured pubs, restaurants and cafes.

“This must go hand in hand with getting Britain growing again. By joining the EU single market and customs union, we can grow the economy to cut taxes and cut bills.

“The Chancellor’s ability to deliver real change will determine whether his Budget is a pass or a fail.”

open image in gallery Reform UK Treasury spokesman Robert Jenrick called for a ‘break-glass Budget’ (Jonathan Brady/PA) ( PA Wire )

Reform UK’s Treasury spokesman Robert Jenrick accused Mr Healey of “fiddling while the economy burns”.

“Borrowing costs are soaring, national debt has surpassed £3 trillion, and the tax burden is at a record high. We need a break-glass Budget that finally puts the economy back on track,” he said.

“The only way to give hardworking families and businesses relief is to first reduce spending. That’s why Reform has identified £40 billion of waste that can be cut immediately so households can get back £1,300.

“The test tomorrow is whether Healey is strong enough to take those tough decisions, or whether he will capitulate to Labour backbenchers just like Rachel Reeves.”

News.title: Nigeria’s women and girls impacted the most by British and US funding cuts, committee is told
News.content:
UK and US aid funding cuts in Nigeria have impacted the country’s women and girls more than other groups, MPs were told on Tuesday.

Nigeria has been among the hardest-hit countries as many Western governments have slashed overseas development budgets to increase defence spending.

At the International Development Committee’s first hearing on the impact of aid cuts on global health in Africa, MPs were told that UK government cuts had impacted water, sanitation, and hygiene (WASH) programmes in Nigeria significantly, putting women and girls at risk.

“WASH is one of the lowest-funded areas in UK government support to Nigeria. WASH enables girls to stay in school, enables them to manage their menstruation effectively, enables women to give birth safely, and protects the lives of children under 5,” Evelyn Mere country director of Water Aid Nigeria said.

“The UK government says one of its priorities is that it will educate girls, empower women and make sure their voices are heard. It means that the UK says one thing, but with the aid cuts does another,” she added.

The British Foreign, Commonwealth, and Development Office (FCDO) announced earlier this year it would reduce its aid spending in Nigeria by 50.2 per cent over the next three years, from £136 million in 2025 to £68 million by 2029.

Nigeria has also faced substantial funding reductions from the US after the Trump administration shuttered USAID, the government’s foreign assistance arm. This included more than $600 million (£450 million) in health funding.

An FCDO internal impact assessment, published in July 2025, acknowledged that the biggest casualties of African funding cuts would be frontline WASH and women’s health programmes.

“Overall, any reductions to health spending risk an increase in disease burden and ultimately in deaths, impacting in particular those living in poverty, women, children and people with disabilities,” the assessment concluded.

News.title: Taliban forbids ‘un-Islamic’ sight-saving operations
News.content:
Hundreds of people each year will be denied sight-saving operations in Afghanistan after the Taliban forbade corneal transplants, doctors have told the Telegraph.

Officials have ruled that the transplant procedure is not permitted under Islamic teachings and have ordered surgeons to halt operations.

It is the latest in a stream of edicts limiting access to health care issued by the regime since it swept to power in 2021.

The edict came just months after a medical charity had helped train up local doctors to conduct operations in the Afghan capital, Kabul, and the eastern city of Jalalabad.

Doctors say there is a severe need for corneal transplants in Afghanistan to restore sight in patients injured in explosions and accidents.

Dr Noor Zaman Hashim of Noor Eye Hospital in Kabul said his staff had conducted 90 transplants in recent months, before the programme had been halted by the Taliban order.

He said the hospital had a growing waiting list, comprising mostly young people who had lost their eyesight because of trauma, injuries, explosions and welding-related accidents.

“Decades of violence have devastated Afghanistan’s healthcare infrastructure. We neither have sufficient ophthalmologists nor locally available corneas to meet the demand for transplants,” he said.

“The Taliban have verbally instructed us to stop the transplants. Nobody has the courage to defy their orders because of the risk of severe punishment,” he said.

News.title: The silent war: As Israel chooses a new leader Gazans wait for life to begin again
News.content:
One year after the ceasefire, Gaza’s health system is still on its knees. Of Gaza’s 228 primary care facilities, only just over half are functioning, according to the WHO.

Medicines are getting in, with almost 87 per cent of requests granted, says the WHO.

It means that someone with a fever or a minor injury can be treated but if it’s anything more complicated there are few options.

None of Gaza’s 36 hospitals are fully functioning, with just 19 partially working, according to the WHO.

There is no MRI scanner anywhere in the Strip, only about 30 per cent of facilities have basic X-rays, and only 12 to 17 per cent have dialysis capability, according to Physicians for Human Rights-Israel (PHRI), a medical NGO founded by Israeli doctors

Chronic illnesses are getting worse. Sally Saleh, head of health and emergency response at Medical Aid for Palestinians (MAP), says there is no capacity to monitor patients or guarantee consistent medical access, so preventable complications from cancer, kidney disease and diabetes will accumulate.

“We need to move beyond simply keeping services alive from one week to the next,” she told The Telegraph.

Power is the biggest hurdle, doctors say. Gaza’s electricity grid has been dead since Israel turned off the supply in October 2023, so hospitals rely on expensive and unreliable generators.

Dr Ahmed Muhanna of Al-Awda Hospital in central Gaza said that when his generators broke down, the hospital rented one for $1,200 a day, but it may only run for 10 hours.

Fuel and spare generator parts are in short supply – but Cogat blames Hamas for stealing fuel and it says that because “Hamas operates inside hospitals” it has to monitor where spare parts end up.

One major problem for those trying to get supplies into the Strip is Israel’s ban on “dual use” items, material it deems serves both a civilian and military purpose. Items that have been blacklisted include generators and metal tent poles.

Cogat says generators, X-ray machines and oxygen concentrators are allowed in under monitoring arrangement with aid groups. But aid agencies told The Telegraph that the rules on what is permitted change from day to day.

Israel allows 15 trucks of dual-use items to enter every week. But the WHO says repeated delays in bringing medical equipment, prosthetics and diagnostic tools into Gaza are delaying patients’ recovery.

In the last six months alone, a single shipment of prosthetics and assistive devices for amputees was rejected four times, the WHO added. It is particularly concerning as Gaza is now home to “the largest cohort of child amputees in modern history”, according to the UN.

“Every rejection means another delay for someone who has already lost a limb and is simply waiting for the chance to walk again,” said Dr Reinhilde Van De Weerdt, WHO Representative in the Occupied Palestinian Territory (OPT).

In July Cogat said over 10,300 pallets of health products had been approved since the start of the year, but only 3,238 had reached the crossing. It blamed “a delivery bottleneck” among the organisations that requested them rather than a “Cogat controlled supply bottleneck”.

Crumbling hospitals mean that around 20,000 patients, including 4,000 patients, need urgent medical evacuation. The WHO says about 5,700 patients have been evacuated since the ceasefire. Save the Children estimates that at the current rate the backlog would take four and a half years to clear.

Cogat disputes WHO and UN figures, and says that it has approved the majority of evacuation requests.

News.title: Harry Kane ends England’s 25-year wait for Ballon d’Or winner
News.content:
The 70th Ballon d’Or ceremony takes place at the London Palladium as England and Bayern Munich striker Harry Kane aims to become the first Englishman in more than 20 years to win the award. Michael Owen was the last Englishman to win the award back in 2001.

The choice of London as the host city pays tribute to the award’s inaugural winner, England’s Stanley Matthews, who won it in 1956. This also marks the first time the ceremony will be organised outside France. Kane, who scored over 70 goals for club and country in the relevant year, is among the favourites for this year’s award alongside the likes of Barcelona and Spain’s Lamine Yamal and Real Madrid and France’s Kylian Mbappe.

Kane won the Bundesliga with Bayern Munich whereas Yamal won both La Liga and the World Cup. Yamal won the Kopa Trophy at last year’s ceremony as the best men’s young player.

Last year’s winners were Spain and Barcelona midfielder Aitana Bonmati and France and Barcelona forward Ousmane Dembele. Dembele is aiming to become just the 11th man to win the top prize at least twice, although it would appear to be very unlikely that the Frenchman will be winning the award this evening.

Selected international journalists cast their votes based on the performances of players throughout the season. The panel consists of one representative per country from the top 100 nations in the Fifa men’s world ranking and the top 50 in the women’s world ranking. Each voter ranks their top 10 candidates, with points distributed on a descending scale. They vote based on three factors: individual performance, team achievements, and class combined with fair play.

In total, 13 trophies will be presented across the men’s and women’s game, including the two man Ballon d’Or awards, the best young players and best teams. The awards take into account achievements from August 3, 2025, to July 19, 2026 (August 16 for the women).

The official ceremony begins at 8pm GMT.

News.title: Nurse accused of spreading Ebola murdered by mob
News.content:
A nurse was killed and a teacher badly injured in a mob attack after being accused of spreading Ebola in the water supply in Congo.

The unnamed victims were set upon in Bafwasende territory of Tshopo province after a group of young people accused them of being responsible for the outbreak of the haemorrhagic fever.

The nurse was killed outright and the teacher, who local media reported was close to the health worker, only survived after being rescued by police.

The World Health Organization (WHO) condemned the attack, which is only the latest incident of health workers being attacked by suspicious, scared or angry locals.

Medical workers have been forced to deal with widespread rumours that the outbreak – the world’s second largest – is spread by them.

Other conspiracy theories claim the outbreak is a money-making hoax for aid agencies, or that foreigners are using it as a pretext to grab the country’s minerals.

Strict rules imposed on how to conduct funerals in order to stop mourners becoming infected, have become another flashpoint.

Last month, a Congolese politician was beaten to death in North Kivu after publicly defending the government’s response.

He had been calling on the public to obey response measures, particularly social distancing and hand washing, on a radio show.

News.title: ‘Our world is yellow’: Fears for children as sickening smog blankets Indonesia
News.content:
For two months now, Natanael Undas has opened his curtains not to blue skies, but a sickening sepia haze that blocks out any sunlight. As the relentless fires smoulder nearby, his city looks “more like Mars” than Indonesian Borneo.

“We start our day in yellow, and we end our day in yellow,” the 32-year-old headteacher told the Telegraph. “When you inhale and take a breath, it feels like you’re choking. Your eyes hurt, your nose hurts… when you go outside, it feels like someone is burning dry leaves next to you.”

Palangkaraya, the capital of Central Kalimantan, is on the front lines of an environmental crisis that has cloaked much of Southeast Asia in a toxic haze for months.

According to Nusantara Atlas, an open-access platform that tracks deforestation, fires have torched roughly 1.9 million hectares across the archipelago so far this year – including one million hectares in September alone.

“I’ve seen burning in the city, burning in the forests, burning near the river, burning in the peatlands, burning near the street – it’s devastating,” said Mr Undas. “It’s the longest burning season I’ve seen. Usually the rainy season comes in October, but everything is still on fire.”

News.title: Britain sanctions warlords accused of rape in Sudan
News.content:
The British government is to sanction senior military and militia commanders accused of atrocities, including rape and sexual violence, during the fall of the city of El Fasher in Sudan.

At least 15 commanders from both the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) and Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) have been sanctioned after investigations found they used rape as a weapon of war during the brutal siege of the Sudanese city in October last year.

The siege, perpetrated by the RSF paramilitary group who have been battling SAF since 2023, resulted in the massacre of at least 60,000 people.

The fall of the city came after an 18-month blockade in which the city’s population were deliberately starved into submission, according to a report from the UK-government funded think tank the Centre for Information Resilience.

Reports from aid organisations, UN investigators, and eyewitness accounts have previously found that rape was used on a mass scale by both sides.

In one incident, aid workers said at least 54 children were raped or sexually assaulted by RSF fighters while fleeing the city to Tawila, a town 25 miles west of El Fasher.

Sports.title: Khan backs new inquiry to improve welfare, health and safety in boxing
Sports.content:
Boxing lags behind other sports in welfare and safety standards; leading UK King’s Counsel launches inquiry to improve standards across boxing and combat sports; Global Fighters Association aims to establish boxing’s first trade union

Former world champion Amir Khan is among a growing number of boxers backing a King’s Counsel-led inquiry aimed at improving welfare, health and safety standards across boxing and other combat sports.

Khan is one of Britain's most decorated boxers who won multiple world championship belts across several weights.

He has backed the Global Fighters Association's (GFA) appointment of leading UK barrister Jonathan Caplan KC to lead a "root-and-branch" inquiry into the safety, governance and treatment of boxers at every level of the sport.

What's happening?

Jonathan Caplan KC has been tasked with leading an inquiry to gather evidence from within boxing and other combat sports in order to raise standards around welfare, health and safety and governance issues.

He intends to consult a broad range of stakeholders, including fighters, coaches, physiotherapists, doctors, surgeons, referees, judges, promoters, boards of control, governing bodies, media commentators, venue operators, managers, and the friends and families of fighters.

Caplan, speaking to Sky Sports said: "We will publish I hope far-reaching recommendations explaining our conclusions.

"We're doing this inquiry late, it should have been done a long time ago.

"There have been other significant inquiries into sport. An MP-led select committee held an inquiry into concussion in sport around two years ago, while the Whyte Review examined allegations of physical and emotional abuse in British Gymnastics. Combat sports are now crying out for the same level of detailed scrutiny. The welfare of participants across all combat sports must be fundamental to what we're trying to achieve. This inquiry is long overdue, and it's something that has never been done before."

Why is this happening now?

The inquiry has been commissioned by the Global Fighters Association (GFA), which aims to establish itself as the first trade union representing boxers and participants across other combat sports.

The GFA's goal is to become a collective voice for everyone involved in combat sports, from those training and competing at their local gym to professional athletes who depend on the sport for their livelihood. Its ambition is to represent participants at every level, both inside and outside the ring.

While the sport's biggest stars generate a significant proportion of its revenue, for every global superstar such as Anthony Joshua or Tyson Fury, there are hundreds of fighters further down the ladder working hard to make a living from the sport. Their welfare, financial security and long-term health are among the issues the inquiry aims to address.

Paul Smith enjoyed a professional boxing career spanning 2003 to 2017, competing at middleweight and super-middleweight. During that time, he won both English and British titles and challenged for a world title on three occasions.

Image: Paul Smith boxed professionally and is now a trainer

Now a trainer and co-founder of the GFA, Smith told Sky Sports: "The average fighter going to work every day is just trying to make a living from professional boxing. There is enough money in the sport for them to earn a living, but at the moment, it's simply not reaching those fighters.

"There isn't a system in place that adequately protects fighters when it comes to health and safety. We've seen so many people injured in the ring and, unfortunately, boxing isn't a sport where you simply lose a race. You can suffer serious injuries, be hit and even be killed. As sad as it is, it happens."

Smith added: "We want to establish a union where fighters feel safe and know they have someone on their side. If something goes wrong, they should be able to pick up the phone and speak to someone who can support them straight away.

"There are so many situations where rules may have been breached and a fighter is required to attend a hearing or answer questions. We want a GFA representative to be there alongside them, ensuring they have support and someone looking after their interests. The same applies if they have a disagreement with their manager or become involved in a dispute."

The GFA says that, in recent months, several fighters have suffered serious injuries in and around the ring, leaving their families to rely on public fundraising pages and the goodwill of fellow fighters and promoters to cover emergency medical treatment and rehabilitation costs. The association argues that these cases highlight the need for a more robust, sport-wide system of protection and support for fighters.

Former world champion Amir Khan also voiced his support for the initiative, saying: "There has to be an organisation that sits above everything, somewhere we can all turn to when something goes wrong, whether it's in training, at a weigh-in, with a contract or even in retirement. The GFA is that organisation."

Who else is involved?

Founded in 2022, the Global Fighters Association (GFA) is stepping up its efforts to improve welfare and safety across boxing and other combat sports, with its ambitions now extending beyond a group of former fighters campaigning for change.

The association's chair-designate is Simon Bazalgette, former chief executive of the Jockey Club and an independent non-executive director of the English Football League (EFL). His experience across professional sport brings an additional perspective to the GFA's mission.

Bazalgette said: "Over the last decade or so, professional sports such as rugby, football and horse racing have raised their game when it comes to the welfare of the participants."

Image: Khan is one former high-profile boxer who is backing the inquiry

"They recognise that the brand of the sport increasingly depends on demonstrating that best-in-class welfare underpins any aspiration to grow the audience and the commercial value of the sport.

"It is striking that combat sport is one of the last workplaces with no professional representation for its workers, meaning little protection, no minimum health and safety standard, no independent pension scheme, no insurance floor, and no single body a fighter can turn to when something goes wrong."

When will the inquiry report its findings?

Jonathan Caplan KC confirmed he intends to conduct several inquiries, with the first focusing on health and safety in boxing and other combat sports. He hopes to publish the initial report by spring 2027.

Speaking to Sky Sports, Caplan said he would examine how other sports have approached similar challenges and consider the lessons that could be applied to combat sports.

"I'm certainly very interested in looking at comparative sports, the conclusions they've reached and the regulatory overviews that have been carried out.

"For example, a DCMS select committee inquiry into concussion in sport is going to be of great interest to me. I'll be looking at what's already been done elsewhere and, where it's relevant, we want to learn from it and apply those lessons."

Caplan stressed that the inquiry would be evidence-led, with fighters and their families contributing first-hand accounts to help inform its findings and recommendations.

"The whole purpose is to produce a comprehensive and reasoned report. We'll be speaking to fighters and their families to gather case studies. Those who choose not to follow the proposals we put forward will have to explain why, particularly if the evidence supports them.

"I suspect the evidence is going to point to quite a lot of innovations that are necessary and long overdue. I don't think anybody wants to see those recommendations ignored, and I don't think anyone wants to be the person who fails to act on sensible recommendations."

Sports.title: Wolff rejects Marko's doubts over Russell's future F1 title hopes
Sports.content:
Mercedes chief Toto Wolff has rejected Helmut Marko's suggestion that George Russell has little chance of becoming Formula 1 world champion in the future after being outperformed by his team-mate Kimi Antonelli this season.

Antonelli won the United States Grand Prix on Sunday to move to the brink of being crowed the sport's youngest ever champion, with the 20-year-old only needing to finish ninth this weekend in the Mexico City Grand Prix to seal the title with four rounds to spare.

Perhaps the most shocking element of the Italian's historic campaign has been the way he has outperformed Russell, who had begun the season as the clear title favourite after dominating Antonelli during the latter's rookie season last year.

Speaking ahead of Sunday's race in Austin, former Red Bull motorsport advisor Marko told Sky Germany: "Mentally, it's certainly a massive setback and it's a blow. Russell is no longer the number one driver."

"Antonelli has quite clearly taken that spot from him. But Russell is one of the top drivers. I doubt whether he'll ever have another chance at the world title or be given number one status anywhere."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Highlights from the 2026 United States Grand Prix.

Asked after Sunday's race whether he has a response to Marko's comments on Russell's title pedigree, Wolff said: "I start with Helmut. I mean, he's my Austrian… not so buddy, but I respect his opinion.

"But I think he's wrong on George. George has all the ability. I think the car doesn't suit him.

"I think that at the beginning of the season, it's maybe difficult to cope with a situation where you're feeling like this is my year to come, and then you have this wunderkind on the other side that starts to really chip away.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player George Russell admits the pace of his Mercedes was 'rubbish ', costing him eighth at the United States GP.

"And I believe that in a new season, George, if we provide him a quick car, it's absolutely possible, (he) has absolutely what it takes to win a championship.

"So, I think it's a bit too easy to say, let's forget about all these years where he won in F2 and in F3 in his rookie years and the European championships back-to-back in karting. That's still all there."

'George is not three tenths slower than Kimi'

Russell had performed with great consistency since joining Mercedes for the 2022 season, exceeding expectations by impressing with Lewis Hamilton as his team-mate for his first three years with the Silver Arrows.

His strong form continued in 2025 as Russell maximised an underperforming car to finish fourth in the Drivers' Championship, more than doubling the points total of seventh-placed Antonelli.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Kimi Antonelli got a flying start at the United States Grand Prix as George Russell was handed a five-second penalty.

It therefore came as a major surprise when, after Russell won the season opener in Australia, Antonelli reeled off the first five wins of his career in succession to establish a championship lead that he has never looked like relinquishing.

Wolff believes the major regulation change that preceded the 2026 season is the main reason for Russell's struggles, but says it is on the team to help the 28-year-old rediscover his best form.

"George, for all of us in the team, is a champion and has won in every category," Wolff said. "And I think he merits to be put in the group of the very best ones (drivers). We've seen that last year.

"And this year, we've seen this variability in results. When we land the car in the way that suits him, he's absolutely fast. But when it drops out of that operational window, he struggles, and he struggles more than maybe Kimi.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player George Russell crashes out shortly taking the lead at the Singapore Grand Prix.

"And that is on us. We just have to work it out with him how there can be such a difference in driving, in performance, because George is not half a second slower, three tenths slower than Kimi. That's just absolutely not the case.

"So, what is it that he doesn't like? What is it that we need to do in terms of modifying the car, setting it up in a different way for him to go fast? Because it's all there, the intelligence, the ability, the determination."

Sports.title: Fleetwood Town stun Arsenal on penalties: Carabao Cup fourth round – live
Sports.content:
4m ago 18.20 EDT “The star of the show was clearly the little girl with a giant sparkly hat and a Fleetwood scarf on her dad’s shoulders to the right of the goal, where the penalty kicks were taken,” writes Kari Tulinius. “What a night she’s having! She’ll remember that for the rest of her life.” Share

5m ago 18.19 EDT Jay Lynch talks to Sky! “My voice has gone! The whole team was magnificent, every one of them. We took heart from Grimsby beating Manchester United last season, it felt comparable. It means so much to the whole town.” Conor Haughey is asked to describe his winning spot-kick. In a broad Ulster accent, he says: “I smashed it in and then ran like fuck.” Lovely stuff. View image in fullscreen Fleetwood’s shootout heroes, keeper Jay Lynch and winning penalty goalscorer Conor Haughey, pose after their famous victory. Photograph: Carl Recine/Getty Images Share Updated at 18.24 EDT

8m ago 18.15 EDT Fans pour onto the pitch as Fleetwood players run to embrace their kids on the touchline. The manager, Matt Lawlor, has tears in his eyes – he can’t believe what he’s just seen. Neither can I. Fleetwood are into the quarter-finals, beating a team 84 places above them in the pyramid – and in reality, the gulf is even bigger than that. Cup football, eh? They’ve tried to kill it, but the magic will never die. View image in fullscreen Ronan Coughlan of Fleetwood Town celebrates with his baby. Photograph: Carl Recine/Getty Images View image in fullscreen Winning penalty taker Conor Haughey celebrates with fans. Photograph: Ryan Browne/Shutterstock Share Updated at 18.21 EDT

14m ago 18.10 EDT Fleetwood win 5-3 on penalties! It’s centre-back Conor Haughey who steps up … and smashes it into the top corner. Fleetwood, 18th in League Two, have dumped Arsenal out of the Carabao Cup! View image in fullscreen Fleetwood Town's Rhys Bennett and teammates celebrate winning the penalty shootout. Photograph: Jon Super/Reuters Share Updated at 18.21 EDT

16m ago 18.08 EDT Cannon scores! Fleetwood 4-3 Arsenal Of course he does. Seven clinical penalties dispatched so far … Share

16m ago 18.07 EDT Gyokeres scores! Fleetwood 3-3 Arsenal Straightforward stuff from Gyokeres, who blooters it into the top corner. Share

17m ago 18.06 EDT Davies scores! Fleetwood 3-2 Arsenal The breeze whips up, nudging the ball off the spot – but Will Davies is unfazed, whipping the ball in the opposite direction as Meslier dives to his left. Share

18m ago 18.05 EDT Havertz scores! Fleetwood 2-2 Arsenal Kai Havertz, waster of many chances tonight, sends Lynch the wrong way to level things up. View image in fullscreen Arsenal's Kai Havertz finds the net. Photograph: Jason Cairnduff/Action Images/Reuters Share Updated at 18.07 EDT

19m ago 18.05 EDT Neal scores! Fleetwood 2-1 Arsenal Perhaps Fleetwood’s best player on the night, Harrison Neal steps up … and belts it into the roof of the net! Share

20m ago 18.04 EDT Odegaard scores! Fleetwood 1-1 Arsenal Right in the corner, beyond Lynch’s despairing dive. View image in fullscreen Arsenal's Martin Odegaard scores a penalty in the shootout. Photograph: Nick Potts/PA Share Updated at 18.08 EDT

20m ago 18.03 EDT Penalty shootout Fleetwood 1-0 Arsenal: Coughlan strokes the ball into the corner to open the shootout, with Meslier going the wrong way. Share

22m ago 18.02 EDT Here we go, then. Because of Dowman’s red card, one Fleetwood player has to sit this out – it’s Jake Batty who draws the short (or long?) straw. Share

25m ago 17.58 EDT Full time! Fleetwood 1-1 Arsenal Fasten your seatbelts – we’re going to penalties. Share

26m ago 17.57 EDT 94 mins: At the other end, Rooney’s cross is shanked into the air by Ben White, and Meslier can’t keep it in play. Corner … headed away by Konsa at the near post. Share

27m ago 17.56 EDT 93 mins: Eze miscontrols the ball but is then brought down, and Arsenal have a free kick. It’s worked to Guimaraes, who floats the ball … straight into Lynch’s gloves. Share

28m ago 17.56 EDT 92 mins: Another chance! Eze gets another chance to whip the ball in and find Havertz, whose downward header spins wide of goal! Share

29m ago 17.55 EDT 91 mins: Another save from Lynch, this time tipping Odegaard’s swerving effort away. Havertz appealed for a penalty, and there’s another shout for handball as Eze’s cross hits Haughey. Share

30m ago 17.54 EDT 90 mins: Huge save! It looks like Arsenal have got out of jail here, with Ben White unmarked and shooting on goal from eight yards out … but Lynch repels it at his near post! Share

31m ago 17.52 EDT 88 mins: Andy Cannon was also booked in that skirmish, while Mikel Arteta did not look remotely impressed with Dowman as he trudged off, offering only a frosty word or two in the teenager’s direction. Share Updated at 18.01 EDT

33m ago 17.50 EDT Max Dowman sent off for Arsenal! There’s a scuffle between Dowman and Neal near the halfway line, and the Arsenal youngster appears to strike out after a hefty challenge. There’s an almighty melee before Michael Salisbury intervenes … and sends Max Dowman off! It looks harsh on first view, but Arsenal will have to see this out with 10 men. View image in fullscreen Finley Potter and his Fleetwood Town teammates rush over to let Max Dowman know what they thought of his challenge. Photograph: Jon Super/Reuters View image in fullscreen Cue the stramash. Photograph: Ryan Browne/Shutterstock View image in fullscreen And then an early bath for Max Dowman. Photograph: Nick Potts/PA Share Updated at 17.59 EDT

36m ago 17.48 EDT 83 mins: Oof! Andy Cannon can see the headlines, but his header is blocked by Meslier and from the rebound, the keeper is down quickly to block Will Davies’ shot from a tight angle. View image in fullscreen Will Davies of Fleetwood forces a save from Arsenal keeper Illan Meslier. Photograph: Phil Oldham/Shutterstock Share Updated at 18.01 EDT

38m ago 17.46 EDT 82 mins: For Arsenal, Bruno Guimaraes and Ezri Konsa replace Zubimendi and Lewis-Skelly. Will Davies is on for Fleetwood, in place of goalscorer Loupalo-Bi. Share

40m ago 17.44 EDT 81 mins: Eze fires an aimless effort into a wall of red shirts, then is flagged offside when the ball comes back to him. Some more changes coming up … Share

41m ago 17.43 EDT 79 mins: A sniff of a half-chance for Loupalo-Bi as he breaks into the Arsenal half, but Mosquera shakes him off the ball before Coughlan can catch up. Share

42m ago 17.42 EDT FT: Bradford 2-0 Peterborough The League One promotion-chasers are into the quarter-final draw. Can Fleetwood join them? Ten-odd minutes to go … Share

43m ago 17.40 EDT 76 mins: It’s full attack-v-defence now, but Ben White releases the pressure by wandering offside. Behind the Fleetwood goal, we can see a solitary lad watching from his bedroom window. Share

45m ago 17.39 EDT 74 mins: Odegaard’s delivery is half-dealt with, before Havertz crunches a cross into the side netting. Share

45m ago 17.38 EDT 73 mins: It’s time! Andy Cannon is on, replacing Mark Helm. There’s a free kick to deal with before any heroics, with Batty booked for hauling Dowman down. Share

48m ago 17.36 EDT 72 mins: It’s played short and Dowman goes for goal, but his effort from 18 yards is held by Lynch at the near post. Share

49m ago 17.35 EDT 71 mins: The Fleetwood fans are still in fine voice, with chants for Rooney, Coughlin and “boring, boring Arsenal” – who have won a corner after Lewis-Skelly’s shot was blocked. Share

50m ago 17.34 EDT 70 mins: Arsenal deal with the corner when Batty steps offside, but the clock keeps ticking, and penalties are now just over 20 minutes away. Share

51m ago 17.33 EDT 68 mins: Coughlan has been in decent goalscoring form and makes his presence felt straight away, jostling the Arsenal centre-backs and earning a throw-in. There’s also a bit of afters between the towering Shaun Rooney and Odegaard, who does a good job of not looking scared. Share

54m ago 17.30 EDT 66 mins: And a change for Arsenal, with Eberechi Eze replacing O’Neill, who set up the equaliser as part of a very promising performance. Share

Sports.title: An unmanageable club? Carrick the latest to suffer in Manchester United’s faded grandeur
Sports.content:
Should any football club fit the Great Man theory of history it is Manchester United. In the past 100 years, only Matt Busby and Alex Ferguson have knocked the club into shape. A pair of 20th-century Scotsmen, born 15 miles apart in Bellshill and Govan respectively, found the key. Otherwise, United has been a managerial dustbin, Michael Carrick the latest likely lobbed on the pile.

Busby and Ferguson built the club around themselves, possessing the charisma to convince others that theirs was the path to follow. Carrick, an insider, a club man, is falling victim to the same isolation as his predecessors in failure. Bruno Fernandes and Lisandro Martínez going off-piste in TV interviews to depth charge Carrick were actually following club tradition. With glamour comes decadence, the faded grandeur that has so often chased a United manager out the door.

Beyond Busby and Ferguson, each United manager who also served felt the lash of desperation of a falling giant. Each of their defenestrations has featured an infighting that would not have been out of place in ancient Rome. Favouritism, nepotism, self-interest, entitlement, complacency and sentimentality have been the betrayal of a legend, to use the title of Michael Crick’s and David Smith’s “j’accuse” book from 1989. Living with the legend and influence of those two managers leads the list of difficulties.

United fans know such history too well. “You lousy bastards, you let him down,” Brian Kidd told teammates when the bullet came for Wilf McGuinness, Busby’s immediate successor, in December 1970. Busby himself had done the deed. A December 1972 meeting at Selhurst Park with Tommy Docherty as Crystal Palace beat United 5-0 hastened the end for Frank O’Farrell.

View image in fullscreen Alex Ferguson shows off the team hat and scarf after his appointment as Manchester United manager in November 1986. Photograph: Gerry Crowther/Mirrorpix/Getty Images

Docherty’s turn came. His sacking in 1977 after an affair with the physio’s wife was announced by the club secretary, Les Olive, from behind the oak door of the chairman Louis Edwards’ Cheshire mansion. Dave Sexton was sacked in 1981 despite winning his last seven matches. Falling attendances at “Cold Trafford” did for “Whispering Dave”. Ron Atkinson turned his November 1986 sacking into a party in the office that also housed the club sunbed. Big Ron’s parting gift was the hangovers that greeted Ferguson’s first day in charge.

Ferguson’s predecessors had been intimidated by the fog of pipe smoke wafting down Old Trafford’s corridors. O’Farrell had needed to ask Busby if the former manager could vacate the manager’s office. “A fantasy world” is how O’Farrell described Busby’s coterie of gossipy former players who teed off with “the old man” at Davyhulme golf course. “There was no reality in the myth,” the Corkman dubbed “O’Failure” said in 1991.

Busby’s indulgence of George Best, careering towards oblivion, created problems O’Farrell found unsolvable. Docherty showed the political wiles to jettison Best in January 1974 but also shelling Bobby Charlton, Denis Law and Paddy Crerand created enemies. Falling in love with Mary Brown, with whom Docherty remained for the rest of his life, was enough for a boardroom moral majority to rid themselves of their turbulent manager.

Ferguson’s successors must deal with his continued presence, the face in the crowd photographers and TV directors seek. His patronage of Malcolm Glazer’s 2005 takeover is a dubious legacy dragging down those who have followed him. Ferguson mostly keeps his own counsel, a well-remunerated club ambassador until Sir Jim Ratcliffe cancelled a £2m annual stipend in 2024. There have been slips. “You should always start with your best players,” Ferguson told the mixed martial arts fighter Khabib Nurmagomedov in 2021 when Ole Gunnar Solskjær had dropped Cristiano Ronaldo, loose talk escaping to social media.

Ferguson’s part in Ronaldo’s disastrous return to Old Trafford evidenced continuing back-channel influence, echoing Busby and Best. Carrick, during his press conference last Friday, mentioned his chats with his former boss. The omission of Fernandes for the Bournemouth game, left to sulk on the bench in club tracksuit, was classic Fergie politics.

View image in fullscreen The Sir Matt Busby statue alongside the Manchester United club crest at Old Trafford. Photograph: Conor Molloy/ProSports/Shutterstock

A Ferguson facsimile is a fool’s errand. Carrick might have learned the lessons dished out to Solskjær, to whom he was assistant. After refusing to use Ferguson’s parking space and misty-eyed chat of “the boss”, nobody was buying the affable, gentle Norwegian cosplaying as a Glaswegian hard man.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Not that an injection of the alpha male has been much more use. Time has been kinder to the Louis van Gaal and José Mourinho regimes as subsequent failures pile up, but both failed to embrace the expectations of attacking football.

Not that other club traditions were avoided. The subterfuge that brought in Mourinho was as dastardly as any of the post-Busby knifings. “People know him as a larger-than-life character,” the executive vice-chairman Ed Woodward said on Van Gaal’s 2014 appointment. “My wife had to find out when she was in the lift with Woodward’s family,” Van Gaal said of finding, in the haze of celebrating the 2016 FA Cup final victory, that he was being replaced. His former Barcelona assistant had successfully lobbied Woodward. Attempts have been made by the Glazers’ operatives and, since December 2023, Ratcliffe’s Ineos, to corporatise and professionalise but United’s innate excess and anarchy keeps overtaking rationale.

View image in fullscreen José Mourinho during his tenure as Manchester United manager, in November 2018. Photograph: Nigel Roddis/EPA

Using the means of a Netflix special, Mourinho has retrofitted his part in the story, he and Ferguson revealing together the fact he turned United down in 2013. The inference is that if Mourinho had arrived then all would have been roses. It is an unconvincing attempt at airbrushing both men’s reputations. Where does that leave David Moyes, the immediate successor painted as afterthought? In July 2013, Ferguson was celebrated as kingmaker, Moyes the rightful heir.

Moyes’s reputation is another enhanced by failures that followed, including Mourinho’s grumpy, fractious tenure. When emerging reluctantly from his Lowry Hotel bolthole, the Portuguese reduced himself to mocking club history with “football heritage” rants. Such a scorched-earth policy was echoed by Ruben Amorim, while Erik ten Hag’s retention by Ineos in summer 2024 was as confusing to Ten Hag as to everyone else.

An unmanageable club? Busby and Ferguson showed it can be done, though the chance of another empire recedes the longer the vanity, plotting and self-interest that personify United continues. And for that, Busby and Ferguson deserve a share of the blame.

Sports.title: Arise, Sir Harry? Downing Street hints at Kane knighthood after Ballon d’Or win
Sports.content:
Downing Street has hinted that Harry Kane deserves a knighthood, ­praising the England captain’s “extraordinary achievement” as the first English winner of the Ballon d’Or in 25 years.

The prime minister’s spokesperson said Andy Burnham sent praise and congratulations to the England captain, who was announced as the men’s winner of football’s most prestigious individual award at a ceremony on Monday night.

No 10 said it hoped it would be the prelude to a trophy to celebrate with England “before too long” – alluding to hopes of an England win when the country co-hosts the European Championship in 2028 with Scotland, Wales and the Republic of Ireland.

11:25 Harry Kane triumphs with historic Ballon d’Or win - The Latest

The Bayern Munich player is the first Englishman to win the award since Michael Owen in 2001.

“The PM would like to congratulate Harry Kane on winning the Ballon d’Or,” the spokesperson said. “To be the first Englishman to win it in 25 years is an extraordinary achievement, and what a moment to do it here at home.

“Seventy years after Sir Stanley Matthews won the inaugural award, it caps a remarkable season and Harry continues to set a brilliant example to young players across the country, and the PM knows the whole nation will be incredibly proud of him. And, hopefully, there’s another trophy to celebrate with England before too long.”

Asked whether Burnham would like to see Kane receive a knighthood, she said: “I think everyone would agree, Harry Kane has given an enormous amount to English football, and this is a very special moment for him and the country, but, as ever, I’m not going to pre-empt the honours process.”

Kane received the award at a ceremony at the London Palladium on Monday night, beating Kylian Mbappé of Real Madrid and Barcelona’s Lamine Yamal. He is the fifth English player to win the award, the list also including Kevin Keegan and Sir Bobby Charlton.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Burnham cannot decide whether to hand Kane a knighthood, but ministers and departments can make recommendations to the honours committee, as can private individuals. The sport committee includes the presenter Sue Barker and the chief executive of the Football Foundation, Robert Sullivan.

Kane holds an MBE, awarded after England’s success in reaching the semi-finals in the 2018 World Cup. Players are often not awarded knighthoods until after retirement. The former England captain Sir David Beckham received his knighthood last year, as did the former England player and manager Sir Gareth Southgate.

Before those awards, the most recent was the former Scottish player and Liverpool manager Sir Kenny Dalglish. Owen, also a former Liverpool player, has not received a knighthood, and nor did Keegan, the former Newcastle player and manager who was also England’s captain and manager.

Sports.title: Kane’s Ballon d’Or triumph a glorious riposte to celebrity fawning of ceremony | Barney Ronay
Sports.content:
Well, there’s something new. Football: now available in new, genuinely heartwarming flavour.

There was a lovely moment at London’s Palladium theatre on Monday, with the clock creeping towards 11pm at the end of a startlingly shrill and bloated evening of never‑ending awards and never-ending award‑related excitement.

Not just for Harry Kane, who is now the 2026 men’s Ballon d’Or winner, and in the process placed indelibly in that lineage of elite footballers. But also, frankly, for anyone watching, as Kane stood on stage gazing a little shyly at his golden orb, and kicked off his speech by thanking everyone, paying tribute to everyone, everywhere, then finally cracking into tears and a strangled croak as he thanked his parents for sacrifices made, his wife for always being there, and even, in slightly jarring vibe-shift from the warm honeyed tone, José Mourinho.

11:25 Harry Kane triumphs with historic Ballon d’Or win - The Latest

Even Kane’s biggest advocates will rarely claim their man is one of a kind, sui generis, in the mode of the Ronaldo-Messi godhead. But Kane is exactly this in his own admirably humble way.

Not just an exceptional footballer, the best, most deserving men’s player in the world this year, a European golden boot, scorer of 89 goals since August 2025, Bundesliga champion, World Cup semi-final captain, model of extreme professionalism and care. He’s also quite clearly the nicest man, if not just in football, then possibly the world.

Or at least it felt like that as he walked off in that very dear and tender way, the centre of the world in that moment, but also just keen to get off the stage and let everyone get on with clearing up.

It would be wrong to say Kane’s victory in the final vote of the night redeemed the grotesqueness of the ceremonies itself. There was a roomful of hugely deserving winners here. But Kane hits particularly hard.

View image in fullscreen Alexia Putellas and Harry Kane pose with their trophies at the end of the 2026 Ballon d’Or awards ceremony in London. Photograph: Tolga Akmen/EPA

And the Ballon d’Or is, let us be clear, a horrendous event, albeit a supremely popular horrendous event. There was the usual pomp around the ceremony, staged this year at a fancy theatre close to Oxford Circus.

This isn’t sport. It’s celebrity culture, red‑carpet fawning, the worship of images and people, and fame. Football isn’t supposed to be cocooned this way, to send the message that there are barriers and ropes and special people. Yeah, well, good luck with that.

The night kicked off with French Montana in spotless white tuxedo performing on an open-air double-decker bus. He definitely speaks, clearly, carried well, seemed enthusiastic. If it all goes south from here, the evidence suggests French Montana could, at the very least, get a job as a London tour bus operator.

View image in fullscreen French Montana performs during Ballon d’Or award ceremony in London. Photograph: Rasid Necati Aslim/Anadolu/Getty Images

Before long Thierry Henry and Kate Scott glided on stage, half an hour late, to add a little deft and easy charm to a furious schedule of pots and prizes.

And the awards came thick and fast. The Spain manager, Luis de la Fuente, was named coach of the year. “I hope in the future I will become in English better,” were his first words at the lectern, throwing his hat in the ring for a disastrous pension-padding six months at Manchester United two years from now.

There was a lovely moment as Burna Boy came on to present the Socrates award for charitable works to Bukayo Saka. He was asked if there were footballers who had inspired his love for the game. At which point he looked at Thierry and said, “definitely, one of them’s standing right there”, and of course he said it in his Burna Boy voice, looking Thierry deep in the eyes so smooth and deep, just almost an impossibly sexy moment.

The Ballon d’Or can be unintentionally hilarious at times such as these. There were just so, so many video tributes, so much excitingly portentous music. This is a stage where everyone happening at every moment is very clearly the most important thing ever to happen, superseded only by the next thing to happen on that stage, and then the thing after that.

View image in fullscreen The hosts of the ceremony: Kate Scott and Thierry Henry. Photograph: Matthew Childs/Action Images/Reuters

The degree of fawning is startling at first, but glazed by familiarity before long. At one point Cristiano Ronaldo appeared very briefly in a fact-cut big-screen montage and the crowd shrieked a song, clutched its hand to its fevered throat, collapsed into the aisles in sheer priapic excitement.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Although by the time the original Ronaldo emerged onstage at 10.44pm, there was a sense of the genuinely vertiginous company Kane was about to join. Ronaldo read out the name inside the envelope, and the hall collapsed into cheers and yells and roars as Kane appeared onstage.

And yes the Ballon d’Or is a fundamentally silly thing on its own terms. It jars with the basic concept of team sport, promoting instead the opposite of sport, the opposite of team culture, the modern disease of fawning parasocial engagement with star names. In many ways the world would be a better place if the Ballon d’Or was simply abolished, as an example to all who pore over reels and clips and the imagined qualities of their celebrity paramours.

But it is also fascinating, unignorable, and endlessly moreish. All the more so this time. Kane as the Ballon d’Or 2026 is a genuinely fine, uplifting, instructive moment in the spotlight.

View image in fullscreen Bukayo Saka delivers his speech after accepting the Sócrates award from Burna Boy. Photograph: Jeff Spicer/Uefa/Getty Images

It is always tempting to talk about the journey these players make. Everyone has a backstory. Most footballers come from adversity. Kane has this, in his own way, 16 years into a professional career which has names such as Leyton Orient, Millwall, Leicester and Norwich on the timelines. He was unexceptional as a junior, didn’t stand out as particularly skilful or big or outstanding in his numbers. He played as a holding midfielder for a bit while Spurs decided what to do with him.

Kane worked relentlessly. He was Millwall young player of the year in 2012, fitting bookend to the Ballon. He made it because he simply refused to go away, to stop working, honed instead the deeper skills in his quiver, the purity of his shooting, the range of his passing long and short.

And Kane is exceptional in other ways. Without ever peacocking around promoting his brand, without really trying he remains the most likable, authentic, role‑model‑ish modern-day England player. For a man who never talks big or acts big he has a happy knack of becoming the key player wherever he goes. Perhaps Kane has become cool now. He has always been likable, with that mild-mannered air of a kindly Victorian chimney sweep with a hamster in his waistcoat watch pocket. In the Bayern years, Kane has become leaner, more glossed and handsome, jawline, tan, iconic Vampire hairline.

Mainly he expresses a common confusion about what talent really is. Talent isn’t simply moments. Talent is also application, focus, craft, the ability to work, to make others better.

View image in fullscreen Harry Kane celebrates after scoring a penalty against Paris Saint-Germain in last season’s Champions League. Photograph: Christophe Ena/AP

And yet his elite career has also been oddly grudging. Somehow the idea has always been out there that Kane is undeserving of these accolades, despite his own mildness and humility, his obvious team qualities, his relentless delivery of goals, effort, leadership. It is a genuinely odd conclusion given the opposite is so manifestly true, that this is an entirely uplifting story of overachievement, of hard work and applied intelligence, as opposed to the kind of talent that just needs to be flame‑throwered in the right direction.

It is undeniably true that Kane’s levels can drop dramatically when he can’t perform at his full physical capacity. There have been moments where it has been tempting to wonder if he’s gone far enough as England’s captain in the past few years, if his body and his talent deserve a little care.

Well, that just shows how wrong you can be.

Sports.title: Donnarumma gets Maresca’s backing; Iraola feels bond growing at Anfield
Sports.content:
1. Maresca: ‘He’s a strong character’

Enzo Maresca has given his backing to Gianluigi Donnarumma after the goalkeeper’s costly errors in Manchester City’s recent defeats against Paris Saint-Germain and Aston Villa.

Donnarumma was at fault for Nicolas Jackson’s game-winning strike at Villa Park on Saturday, the forward’s long-range shot squeezing under the Italian’s body and leading to City’s first league defeat of the season. Against PSG in the Champions League this month, Donnarumma was at fault for Désiré Doué’s and Maghnes Akliouche’s goals as City lost 4-2 against the holders.

“As a football player or manager, when you don’t get results or make some mistakes, it’s normal. It’s a consequence,” Maresca said. “Gigio since we started is doing well. Like any manager or player making some mistakes, it’s part of the season.

“They [footballers] play so many games and minutes that sometimes it’s impossible not to make mistakes. He’s a strong character. He knows that when he makes a mistake, he doesn’t need us to tell him – sometimes it’s so clear so they recognise this.”

Marc Guéhi has been in uneven form, too. The defender was culpable for Jackon’s opener on Saturday. He also conceded a late penalty in the previous weekend’s 3-2 win against Ipswich, and made an early mistake that led directly to Lamine Yamal scoring for Spain against England in the Nations League last month.

“I am completely happy with Marc,” Maresca said. “The way he reacts is fantastic, he is a top guy. He is one of the captains, he is a leader and I love Marc. Same as Gigio, when they make some mistakes it is recognised.”

Donnarumma will be rested for Brighton’s visit in the Carabao Cup on Wednesday. Maresca said: “After the Villa game we gave five players three days off to recover the energy: Erling [Haaland], Rúben [Dias], Elliot [Anderson], Gigio and Josko [Gvardiol]. They are all on holiday. Three days off, energy, go, come back with full energy then we go again.”

Geronimo Rulli will again deputise for Donnarumma against Brighton. JJ

Sports.title: Pierre Sage given more time by Crystal Palace but remains under pressure
Sports.content:
Pierre Sage has been given more time to turn around Crystal Palace’s fortunes but he remains under huge pressure and could be dismissed if they lose against Tottenham on Saturday.

The Frenchman’s position was in serious doubt after another poor performance in the 2-0 defeat against Newcastle at the weekend. That followed a 5-0 thrashing against Brighton when Sage was warned that he could be dismissed if results did not improve quickly.

However the club’s chair, Steve Parish, has decided not to act given the tight turnaround in Palace’s schedule: the side face Fulham at Craven Cottage in the Carabao Cup on Wednesday, before their trip to Tottenham in the Premier League. But Sage, who attended the Ballon d’Or ceremony in London on Monday evening, is understood to have been left in no doubt that the meeting with Spurs on Saturday is crucial to his future.

Palace are 17th and have conceded 19 goals in eight Premier League matchesthis season – the highest in the division. But, it is understood, Sage retains the support of his squad, with two leading players having sent him messages saying that they still have faith he can turn things around.

Palace’s hierarchy are said to be split over whether to fire the former Lens manager after only 12 games in charge, with some in favour of bringing in Thomas Frank or Sean Dyche to steady the ship. The former Wolves manager Rob Edwards has also been mentioned as a potential contender.

There is sympathy for Sage at boardroom level given that Axel Disasi – who was signed on loan from Chelsea to replace the key defender Maxence Lacroix – has only just returned from a three-match suspension. There were also signs of improvement in the 2-2 Europa League draw at Besiktas in midweek, with Sage believed to have been delighted with Jean-Philippe Mateta’s response since returning from injury. The France striker is in the final year of his contract but failed in an attempt to have it ruled invalid by an independent Premier League tribunal and Fifa.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

There are concerns about Ismaïla Sarr, however, who missed the defeat against Newcastle after a recurrence of the groin injury that ruled him out earlier in the season. The Senegal forward has made no secret of his disappointment after Palace rejected a bid from Liverpool in the summer and Sage needs the club’s player of the year last season back on the pitch if they are to recover from a poor start to life after Oliver Glasner.

Sports.title: Police called to Florida soccer game after parents say three-year-old benched for being too good
Sports.content:
Police were called after a dispute involving the parents of a three-year-old player at a soccer game in Florida over the weekend.

The boy’s parents can be heard on police body cameras saying their son, Nevada, had been kicked out because he was too good at soccer and was embarrassing the other children. However, an organizer at the game said Nevada had pushed other children and his parents had become argumentative when their son was taken out of the game.

In police body camera footage the organizer of the event, who works for i9 Sports, a youth sports group, can be heard saying Nevada’s parents had caused a disturbance.

“The kid is good. He’s great. Really good,” the organizer says in the footage. “He’s very advanced compared to the other ones, so he’s scoring a lot of goals. But he’s pushing the kids ... So, I try to tell him, don’t push; we want to play without pushing, right?”

In audio of the 911 call, the organizer says Nevada’s mother was being “really, really disruptive, following me around and calling me names in front of this whole bunch of people.”

Nevada’s parents posted a clip of their son at the event in which he can be seen dribbling around older children with ease. The video has since gone viral. Nevada cannot be seen pushing any other children in the footage posted by his parents.

Allow Instagram content? This article includes content provided by Instagram . We ask for your permission before anything is loaded, as they may be using cookies and other technologies. To view this content, click 'Allow and continue'. Allow and continue

“They’re mad at my son because he actually plays soccer. They’re literally kicking him out of this place because he’s good at soccer,” his mother says in the body camera footage. “First, they said he’s not passing, but nobody’s catching the ball when he’s passing.”

The i9 Sports worker told police they were willing to give Nevada’s parents a refund if they left.

“I just want him out. Immediately,” the organizer told police. “Just give me their names so I can give them their refund.”

The Winter Park Police Department said the family agreed to leave the event and no one was arrested.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Twice weekly Sign up to Soccer Desk Jonathan Wilson and Guardian journalists bring expert analysis and reporting on the biggest stories in soccer. Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

“The family stated the game was over and they were leaving. The family was cooperative with the officers,” the department wrote in a statement on its website. “No one was arrested, trespassed, or forced to leave the park.”

i9 Sports said it was reviewing the incident and had contacted Nevada’s family.

“We are aware of concerns being shared regarding an incident at a local i9 Sports program, and we take them very seriously,” i9 Sports said in a statement. “The respectful treatment and well-being of every child and family matter deeply to us.”

One officer appeared to want to see more of Nevada though. “I kind of want to see him play. I bet he’s good,” he can be heard saying to another officer on body camera.

Sports.title: Kylian Mbappé apologises after being dropped by Chinese brands for Mao Zedong comment
Sports.content:
Kylian Mbappé has apologised after the Real Madrid forward was dropped by major Chinese brands for apparently joking about Mao Zedong in a video that has gone viral. There were also signs of broader repercussions, with the state-run Chinese digital newspaper The Paper reporting that public television was suspending broadcasts of matches from La Liga.

The offending video shows Mbappé saying that the funniest internet meme he had seen involving him was of his face photoshopped on to that of “some guy – I think he’s a Chinese dictator”. This was an apparent reference to a meme of Mbappé superimposed on an image of Mao.

“My comment was ill-judged, and I now understand that it hurt many people in China and in Chinese communities around the world. I apologise to everyone my words have upset,” Mbappé said in a statement in French, Chinese and English.

Spain’s La Liga also apologised, saying it “deeply regrets the offence that Kylian Mbappé’s recent comments have caused among Chinese fans. These comments were made in a personal capacity and do not represent La Liga.” In China, jokes about Mao, the country’s founding leader who died in 1976 – and whose drastic policies are also blamed by historians for mass starvation and millions of deaths – remain taboo.

The beverage giant Dongpeng, which during this year’s World Cup ran adverts with AI-generated images of Mbappé consuming its sport drink, said it was terminating all cooperation with the France captain. “Our company firmly opposes and has a zero-tolerance policy towards any behaviour that offends national sentiments,” Dongpeng said in a statement.

Mengniu, China’s largest dairy producer, and cheese maker Milkground also said that they were cutting ties with Mbappé, who until now was hugely popular among Chinese fans with millions of social media followers. “Dongpeng Beverage ends cooperation with Mbappé” was the top-trending topic on Chinese social media site Weibo with 430m views.

One Weibo user said the “extremely serious wrong remarks … crossed the red line” and others urged Dongpeng to remove Mbappé’s image from their bottles. Dongqiudi, one of China’s biggest online football outlets, said Mbappé’s remarks were “offensive to China and the Chinese people”.

View image in fullscreen Two Chinese brands have ended deals with Kylian Mbappé after he allegedly referred to Mao Zedong as a ‘Chinese dictator’. Photograph: Karwai Tang/WireImage

In an interview with the French sports newspaper L’Equipe last month, the 27-year-old Mbappé addressed a previous meme depicting him as a military dictator. “There’s a part of it that’s funny … but there is another part that’s a bit less funny because of the damage such people have caused throughout history,” he said.

China’s foreign ministry said it was aware of the reports regarding Mbappé, who on Monday finished runner-up to Harry Kane in the Ballon d’Or award for the world’s best player. “Words and actions that hurt the feelings of the Chinese people will naturally be met with unanimous rejection from all sectors of Chinese society,” spokesperson Guo Jiakun told a regular briefing.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

The Paper cited sources at the state broadcaster saying that CCTV has suspended all broadcasts of La Liga matches, and removed all s involving Mbappé. On the CCTV website, La Liga matches this weekend were still on its online viewing schedule.

Global sports stars who have commented on sensitive topics such as Taiwan, Tibet and Hong Kong have previously caused controversy in China and been dumped by sponsors there. The former NBA player Dwight Howard referred to Taiwan as a country in 2023 as he appeared in a video with the island’s then vice-president and current president, Lai Ching-te, sparking fury on Chinese social media. Beijing claims Taiwan is part of its territory and has threatened to use force to bring it under its control.

The Houston Rockets general manager, Daryl Morey, posted a tweet in 2019 supporting Hong Kong protests, leading to China suspending sponsorship deals with the NBA and pulling games off Chinese television for a year.

Fans in China made their feelings clear. “I used to really enjoy watching Mbappé play on the pitch,” Zhang Jingqi, 30, who works at a mall in Beijing, said. “But ever since this news broke yesterday I have lost that admiration, sorry to say.”
