The White House says its efforts aim to secure elections. But McDaniel says credible evidence of voter fraud significant enough to affect election outcomes in the U.S. has never been found. ➡️ With the elections a week away, Polymarket has already investigated "dozens" of bets on its prediction markets concerning the midterm elections, according to Shana Bautista, the company's head of global intelligence and investigations.

Israelis are voting today in an election that will shape their country's future. This marks the first time since the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas attacks that Israelis can choose their leaders. Voters will decide whether to keep Israel's far-right, longest-serving prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, or replace him with Gadi Eisenkot, a former military chief promising more diplomacy and less extremism. Here's what you need to know about the leading candidates, the issues shaping the vote and what could happen next.



Sponsor Message

🎧 NPR's Ruth Sherlock says a high voter turnout is expected, and many people casting their votes believe this is a critical election for the country's future. Israelis abroad have flown in to participate. At a polling station, Sherlock met Itamar Ariel, who believes that only Netanyahu can ensure Israel's security, even though the country faces problems. Others in the country believe Netanyahu should be voted out due to security failures. Those wanting change in leadership want an investigation into how the Oct. 7 attacks in Israel happened, which Netanyahu has blocked. Sherlock says by Wednesday morning, we should see which side secures the most seats in Parliament, but the vote count could continue for days, and the prime minister won't be determined until after days or possibly weeks of negotiations between the parties.

Life advice

toggle caption i Olga Pankova/Getty Images/Moment RF

Hours of screen time at your desk can turn you into a stiff, bleary-eyed version of yourself. Prolonged sitting can take a real toll, but a few smart habits can help reset your body and mind. Here are Life Kit's best strategies to help with the discomfort and health risks that can come from sitting at a desk all day.

🧘 Walking for five minutes every 30 minutes helps combat fatigue, weight gain and joint pain, reducing the risk of chronic diseases like obesity, heart disease and cancer.

🧘 If your back aches from slouching at your desk, rotate your spine to relieve stress and enhance flexibility by mimicking its natural movements.

🧘 Fidgeting indicates a need to change your position. Pay attention to your body and switch between sitting, standing, reclining and moving.

🧘 To relieve eye strain from screen time, stretch your eye muscles. Hold your arm straight in front of you, thumb pointing up. Move your arm in a big circle while keeping your head still and follow your thumb with your eyes.

Sponsor Message

Subscribe to the Life Kit newsletter for expert advice on love, money, relationships and more.

Picture show

toggle caption i Tommy Trenchard for NPR

Forget flying brooms. Cape Town is home to South Africa's real-world Hogwarts: the College of Magic. Every Saturday, almost 200 students ages 10 to 18 attend classes in a variety of things, including puppetry, mime and clowning, juggling, card tricks, illusions, mentalism, stage magic, theater production and escapology. In 1980, David Gore and a friend came up with the idea of starting a magic school. At the time, South Africa was grappling with apartheid, a brutal system of racial segregation. But from day one, the establishment was multiracial, even though state schools were still strictly segregated. Almost 50 years later, the College of Magic continues to stand out in a city that remains deeply divided along racial and economic lines. These photos capture how the school has turned young dreamers into magicians.

3 things to know before you go

toggle caption i Ryan Kellman/NPR

Blue crabs in the Chesapeake Bay are threatened by invasive blue catfish. To tackle the problem, officials are creating kid-friendly catfish recipes that meet federal dietary requirements for school lunches in Maryland and Virginia. Microsoft sent memos yesterday to about 60,000 employees, offering voluntary buyouts to further reduce its headcount. The offer is available to roughly one quarter of its workforce. (via KUOW) The Archdiocese of New York has agreed to pay $800 million to settle claims from around 1,300 people who say they faced sexual abuse by clergy members and lay workers.

This newsletter was edited by Suzanne Nuyen.

World.title: Big wins, shocking losses, and goodbye to a 46-year mayor: what to know about Ontario's 400+ elections
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

There were more than 400 municipal elections in Ontario Monday, so naturally the results were all over the map.

From an anti-incumbent wave that hit many politicians, including one of Canada's longest-serving mayors, to several big cities that brought back almost every incumbent, here are some of the key headlines and takeaways from last night.

Chow wins easily in Toronto

After polling had suggested a "statistical dead heat," Toronto's incumbent Mayor Olivia Chow defeated challenger Brad Bradford with relative ease.

Political strategist Blue Knox, who served as former mayor John Tory's director of communications, said the Chow campaign struck a nerve with Torontonians by going after Bradford's pledge to create a public utility company to handle the city's water and wastewater. Chow said it would mean the city losing control of an asset and opening the door to privatization.

"Canadians like for their public institutions to stay public," Knox said.

Chow will oversee a progressive, new-look council with several of her key allies elected, putting her in a strong position to pursue her agenda.

Mississauga's first male mayor since 1978

Polling at only 12 per cent as recently as August, Alvin Tedjo climbed from those depths to the Mississauga mayor's chair, defeating incumbent Carolyn Parrish and former mayor Bonnie Crombie.



Tedjo is just the fourth person to hold the job in nearly half a century, marking a significant generational shift in a city long led by political veterans. He's also the first man to hold the job since 1978.

WATCH | Tedjo wins: Alvin Tedjo wins Mississauga mayoral race | Duration 1:01 Breaking news: Alvin Tedjo has won the 2026 Mississauga mayoral election. Tedjo was elected as Ward 2 councillor in 2022, and gained attention after being the only mayoral candidate endorsed by the Peel police union. He secured the election following concessions from his rivals.

Horwath out in Hamilton

Since amalgamation in 2000, Hamilton's incumbent mayors have lost their seats more often than they keep them, and that held true on Monday. Andrea Horwath, the former Ontario New Democratic Party leader and former Hamilton Centre MPP, was unable to secure a second term.

The new mayor is Keanin Loomis, former president and CEO of the Canadian Institute of Steel Construction and former head of Hamilton's Chamber of Commerce, who will be joined by eight new councillors in a strong vote for change in the city.

Milton's 46-year mayor ousted

At least two dozen incumbent mayors lost their seats Monday, including nine who had served their cities for more than a decade.

Gordon Krantz, Canada's longest-serving mayor of a major municipality, had been in charge of Milton council since 1980. He lost handily to councillor George Minakakis.

And in Sarnia, the area's Chamber of Commerce CEO Carrie McEachran defeated mayor Mike Bradley, who had held the chair since 1988.

Other long-time mayors who lost include Oakville's Rob Burton (20 years) and Niagara Falls' Jim Diodati (16 years).

Some larger cities stay the course

The winds of change did not sweep away everyone in Ontario.

Ottawa, Brampton, London and Kitchener were among the communities that kept their mayors and most of their councils.

Zack Taylor, an associate professor of political science at Western University in London, said limited information about candidates can make it harder for challengers to gain traction. Taylor described the London campaign as relatively quiet compared with some previous election cycles.

“It could just be that [London Mayor] Josh Morgan benefited from incumbency and also not really having any kind of scandals occur,” Taylor said.

Mark Sutcliffe gives a victory speech after being re-elected as mayor of Ottawa on Monday. (Keito Newman/The Canadian Press)

A good night for women

Niagara Falls, Port Colborne and North Bay each elected their first female mayors, Ottawa's council has more women than men for the first time since the 2001 amalgamation, and the community of Merrickville-Wolford elected an all-female council.

At her victory party, Niagara Falls mayor-elect Lori Lococo downplayed the accomplishment.

"I always hope that people vote for people based on their experience and skills, not because of their gender," she said.

Women made up 32 per cent of the candidates province-wide.

WATCH | North Bay's new mayor: North Bay mayor-elect Maggie Horsfield speaks with reporters | Duration closed caption 2:14 Maggie Horsfield has won the election in North Bay, Ont., making her the first woman mayor in the city's history. She spoke with reporters at her election night event.

Taxes, homelessness were key issues

Taxes were a running theme across many municipalities.

Tedjo in Mississauga promised a two-year tax freeze; Loomis in Hamilton promised to get taxes "under control"; and Windsor's new mayor Fred Francis promised to hold the line on taxes.

Other popular discussion points during the campaign were homelessness, encampments and community safety. These were key issues in places like Windsor, Thunder Bay and Oshawa.

Thunder Bay councillor-elect Julie-Ann Colquhoun said she wants to "help build a community where people feel safe … and people experiencing homelessness are supported with an understanding of the complexities they face."

World.title: Trump wades into Canadian politics with kudos for Parti Québécois, B.C. Conservative wins
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

While he's fully engaged in a tight midterm election battle in his own country, U.S. President Donald Trump is still finding time to step into politics north of the border by congratulating the newly elected premiers of Quebec and British Columbia.

Praise for the sovereignist premier of Quebec, Paul St-Pierre Plamondon, and Conservative premier-designate Lorne Doerkson, came Tuesday in a pair of posts on Trump's Truth Social platform.

The highly unusual move breaks with the tradition of U.S. presidents and Canadian prime ministers only offering public congratulations to their direct counterparts.

Trump's praise of St-Pierre Plamondon came with a dig at Prime Minister Mark Carney. He linked to an article in the Irish Times carrying the headline: "Separatists win Quebec provincial election in blow to Mark Carney."

Bloc Québécois Leader Yves-François Blanchet responded by suggesting Trump's comments would be more relevant if he wanted to talk about cutting tariffs.

"Actually Mr. Trump is unpredictable and not so meaningful of what he says.... There's no lost love between Quebecers and Mr. Trump," Blanchet said.

WATCH | Bloc leader on Trump's comments: Trump congratulating new Quebec premier 'not so meaningful': Bloc leader | Duration closed caption 0:52 Bloc Québécois Leader Yves-François Blanchet says there's 'no lost love' between Quebecers and U.S. President Donald Trump. Trump's comments would only be 'relevant' if they were about mutually reducing tariffs, said Blanchet.

The salute to Doerkson's "big victory" was described by the president as an example of conservatives " moving strong in Canada ."

Trump first congratulated the incoming B.C. premier on the night of his election win, in a post that was shared by U.S. Ambassador Pete Hoekstra on X.

The B.C. Conservatives' win on Saturday was the party's first victory in about a century, a fact noted in that post.

Conservative doesn't equal MAGA

Hoekstra's message was reposted by several prominent Conservatives who, rather than join in the celebration, criticized the president for his lack of knowledge about Canada and his ambassador's decision to amplify it.

"It is impressive how bad you are at understanding the basic elements of your job or the simple truths of the country you are privileged to live in," former Conservative cabinet minister James Moore wrote to Hoekstra.

Stephen Harper's former communications director, Dimitri Soudas, quoted Doerkson's comments from September about "unacceptable threats, tariffs and rhetoric from a bully south of the border" as he shared Hoekstra's post.

Ken Boessenkool, a former senior policy adviser to Harper and the federal Conservative Party, tried to explain that being conservative in Canada doesn't mean being aligned with Trump.

"The MAGA party in B.C. is called One B.C. They got 1.5 per cent of the vote. More than Trump would get, I suspect," Boessenkool said in a post on X, referring to Trump's "Make America Great Again" movement.

"Like you, they are an embarrassment to the concept of conservatism."

Election interference and endorsements

Polls show Trump's dispute with Canada is deeply unpopular among American voters in both major parties.

Many online drew attention to the irony of the Trump administration's accusations that Canada is interfering in the U.S. midterm elections — where polling suggests the Republicans are struggling — while poking his own nose into Canada's politics.

The U.S. Embassy in Ottawa released a "fact sheet" last week pointing to instances that could amount to "potential interference in U.S. elections" including the Nov. 3 midterms.

That accusation came despite Trump's record of endorsing political candidates around the world since returning to the White House.

Since early 2025, Trump has backed presidential or prime ministerial candidates in Poland , Honduras , Colombia and Japan .

Most recently, he voiced support for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu .

World.title: Alberta bill would stop provincial entities from considering diversity, equity and inclusion in hiring
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

New Alberta legislation seeks to stop the provincial government and other public entities from considering diversity, equity and inclusion in hiring decisions.

Justice Minister Mickey Amery tabled legislation Tuesday that would prevent the provincial public service, provincial Crown corporations, publicly funded post-secondary institutions, school boards and municipalities from hiring employees based on “personal characteristics,” according to a government news release.

“Hiring decisions should be about who is best qualified for the job, and these changes will help ensure that fairness is at the heart of hiring,” Premier Danielle Smith is quoted as saying in the news release.

Amery’s statement in the release says public-sector hiring should be based on merit, qualifications and competence.

The legislation — the first bill of the fall sitting — proposes to do this by amending the Alberta Human Rights Act so that employers may not consider characteristics protected by the act — such as gender identity, race, religion or disability — in hiring and promotion decisions. However, the government could grant exemptions in regulations.

WATCH | 'Merit' hiring, data centres, report cards: Alberta government lays out agenda for upcoming fall sitting | Duration closed caption 1:27 With the fall sitting set to get underway next week, the provincial government is unveiling its priorities. Proposed new bills are expected to focus on data centre protections, standardized report cards, and bike lanes. But as CBC’s Ted Henley reports, the province says Albertans shouldn't expect any movement on the referendum immigration issues, yet.

The amendments would also prevent provincial entities from requiring employees to participate in diversity, equity or inclusion training. Workplace training must be “ideologically neutral and focused on job-related duties and skills,” a briefing note about the proposed amendment says.

In a technical briefing, officials said the legislation would not prevent post-secondary institutions from tailoring programs for particular students, or reserving spots for those with unchangeable characteristics, such as training for Indigenous teachers, doctors or lawyers.

The law would also apply to some private or non-profit organizations that receive government funding. However, officials said it would be up to the Alberta Human Rights Commission to determine which organizations, and only after someone files a complaint.

Consequences for threatening sextortion

If passed, Bill 33, the Justice Statutes Amendment Act, 2026 (No. 2), would also expand provincial legislation to give victims recourse when someone shares intimate content of them without their consent.

The bill would rename and expand the Victims of Non-consensual Distribution of Intimate Images Act to include victims of sextortion, which is when someone threatens to distribute intimate videos, images or other content to blackmail another person.

If passed by the legislature, the amended law would include digitally altered media, such as AI-generated content including deepfakes, and would allow a victim to sue anyone who shares or threatens to share the media without their consent.

It would allow a person to withdraw consent at any time, unless they have signed a legal consent agreement.

The legislation would create a new provincial offence carrying a fine of up to $10,000, up to two years of jail time, or both.

At the technical briefing, officials said the provincial law is intended to cover what they say are gaps in federal criminal law, and give victims more avenues of recourse. Officials said a provincial law allowing a victim to sue someone for threatening to share intimate content would be the first of its kind in Canada.

Federal law, which was updated in June , allows a prison sentence of up to 10 years for distributing or threatening to distribute intimate images, including non-consensual deepfakes, without consent.

The bill would also update the Education Act. For instance, principals have the ability now to suspend or expel a student who shares intimate images of another student without their permission. The amendment would allow them to discipline a student who only threatens to do so, and add sound, video or any other media to the list of possible content.

World.title: 'Healthy' to have conversation on abolishing Indian Act, First Nation chief says
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Some First Nations people in Manitoba say they agree with Premier Wab Kinew that Canada should abolish the Indian Act — even if they believe it will take a long time to find a way forward.

As First Nations leaders and Canada's first ministers convened in Ottawa on Monday, Kinew called on the federal government to do away with the 1876 law, which initially controlled almost every aspect of First Nations people's lives. While it's changed, the law remains the overarching legal document for First Nations.

Minegoziibe Anishinabe Chief Derek Nepinak said it's "healthy" for the country to have that conversation, even if it can be polarizing.

"There's a deep history here," he said. It's "not always on the agenda, but nonetheless a very critical conversation that needs to be had."

Kinew made the comments during a meeting of federal, provincial and First Nations leaders to discuss Indigenous rights, saying his proposal received an "open-minded reception" from others at the summit.

But some were not enthused.

In Manitoba, Bunibonibee Cree Nation Chief Sheila North said Monday that chiefs she spoke to thought it was "inappropriate" for the premier to be calling for the abolition of the act given his position as leader of a province that's historically broken its promises to First Nations.

Frank Deer, an Indigenous education professor at the University of Manitoba, said the premier — who is Anishinaabe — is in a "unique position" to push the issue forward.

"I agree with him that it is time to consider moving on from this rather dated approach toward categorizing native people in Canada," Deer said.

"I think some of the history that's associated with the Indian Act should give Canadians pause to consider why it is time to be looking at transferring the focus towards something new."

The law dismantled traditional forms of governance and, at one point, outlawed ceremonial practices.

It even affects First Nations people after they die. The Indigenous Services minister is required to approve wills for people living on reserve and has the power to void them altogether.

The act has received many amendments over the years, but it remains in place.

In 1969, a proposal from Pierre Trudeau's government to abolish the law, in what's known as the White Paper, drew widespread criticism from First Nations leaders, who saw it as an attack on their rights and an attempt to assimilate Indigenous people.

The document, authored by Jean Chrétien while he was Indian affairs minister, called for an end to Indian status, the absorption of First Nations people as ordinary citizens, the termination of treaties and the privatization of reserve lands.

Carney open to reform

Prime Minister Mark Carney — who told reporters he was open to abolishing the act following Kinew's comments — said Tuesday that a process to review the legislation would not necessarily lead to it being terminated.

The federal government will work with First Nations and the provinces and territories to suggest possible replacements for it, Carney said.

Most First Nations chiefs agree the Indian Act is outdated and restrictive, but there is little consensus on what should replace it.

WATCH | Carney open to abolishing Indian Act: Carney ‘very open’ to abolishing the Indian Act | Duration closed caption 2:11 Speaking at the Assembly of First Nations, Prime Minister Mark Carney said he is open to reforming or abolishing the Indian Act and has asked his ministers to work in partnership with First Nations to ‘chart that path together.’

Mike Sutherland from Peguis First Nation said abolishing the law is a "big ask."

"It's one thing to say, the other thing to do it," Southerland said at an event marking the opening of an Indigenous-led business incubator in Winnipeg Tuesday.

"It's something that we would like to see, but you know, how long is it going to take us to get there?"

Nelson Nepinak from Skownan First Nation said after 150 years, it's time to get rid of the law altogether.

"It's time for First Nations to go into self-government and start governing themselves appropriately," he said.

"We have the young people that are highly educated. We have our staff in our First Nations communities that can do the same job [Indigenous Services Canada] is doing."

Activist warning

The main conversation about the Indian Act for the past year has been about how it determines status. Amendments proposed by the Senate would introduce a one-parent rule that would allow families to pass on Indian status as long as one parent has it.

Indigenous Services Minister Mandy Gull-Masty has criticized the proposal a "one-solution blanket," saying more consulations are needed.

There are policies in place if a First Nation decides to opt out of the Indian Act, with several communities having negotiated self-government over their territories.

Gull-Masty's community, the Cree First Nation of Waswanipi, is one of those self-governing communities, under the 1975 James Bay and Northern Quebec Agreement — in which Chrétien played a leading role.

Talk of reforming or abolishing the Indian Act comes as Carney works to speed up development of major projects alongside the provinces and Indigenous Peoples.

His government's Building Canada Act initially gave Ottawa the power to sidestep the Indian Act. That provision was removed in response to calls from the Conservatives and the Bloc Québécois.

Janice Makokis, a lawyer and Idle No More organizer, said the current talk of abolishing the Indian Act is an echo of federal efforts decades earlier that triggered unrest among First Nations people and leaders.

"We must scrutinize whether the language of modernization and economic partnership is being used to shift power away from our nations, while opening our territories to development," she said in the foyer of the House of Commons.

"Our rights existed before the Indian Act; they do not depend on the Indian Act. But abolishing it without a process directed by First Nations themselves risks another era of paternalism, of Canada deciding what our freedom should look like then writing the rules for us."

World.title: This year will be a super-duper El Niño. Here's what Canadians can expect this winter
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

No doubt, most Canadians have heard of this year's El Niño, a warming in an area of the central Pacific Ocean that has an influence on weather patterns around the world and which drives up the global temperature. Early forecasts had called for one of the most powerful on record, and it has certainly lived up to its expectations.

This "super" El Niño hasn't even peaked yet — that's expected to happen some time in December — but it has broken records with daily ocean temperatures reaching nearly 3.5 C above the 1991-2020 average. The highest temperature before that was in 2015 at 3.08 C.

It may be hard to imagine, but what happens in the Pacific Ocean doesn't stay in the Pacific Ocean. Instead, this natural phenomenon can bring more rain, droughts or warmer-than-average temperatures across different parts of the world.

So what does this mean for Canada this winter? It depends where you are.

Don't blame El Niño just yet

First, don't blame El Niño just yet for any weather you may or may not like.

Well, not unless you're in Atlantic Canada. That region has already felt the effects of an El Niño, specifically, no hurricanes or subtropical storms.

Early forecasts for this year's Atlantic hurricane season had called for reduced activity in the region, typical of most El Niño years. And those predictions were bang on: there has been only one named storm in the Atlantic basin so far, and the hurricane season ends on Nov. 30.

WATCH | I've tracked El Niño for years — I've never seen this before: I’ve tracked El Niño for years — I’ve never seen this before | Duration 3:17 It’s set to be a record-breaking few months of weather, driven by a 'super' El Niño. As Johanna Wagstaffe explores, a natural surge of warm ocean water is colliding with a planet hotter than ever before, bringing more extreme heat, floods, and droughts. But this 'super' El Niño could also help us prepare for what's coming.

But otherwise, the weather we're experiencing now is just, well … weather.

In terms of El Niño's larger impacts across Canada, Bill Merryfield, a research scientist with Environment and Climate Change Canada, says those generally don't set in until late December.

"They tend to sort of intensify as the winter sets in," he said.

Warm and dry

If you're not a fan of the cold, good news: You can expect a warmer winter.

"We tend to see unusually mild winters really from coast to coast across the provinces. And as an example, winter temperatures during the last two events of this type in 1997 into 1998 [and] 2015 to 2016 in the Prairies were as much as five degrees or more above historical norms."

People practise their golf swings at the Shooters Family Golf Centre in Winnipeg at the end of January 2024. It was the earliest the centre had opened amid unusually warm temperatures in Manitoba. (Jaison Empson/CBC)

The bad news, particularly for the West, is that it tends to be drier, with reduced precipitation. That's not great for the fire risk in some regions experiencing drought conditions, especially heading into 2027, which is expected to be the warmest year on record.

At the moment, according to Berkeley Earth, a non-profit climate analysis organization, 2026 has a 96 per cent chance of being the warmest on record beating out 2024.

"For the high latitude, starting in December, we're going to see much rainier conditions in the western U.S. and southeastern U.S., and we're going to start seeing drier conditions in the northwest U.S. and British Columbia, Saskatchewan, Alberta, the western provinces of Canada," said Zeke Hausfather, a climate scientist with Berkeley Earth.

Yes, it will still be cold

Now, there's no guarantee for anything when it comes to weather, but Hausfather looked at eight of the past strong El Niños, and said that currently 12 of the 13 modelling groups around the world expect those regions to experience 19 per cent less rainfall.

Hausfather also looked at the models for warmth.

"All of Canada is warmer. And again, some of this is climate change, right? Because this is the 1991 to 2020 average," he said. "And it's particularly pronounced in central and northern Canada, and to an extent in Eastern Canada."

This map illustrates the El Niño 2026-2027 forecast for North America from October 2026 to February 2027. Canada is expected to experience a warmer-than-normal winter, particularly in the north. (Zeke Hausfather)

And while it will be warmer than average, that doesn't mean that we won't experience cold days, even days that are colder than normal or days with snowstorms.

Hausfather says most of north central Canada is going to be two degrees warmer than normal. "So you're still going to have a lot of variation day to day and week to week," he said. "Weather isn't going away."

World.title: Transport minister questioned over Air Canada's use of safety exemption to deny compensation
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A Go Public investigation revealed Air Canada shuffled planes around, cancelled flights — claiming safety-related maintenance — then denied compensation. Minister of Transport Steven MacKinnon says he is 'reluctant to give them instructions' as the airline is an independent agency.

Minister questioned after Go Public investigation into airline's use of 'safety-related maintenance' exemption

Canadians across the country want federal Transport Minister Steven MacKinnon to come down hard on Air Canada and WestJet, the country's major air carriers.

The calls come after two CBC Go Public investigations revealed both Air Canada and WestJet cancelled flights — citing safety-related maintenance — then used those working planes on other routes and denied passengers compensation.

On Parliament Hill Monday, MacKinnon said the Canadian Transportation Agency (CTA) is an "independent agency."

"I'm reluctant to give them instructions directly," he told CBC News.

In dozens of emails to Go Public, passengers on various air carriers outline how they had their flights cancelled due to maintenance and were denied compensation — and now wonder if they too were wrongly denied.

"This is probably just a small tip of the iceberg," said Montreal lawyer Sylvie De Bellefeuille, a consumer advocate with Option consommateurs.

Concerns raised about maintenance loophole

De Bellefeuille and other advocates have urged Ottawa for several years to change the Air Passenger Protection Regulations, so airlines can't use "safety-related maintenance" as a reason to deny compensation.

"We cannot rely on the information that is provided [to passengers]," said De Bellefeuille. "And if they [airlines] lie to the authorities, that's even worse."

The European Union only allows airlines to cite maintenance in rare circumstances.

Got a story you want investigated? Contact Erica and the Go Public team gopublic@cbc.ca

The emails to Go Public follow a story we reported earlier this week about Juan Rojas, a Gatineau, Que., man whose flight from Montreal to Bogota was cancelled due to "unforeseen aircraft maintenance."

Under the protection regulations, passengers can be entitled to up to $1,000 for delayed flights, but only if the delay is within the airline's control and not required for safety.

Air Canada denied Rojas compensation. He escalated his claim to the CTA, where Air Canada submitted documents showing a plane had to be taken out of service after getting struck by a catering truck.

But Rojas did some digging and learned the broken plane was a different aircraft — not the one originally assigned to his flight.

"They are clearly misrepresenting information," said Rojas. "To cheat the system to avoid paying $1,000."

WATCH | Passengers speak-up about compensation denial: Growing number of WestJet passengers question compensation denials over maintenance | Go Public | Duration closed caption 2:18 Go Public uncovers more cases of WestJet passengers denied compensation after plane swaps. Passenger advocate calls it 'fraud.'

The regulator sided with Rojas and ordered Air Canada to pay him the compensation. Though Rojas asked for one, the CTA declined to issue an administrative penalty.

Michael Odobas of Vancouver said he was incredulous that Air Canada submitted records about a different plane and faced no consequences.

"If an airline can incorrectly deny compensation, lose a regulatory dispute and face no financial penalty … what incentive does it have to comply (with the rules)?" wrote Odobas in an email to Go Public.

"That's a question Canadians deserve an answer to."

Should airlines face 'profit-altering fines?'

Conservative MP Dan Albas (Okanagan Lake West—South Kelowna) also raised the issue when MacKinnon appeared Monday before the standing committee on finance.

"Does swapping aircraft to another route qualify as a safety exemption?" he asked.

"The CTA is the regulator," the minister replied.

Conservative transport critic Dan Albas questioned the transport minister on Monday about the safety-related maintenance exemption. (CBC)

The regulator also didn't fine WestJet in cases where that airline denied people compensation while incorrectly claiming safety-related maintenance — cases Go Public reported on earlier this year.

At the time, WestJet's vice president of airline operations said, "when an unexpected issue occurs, WestJet carefully considers the approach that minimizes disruption for the greatest number of guests overall."

WATCH | Understanding how it works: How a 'maintenance loophole' is costing air passengers compensation | Go Public | Duration closed caption 2:11 Air Canada has been accused of using a safety maintenance 'loophole' to deny compensation for cancelled flights. Advocates are urging the government to adopt regulations from other countries that prevent airlines from citing safety maintenance to avoid payouts.

"I'm profoundly troubled that this type of dishonest behaviour is going unpunished," said Gabor Lukacs, founder of Air Passenger Rights.

"That behaviour should be stopped. … And the only way would be to issue profit-altering fines."

In a statement to Go Public, Air Canada said it's allowed to move planes around, cancel flights and deny compensation — calling it a "commercial decision."

That position conflicts with previous CTA decisions saying airlines can do what they want with their flight schedules, but must provide compensation to affected passengers unless a mechanical issue is the direct cause of a cancelled flight.

World.title: U.S. and Cuban officials get into shouting match on floor of United Nations
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

U.S. and Cuban officials engaged in a stunning shouting match on the floor of the United Nations General Assembly on Tuesday, the latest in a series of public spats between the longtime adversaries over Washington's escalating economic campaign against Havana.

The interaction began shortly after U.S. Ambassador to the UN Mike Waltz took the podium to argue against supporting the annual resolution this week condemning the decades-long U.S. economic embargo against the island country.

As Waltz was detailing years of alleged corruption by the socialist government, members of the Cuban delegation, including Foreign Minister Bruno Rodríguez Parrilla, began to slam on their designated table and yell for a point of order.

Then, as UN officials sought to tone down the outbursts, Rodríguez Parrilla walked down the aisle to the head of the General Assembly and yelled at Waltz, "You are a liar!"

Waltz responded, "You understand who you're dealing with? This is America. Back up."

WATCH | The confrontation at the UN: Shouting erupts at UN embargo vote as U.S., Cuban officials face off | Duration closed caption 1:55

While the moment represented a shocking break from diplomatic decorum traditional to the UN, it perfectly captured the heightened tensions between Cuba and the U.S. as President Donald Trump's administration seeks to force changes to Cuba's political system by increasing its already punishing economic campaign.

The Caribbean country — already facing the dire impact of longtime economic and financial troubles — is now being pushed to a breaking point after Trump announced in late January that he would impose tariffs on any country that sells or provides oil to Cuba. The warning has effectively cut off fuel to the island, leading to widespread power outages that affect basic activities such as cooking, the water supply and internet and telephone services.

Cuban officials have also repeatedly stressed that as U.S. officials demand that Cuba open up to private investment, Washington keeps piling on sanctions that stymie the very economic opening it has sought for decades.

A woman walks past a pool of sewage on a Havana street as water and electricity shortages threaten health and hygiene in the island nation. (Ricardo Arduengo/Reuters)

The outbursts Tuesday came a week after a similar interaction between Waltz and his Cuban counterpart, Ernesto Soberón Guzmán, outside a U.S.-hosted panel with Cuban dissidents and former prisoners that sought to highlight allegations of the oppressive behaviour of the island's government.

Waltz and other U.S. officials have been using these public events and gatherings at the world body to try to persuade UN member states to vote on Wednesday against the annual resolution, which is aimed at calling out the U.S. government's "maximum pressure policy" against Cuba.

For the past 34 years, the resolution has received overwhelming support. Last year, the vote was 165-7, with 12 abstentions. Argentina, Ukraine and Hungary opposed the measure for the first time.

Canada has consistently voted in favour of the annual resolution. Earlier this year, Global Affairs Canada announced it was providing $5.5 million in new support to Cubans, following $8 million it provided in February in accelerated funds to help scale up food aid to the nation.

While such resolutions are not legally binding, they do reflect world opinion.

World.title: Meet Canada's 5 Eurovision finalists
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The first-ever group of Canadian Eurovision finalists have been chosen, setting up who will vie to make history as the country's first entrant into the long-running song competition.

The five finalists — selected by a jury of music industry professionals and public broadcasting executives — include Quebec pop showman William Cloutier, bilingual Acadian singer-songwriter Josiane, Montreal-to-Toronto dance-pop artist Rêve, Ottawa-born hitmaker Talk and B.C. singer-songwriter Tyler Shaw.

Held annually since 1956, the Eurovision Song Contest is considered one of the world’s biggest live music spectacles, known for its extravagant costumes and performances. More than 130 million viewers across 35 countries watched the most recent edition.

Here's a closer look at the finalists battling to represent Canada at the 2027 Eurovision Song Contest in Bulgaria — and how Canadians can help choose the winner.

William Cloutier: Qu e bec's 'Prince of Pop'

William Cloutier is a Canadian pop singer from Victoriaville, Que. (CBC/Radio-Canada)

Cloutier was drawn to the stage early, appearing on the youth talent show La cour des grands at 12, before winning the teen reality TV singing and dancing competition Mixmania at 16. He went on to study theatre, then returned to music and won Quebec's Star Académie in 2021.

He's also taken on one of French-language musica l theatre's biggest roles, playing Johnny Rockfort in Starmania more than 360 times across Europe and Qu e bec. His 2022 album On ira earned an ADISQ nomination for album of the year (given out by a non-profit organization that supports the independent music industry in Queb ec) , and he followed it up with 2025's L'amour.

"It's a dream. I have the chance to live my childhood dream, making music, singing for people on the stage," Cloutier told CBC News. He said he wants to bring his personality — and his voice — to Eurovision, adding, "I want to sing my life on the stage."

WATCH | William Cloutier:

Josiane: Bilingual pop with Acadian roots

Josiane is an Acadian singer-songwriter from Dieppe, N.B. (CBC/Radio-Canada)

The Dieppe, N.B., singer-songwriter performs under her first name and moves between French and English pop, with a sound shaped by her Acadian heritage and distinctive Chiac phrasing. She won La Voix, the French Canadian edition of the The Voice singing competition, in 2020 and released her debut album, Take Care, in March 2026.

She says her music explores resilience, heartbreak and self-worth. Her song Lose It All has amassed over six million streams.

Josiane sees Eurovision as a chance to connect with audiences across Canada and beyond. "I want to capture a lot of my vulnerability with a big, powerful performance," she told CBC News.

WATCH | Josiane:

Rêve: Made for the dance floor

Rêve is a Montreal-born, Toronto-based electronic and dance-pop singer-songwriter. (CBC/Radio-Canada)

The Juno-winning artist blends contemporary pop and R&B with '90s eurodance. Born and raised in Montreal and now based in Toronto, Rêve broke through in 2021 with songs including Ctrl + Alt + Del, Big Boom and Whitney.

Her music draws on club culture, her French-Canadian roots and the communities that have shaped her. She sees the dance floor as a place for both escape and connection — a perspective that could make for a lively Eurovision performance.

Rêve envisions a performance that is "high energy but also emotional," combining "soaring vocals, dazzling choreography" and striking visuals. She called being selected "the greatest honour of my life."

WATCH | Rêve:

Talk: The colourful storyteller

Talk is a Canadian singer-songwriter and multi-instrumentalist from Ottawa. (CBC/Radio-Canada)

The Ottawa-born singer-songwriter rose to global attention with Run Away to Mars, written during what he calls a lonely night. He followed it with the album Lord of the Flies & Birds & Bees and a sold-out international tour.

Talk won the 2024 Juno award for breakthrough artist of the year. His next concept album, The Ballad of Ozzy Moon, is scheduled for release in early 2027.

Talk told CBC News he has watched Eurovision for 15 years, making this opportunity more than just a career move.

"This actually means something," he said. He's already been writing songs and building a team in case he's selected, and hopes to bring something "a little more mysterious, a little more dramatic" to the stage.

WATCH | Talk:

Tyler Shaw: Pop with international reach

Tyler Shaw is a Canadian singer, songwriter, music producer and actor born in Richmond, B.C. and raised in nearby Coquitlam, B.C. (CBC/Radio-Canada)

The Richmond, B.C.-born Chinese Canadian singer, producer and actor broke through with Kiss Goodnight in 2012. He found a new audience in 2022 with Love You Still (abcdefu Romantic Version), his take on Gayle's hit song.

Shaw toured Europe for the first time in 2026, playing sold-out shows in Germany, Austria and the U.K.

Shaw told CBC News that representing Canada would mean "everything," especially after living in several parts of the country and building connections across it.

"I feel like I’ve been literally training for this for the past 14 years," he said. He added that being part of the selection process is a win in itself, with "a lot of opportunities" possible regardless of the outcome.

WATCH | Tyler Shaw:

How the finalists were chosen

The five finalists were selected from 325 applications submitted between Aug. 31 and Sept. 9. CBC/Radio-Canada's music teams narrowed the entries to 15, then a jury of music industry professionals and public broadcasting executives chose the final five.

Applicants were assessed on vocal ability, stage presence, artistic experience, musical vision and availability, as well as their potential to deliver a strong performance on an international stage.

The jury included Montreal International Jazz Festival programming director Maurin Auxéméry, choreographer Samuel Chouinard, television composer Orin Isaacs, social media strategist and Eurovision specialist Shawn Myers and soprano Élisabeth St-Gelais. CBC executive vice-president Douglas Smith and Radio-Canada executive vice-president Dany Meloul also took part.

PHOTOS | Meet Canada's finalists for Eurovision:

How to vote

Now, voting is in the public's hands. On X, Prime Minister Mark Carney urged Canadians to take part, writing: "Canada is going to Eurovision 2027. It's up to you to decide who takes the stage. Cast your vote by November 5" in English and in French.

Canadians can watch the finalists' performances at CBC.ca/eurovision and vote for their preferred artist up to 10 times.

The voting window is open over the next 10 days, closing on Nov. 5 at 11:59 p.m. PT, with the winner to be announced by December. PricewaterhouseCoopers LLP is overseeing the voting system and tabulation of results.

Canada is the first new country to join the Eurovision Song Contest since Australia in 2015.

World.title: Colombia’s government claims Petro exploited 48 women as president
World.content:
The administration chief of Colombia’s President Abelardo De la Espriella told Congress that former President Gustavo Petro hired at least 48 women who were “trapped and exploited” for presidential parties.

During a hearing, DAPRE director Carlos Andres Rios claimed that Petro had 48 women “working in the Presidency, who were unfortunately exploited through temporary work contracts.”

We’re going to prove this to the Colombian people: how, unfortunately, the Casa de Nariño was set up, organized, and designed not for governing, but for partying there every day, bringing women there and engaging in behavior we should not be engaging in—behavior that sets a bad example. DAPRE director Carlos Andres Rios

“Forty-eight women are already speaking with us about how, through a contract and an OPS, they were trapped and exploited in order to be with President Petro,” said Rios.

Former DAPRE director Angie Rodriguez, who was sacked by Petro in July, doubled down on her successor’s allegations and asked the former president to prove that the president managed a network of women, including child transvestites.

Were there transvestite children there? Answer me, Mr. President. Were there transvestite children there? I am asking you a question, and I have every right to ask it. Were there? And if there weren’t, uh… prove that what I am saying is a lie. Angie Rodriguez

Last but not least, far-right magazine Semana published an interview with a woman identified as Deicy Jimenez, who claimed she as hired by Petro after meeting him on an adult website.

Jimenez even told Semana’s former presidential candidate Vicky Davila she trafficked drugs for the former president when he was senator.

VD: What happened on the day you say you transported drugs for Petro? DJ: Yes, I was traveling, and he asked me as a favor to bring him some drugs. VD: Were you outside of Bogotá? DJ: Yes. VD: How do you recall that favor Petro asked of you? DJ: He asked me as the favor to bring him some drugs. VD: Did you buy them? DJ: Yes, I bought them somewhere. He gave me money. VD: Did he give it to you in cash or deposit it for you? DJ: In cash. VD: How much money? DJ: Three million pesos. VD: What kind of drugs did you buy? DJ: Cocaine. VD: Where did you buy it? DJ: I bought it from some people. I can’t say (publicly) their names or the location. VD: Is it a gang? DJ: Yes. VD: Did he know you were going to buy the drugs from that gang? DJ: Yes. VD: At that time, was he a senator or the president? DJ: A senator. VD: How did you bring that drug in? DJ: I brought it through the airport. VD: You mean, on a plane? DJ: Yeah. VD: Did you get on a plane with Petro’s drugs? DJ: Yes. VD: How were the drugs packaged? DJ: In bags. VD: Like individual doses? DJ: Yes. VD: And where did you hide the drugs? DJ: In my suitcase.

In a response, Petro denied having hired women for sex and claimed that the far-right attack were the result of authorities’ failure to sustain corruption allegations.

World.title: “Brazil and Colombia need each other,” says De la Espriella
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella recognized the election victory of his Brazilian counterpart Luiz Ignacio Lula, who defeated far-right candidate Flavio Bolsonaro on Sunday.

In a post on social media platform X, the Colombian President said that “in the Colombian presidential campaign, President Lula openly supported Ivan Cepeda, and I won. In the Brazilian campaign, I supported Bolsonaro, and Lula won.”

“Neither does Lula decide for Colombians, nor do I decide for Brazilians. THE PEOPLE DECIDE! And when the people speak at the polls, their will is respected because it is sacred,” the president added.

Lula and I have major and profound political and ideological differences, but we agree on one fundamental point: Brazil and Colombia need each other. No other consideration can take precedence over the interests of our nations. Colombia and Brazil are sister nations, facing enormous shared challenges and opportunities.

President Abelardo de la Espriella

De la Espriella stressed that “we have much to do and much work to carry out for the benefit of our peoples” an ought to “fight against narco-terrorism and illegal mining, the protection of the Amazon, and the well-being of our citizens.”

Lula was the first leftist candidate and critic of US President Donald Trump to win an election, triggering celebrations among leftists throughout the continent.

De la Espriella, a US citizen, has been among the most fanatic among Trump supporter in trying to align his domestic policies to US foreign policy.

World.title: De la Espriella sacks interior minister after Congress bungles Colombia’s 2027 budget
World.content:
Colombia President Abelardo de la Espriella sacked Interior Minister Rodrigo Lara hours after Congress found a procedural flaw in the passed 2027 budget, which makes the law invalid.

In a post on social media platform X, De la Espriella briefly thanked Lara and announced he would be replaced by the ambassador to the Organization of American States, Alejandro Ordoñez.

The news surprised the interior minister, who suddenly left a congressional debate on a law to facilitate the demobilization of illegal armed groups after receiving a message on his phone.

Lara was apparently held responsible for the blunder of Congress, whose two houses approved the 2027 budget but with conflicting versions of an article on financial risk-coverage mechanisms for the Ministry of Finance.

By the time the error was detected, the budget debate had passed its October 20 deadline, forcing De la Espriella to issue a decree that would convert an older version of the budget bill into law.

The interior minister was the administration’s primary political liaison responsible for managing legislative procedure and whip operations in Congress.

Lara’s job was already under pressure after he failed to convince Congress to cede its presidency to the president’s candidate.

While Ordoñez returns from Washington, Justice Minister Ivan Cancino will assume the role of interior minister.

The incoming interior minister is an ultra conservative Catholic with ties to the Society of St. Pius X, which considers the modernizing reforms of the Catholic Church heresies and errors, and was declared in a schism with the church in June.

In Colombian politics and particularly among the opposition, Ordoñez is mainly remembered as the inspector general who illegally removed former President Gustavo Petro from his post as mayor of Bogota in 2013.

Petro was ultimately reinstated and would become president of the country in 2022.

World.title: Colombia’s Congress approves De la Espriella’s 2027 budget
World.content:
Colombia’s Congress agreed to increase the government’s 2027 budget despite promises by President Abelardo de la Espriella to reduce public spending.

Next year’s budget will be COP634.9 trillion, almost $204 billion, which is 16% more than last year’s budget and 10% higher than the proposal made by former President Gustavo Petro.

According to Finance Minister Miguel Gomez, the budget seeks to bring the State’s finances in line with reality.

The budget was approved in both the Senate and the House of Representatives with the support of De la Espriella’s government coalition.

The Historic Pact, the only leftist opposition party, rejected the budget and boycotted the vote.

On behalf of the national government, I would like to thank you all for your work over the past few months in passing the budget. I would also like to thank the opposition for the strength with which they defended their views. The message that Congress has sent today regarding the government’s economic policy is very important. It is the first step toward putting the country’s economy back on track toward growth, fiscal responsibility, and addressing the nation’s needs. Finance Minister Miguel Gomez

The budget seeks to reimpose the neoliberal model that had been abandoned by Petro and reduce public debt.

According to Green Party representative Jaime Raul Salamanca, who opposed the budget, funding for free higher education was cut in half from COP800 billion ($254 million) to COP400 billion (127 million).

“This cut raises concerns about its potential impact on the continuity and scope of this policy, which has enabled thousands of young people to enroll in public institutions of higher education,” said Salamanca.

The budget also cut the budget for the war crimes tribunal JEP, which could endanger the future of the peace process with the FARC and is opposed by the government.

World.title: De la Espriella announces “open, resolute, and patriotic struggle against wokeism”
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella announced an “open, resolute, and patriotic struggle against wokeism” as part of his “cultural counterrevolution.”

During a visit to the Culture Ministry, De la Espriella described wokeism as “an ideological paradigm that aims to transform moral, cultural, and social foundations in the West, perverting values, family tradition, and national identity.”

According to the president, Culture Minister Paola Holguin was a general in the “cultural counterrevolution.”

Culture has an enormous capacity to shape society, and that is why the State has a moral, inescapable, and political duty to prevent cultural spaces from being taken over by social communism, which is atheist and an enemy to the fundamental values upon which the nation of Colombia is built. This is where that cultural counterrevolution will begin. President Abelardo de la Espriella

De la Espriella said that Holguin, the daughter of a reported money launderer, would lead the “Culture War” against the “extreme left,” which has “permeated all parts of society, particularly the cultural and academic spheres.”

I want to be clear about this: we are going to wage an open, resolute, and patriotic struggle against wokeism, which is nothing more than an ideological movement that aims to transform the moral, cultural, and social foundations of the West, corrupting values, family tradition, and national identity. President Abelardo de la Espriella

Earlier in the day, the National Museum removed all references to members of the exterminated Patriotic Union party, slain guerrilla leader and presidential candidate Carlos Pizarro, and the struggle for the rights of Colombia’s LGBT+ community.

References to Colombia’s former guerrilla movements was “terrorism apology, which is “exactly what we have come to confront” in an attempt to “recover pride for Colombian culture.”

Atheists, the Pizarro family and gay rights activists rejected the president’s attempts to remove them from mainstream culture.

World.title: Colombia’s first lady promises transparency over earthquake donations
World.content:
Colombia’s first lady, Ana Lucia Pineda, vowed to reveal how much money she collected and spent in response to the August 10 earthquake that affected hundreds of thousands of people.

Amid mounting public pressure about where the money had gone, Pineda went on the morning program of public television channel Nuestro Caribe to promise that her foundation, Luz y Sonrisas, will take its finances public on Friday.

Carrying a white folder, the wife of President Abelardo de la Espriella stressed that “in the foundation’s accounts rest all, absolutely all of the monies from the donations we received during the ‘Colombia One Single Heart’ campaign” that was announced on August 12.

“A lie is not going to tear down the truth of who I am or what I represent, or how my children recognize me,” said Pineda.

Luz y Sonrisas was one of three NGO’s that were promoted by the De la Espriella government to collect contributions for victims of the earthquake.

Pineda’s foundation was the only one that could receive contributions from abroad.

Earlier in the week, news program Noticias Uno revealed that her foundation that was founded on July 7 lacked the tax exemption that would allow it to accept donations, a process that usually takes months.

In a press statement, tax office DIAN subsequently said that it had granted the tax exemption to the first lady and that she could legally accept financial contributions.

Pineda did not say how much money she had received, but said that she stopped supporting the initial relief efforts “because the humanitarian aid was sufficient, it was huge.”

The first lady vowed she had saved the donations for the reconstruction phase “because I have also taken the initiative to build and return to the victims a house that is durable for the families who lost everything.”

World.title: Colombia’s opposition takes to the street to protest De la Espriella
World.content:
Despite intimidation attempts by the national government and the police, tens of thousands of people took to the streets throughout Colombia to protest the far-right government of President Abelardo De la Espriella.

The protest had been organized by social organizations, labor unions and the country’s largest opposition party, the Historic Pact.

Opposition leader Ivan Cepeda, who joined the protests in Bogota, told a reporter that the government is “exercising a mafia-style rule in the service of the worst elements of Colombian politics—the drug trade.”

Contrary to what De la Espriella is saying, this is not a government that opposes drug trafficking; it is a government that supports the drug trafficking cartels, the paramilitaries, and the ultra-conservative forces that want to destroy people’s rights, the democratic advances made by President Gustavo Petro, and the progress achieved by the popular movement over the past four years. Senator Ivan Cepeda

“That’s why we’re here; we won’t allow people’s rights to be violated or trampled upon,” said the senator.

Hours ahead of the protest, the president signed off on a decree that changed the police response to protests and accused the organizers of being “instigators of evil” who “seek to once again cause chaos.”

Human rights organizations denounced that the security forces put snipers on the roofs of buildings in Bogota and in Cali, a helicopter flew over the heads of the protesters.

The protests sought to test the waters for an even larger “national strike” that is set for November and shut down parts of the country in 2021.

“We are only warming up,” warned Cepeda, who has yet to recognize De la Espriella as Colombia’s legitimate president after losing the elections in July.

World.title: Colombia’s national strike organizers “are instigators of evil,” claims De la Espriella
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella called labor unions and social organizations who organized anti-government protests for Wednesday “instigators of evil” who “seek to once again cause chaos.”

In an address to the nation, De la Espriella stressed that the security forces were instructed to allow peaceful protests, but warned the protesters that “if they intend to set Colombia ablaze, they will face the determination of the tiger and his government to do what is lawfully required—which is to defend the lives, honor, and property of all Colombians.”

Wednesday’s protests are a preparation for a national strike that is set to take place in November and is supported by the country’s political opposition to the far-right government.

According to the president, “those who are promoting the strike and seeking to use it to once again cause chaos and destabilize the government are the very same people who left the country bankrupt, on the brink of a blackout, with the healthcare system in intensive care, energy sovereignty compromised, and public resources plundered and looted.”

“They are instigators of evil, not fighter for freedom,” said De la Espriella.

If they intend to set Colombia ablaze, they will face the determination of the tiger and his government to do what is rightfully required—which is to defend the lives, honor, and property of all Colombians. President Abelardo de la Espriella

The president stressed that he would be signing a decree that regulates public protests in an attempt to avoid the chaos that erupted during massive strikes in 2019 and 2021 an killed 80 people.

De la Espriella additionally is expected to present an “anti-terrorism stature” to Congress, which could see the prosecution of protest organizers on terrorism charges, according to opposition leaders and security experts.

World.title: Brazil investigates whether Flávio Bolsonaro left the country via Argentina after his defeat
World.content:
Brazil investigates whether Flávio Bolsonaro left the country via Argentina after his defeat

27th Tuesday, October 2026 - 16:32 UTC Full article

Judge Alexandre de Moraes ordered Bolsonaro, who is under investigation by the court, to surrender his ordinary and diplomatic passports within 24 hours and barred him from leaving the country

Brazil’s Federal Police are checking with Argentine authorities whether Senator Flávio Bolsonaro, defeated by Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva in Sunday’s presidential runoff, left the country across the Argentine border, after he failed to hand over his passports within the deadline set by the Supreme Federal Court. His campaign and the Argentine government deny that he has left Brazil.

Supreme Court Judge Alexandre de Moraes on Monday ordered Bolsonaro, who is under investigation by the court, to surrender his ordinary and diplomatic passports within 24 hours and barred him from leaving the country. In a video posted on social media, the senator said Federal Police officers served him notice “in the middle of the street” as he left the Brasília home of his father, former president Jair Bolsonaro, and he agreed with his lawyers to hand over the documents on Tuesday morning. The deadline passed without police confirming the handover, and the passports were cancelled, according to the Brazilian press.

Argentine newspaper Infobae reported early on Tuesday that Bolsonaro had entered Argentina at Puerto Iguazú, in the Triple Frontier area, at around 2 a.m. using his national identity card, valid for travel between Mercosur countries, in order to continue to the United States on a private plane. According to the newspaper, it was a Gulfstream G400 owned by Argentine company Baires Fly, which requested immigration clearance for four passengers and three crew. Records on the Flightradar24 platform show the aircraft flew from Buenos Aires to Puerto Iguazú on Monday night.

Federal Police sources quoted by the newspaper Metrópoles said Bolsonaro had not passed through any official Brazilian border checkpoint, though they acknowledged it is possible to cross the border without being checked. His campaign’s general coordinator, Rogério Marinho, denied he had left the country, and the Argentine government also rejected the report. Since Tuesday morning, his allies had been unable to reach him, according to a columnist for the UOL news portal.

His brother Eduardo Bolsonaro, who has lived in the United States since 2025 after being convicted by the Supreme Court of coercion in the case over their father’s coup attempt, said on Friday that Flávio should leave the country if he lost. The senator refused to recognise Lula’s victory and later said he would “organise the opposition”. US President Donald Trump said on Monday, without offering evidence, that the election looked “rigged”.

World.title: A judge appointed by Jair Bolsonaro rejects his son’s case for annulling the election
World.content:
A judge appointed by Jair Bolsonaro rejects his son’s case for annulling the election

26th Monday, October 2026 - 13:39 UTC Full article

“Even before all these circumstances, we took all the necessary measures and were entirely successful. I repeat: there was no change resulting from the court ruling,” Nunes Marques said

The president of Brazil’s Superior Electoral Court, Kassio Nunes Marques, who was appointed to the Supreme Federal Court by former president Jair Bolsonaro in 2020, said on Monday that the extension of voting hours did not change the result of the runoff won by Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva. Senator Flávio Bolsonaro, the former president’s son, had cited the extension in refusing to recognise his defeat and calling for the election to be annulled.

“Even before all these circumstances, we took all the necessary measures and were entirely successful. I repeat: there was no change resulting from the court ruling,” Nunes Marques told a press conference.

On Sunday night, Bolsonaro called it “unacceptable” that Supreme Court Judge Cristiano Zanin, whom he called “Lula’s lawyer” for having defended him in the Lava Jato cases, ordered at 5.01 p.m., when polls were due to close, an extension of voting until 7 p.m. “There is a lot to clarify before Brazil recognises this outrage that has just happened,” he said. “I will never know how many votes I could have had.”

Zanin ordered the extension at the request of Lula’s coalition, which reported a lack of buses to carry voters in cities such as Salvador and São Paulo. Bolsonaro’s campaign, for its part, had asked the electoral courts to extend voting in municipalities affected by rain, flooding and power cuts in states such as Minas Gerais and Rio Grande do Sul. The measure applied only to polling stations still open; those that had closed at 5 p.m. did not reopen and followed the usual counting procedure.

Lula won with 51.78% of valid votes against Bolsonaro’s 48.22%, a margin of about 4.4 million votes. There is no record yet of the senator’s campaign having filed a formal challenge.

World.title: Debt, inflation and a hostile Congress: the economic challenges of Lula’s fourth term
World.content:
Debt, inflation and a hostile Congress: the economic challenges of Lula’s fourth term

26th Monday, October 2026 - 13:29 UTC Full article

Public debt has risen by more than ten points during the current term and exceeds 82% of GDP, driven by growing mandatory spending

Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva will begin his fourth term as Brazil’s president on January 1 with an economy that has grown more than expected and record-low unemployment, but with fiscal imbalances that markets punished heavily on Monday, the first trading day after his re-election. The dollar rose more than 12% at one point to 5.60 reais, the Ibovespa index triggered an automatic trading halt at the open and long-term interest rates jumped almost two points.

The reaction reflects investors’ bets on a victory by Senator Flávio Bolsonaro, who promised sharp spending cuts. On Friday, the dollar had closed at 4.99 reais and the Ibovespa at 205,082 points, close to the record it reached after the first round. Analysts agree that the president’s first test will be the make-up of his economic team and his fiscal framework. These are the five main challenges he faces.

Debt

Public debt has risen by more than ten points during the current term and exceeds 82% of GDP, driven by growing mandatory spending, which leaves less than 8% of the federal budget for adjustable items. Lula has at times played down concerns over debt, arguing that stronger growth will solve the problem. His team has pledged to keep the current fiscal rules, which cap spending growth and set primary surplus targets, but meeting them will be harder given the commitment to raise the minimum wage above inflation, which also increases pension costs, and the new benefits announced during the campaign.

Inflation and interest rates

The Central Bank has cut the Selic rate five times in a row to 13.75%, but annual inflation exceeded the 4.5% tolerance ceiling in September, against a 3% target. The Monetary Policy Committee meets on November 4, and the real’s depreciation complicates further cuts. Lula proposes lowering rates through greater fiscal discipline without touching social programmes, while most economists argue a faster decline would require spending cuts.

Household debt

According to credit agency Serasa, nearly 84 million Brazilians and 9.3 million companies are behind on payments, a record attributed to high interest rates. The government is preparing new relief measures, such as buying distressed mortgages from banks at a discount and forgiving tax debts for small business owners, which analysts see as temporary relief.

A hostile Congress

Bolsonaro’s Liberal Party will hold the largest bloc in both the Chamber of Deputies and the Senate, in the most conservative Congress since the return to democracy. That will hamper the government’s plans to cut tax exemptions and the approval of appointments to the Central Bank, regulators and the Supreme Court, which were already difficult during the current term. Bolsonaro, moreover, does not recognise the result and has said he will seek to annul the election.

Tax reform

The new value-added tax, approved in 2023, takes effect in January, but the government has yet to set its effective rate, which independent analysts put at around 28%. The government also postponed during the campaign a bill for a selective tax on products harmful to health or the environment, such as tobacco and alcohol.

World.title: Trump insults Norway and rejects its immigrants for not giving him the Nobel Peace Prize
World.content:
Trump insults Norway and rejects its immigrants for not giving him the Nobel Peace Prize

26th Monday, October 2026 - 13:24 UTC Full article

Trump has made no secret of his wish to win the prize

US President Donald Trump lashed out at Norway at a rally in Port Huron, Michigan, on Sunday, saying Norwegian immigrants are not welcome in the United States because the Nobel Committee did not award him the Peace Prize. Norwegian Foreign Minister Espen Barth Eide replied that the committee is independent.

“Frankly, Norway stinks. Norway has become a shithole country, in fact,” Trump said at a campaign event a week before the November 3 midterm elections. The president said he would welcome immigrants from certain countries but not from Norway, “because I didn’t get the Nobel Prize. So I don’t want anybody from Norway.”

“He knows very well that the Nobel Committee is independent. We have reminded him of that, in case anyone had any doubts, and that remains the case,” Barth Eide told Norwegian public radio NRK on Monday.

Trump has made no secret of his wish to win the prize. This year the Nobel Committee awarded it to South African jurist Navi Pillay, a former International Criminal Court judge and former UN High Commissioner for Human Rights, a decision Trump called “shameful and embarrassing”. Last year, when the prize went to Venezuelan opposition leader María Corina Machado, he also expressed anger at not being recognised. In 2018, during his first term, he was heavily criticised for using similar language about Haiti and several African countries.

World.title: Trump questions Lula’s victory as most of the region, including the right, congratulates him
World.content:
Trump questions Lula’s victory as most of the region, including the right, congratulates him

26th Monday, October 2026 - 13:16 UTC Full article

“They just applied the Biden playbook in Brazil. Bolsonaro had a big lead in the first round and was the clear favourite. But communists don’t give up power once they get it,” Trump said

US President Donald Trump cast doubt on Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s re-election in Brazil and compared it with the 2020 US election, while most Latin American governments, including several right-wing allies of Washington, congratulated the Brazilian president. In Argentina, President Javier Milei remained silent.

“They just applied the Joe Biden playbook in Brazil. Bolsonaro had a big lead in the first round and was the clear favourite to win the second. But communists don’t give up power once they get it,” Trump said, according to the EFE news agency, without offering evidence of irregularities. Trump has never acknowledged his defeat by Biden in 2020. The White House has not formally commented on the result, which Senator Flávio Bolsonaro also refuses to recognise and has said he will seek to annul.

One of the first to congratulate Lula was Uruguayan President Yamandú Orsi: “I have just spoken with Brazil’s president-elect, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, a friend. I congratulated him on his victory and on the democratic celebration that an electoral process represents.” Governments of the opposite ideological stripe also did so. Chile’s José Antonio Kast, an ally of the Bolsonaros, said the two countries “have a lot of future in common”; Paraguay’s Santiago Peña hailed “this great democratic day”; and Bolivia’s Rodrigo Paz noted that Bolivia and Brazil are “neighbouring and brotherly countries”. Ecuador’s Daniel Noboa called for working together against “common enemies”, and Panama’s José Raúl Mulino pledged to keep “working together”. Mexico’s Claudia Sheinbaum said: “Long live democracy, the people of Brazil won.”

In Argentina, Milei, who backed Bolsonaro during the campaign and even accused Lula of seeking to “steal” the election, had issued no congratulations. The Peronist opposition, by contrast, celebrated. Former president Cristina Kirchner spoke of “a genuine electoral 17 October”, referring to Peronism’s founding date; Buenos Aires governor Axel Kicillof of “a historic night”; and former presidential candidate Sergio Massa wrote: “Today, as yesterday, on Lula’s side of life.”

Former Chilean president Gabriel Boric, who followed the vote in Brazil, thanked Lula “for never giving up the fight”. Congratulations from right-wing leaders such as Kast, Peña and Paz reflect the weight of Brazil, the region’s largest economy and the main trading partner of several of its neighbours. Lula will begin his fourth term on January 1.

World.title: Milei stays silent on Lula’s victory as Kast and Peña congratulate him
World.content:
Milei stays silent on Lula’s victory as Kast and Peña congratulate him

26th Monday, October 2026 - 13:05 UTC Full article

Neither the president nor Foreign Minister Pablo Quirno had issued a statement on the result, according to the Argentine press

Argentine President Javier Milei had not congratulated Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva on his re-election in Brazil by Monday, unlike other right-wing South American leaders such as Chile’s José Antonio Kast, Paraguay’s Santiago Peña and Bolivia’s Rodrigo Paz. Milei, who publicly backed Senator Flávio Bolsonaro during the campaign, met his cabinet at the Casa Rosada first thing in the morning.

Neither the president nor Foreign Minister Pablo Quirno had issued a statement on the result, according to the Argentine press. “We have to wait,” official sources said. During election night, Milei shared social media posts questioning the extension of voting hours in Brazil, and on Monday he shared a message against the “average leftie”. Bolsonaro does not recognise Lula’s victory and has said he will seek to annul the election.

Kast, for his part, said he had spoken with Lula: “I have just spoken with the President of Brazil, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, and congratulated him on the election result.” The presidents of Mexico, Panama and Uruguay also congratulated the Brazilian leader, according to the newspaper La Nación.

Within the Argentine government, Bolsonaro’s defeat came as a surprise. “The rejection of Bolsonaro was very strong,” an official told the Noticias Argentinas news agency. At the Casa Rosada, the result is attributed to Lula’s latest economic measures, the shorter working week and the rejection the candidate generated among women and young people. A political figure who regularly visits government headquarters told Infobae the defeat weakens the idea of an international right-wing alliance that Milei had promoted. The Peronist opposition, by contrast, celebrated the re-election: Cristina Kirchner, Axel Kicillof and Sergio Massa linked it to Argentina’s 2027 elections.

Relations between the two presidents are strained. Milei repeatedly called Lula a “thief” and last week said he hoped he would not “steal” the election. In July, Brazil recalled its ambassador in Buenos Aires for consultations after earlier insults from the Argentine president. Brazil is Argentina’s main trading partner, and the two countries are Mercosur’s largest economies.

World.title: Brazil’s real plunges more than 8% and São Paulo stocks slump after Lula’s victory
World.content:
Brazil’s real plunges more than 8% and São Paulo stocks slump after Lula’s victory
