World.title: Quebec’s separatist leader threatens to play spoiler at Carney’s EU summit
World.content:
Ottawa also turned down a September request from the previous Quebec government to host a reception on the sidelines of the summit, Sarrazin noted.

Prime Minister Mark Carney hit back, saying St-Pierre Plamondon had himself turned down an invitation to the Thursday night summit dinner. “It’s his decision to leave an empty chair again,” Carney told reporters in French.

The tiff threatens to overshadow an international gathering that Carney, Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and European Council President António Costa have billed as a step change in mutual relations, driven by U.S. President Donald Trump’s aggressive tariffs and scorn for the postwar Western consensus.

Early drafts of the joint declaration include a digital trade deal and a pact that lets the European Investment Bank finance Canadian critical minerals projects. Many of those deliverables fall under provincial jurisdiction, such as natural resources.

“'When you’re not at the table, you’re on the menu,' Prime Minister Carney told us,” Sarrazin said in her statement. “The federal government has chosen to prevent Quebec from having a say on its own territory.”

Whatever agreements are signed at the summit, “Quebec is sovereign in its fields of jurisdiction internationally, so it will have the last word,” Sarrazin warned.

World.title: EU eyes global tax deal revenue to boost next budget
World.content:
Costa, who is brokering budget talks, is pressuring leaders to reach a budget deal among themselves by the end of the year — before elections in Poland, France and Italy threaten to derail the negotiations.

Yet after more than a year of haggling, EU governments are still at odds over five proposed new taxes that the Commission estimates would generate €65 billion per year.

Among the options on the table, a corporate tax known as CORE — which charges a lump sum on companies’ revenues exceeding €100 million — has emerged as the most unpopular option and is particularly toxic in Germany.

To break the deadlock, French President Emmanuel Macron supported funneling part of the tax on multinationals to the EU budget during a leaders’ summit in October, said two of the diplomats. They were granted anonymity, like others, to discuss the sensitive plans.

Supporters argue that this idea could garner more political support than CORE as it targets companies’ profits as opposed to their revenue.

“The corporate income tax is about taxing companies based on their profitability. CORE is not about that, CORE is about taking a toll blindly,” said Pascal Saint-Amans, a former OECD official and one of the architects of the global tax arrangement.

World.title: EU prepares for a grim future with new climate-proofing law
World.content:
“There is no alternative to continue to cut emissions more forcefully and to move full-frontal into clean energy,” Climate Commissioner Wopke Hoekstra told reporters. “But at the same time, we do have to acknowledge that the problems we're facing have morphed into something that is so large that just doing that alone unfortunately no longer is good enough.”

The Commission’s proposed Climate Resilience Law asks governments to draft plans to prepare for a world that’s 2 degrees Celsius hotter in 2050 and 3C hotter by the end of the century, aligning with the United Nations’ latest projections that current global climate policies can only limit warming to 2.8C.

The same U.N. report also warned that the world can no longer limit warming to 1.5C, the lower bound of the Paris Agreement’s dual goals, and that steep emissions cuts are needed to achieve the best-case scenario of halting the rise in global temperatures at 1.8C.

The Commission insisted that Tuesday’s package did not amount to Brussels resigning itself to catastrophic levels of warming.

“Let me just be crystal-clear on the 1.5C, that remains our goal,” said Hoekstra. “At the same time, it would be unwise not to prepare for… the current trajectory the world is on.”

Regulation for the deregulation era

Under the proposed law, governments are “encouraged” to take the 3C scenario into account when designing policies, budgets and investments.

World.title: Frontex soll soziale Medien auf Hinweise zu illegaler Migration überwachen
World.content:
BRÜSSEL – Die Europäische Kommission stellte am Dienstag Pläne für eine umfassende Reform von Frontex vor. Damit sollen die Befugnisse und Kapazitäten der Agentur im Kampf gegen irreguläre Migration ausgeweitet werden. Künftig soll Frontex eine größere Rolle bei der Rückführung von Menschen ohne Aufenthaltsrecht übernehmen und Rückführungsmaßnahmen auch außerhalb der EU durchführen können. Zudem soll die Behörde neue Kompetenzen bei der Überwachung sozialer Medien erhalten.

Welche Rolle soziale Netzwerke bei der Verbreitung von Informationen spielen, die irreguläre Migration begünstigen können, zeigte sich im Juli in der spanischen Exklave Ceuta. Dort hatten innerhalb weniger Stunden Tausende Migranten unerlaubt die Grenze überquert.

Nach den neuen Plänen soll Frontex ein Zentrum zur Überwachung und Reaktion auf Online-Inhalte einrichten. Dieses soll öffentlich zugängliche Beiträge in sozialen Medien auswerten, um Entwicklungen zu erkennen, die für den Schutz der EU-Außengrenzen relevant sind. Darüber hinaus soll die Stelle Maßnahmen gegen illegale Online-Inhalte unterstützen, die mit Sicherheitsrisiken an den Grenzen zusammenhängen, erklärte die zuständige EU-Kommissionsvizepräsidentin Henna Virkkunen am Dienstag vor Journalisten.

World.title: EIB to sign framework deal with Canada on critical raw materials
World.content:
A Canadian flag flies by the waterfront of Lake Ontario in Toronto, Canada on Aug. 27, 2026. | Cole Burston/AFP via Getty Images

The European Investment Bank is due to sign a framework agreement with Canada this week that will pave the way for investments into critical raw materials and other areas, a Bank official told POLITICO.

The deal with the long-term lending arm of the European Union is expected to be signed on the sidelines of an EU-Canada summit on Thursday in Montreal, said the official who was granted anonymity to discuss internal preparations.

Such a deal would mark a concrete step toward closer ties amid broader discussions about cooperation on arctic security and the EU’s potential offer of “associate member” status to Canada. The summit will aim to highlight deepening ties between like-minded partners.

World.title: EU divisions persist on ‘associate member’ label for Canada
World.content:
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, left, speaks with European Parliament President Roberta Metsola in the hemicycle of the European Parliament in Strasbourg, France on Sept. 17, 2026. | Jean-Christophe Verhaegen/AFP via Getty Images

BRUSSELS — The EU was split Tuesday over whether to offer “associate membership” status to Canada, with several countries refusing to sign off on a statement containing that phrase just 48 hours before a summit between the two sides in Montreal.

After EU capitals could not agree on the language in the statement in talks between ambassadors Monday, they used the so-called silence procedure on Tuesday. That meant a new text would be adopted automatically without a formal meeting or vote, if no countries objected by midday.

But Germany, which is leading the push to have the term “associate member” fully removed from the text, was among at least four countries that broke the silence procedure before that deadline, said two EU diplomats, granted anonymity to speak freely. That means the topic will be discussed Wednesday at another meeting of EU ambassadors, just one day before the EU-Canada summit kicks off.

World.title: Frontex gets power to track migration talk on social media
World.content:
This article is also available in: German

The role of social media platforms in spreading information that contributes to illegal migration was central to the crisis in the Spanish exclave of Ceuta. | Tomohiro Ohsumi/Getty Images

The EU's border agency, Frontex, will be able to monitor social media for information about migration flows.

The European Commission on Tuesday unveiled a revamp of Frontex, strengthening its capabilities and capacity to tackle illegal migration. It will play a more prominent role in deporting people with no legal right to remain in the EU, including new powers to carry out return operations beyond the bloc’s territory and new oversight on social media.

The role of social media platforms in spreading information that contributes to illegal migration was central to the crisis in the Spanish exclave of Ceuta, where thousands of migrants illegally crossed the border within a few hours in July.

World.title: French government mulled blocking social networks and mobile internet amid protests
World.content:
Contacted by POLITICO, officials from Lecornu's office, the technology ministry and the interior ministry did not deny the move nor the letter's existence.

The government feared that the scenes of violence seen on Oct. 17 could repeat or escalate on the following weekend — a concern that did not materialize, as far fewer incidents were recorded on Oct. 24.

“What they wanted, above all, was to block the communication channels that allow gangs to meet up and organize,” said the employee of a telecommunications provider, who was granted anonymity to speak freely.

The move, however, would have also prevented peaceful protesters from communicating as well. Blocking access to social networks in a targeted area, such as a specific neighborhood, is not technically possible, while cutting access to mobile internet would cause major disruptions to other key services such as mobile payments, security-surveillance devices and emergency communications.

The government also considered a less radical solution that would disable geolocation display features “to prevent gatherings of people who don’t know each other, for example,” according to the official from the prime minister’s office.

Other limitations on social media access are being discussed in parliament as part of the debate on the so-called “who breaks pays” bill, which would hold people who "knowingly took part" in a riot financially responsible — whether or not they committed property damage themselves.

The same bill would require platforms to remove within 24 hours content that incites physical or sexual assault, theft, destruction, or property damage, “when such content is likely to cause a serious disturbance to public order” and within one hour content that encourages insurrection.

Other lawmakers are proposing measures ranging from tracking troublemakers via algorithmic video surveillance to penalizing online marketplaces that fail to prevent the sale of stolen goods.

World.title: Exit polls suggest no clear victor in Israeli election
World.content:
Exit polls in Israel's key legislative election on Tuesday suggested no clear victor, with both Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and main rival Gadi Eisenkot falling short of a majority.

 

Israel's Channel 13 news initially projected the opposition bloc would have the edge with 53 seats in the 120-seat Knesset, with Netanyahu's bloc set to win around 50. It later dropped the Eisenkot bloc to 52. Netanyahu's Likud party would be the largest single party, with 25 seats, per the broadcaster.

Channel 12, another major pollster, also put the opposition bloc at 52 seats and Netanyahu's at 50. It had the Likud party winning 24 seats.

Arab parties are projected to win a record 18 seats, according to the outlets.

In a post on X, Eisenkot said the exit poll results showed a "complete lack of confidence in Netanyahu and the October 7 government."

Yair Golan, the leader of Israel's left-wing Democrats party, added that the public had "spoken" and "ousted the Netanyahu government."

But Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Sa'ar warned that celebrations from the left were "premature."

"One thing seems quite clear: The Likud is the largest party in Israel," he wrote on social media.

Turnout for the election - Israel's first since Hamas' 7 October 2023 attacks - hit over 77%, according to Israel's Central Elections Committee.

Netanyahu had spent much of the day calling on supporters to get out and vote, painting the election as a "matter of life and death."

The vote is widely seen as a referendum on Netanyahu's leadership.

This is a developing story. Check back here for further details.

World.title: Egypt’s parliament approves military support for Saudi Arabia amid Houthi attacks
World.content:
Egypt’s parliament on Monday authorised President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi to provide military assistance to defend Saudi Arabia if the kingdom requests help, following a wave of attacks by Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthis.

 

The House of Representatives said the decision passed with the required two-thirds majority. It allows el-Sisi, in coordination with Riyadh, to take measures to protect Saudi territory, sovereignty and holy sites against external attacks.

Parliament’s statement did not specify what assistance Egypt would provide or announce that troops were being sent.

On 17 October, Yahya al-Raei, speaker of the Houthi-controlled parliament in Sanaa, warned Egypt against military involvement, saying it would endanger Egypt’s own security and stability.

El-Sisi said last week that any Egyptian military role would be limited to defending Saudi territory and borders, ruling out attacks on Yemen.

The vote came as Saudi Defence Minister Prince Khalid bin Salman joined Pakistani and Turkish officials for talks with Iranian leaders in Tehran. The Saudi foreign ministry said the visit aimed to open channels for negotiations and prevent further military escalation.

Approval after three closed sessions

El-Sisi first sought parliament’s backing on 17 October. MPs met behind closed doors on 18 and 19 October before postponing the decision until Monday.

Deputy Speaker Assem El-Gazzar said nearly 500 MPs had asked to speak during the discussions. Most parties supported the request, but some lawmakers questioned the terms of a possible military mission.

The Egyptian Social Democratic Party instructed its MPs ahead of the vote to abstain. It said parliament had not received enough information about what Egyptian troops would be asked to do, how long they would stay, what the operation would cost or the risks they would face.

While supporting Saudi Arabia’s security, the party warned against an open-ended military commitment and urged Egypt to leave room for diplomacy.

The National Defence Council, chaired by el-Sisi, had endorsed support for Saudi Arabia on 18 October. However, Egypt’s constitution also requires approval from two-thirds of MPs before its armed forces can be sent on combat missions abroad.

Attacks continue as diplomats meet

Saudi, Pakistani and Turkish officials met Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian and other senior officials in Tehran on Monday. Pakistan sent army chief Asim Munir, while Turkey sent intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalin.

Fighting continues between the Houthis and the Saudi-led coalition backing Yemen’s internationally recognised government.

The Houthis said on Monday they had attacked pumping stations on Saudi Arabia’s East-West oil pipeline and King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh. There was no immediate Saudi confirmation of those claims.

The Saudi-led coalition separately said it had intercepted a missile heading towards Riyadh. It also said it had destroyed Houthi missile launchers and storage facilities in Yemen.

The fighting threatens shipping through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait. The waterway forms the southern entrance to the Red Sea and is part of the route to Egypt’s Suez Canal.

Egypt’s main stock index closed 1.7% lower on Monday ahead of the parliamentary vote. Trading had been halted for 30 minutes on Sunday after the broader EGX100 index fell 10%.

Saudi Arabia is a major political ally and financial supporter of Egypt. It provides aid, energy supplies and deposits at Egypt’s central bank.

Egypt joined the Saudi-led coalition in Yemen in 2015, mainly through naval operations. Its combat role was limited.

World.title: Iraq sentences seven French nationals to prison for belonging to Islamic State
World.content:
An Iraqi court sentenced seven French nationals to prison on Tuesday for belonging to the Islamic State group.

 

Iraq's Supreme Judicial Council sentenced Lakhdar Sebouai, Adel Bou Aoun, Anas Abdul Rahman, Ziad Ahmad, Mehdi Sida and Benjamin Van Han to life imprisonment, which under Iraqi law is equivalent to 20 years.

The seventh defendant, Amza Benabed, 24, was given a 15-year prison term. They now have 30 days to lodge an appeal.

Under Iraqi law, decisions handed down by criminal courts are also subject to review by the Court of Cassation, whether or not the defendant has filed an appeal.

The seven men were deemed "particularly dangerous because of their role in threatening Iraq's national security, destabilising Iraq and Syria, and their involvement in inciting terrorist operations in other countries," a court statement said.

They were among 47 French citizens suspected of links to IS. Held in Syria until last year, they were transferred to Iraq so they could stand trial.

Defence lawyers and representatives of the French embassy were present at the hearing.

Islamic State

The Islamic State group swept across Iraq in 2014, seizing vast swathes of territory in the west of the country and in neighbouring Syria, where it established the seat of its self-proclaimed caliphate.

Although the organisation lost control of these areas several years ago, it still has active cells that periodically carry out attacks in both countries.

Iraq is currently holding thousands of people suspected of belonging to IS. They include more than 5,700 detainees transferred from north-eastern Syria after fighting broke out in January between Syrian government forces and the Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF).

The latter had long been guarding the detention centres where jihadist fighters and their families were held following the fall of the caliphate.

Some detainees linked to IS managed to escape during the January clashes, fuelling fears of larger-scale breakouts and leading to the transfer of the remaining prisoners to Iraq.

Iraq's national security adviser, Qasim al-Aboudi, said earlier this month that Syria had requested the transfer to Damascus of around 4,000 Syrians suspected of belonging to IS so that they could be tried there. Baghdad, however, rejected the request.

Al-Aboudi said that once their trials in Iraq were over, some detainees could be sent back to their country of origin to serve their sentences there. It is still not known whether the convicted French nationals could be repatriated.

In the past, Iraq has frequently executed people convicted of terrorism, prompting criticism from human rights organisations. However, the country does not apply the death penalty to foreign nationals whose home country does not provide for capital punishment.

World.title: Norway says 'successful' cyberattacks against the country have tripled in last six months
World.content:
Norway's National Security Authority (NSM) said on Tuesday that the number of "successful" cyberattacks targeting Norwegian organisations had trebled in the last six months as it warned of a continued threat to national security.

 

In a new report, the NSM - which is involved in efforts to counter espionage and hybrid threats - said the country's defence industry and space sector were particularly exposed to cyber risk.

"This also applies to critical infrastructure and service providers to organisations that are important to national security," it said.

"NSM has not previously made this type of assessment public," director Arne Christian Haugstøyl added. "We are doing so now because it is absolutely necessary to strengthen both the resilience and the ability to handle cyber operations in Norwegian organisations."

The report follows increasing warnings across Europe of suspected Russian hybrid attacks, including cyber operations.

In August, Norwegian media reported that a Russian hacker group had declared war on Norway while also claiming responsibility for a distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) attack that had reportedly impacted multiple government digital services.

In its report published on Tuesday, the NSM did not point to a specific actor but said that certain businesses and organisations were being increasingly subjected to reconnaissance and ransomware and DDoS attacks.

The agency also warned of the threat posed by artificial intelligence technology, which it said posed a "serious risk" to Norwegian businesses and organisations.

“AI analyzes large amounts of data and identifies vulnerabilities faster than humans have been able to," Haugstøyl said. "These vulnerabilities open up new opportunities for cyberattacks at a faster pace and on a larger scale.

"This means that the risk is increasing, and the pace at which security measures are implemented must be accelerated."

World.title: Qatar urges Iran to 'show goodwill' by ending threats to the region and reopening the Strait of Hormuz
World.content:
Qatar urged Iran on Tuesday to “show goodwill” by stopping threats against countries in the region and reopening the Strait of Hormuz, as efforts to broker a deal with the United States continued.

 

"We have heard positive statements from the Iranian side on this issue, but they still need to show goodwill,” Ibrahim bin Sultan Al Hashmi, director of the foreign ministry’s Media and Communication Department, told a weekly briefing in Doha.

He said a Qatari delegation’s recent visit to Tehran was part of mediation efforts with Pakistan and other regional partners.

Asked whether the delegation had carried a new proposal, Al Hashmi said messages and ideas were still being exchanged with both sides. He gave no details of a proposal and did not announce a breakthrough.

Both Washington and Tehran had spoken about further escalation as well as the possibility of a diplomatic solution, he said.

“The mediator always holds on to this window of hope,” he said.

Regional security talks

On Monday, Saudi Defence Minister Prince Khalid bin Salman, Pakistan’s army chief Asim Munir and Turkish intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalin met Iranian leaders in Tehran.

The three countries signed the Mecca mutual defence pact in August. Iranian state media said all four countries agreed to continue talks on peace and security.

Al Hashmi said Qatar and its Gulf neighbours were ready to take part in a regional security framework based on respect for sovereignty and a commitment not to attack one another.

He said Saudi Arabia’s efforts complemented the work of Qatar and Pakistan.

The talks come amid continuing attacks on Saudi Arabia by Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthis. Egypt’s parliament on Monday authorised military support to help defend the kingdom.

The US and Iran remain divided over the terms of a deal. Tehran wants the US blockade of its ports lifted and sanctions on Iranian oil exports removed. Washington is demanding that Iran reduce nuclear enrichment.

The war began with US and Israeli strikes on Iran in late February. Iranian restrictions on shipping and the US blockade have severely disrupted traffic through Hormuz, a crucial route for Gulf oil and gas exports.

Brent crude rose above $117 (€105) a barrel last week, its highest level since April, following Iranian attacks on tankers near the strait. Crude flows through Hormuz were around 60% of normal, according to ANZ research.

World.title: South Africa: Athlete traverses 600 monkey bars under a 216-metre bridge
World.content:
South African obstacle course racing world champion Thomas van Tonder completed a world-first crossing beneath the Bloukrans Bridge, navigating 600 suspended monkey bars along more than 280 metres of its towering arch.

 

The athlete finished the Red Bull Bridge Bars challenge in 47 minutes and 37 seconds, suspended beneath the 216-metre-high bridge. Setting off at 10:21 with a heart rate of 150 beats per minute, he immediately faced the course's steepest section, a 45-degree ascent that forced him to pull himself upwards, bar by bar, while facing backwards.

The gruelling ascent pushed Van Tonder's grip beyond its limits, while the descent demanded precise control as gravity pulled him between bars and the tape protecting his fingers wore away. Battling exhaustion, he focused on one bar at a time, completing all 600 without giving up.

Thomas van Tonder described the crossing as “one of my biggest dreams and missions for the last two years” and said: “I have finished what I started.”

World.title: Putin call pits Finland and Norway against Denmark and Sweden
World.content:
A rare Nordic split emerged on Tuesday as the leaders of Denmark and Sweden publicly rebuked their counterparts in Finland and Norway for holding a surprise phone call with Russian President Vladimir Putin.

 

The call was the initiative of Finnish President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre, who recently hosted a round of peace talks in Oslo.

The two leaders urged Putin to end the full-scale invasion of Ukraine and engage in meaningful negotiations to reach a stable, peaceful settlement.

"The discussion was frank and substantive," Stubb said.

"The outcome of this war will have a direct impact on our and the broader European security. Ending the war requires direct discussion," he added.

"We stressed the importance of de-escalation," Støre said.

The read-out made clear that Stubb and Støre had spoken to Putin as "leaders of their respective countries and did not speak on behalf of Europe as a whole".

Immediately after, Stubb and Støre phoned Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, who thanked them for their "active" support.

But the choreography did little to mitigate the backlash from their neighbours.

Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen was highly critical, pointing to Russia's escalation against Ukraine as evidence that Moscow is not serious about diplomacy.

The Kremlin's statement released after the call echoed Putin's maximalist tone.

"I am very sceptical about this independent initiative by Norway and Finland. It was not coordinated with any of us," Frederiksen said shortly after the call became public.

"I don't see any signs that Russia desires peace with Europe, neither in the hybrid warfare taking place every single day, nor in Ukraine."

Frederiksen questioned the effectiveness of the overture and drew a parallel with previous go-it-alone attempts, such as when former Hungary Prime Minister Viktor Orbán flew to Moscow to meet with Putin.

"I honestly don't know what they think can be achieved by this," she said.

"We have previously emphasise, with clear backing from the rest of Europe, that when others have gone solo and, for example, travelled to Moscow, it is crucial that we, Europeans, stand together. That is something many of us have fought for."

Swedish Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson also cast doubt on the initiative, albeit in less harsh terms.

"My impression is that everyone wants peace except Putin. I have pretty low expectations for this kind of (direct) talk," Kristersson said.

"Holding talks that risk splitting the European voice is risky. Now, I'm not saying they have done that at all. I don't yet know what those talks were about," he noted.

"Talks that make Russia more willing to make a decent peace on Ukraine's terms are, of course, good."

In response to the pushback, Støre said Europe should speak with Russia to complement the messages sent by the US administration, which has a different take on the war.

Stubb, Støre, Frederiksen and Kristersson were all in Helsinki, Finland, to attend a leaders-level session of the Nordic Council.

Tuesday's political split is significant given that the four countries always see eye to eye when it comes to Russia's war on Ukraine. They are among the largest bilateral donors to Kyiv and vocal advocates of applying ever-stronger sanctions on Moscow.

World.title: Flavio Bolsonaro flees Brazil for US amid investigation  — reports
World.content:
Flavio Bolsonaro is on the way to the US, according to reports citing people close to the senator. The US State Department said it will issue visas to the senator and his family.

Brazilian Senator Flavio Bolsonaro has left the country for the United States after he was defeated in Sunday's presidential election, Folha de S.Paulo and Reuters reported, citing sources close to the senator.

The US State Department will issue visas to Flavio Bolsonaro and his family to allow them to enter the US, a senior State Department official told Reuters and other news agencies.

Leftist President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, who secured the runoff victory in elections , told supporters outside the presidential residence in Brasilia on Tuesday that Bolsonaro had left the country, but he didn't have information about Bolsonaro's exact whereabouts.

Brazil is "the second country" of the Bolsonaro family, Lula added.

"The first is licking American boots," the reelected president said. "Those who are not liable do not fear. A fellow that secretly leaves his country, that's because he is liable for something."

Bolsonaro wasn't allowed to leave Brazil

The Supreme Court had asked Flavio Bolsonaro, the eldest son of former President Jair Bolsonaro, to surrender his passports to stop him from leaving the country amid investigations into the senator.

It was reported that Bolsonaro had refused to comply with the order, although other reports contradicted this.

The AFP news agency cited a police official as saying that Bolsonaro's passports had been cancelled and there was no official record of him leaving the country.

Brazilian newspaper Folha de S.Paulo reported that Bolsonaro's plane was scheduled to land in either Miami or Dallas.

How did Bolsonaro exit Brazil?

Argentine news outlet Infobae reported earlier today that Bolsonaro had crossed into Argentina to board a plane to the US.

A spokesperson for Argentina's Ministry of Security denied the reports that the conservative Brazilian senator had entered the country.

Brazilian media reports earlier said that the federal police were still searching for him.

Bolsonaro leaves Brazil after losing presidential election: What to know

Bolsonaro lost Brazil's presidential election runoff on Sunday after an incredibly tight voting count through the evening until his challenger, Lula, surged ahead.

Bolsonaro had initially said he would seek to annul the election results, citing alleged irregularities. But Bolsonaro's Liberal Party on Tuesday acknowledged the results.

In a video on Instagram on Monday, Bolsonaro said he had been served with a Supreme Court order to hand over his passports so he couldn't leave the country.

He had said he was planning to hand over his passports, but reports on Tuesday said the deadline had passed leading to their cancellation.

What are the investigations against Flavio Bolsonaro about?

The senator has been accused of laundering money through a sports betting company, money that was deducted from government pensions to senior citizens.

A second investigation is looking into Bolsonaro's connections to a disgraced banker from whom he allegedly accepted millions of dollars to finance the biopic about his father, titled "Dark Horse."

Bolsonaro loses his immunity from prosecution once his Senate term comes to end in February 2027. He has denied wrongdoing in both cases.

Bolsonaro asked to surrender passports: What to know

Bolsonaro said that he had received the Supreme Court order outside the home where his father, Jair Bolsonaro, is under house arrest.

He said the order was issued by Supreme Court Justice Alexandre de Moraes, the same judge who sentenced his father to prison.

He also pointed to comments made by his brother, Eduardo Bolsonaro, who said on a podcast last week that his sibling should leave the country if he lost the election.

Eduardo, who lives in the US, was convicted in absentia in June of illegally lobbying the Trump administration. He was sentenced to four years in prison and a warrant was issued for his arrest.

Brazil's Lula celebrates election victory as Bolsonaro rejects results To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

World.title: Israel election: Anti-Netanyahu bloc ahead, but no majority
World.content:
The president of the German-Israeli Society, Green party politician Volker Beck, said in a TV interview on election day that he believed a change in leadership might be in Israel's interests.

"It would be good for Israel, if it were to come to a change, because I believe that [Prime Minister Benjamin] Netanyahu has squandered a great deal of trust in recent years, both in foreign and domestic policy," Beck said in an interview broadcast on sister channels RTL and ntv.

Beck, a Bundestag lawmaker for more than two decades with the Greens who was perhaps best known as a politician as a campaigner for LGBT rights and advocate of an uncompromising Israeli foreign policy, is not typically associated with stern criticism of Netanyahu or his government.

"Although he has also done some things right and has done some necessary things, a change is really needed" to allow Israel to recoup support among the international community, Beck said, as Netanyahu becomes an increasingly polarizing figure on the world stage.

He also criticized domestic efforts by the Likud-led government to reform the legal system and its influence over politics, saying this would "fundamentally change Israel's character, and should be stopped."

Beck said he hoped that a functioning majority would emerge from the vote, but acknowledged that pollsters anticipated a stalemate. In that scenario, he said, he would personally favor a national unity government incorporating all the major players.

But at present he thought the "divide between the two camps is so deep, that it really would be a bit of a masterstroke to be able to bring them together." He made a similar comment online, saying such a unity govermment "would be good" but was "not very likely."

World.title: EU proposes giving Frontex border agency new major powers
World.content:
The European Commission has unveiled a new plan to give Frontex more resources to ensure the return of irregular migrants, including by supporting non-EU countries. The move comes after the tragedy in Ceuta.

The European Commission on Tuesdayunveiled a new proposal to beef up the powers of the EU border agency in order to empower it to support the return of irregular migrants.

The proposed legislation gives the agency, called Frontex, more resources to act beyond EU territory.

The plan would give the agency the power to support non-EU countries to return migrants to their countries of origin.

The proposal comes as EU member states increasingly focus on returns, saying too many people who are asked to leave the bloc remain.

EU border agency to be beefed up after Ceuta humanitarian crisis of summer

The new role for Frontex comes after the humanitarian crisis in Ceuta this summer.

The tragedy in the Spanish exclave was seized upon by some EU member states as an example of where the EU could do more to block people from reaching the EU.

Italy, for example, placed some temporary border controls on travel from Spain.

Spain's prime minister at the time criticized several EU member states for their "selfish" response to the influx of migrants to Ceuta.

"Today we propose that Frontex becomes the central EU actor on returns," Magnus Brunner, commissioner for internal affairs ​and migration, told reporters.

"It will be able to act faster, with a quick reaction force that can ⁠deploy within ⁠24 hours and spot risks ⁠early, before an ​event becomes a crisis," Brunner added.

How the far right hardened Europe's migration stance To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Frontex to be given wide powers to support deportation of irregular migrants

The ability to deport migrants from non-EU countries means that Frontex could, for instance, deport a Bangladeshi national from Libya, where many migrants start the final leg of their journey into the bloc.

The plan envisages gradually expanding Frontex's standing corps to 30,000 officers by creating a new "European border and return reserve" of 17,000 officers within the next 15 years.

Those officers would remain at the disposal of member states and could be deployed when needed, the commission said in a statement.

The proposal would also create a new EU Return Coordination Center within Frontex and expand the agency's role across the entire deportation process.

It would also include a new online monitoring center to track border-related developments on social media and support action against content linked to border security risks.

Frontex reform criticized by rights groups

Frontex has been responsible for guarding the external borders of the EU as well as ensuring the rights of new arrivals.

It has been criticized for its lack of accountability in the past.

The planned reform shrinks the scope of the agency's internal rights watchdog, with complaints to be referred to national authorities.

"The Commission is pandering to populism and the far right on migration," said Tineke Strik, a Dutch MEP from the Greens/EFA group.

"We need a human rights-based approach to border management and Frontex plays a key role. But instead the Commission ​risks turning Frontex into a European version of ICE," she said.

Edited: Alex Berry

World.title: Mbappe apologizes as Chinese sponsors drop him and TV broadcasts are halted over Mao dictator remark
World.content:
French soccer star Kylian Mbappe has apologized after apparently referring to Mao Zedong as a dictator. Chinese sponsors have dropped him, while state television has suspended Spanish league broadcasts.

France striker Kylian Mbappe apologized after apparently referring to China's founding leader Mao Zedong as a dictator in a video that circulated online.

The controversy prompted three major Chinese companies to sever sponsorship ties with the Real Madrid forward, while Chinese state television suspended broadcasts of Spain's La Liga.

What did Mbappe say about Mao?

The controversy began when a video circulated showing Mbappe discussing his favorite internet meme featuring himself.

In the clip, apparently filmed ahead of an appearance on the French online talk show The Bridge, Mbappe referred to an image depicting his face superimposed on the body of "some guy ... I think he's a Chinese dictator."

The image appeared to depict Mao Zedong, who founded the People's Republic of China in 1949 and ruled until his death in 1976. Jokes about country's former leader and descriptions of him as a dictator remain taboo.

Mbappe has previously been depicted as authoritarian leaders in online memes mocking his perceived influence over teammates and suggestions that he has the power to influence club decisions.

Mbappe has been nicknamed "the dictator" in the European press.

How did Mbappe apologize?

"My comment was ill-judged, and I now understand that it hurt many people in China and in Chinese communities around the world," Mbappe said in a statement.

"I apologize to everyone my words have upset. This was absolutely not my intention. I have deep respect for the Chinese people and their history, and I am sincerely sorry."

Mao remains revered by many in China despite his policies causing tens of millions of deaths (FILE: October 1, 1949) Image: AP

Chinese sponsors cut ties with Mbappe

Chinese beverage company Dongpeng, dairy producer Mengniu and cheesemaker Milkground announced they were ending their partnerships with the French international.

In similarly worded statements, each said that they oppose "any words and actions that hurt national sentiment."

China Media Group, which oversees state broadcaster CCTV, also suspended broadcasts of La Liga matches and removed s featuring Mbappe.

La Liga apologized for the controversy, saying Mbappe's comments were made in a personal capacity and did not represent the Spanish league.

Chinese state broadcaster CCTV subsequently said it would consider Mbappe's apology but would also judge his future actions.

In response to a question about the controversy, China's Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesperson Guo Jiakun said that "words and actions that hurt the feelings of the Chinese people will naturally be met with joint opposition from all sectors of Chinese society."

Why is Mao such a sensitive subject in China?

Mao remains a revered figure in China, where public criticism of the former Communist leader is politically sensitive.

His rule was also marked by disastrous political campaigns, including the Great Leap Forward, which contributed to a famine that killed tens of millions of people.

The ruling Communist Party acknowledges some of his mistakes but maintains that his achievements outweighed them, making criticism of his legacy politically sensitive.

Edited by: Alex Berry
