World.title: The dual nationality dilemma: what Dutch News readers say
World.content:
Earlier this month we asked Dutch News’ readers for their thoughts on taking Dutch nationality, given that in many cases they would have to give up their original passport.

Legislation due to be discussed in parliament in early December should change that, but it now seems likely that foreigners will be excluded from the new rules – which will then only apply to the native Dutch who take on a second nationality.

The rules on dual nationality are complex and discriminatory. If you are married it is easier to become Dutch and retain your original passport, for example. It also gets easier once you reach the age of 65. But many readers are caught up in the complexity of the current “naturalisation” process. They want to become Dutch, but giving up their original nationality will create a new range of problems.

Over 80 readers told us their stories. Here is a selection of their experiences.

An impossible choice

“What I find difficult is that many people who have lived, worked, and contributed to Dutch society for years are forced to make a choice that other Dutch citizens are not required to make. I would gladly embrace Dutch citizenship, but not at the cost of losing an important part of my identity and connection to my family and heritage.” Ahmed, from Egypt

Bureaucratic nightmare

“I’m Chilean and have been living in the Netherlands for around 10 years. A few years ago, I decided to become Dutch. The Dutch naturalisation process itself was clear and straightforward for me. What I could never have imagined was the nightmare I would face in Chile afterwards.

“Renouncing Chilean nationality is effectively irreversible. Once you give it up, you cannot simply apply to get it back …The renunciation brought very serious practical consequences that I was not prepared for. My Chilean nationality was removed and I was deleted from Chile’s national registry.

“This means that I can no longer obtain basic documents such as a birth certificate in the normal way, despite having been born in Chile. Every time I need to deal with something in Chile, including matters concerning my own family and inheritance, I find myself unable to prove that I am the person who appears in their records. I have no Chilean identity documents anymore, and because I have been removed from the registry, I simply no longer exist in the country where I was born.

“The Dutch government describes the renunciation as something you do ‘voluntarily’. But I struggle with that description. If acquiring Dutch nationality means that I have to give up my original nationality in order to become Dutch, how voluntary is that choice really?” Jonathan, from Chile

An easy decision

“I have lived here for 32 years – over half my life. I was born in Ireland but moved here in 1994. My wife is Dutch-born, our kids were born here and my life is here. I became a Dutch citizen about 15 years ago and gave up my Irish citizenship. I regard myself as culturally more Dutch now than Irish and choosing for a single nationality was a very easy decision.” Jim, from Ireland

Global freedom

“My wife loves it here, I’ve passed my inburgering exams, love my job, and contribute over €100k annually in taxes. But despite loving our life here, we’ve decided to leave soon. With the 30% ruling ending for me and the Netherlands requiring naturalising citizens to renounce their original nationality, staying no longer makes sense. My original passport represents my roots, family, and identity – I will never give it up.

“However, I do want the global freedom and security of a second passport. We’ve made the hard decision to move to Canada or the UK, where we can naturalise in five years or less without dropping our original nationality. It’s a sad move for my wife and a tough choice for both of us, but the current legal framework leaves high-contributing expats with very few practical alternatives.” John, from Jordan

Where to retire?

“I have lived in Europe since 2001 and moved to Amsterdam in 2018 as I wanted to remain in Europe. As I am coming into the end of my career we are contemplating where we want to retire but have no mobility as our permanent residence is tied solely to the Netherlands.

“Right now, given the political situation in Canada, it pains me to surrender my nationality as I am a proud Canadian, but I must contemplate our future as a family that wishes to remain in Europe with the option to reside in a sunnier climate. It is also a shame given the long history between Canada and the Netherlands and the increasing closeness of Canada to the EU. After 25 years in Europe I am firmly European, but it feels unfair to force me to deny that I am also Canadian.” Adele, from Canada

Discrimination

“As I am not married, I am not able to apply for Dutch citizenship without renouncing my Australian citizenship. I find this quite disappointing and even discriminatory, given that, if I had a partner or spouse, I’d be allowed to have both. For that reason I have remained an Aussie, even though I’m not planning on moving back to there anytime soon.” James has lived in the Netherlands for more than 20 years.

Sister separation

“I have given up my nationality (British) and am now Dutch. The complete irony is I’m an identical twin so now I’m an identical twin where my sister has a different nationality. After Brexit I worry about how that may impact us when we are 80 and are less able to travel.” Tina, from Britain

Rise of the far right

“I declined on three occasions an invitation to attend the naturalisation ceremony because I found it difficult to give up my Filipino citizenship. The Philippines allows dual nationality while the Netherlands requires full allegiance.

“In the end, I had to make what felt like a very hard decision of renouncing my Filipino citizenship because PVV was the biggest party at the time. I was worried that living in the Netherlands would be difficult on account of the radical right leaning becoming the biggest political party.” Brian, from the Philippines

Family ties

“I would love to apply for Dutch nationality, but because I still have family in the US, including an adult child and aging parents, I cannot give up my American passport.

“Sometimes the US does not allow people who have relinquished their passports to return, because they are considered a greater risk for overstaying their visas when compared to other visitors. I cannot risk being unable to visit my family, so I am applying for permanent residency instead of a Dutch passport.” Rick, from the US

Practical reasons

“I come from another EU country, and for me there is currently no possibility of becoming a Dutch citizen without renouncing my original nationality. As someone from a small country, this is not an easy decision. It is difficult not only for emotional reasons, but also for practical ones.

“I was born and raised in my country of origin, and my entire family still lives there. My nationality is therefore more than just a passport or a legal status; it is an important part of my identity and my connection to my family and where I come from.

“At the same time, my children were born and raised here in the Netherlands. They speak Dutch, attend Dutch schools, and grow up with Dutch traditions and culture. The Netherlands is their home. Yet, despite being fully part of Dutch society, they are not Dutch citizens and therefore cannot enjoy all the rights that come with citizenship, most notably the right to vote in national elections.

“This creates a difficult situation for families like mine. We can be deeply integrated into Dutch society and consider the Netherlands our home, while still facing a choice between retaining the nationality we were born with and becoming Dutch citizens.

“For me, this is not about rejecting my country of origin or refusing to become part of Dutch society. It is about wanting to preserve both parts of my identity and, at the same time, fully belong to the country where my children are growing up.” Anon

Some names have been changed to protect the privacy of the individuals concerned.

Our thanks to everyone who got in touch, and we will be contacting more of you in the coming period.

If you would like to comment on this article, or have any additional thoughts, don’t hesitate to get in touch via editor@dutchnews.nl. We will be publishing a series of articles focusing on dual nationality in the coming months.

World.title: Netherlands to stay away from Eurovision Song Contest after all
World.content:
The Netherlands will not take part in next year’s Eurovision Song Contest after public broadcaster NPO said there was “not enough support” for sending an act.

The decision reverses a previous U-turn after AVROTROS, the broadcasting company that is usually responsible for the Dutch entry, said it would boycott the contest for a second year in 2027 because of Israel’s continued participation.

NPO said last month it would make alternative arrangements to participate in the contest in the Bulgarian coastal city of Burgas next May.

But on Tuesday Jet de Ranitz, chair of NPO’s board of directors, said after holding talks with networks and staff that there was “not enough support” for a Dutch entry.

AVROTROS said in September it would be staying away until “transparent rules” were drawn up on countries involved in military conflicts to restore the “neutrality” of the event.

The Netherlands was one of five countries not to send an entry last year, but news broadcaster NOS still sent a team to cover the event and will do so again next year. Ireland has also said it will continue its boycott in 2027 and is not broadcasting the contest.

Staff critical

Around 500 NPO employees signed a letter a week ago criticising the broadcaster’s decision to look for a replacement for AVROTROS, saying that “the desire to take part in an entertainment programme is considered more important than the countless lives of people who are being murdered.”

De Ranitz did not directly mention Israel’s participation, but said NPO had concluded after consulting broadcasting licence holders that “it is too early at the moment to take part in the Eurovision Song Contest”.

“Because of the sensitivities around the issues that are taking place now, we have decided to step aside for now,” she said.

NPO is in charge of the Dutch broadcasting infrastructure, but programmes are made by autonomous licensed companies.

The European Broadcasting Union, which organises the song contest, said it regretted NPO’s decision. It said it recognised the “deep-rooted and genuine opinions about the song contest and that they vary strongly”, but argued the event was an opportunity to bring unity to a “divided world”.

Culture minister Rianne Letschert said NPO had made an “editorial decision” and it was not her place to intervene.

“The song contest is an event that touches many people and understandably gives rise to widely differing opinions,” she said. “I understand that none of the broadcasters are prepared to take over the entry for the song festival for 2027.”

World.title: US chooses Poland to host service facility for Patriot missiles
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. The United States has chosen Poland to host a new centre for servicing and maintaining missiles used in Patriot air defence systems, in a decision described as “historic” by both Washington and Warsaw. It was chosen ahead of bids from four other European countries. The new centre, the first of its kind ot be located outside the US itself, will “dramatically shorten turnaround times and further secure critical supply lines”, said the US Department of War, announcing the decision on Tuesday. Undersecretary of War Michael P. Duffey added that the choice of a country on NATO’s eastern front “sends a clear message [that] the Alliance is united, serious about deterrence, and ready to back our words with action”. Poland Selected to Host Historic PAC-3 Missile Maintenance Facility, Strengthening Allied Burden-Sharing and Transatlantic Security – U.S. Department of War – Release | @DeptofWar https://t.co/2caqADRRx8 — US Embassy Warsaw (@USEmbassyWarsaw) October 27, 2026 The decision was welcomed by Polish leaders, with defence minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz saying that it shows “Poland is a trusted ally and holds an extremely important place on the map of global security”. His deputy minister, Magdalena Sobkowiak-Czarnecka, said that Poland was chosen ahead of rival bids from Germany, the Netherlands and Norway to host the facility. However, US ambassador to Poland Thomas Rose indicated that Sweden, not Norway, was the fourth candidate. Kosiniak-Kamysz and Sobkowiak-Czarnecka both pointed to the role President Karol Nawrocki had played in securing the deal. On many issues, the government is in conflict with the opposition-aligned president, but the two sides worked together on the Patriot bid. Historyczna decyzja! Centrum serwisowania pocisków PAC-3 do systemów Patriot powstanie w Polsce! 🇵🇱 O europejską lokalizację tej inwestycji rywalizowały cztery państwa, obok Polski – Niemcy, Holandia i Norwegia. Już na etapie składania wniosków polska oferta została oceniona… pic.twitter.com/wUgFhzlzUk — Magdalena Sobkowiak (@magdasobkowiak) October 27, 2026 Nawrocki, a conservative, is a close ally of his US counterpart, Donald Trump. The Polish president’s national security advisor, Bartosz Grodecki, claimed that it was “thanks to a conversation between” the two presidents that the new Patriot servicing centre was being established in Poland. The head of Nawrocki’s foreign policy office, Marcin Przydacz, meanwhile, thanked Washington for choosing Poland to host the new centre. “The Polish-American alliance and the good atmosphere in relations once again yield results,” he declared. “We can see what positive effects the President’s activity brings for Poland.” Poland is one of a number of European countries that operate Patriot air defence systems. Others include Germany, Greece, the Netherlands, Romania, Sweden and Ukraine. The new centre will service the PAC-3 missiles used in Patriot batteries. The competition to host the facility was announced in July, with the selection made by the US government in conjunction with American defence giant Lockheed Martin, the producer of missiles. In its press release, the Pentagon emphasised that, although Poland would host the new centre, its work would “be underpinned by robust, transatlantic industrial cooperation, with critical supply chain integration led by Germany, the Netherlands and Sweden”. Sweden will deploy Patriot air defence systems and around 100 accompanying military personnel to Poland later this year to protect the NATO logistics hub in the city of Rzeszów, which is the main conduit for aid to Ukraine https://t.co/cq9p7OVO7E — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 6, 2026 Global demand for Patriot systems has risen significantly, with the United States expending at least 1,500 interceptors in its war with Iran, according to the Center for Strategic and International Studies. Patriot systems have also been crucial in Ukraine’s defence against Russian ballistic missile attacks, although Ukraine’s supply of missiles is now almost entirely exhausted. After Trump recently suggested that he would authorise Ukraine to produce its own missiles, Poland offered to host any such factory, to ensure its security. However, today’s announcement concerns a site for maintaining and servicing, rather than producing, the missiles. Poland has proposed that, if the United States grants Ukraine permission to produce its own missiles for Patriot air-defence systems, the facility could be located on Polish territory to ensure its security https://t.co/jaQng5wtGg — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 28, 2026 The decision cements Poland’s position as one of Washington’s most important security partners in Europe. War secretary Pete Hegseth has praised Poland as a “model ally”, noting that it has for years met NATO’s defence spending targets, unlike many other member states. Poland has also been a significant customer for US defence firms. Between 2021 and 2025, Poland was NATO’s biggest arms importer, with 44% of the equipment it purchased coming from American suppliers. Last year, Poland signed a $2 billion deal for the US to provide logistical support and training for Patriot systems. This year, it was announced that Polish state defence group PGZ would become the first European producer of American Barracuda-500M cruise missiles. Poland will become the first country in Europe to produce cruise missiles developed by US defence firm Anduril Industries The agreement will "transform the continent's defence industry", claims Anduril https://t.co/LPJnwOLfp2 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 7, 2026 Warsaw is also currently lobbying for a new permanent US military base to be established in Poland, with the government and the president once again putting aside their differences to promote the idea. Last month, Nawrocki claimed that the proposed base, which he said would be called “Fort Trump”, was “confirmed”. However, Washington has not publicly announced any final decision. World.title: Germany’s economy minister hails Poland as “example of great success”
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Germany’s economy minister, Katherina Reiche, has praised Poland as an “example of great success”, saying that it offers a model for other countries. Speaking at the fourth Polish-German Economic Forum in Warsaw, which she opened on Monday alongside Polish finance minister Andrzej Domański, Reiche. Reiche highlighted the deepening trade ties between the two countries. She noted that bilateral trade last year exceeded €180 billion for the first time, up from €25 billion in 2000, reports Deutsche Welle. Germany has been Poland’s biggest trading partner for decades, although recent data suggest that China, for the first time in history, overtook Germany as Poland’s largest source of imports in July this year. Germany has also long been a major investor in Poland. But Reiche welcomed growing recent investments by Polish companies in Germany, which she said was helping to create jobs. Earlier this year, for example, Poland’s largest manufacturer of trains and trams, Pesa, announced the acquisition of German rival HeiterBlick as part of its efforts to expand its operations across Europe. Reiche noted that around 1,000 Polish companies have invested in Germany while about 1,600 German companies have invested in Poland, reports Reuters. Poland’s largest manufacturer of trains and trams, Pesa, has announced the acquisition of German rival HeiterBlick as it seeks to expand its operations across Europe https://t.co/N1wE1aYL5m — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) January 12, 2026 Among leading German firms with a presence in Poland are carmakers Mercedes-Benz, which recently invested around €1 billion to build its first electric-only van plant there, which produces its Crafer vans at a plant near the city of Poznań. Reiche also pointed to Poland’s stellar economic performance since joining the European Union in 2004, noting that its GDP has grown by an annual average of 3.8% over that period – twice the EU-wide average. Poland’s economy is on the verge of becoming the 20th largest in the world, with the country hoping to become part of the G20. Meanwhile, Domański used his remarks at the Polish-German Economic Forum to warn Europe against repeating past mistakes as it confronts a rapidly changing geopolitical landscape. He said the continent faced a “unique” historical moment. “The world is changing faster than ever, and we are facing new geopolitical, strategic, and technological challenges.” Europe would need a strong economy and new sources of growth to meet those challenges, he added, warning against what he called “economic naivety” and urging Europe – and Germany in particular – not to return to its previous approach to Russia. “I would like to state this very clearly: Europe must learn from the past. Under no circumstances can there be a return to the previous approach toward Russia. Poland will never agree to that,” Domański said, noting that this position applied in particular to renewed use of Russian energy imports. “We will only be resilient once we are truly independent of external, unstable suppliers of raw materials,” he added, emphasising that Poland and Germany must “work together to modernise the European energy market, focus on technological change and bear security in mind”. Debata ministra @Domanski_Andrz i minister @BMWE_ Katherina Reiche podczas IV Polsko-Niemieckiego Forum Gospodarczego. 💬 Powinniśmy skupić się na cenach energii, ale potrzebne jest znacznie bardziej zdecydowane podejście do ochrony rynku europejskiego. I nie chodzi tu tylko o… pic.twitter.com/NVPUjwx7jA — Ministerstwo Rozwoju i Technologii (@MRiTGOVPL) October 26, 2026 Following the forum, Domański and Reiche attended a meeting of the Friends of Industry, an informal initiative bringing together EU member states to coordinate positions on industrial policy, competitiveness and the operating conditions for European industry. The meeting was attended by representatives of 21 EU member states and European Commission Vice-President Stéphane Séjourné. Discussions focused on protecting and strengthening European industry’s competitiveness and economic security amid geopolitical challenges. “Today, we are facing the consequences of the fact that, in the past, competitiveness was often relegated to second, third or fourth place. Competitiveness took a back seat to other priorities, with the result that European industry now faces serious challenges,” said Domański. He proposed making competitiveness a core EU policy priority, cutting red tape, strengthening the single market, lowering energy costs, investing in strategic technologies such as AI, and tightening trade protections against unfair foreign competition. World.title: Witness testifies Polish president discussed “making money bringing girls” to hotel where they worked 20 years ago
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. A former colleague of Polish President Karol Nawrocki from when he worked as a security guard in a hotel two decades ago testified in court that he told her it was possible to “make some extra money by bringing in girls”. She says she saw him escort a woman onto the premises. The testimony was given after the president himself sued the owner of a website that, just before last year’s presidential election, published claims that Nawrocki had been involved in procuring prostitutes while working at the luxury Grand Hotel in the town of Sopot. The court case began in September but, until now, hearings have been held behind closed doors. However, the judge decided that today’s session would be open to the public, with two former colleagues of Nawrocki giving evidence. The president himself is due to appear before the court in January. 🗣️ "Moją automatyczną oceną było, że to prostytutka i alfons." Nowe zeznania w procesie Karola Nawrockiego z wydawcą Onetu. Przed sądem stanęła była współpracowniczka prezydenta z sopockiego Grand Hotelu. pic.twitter.com/Cn6KyMSjcv — tvp.info 🇵🇱 (@tvp_info) October 27, 2026 In May last year, less than a week before the second round of the election, in which Nawrocki was standing in a run-off against rival Rafał Trzaskowski, Onet, a leading news website, published an article titled “Karol Nawrocki and the secrets of the Grand Hotel”. It claimed, based on information provided by unnamed former colleagues of the future president, that he had “participated in bringing prostitutes for guests of the Grand Hotel in Sopot while working there as a security guard” almost 20 years earlier. Onet said that its interlocutors wished to remain anonymous for their own safety, but had expressed their willingness to testify in court if required. The revelations caused a major scandal, but were vigorously denied by Nawrocki, a conservative candidate aligned with the right-wing opposition, who called them a “pack of lies”. He then went on to narrowly defeat Trzaskowski in the election. Conservative presidential candidate @NawrockiKn says he will sue news website @onetpl for claims it published today that he procured prostitutes for clients at a luxury hotel when working there as a security guard. He called the report "a bunch of lies" https://t.co/WZ4rZWfFT1 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 26, 2025 Nawrocki then sued Ringier Axel Springer Polska (RASP), the Polish subsidiary of a German-Swiss media house that owns Onet, demanding an apology. RASP stood by Onet, saying that its reporting was “factual”. At today’s hearing, one of Onet’s sources, Natasza Geldon, who had worked at the hotel in 2006 and 2007, was questioned. She said that, one evening, she had noticed Nawrocki leading a man and a woman into the hotel, before then taking only the woman into an elevator and returning alone. This had struck her as unusual, because staff were not supposed to escort guests into the hotel, “let alone take them upstairs” in the lift, said Geldon, quoted by broadcaster TVP. “When Karol came back downstairs, I asked him what was going on,” continued the witness. “He said it was possible to make some extra money by bringing girls in, and asked if I wanted to join in.” Geldon refused the offer, telling the court that, “as a young girl, 19 years old, I had the impression that a pimp had been coming in with a prostitute”. However, when asked to confirm if she had seen prostitutes in the hotel, Geldon said: “I don’t know. It’s hard to say. It was just that one incident.” A second witness, Łukasz Franczak, described as a longtime friend of Nawrocki who worked alongside him in security at the Grand Hotel, also gave evidence on Tuesday after being called by Nawrocki’s legal team. He testified that there had been prostitutes in the hotel. However, he added that he had not heard of any organised operation to supply them to guests; nor had he witnessed Nawrocki procuring prostitutes or discussing payment for them, reported Onet from the hearing. Franczak’s testimony was welcomed by Nawrocki’s former national security advisor, Sławomir Cenckiewicz, who said that it showed those making claims against the president have no evidence of his involvement in any wrongdoing. Oni się wszyscy teraz nakręcają jak szaleni, nie czytając tego co sami piszą na własnej stronie… No i dowiedzieli się dzisiaj, że w hotelach bywają prostytutki 🙂 A ja to wszystko czytam na bieżąco, a tam słynny Łukasz z Gdańska, ulubiony świadek-historyk Antka Dudka, i… https://t.co/9sKGZT4PpD — Sławomir Cenckiewicz (@Cenckiewicz) October 27, 2026 RASP’s lawyers have called for Nawrocki himself to testify in the case. The president’s legal team wanted him to provide his testimony in writing, according to Onet. But on Tuesday, judge Aleksandra Orzechowska ordered Nawrocki to give testimony directly – either in person or remotely – at the next hearing, which is scheduled for 18 January 2027, reports broadcaster TVN. World.title: Polish far-right leader charged over confrontation with abortion doctor and inciting hatred against Jews
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Polish far-right leader Grzegorz Braun has been charged with six alleged crimes, including inciting hatred against Jews and vandalising an LGBT+ exhibition. The other four allegations relate to an incident in which he confronted a doctor who performed a late-term abortion. The charges are the latest in a long line of legal cases against Braun, who is already on trial for attacking a Jewish ceremony in Poland’s parliament. However, his party continues to poll strongly, and may play a significant role in deciding what kind of government is formed after next year’s elections. Do sześciu razy sztuka. Grzegorz Braun dostał zarzuty, w tym za uwięzienie ginekolożki Gizeli Jagielskiej Wcześniej europoseł Grzegorz Braun pięć razy unikał przedstawienia zarzutów w Prokuraturze Okręgowej we Wrocławiu. Zainterweniował Prokurator Generalny Waldemar Żurek.… — Bartosz T. Wieliński 🇵🇱🇪🇺🇺🇦🇬🇱 (@Bart_Wielinski) October 26, 2026 As a member of the European Parliament, Braun enjoys legal immunity from prosecution. However, in November 2025, the EP stripped him of immunity to face the six charges. Subsequently, prosecutors tried five times to present Braun with the charges. However, he evaded those attempts by filing motions to have prosecutors excluded from the case or simply by leaving the prosecutor’s office before the charges were read. In July, Poland’s justice minister and prosecutor general, Waldemar Żurek, filed a motion to the EP for permission to forcibly detain Braun and present him with the charges. That application has not yet been considered but, on Monday, Braun finally attended the prosecutor’s office and heard the charges. Afterwards, Braun told a small group of his followers and the media outside the office in Wrocław that he was the victim of a “state lynching” carried out by “the prosecutor’s office of the Hannukah cannibals, racists and genocide perpetrators”. Four of the charges against Braun relate to an incident in April 2025, when he entered a hospital and confronted a gynaecologist who had been involved in a late-term abortion that had drawn controversy and condemnation from right-wing groups. Braun claimed he was carrying out a citizen’s arrest, but is now charged with deprivation of liberty (for preventing the doctor from leaving her office), violating bodily integrity (by pushing her and holding her down), as well as insult and slander. The maximum sentence for those crimes is five years in prison. In separate proceedings, prosecutors later found that the doctor had not violated Poland’s strict abortion laws by terminating the pregnancy in the ninth month. The fifth charge Braun is now facing stems from an infamous incident in December 2023, when he attacked a Jewish Hanukkah celebration in parliament, putting out the candles with a fire extinguisher. Braun is already on trial over the incident itself. Now, however, prosecutors have charged him over a YouTube interview he gave shortly after the attack, in which they say he “described Hanukkah as a Satanic and racist celebration posing a threat to Polish Catholics, which should be counteracted”. For those remarks, he has been hit with a joint charge of inciting religious hatred and the obstruction of religious acts. The maximum penalty for those offences is a three-year jail term. Finally, Braun has been charged with destruction of property for an incident during his presidential campaign in March this year when he vandalised an exhibition about the local LGBT+ community in the city of Opole, spray-painting “stop the propaganda of perversion” on it. Police are investigating far-right presidential candidate and MEP Grzegorz Braun after he vandalised an LGBT+ exhibition. The city where it took place immediately cancelled a meeting he was due to hold there and is seeking compensation for the damage https://t.co/EbDpMzmpFw — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 20, 2025 Braun has pleaded not guilty to all the charges against him, as he has done with a string of other charges for various offences relating to his antisemitic, anti-Ukrainian and anti-LGBT rhetoric and actions. In September, he was stripped of immunity by the EP for the sixth time in order to hear charges of Holocaust denial for his claims that the gas chambers in the Nazi-German death camp of Auschwitz are “fake”. Braun’s high-profile stunts have seen his popularity surge among a section of the electorate. He finished a surprise fourth in last year’s Polish presidential election, with over 6% of the vote, and his Confederation of the Polish Crown (KKP) party is now polling around 9%. If it manages to secure that level of support at next autumn’s parliamentary elections, KKP could become a key player in deciding what kind of government can be formed after what looks likely to be a very close contest between the ruling coalition, which ranges from left to centre right, and the right-wing and far-right opposition. World.title: Poland and Vietnam announce strategic partnership during Tusk visit to Hanoi
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Poland and Vietnam have upgraded their ties to a strategic partnership, pledging to deepen cooperation in trade and investment, security and defence, as well as education, science, technology and cultural exchanges. “Vietnam and Poland share a success story in terms of development,” declared Prime Minister Donald Tusk at a joint press conference with his Vietnamese counterpart Lê Minh Hưng in Hanoi on Monday. “The time has come to turn our successes into joint actions that will open up more opportunities.” The announcement comes amid a broader flurry of Polish diplomacy in Asia, with Tusk arriving in Hanoi following a visit to India and President Karol Nawrocki visiting the Philippines earlier this month. Poland also recently signed new strategic agreements with South Korea and Japan. 🇵🇱🤝🇻🇳 Polska i Wietnam wchodzą na poziom partnerstwa strategicznego! ✅ Podczas wizyty w Hanoi premier @donaldtusk oraz szef wietnamskiego rządu Lê Minh Hưng podjęli decyzję o podniesieniu wzajemnych relacji do rangi partnerstwa strategicznego, otwierając nowy rozdział we… pic.twitter.com/CCvHmc3eva — Kancelaria Premiera (@PremierRP) October 26, 2026 Tusk, who was making the first visit by a Polish prime minister to Vietnam in 16 years, pointed to the two countries’ rapid recent economic development. “Within a single generation, Vietnam achieved middle-income status”, while “Poland recently joined the ranks of the world’s 20 largest economies”. In fact, while Poland was forecast to join the world’s 20 largest economies last year, it eventually fell narrowly short. However, it is expected to soon overtake Switzerland, the current holder of 20th place. Tusk said that, during his visit, he had often heard people say that “Poland is the Vietnam of Europe and Vietnam is the Poland of Asia”. Last year, Hưng’s predecessor, Phạm Minh Chính, became the first Vietnamese prime minister in 15 years to visit Poland. The two countries first established diplomatic relations in 1950, and both leaders emphasised Poland’s large Vietnamese community, which dates back to students arriving around that time. Speaking on Monday, Hưng noted the two countries’ strong traditional ties, adding that Vietnam always remembers and is grateful for Polish support and assistance during his country’s struggle for independence and national reunification, reports the Vietnamese News Agency (VNA). The Vietnamese are Poland's largest non-European migrant group. Photographer Zula Rabikowska, through her images and interviews, offers an insight into their experiences, identities and the challenges they face https://t.co/tsRwHINapQ — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) December 27, 2019 The new strategic partnership agreement signed by Tusk and Hưng pledges to “bring tangible benefits to both nations and contribute to peace, stability, cooperation and prosperity”. It contains commitments to “maintain regular high-level contacts”, reduce non-tariff barriers to trade, and strengthen cooperation on defence, including trade in military equipment. On Sunday, Poland’s deputy minister for state assets, Konrad Gołota, told the Polish Press Agency (PAP) that negotiations are already underway for Vietnam to buy Polish Krab howitzers and Rosomak armoured fighting vehicles, among other hardware. Polish arms firm Mesko has announced the best financial results in its 100-year history. Record revenues and profits were driven in large part by international demand for Mesko's flagship Piorun air-defence system, which has proved successful in Ukraine https://t.co/Dx1yY54qCP — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) April 16, 2026 Tusk, pointing to Poland’s current trade deficit with Vietnam, said that Warsaw’s “priority remains a better balance in trade”. “The sectors in which the Vietnamese side is most interested, and in which we really have something to offer, are the arms industry, satellite and space cooperation, pharmaceuticals and food, especially dairy products,” he added. Tusk also announced that the number of annual Polish-Vietnamese student exchanges would rise by 250% and noted that Poland’s national carrier, LOT, would resume direct Warsaw-Hanoi flights in the first quarter of 2027. Poland is taking steps to attract more foreign students as universities face lower enrollment due to demographic decline. Turkey, South Korea, Vietnam and Uzbekistan are among the countries with which the government is cultivating stronger academic ties https://t.co/r878KqS5OV — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) April 25, 2026 The Polish prime minister acknowledged differences between Poland and Vietnam’s approach to Russia’s war in Ukraine. Vietnam, which has long maintained close ties with Moscow, has avoided condemning the Russian invasion. But he emphasised his belief that, “because of their history, wartime experience and international relations, both Vietnam and Poland can contribute a great deal to the peace process”. Tusk’s trip to Vietnam follows a three-day visit to India, where he and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi announced a goal of doubling bilateral trade by 2030. Poland and India's PMs have, after meeting in New Delhi, outlined aims to double bilateral trade by 2030 and expand cooperation in mining, shipbuilding, energy, space and defence technologies Polish-Indian relations are "gaining speed", said @narendramodi https://t.co/iIVIkCXnvr — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 22, 2026 In April, Tusk visited South Korea, upgrading Poland’s relations with the country he described as Poland’s “most important ally after the United States”, and deepened Poland’s strategic partnership with Japan on the same tour. Earlier this month, Tusk also announced plans to visit China before the end of the year. Meanwhile, President Nawrocki visited the Philippines this month as part of a bid to secure backing from Asian nations for Poland’s hoped-for membership in the G20. World.title: Two thirds of Poles support liberalising abortion law, finds new poll
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Just over two thirds of Poles support liberalising the country’s abortion law, which is among the strictest in Europe, according to a new poll. However, most do not favour introducing abortion on demand, as protesters called for during demonstrations last week. The findings come shortly after parliament approved legislation intended to ease access to abortion. But the measures face a potential veto from right-wing, opposition-aligned President Karol Nawrocki. 🔴 Sondaż dla @rzeczpospolita: Niemal 7 na 10 Polaków chce liberalizacji przepisów ws. aborcjihttps://t.co/f7mxwygIxz — Rzeczpospolita (@rzeczpospolita) October 25, 2026 In 2020, Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal (TK) outlawed abortions in cases where a severe defect is diagnosed in the foetus. That means pregnancies can now only be legally terminated in two cases: where they result from a crime (such as rape or incest) or if they threaten the mother’s life or health. In a new poll by SW Research for Rzeczpospolita, a leading newspaper, a total of 67.2% of respondents said that they want to liberalise that law. However, only 37.7% favoured introducing abortion on demand up to the 12th week of pregnancy. Meanwhile, 29.5% preferred the softer option of returning to the situation from before the 2020 TK ruling – often referred to the “abortion compromise” in Poland – in which terminations were only available in three cases. A further 16.2% supported maintaining the current abortion law; 6.0% wanted to make the rules even tougher (which would involve removing one or both justifications for abortion that currently exist); and 10.6% said they had no opinion. The poll found that support for liberalisation of abortion was stronger among women (73.8%) than men (60.3%). The latest findings are consistent with previous polling, which tends to show that a significant majority supports liberalising the abortion law but that there is not a majority in favour of abortion on demand (although some individual polls have narrowly found such a majority). One member of Poland's likely new ruling coalition, The Left, says polls show a majority in favour of abortion on demand. In fact, they do not. And this issue is likely to be one of the hardest for the incoming government to resolve, writes @danieltilles1 https://t.co/4Nze9wwEC3 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) November 20, 2023 The issue has caused significant political disputes in Poland, not only between the right-wing opposition and the more liberal ruling coalition, but also within the coalition itself. Prime Minister Donald Tusk’s centrist Civic Coalition (KO) and one of its partners, The Left (Lewica), favour introducing abortion on demand. However, more conservative elements of the government, especially the centre-right Polish People’s Party (PSL), prefer a return to the pre-2020 “compromise”. Much of the right-wing opposition, meanwhile, favours maintaining the status quo. However, some more moderate elements of the opposition have suggested it would be best to reverse the TK ruling and return to the “compromise”. Protests took place in towns and cities around Poland on Thursday evening, demanding that the government fulfil its promise to liberalise the country’s strict abortion laws https://t.co/q7eK7mV9zr — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 23, 2026 In 2024, due to disputes within his coalition, Tusk declared that it was unlikely there would be any abortion reform during the current parliamentary term due to differences within his coalition. However, last week the issue was revived, with the government’s majority in the Sejm, the lower house of parliament, approving a bill that would reverse the 2020 TK ruling (but not introduce abortion on demand). It also passed another bill decriminalising providing help to women in obtaining unlawful abortions. After both bills go through the upper-house Senate, which can suggest amendments but not block them, they will pass to President Nawrocki, who can sign them, veto them, or send them to the TK for assessment. Given that Nawrocki is aligned with the right-wing opposition, has declared his opposition to abortion, and has vetoed a record number of government bills, it is widely expected that he will seek to block efforts to liberalise the abortion law. World.title: Time is running out for Germany to pay Polish WWII victims the compensation they deserve [Opinion]
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. By Philipp Fritz, Warsaw correspondent for Die Welt (which first published this article in German here) Negotiations on compensation for the still-living victims of the German occupation of Poland have been going on for years. There are some 30,000 to 50,000 such survivors, but their number dwindles every week. Berlin should act now. No “humanitarian gesture” has emerged. “The draft budget currently reflects the fact that no decision has been made,” said Josef Hinterseher, a German foreign office spokesman, at a press conference in late September. He thereby confirmed what many observers had suspected: survivors of concentration camps, ghettos and death marches, former forced workers and participants in the Warsaw Uprising who are still living in Poland will not receive any compensation, one-off payment or monthly pension from the German government. The German chancellor has announced that his country will offer support to surviving Polish victims of WW2 and will help strengthen Poland’s eastern border. However, in both cases he did not provide details of what these measures will involve in practice https://t.co/gKX6142Alo — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 2, 2024 Just a few sentences later, Hinterseher moved onto the next subject – the fact that two Russian oligarchs were to be removed from the EU’s sanctions list. Or at least, that Berlin had not been successful in opposing this decision. The fact that these two issues were dealt with publicly one after the other shows that the German government is quicker to reach a decision that makes Putin’s supporters’ lives easier than it is with victims of the Nazi terror. It is a declaration of moral bankruptcy. Warsaw and Berlin have been negotiating compensation for the last remaining victims of the German occupation of Poland for years. There are between 30,000 and 50,000 of them – aged over 90, often living alone and in poor health. Their numbers are dwindling every week. The fact that talks are taking place in Berlin ministries but without any decision being taken is met with sadness and fury in Poland. Increasingly, Poles are getting the impression that, even if the Germans manage to put up memorials, they cannot offer survivors tangible help when it is asked for. It is a common view that in Berlin the descendants of the perpetrators are simply waiting for the victims to die so that this pesky issue will sort itself out. Should that happen, those left behind will not forget, and the Germans will hardly be able to forgive themselves. Warsaw is no longer demanding war reparations from Berlin. In December 2023, Donald Tusk’s government switched to talking about “making amends”. Polish foreign minister @sikorskiradek has called on Germany to “think creatively” about compensating Poland for WWII. On a visit to Berlin, he also said that the new government would "end the cold war" waged by the former ruling PiS party against Germany https://t.co/kZ62nUuqqO — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) January 31, 2024 This is not just splitting hairs. In so doing, Tusk put the ball in the German government’s court, giving it the chance to take action and, through a gesture recognising suffering and providing a relatively small sum of money, to offer people tangible help and do a service to the German-Polish relationship. Former German Chancellor Olaf Scholz is reported to have offered Tusk a one-off payment in 2024, but Poland’s prime minister turned the sum down as insufficient. Instead, Polish diplomats are demanding monthly pensions. In any case, we are talking about a few hundred million euro: a relatively small amount compared to the equivalent of €1.3 trillion that Poland’s former ruling national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) party once demanded from Germany, and also in comparison to many other budget items – and yet still there is nothing about compensation in the budget planning. Poland is seeking $1.3 trillion in war reparations from Germany, but Berlin says the issue was legally settled long ago. Legal scholar @MPiatkowski1 examines the arguments of both sides, explains the legal context, and looks at what could come next https://t.co/xsKAY2TukS — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 9, 2022 Rumour has it that, in return for compensation, German foreign ministry officials are asking for a kind of Polish guarantee that in future there will be no more demands for reparations, or at least that at least the German gesture will receive good press in Poland. If that is true, it would be thoroughly indecent, bringing to mind an image of a perpetrator trying to buy his victim’s silence. This reflects a belief in objectification, an ugly bureaucratic mentality stemming from a system in which “work” in a ghetto counts towards statutory pension contributions, but no one can bring themselves to pay compensation. This issue can be resolved at the very top. Chancellor Friedrich Merz would have to work with the relevant ministries – the foreign office and finance ministry – to provide for compensation for the victims in the budget. This would be a belated but major and morally right gesture. If politics is too slow – time really is of the essence – then civil society should take it upon itself to show where it stands. Donations for the still living victims of the German tyranny or a fund from which survivors would receive monthly payments can be created from within society. Business can also get involved. German corporations which were guilty of, for instance, exploiting forced labourers in occupied Poland, or those that emerged from them, such as BASF, Siemens, Volkswagen, BMW and Deutsche Bank, could contribute. Poland covers almost all the costs of maintaining former Nazi-German camps on its territory. It has spent more on this than Germany has paid in compensation to Polish war victims It's time for Germany to fund preservation of the sites, argues @W_Kononczuk https://t.co/08nf4c2jMz — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) January 25, 2026 Right now, since its state elections in September, Germany gives the impression of a country whose compass for right and wrong is broken. As of 6 October, the state parliament of Sachsen-Anhalt has as its vice-president Hans-Thomas Tillschneider of the AfD, a man who wrote on X that “the Poles have been getting on my nerves for a long time now”. In Berlin, not only did the left-wing Die Linke celebrate their electoral success with Israel haters and antisemites, they even tolerate them in their ranks. It is shameful. But now Germany, and particularly its government, has the opportunity to show that the rhetoric of responsibility for the victims is not merely empty words. That, contrary to a mood that does not support it, they are doing what is morally right. Time is running out, Germany – it’s your last chance. World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! We cannot do what we do without your support. Katarzyna Pełczyńska-Nałęcz, the leader of a junior party in Poland’s ruling coalition, has announced her resignation from the government and the leadership of her party, the centrist Poland 2050 (Polska 2050), in protest over a parliamentary vote on Thursday. Poland 2050 (Polska 2050) is set to remain in the government, thereby maintaining Prime Minister Donald Tusk’s parliamentary majority. However, the dispute has highlighted tensions within the ruling coalition just a year ahead of parliamentary elections at which it will seek another term. Dwukadencyjność samorządów została utrzymana. Tak zdecydował dziś Sejm. Wygraliśmy! Zmiana, której chce 75% Polaków dojdzie do skutku! Stało się to jednak pomimo głosów K15X. Koalicja, w tym niestety znaczna część posłów Polski 2050, stanęła przeciw ludziom, a za politykierskimi… — Katarzyna Pełczyńska (@Kpelczynska) October 22, 2026 Pełczyńska-Nałęcz, who serves as minister for funds and regional policy, made her decision in the wake of an unusual voting result in the Sejm, the more powerful lower house of parliament, on Thursday. Another junior partner in the ruling coalition, the centre-right Polish People’s Party (PSL), had proposed a bill abolishing two-term limits for mayors. Those limits had been introduced in 2018 with the aim of reducing corruption and cronyism by preventing local officials from becoming entrenched in power. However, PSL, which has a strong presence in local politics, argues that the limits prevent effective, popular mayors from being re-elected, thereby denying voters the right to decide who they want to represent them. Although the government has a majority in the Sejm, the bill was narrowly defeated, with 213 votes in favour and 215 against, after 15 MPs from the ruling coalition joined with the right-wing opposition in voting against it. Pełczyńska-Nałęcz herself is not a member of parliament, so did not vote. Her party was split, with six MPs voting for the bill, three against, three abstaining, and three not voting at all. Aftewards, Pełczyńska-Nałęcz made clear that she opposed the bill and celebrated the fact that it was blocked. She also announced her resignation from the government and the leadership of her party. “The coalition, unfortunately including a significant portion of MPs from Poland 2050, stood against the people and in favour of backroom political deals,” she wrote. “I am leaving Donald Tusk’s government because values are more important to me than positions.” “I am leaving the party in the hands of its founder, who stepped away but then returned,” she added, referring to Poland 2050’s founder, Szymon Hołownia. “I hope that he remembers what values he came to power in the name of.” Pełczyńska-Nałęcz’s decision follows a year of turmoil for Poland 2050. In September 2025, Hołownia, who had led the party since founding it in 2021, announced that he was stepping down. However, a first attempt to choose a new leader was invalidated in January after technical problems with voting. Hołownia then hinted that he may reverse course and seek to continue leading the party, though in the end that did not happen. In February, Pełczyńska-Nałęcz was chosen as the new leader. That prompted her rival candidate, Paulina Hennig-Kloska, to quit the party, taking half of its MPs with her. They formed a new group called Centrum (Centre). Both Poland 2050 and Centrum remain in the ruling coalition. However, Pełczyńska-Nałęcz has had an uneasy relationship with Tusk. Around half the MPs from Poland 2050, a junior member of Poland’s ruling coalition, have split from the party and formed a new parliamentary caucus. They expressed dissatisfaction with the actions of the party's recently elected new leader, @Kpelczynska https://t.co/IqU4vE1EEe — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) February 18, 2026 On Friday, Tusk, who is on a state visit to India, sarcastically responded to Pełczyńska-Nałęcz’s resignation by saying, “I thought she’d at least call before she left”. He admitted that “cooperation [with her] has not been the easiest for a long time”. The prime minister, however, added that he “does not think [her resignation] will have any impact on the future work of the coalition…My intuition tells me that this is her individual decision”. Hołownia, who currently serves as head of Poland 2050’s parliamentary caucus, confirmed at a press conference on Friday alongside fellow MPs that the party intends to remain in Tusk’s coalition. But he also warned that, without Poland 2050, the government would not have a parliamentary majority. W @PL_2050 dowiedzieliśmy się o decyzji @Kpelczynska z mediów. Zaskakująca rezygnacja przewodniczącej z zaufania wyborców i odpowiedzialności powierzonej jej w bardzo trudnym momencie przez ludzi (w tym mnie) zaledwie po niespełna 1/3 kadencji – dla każdej organizacji byłaby… — Szymon Hołownia (@szymon_holownia) October 22, 2026 The episode highlights the tensions within the ruling coalition, which ranges from left to centre right and contains parties that disagree on a number of issues. It also points to the pressure smaller coalition partners are feeling ahead of next autumn’s parliamentary elections. Only parties that win at least 5% of the vote nationally can enter parliament. But Poland 2050 has been polling at around 1% and PSL is on 3%. In the 2023 election, Poland 2050 and PSL in fact stood together as an alliance called the Third Way (Trzecia Droga), helping ensure that the two parties won enough votes to enter parliament. However, in 2025, they split from one another and confirmed that they would not stand together again. PSL and Poland 2050, the two parties that make up the Third Way alliance, have confirmed that they are splitting and will stand separately at the next elections. They will, however, remain part of @donaldtusk's ruling coalition https://t.co/NduEJY25eE — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 18, 2025 The fact that the bill to end two-term limits for mayors was defeated has also caused tension between PSL and its coalition partners. In the wake of yesterday’s vote, PSL immediately announced that it would push for the introduction of two-term limits for members of parliament, arguing that the same rules should apply to national and local elected representatives. The right-wing opposition has long hoped that it could tempt PSL, the most conservative element of Tusk’s coalition, to quit the government. A recent report even claimed that US President Donald Trump had, at the behest of Poland’s opposition, suggested to PSL’s leader that he leave Tusk.
