World.title: Journalist-Turned-PM Faces Daunting Challenges in Romania
World.content:
What do journalism and diplomacy have in common? For Luca Niculescu, both offer the opportunity of direct engagement with people, demand effective communication, and require an ability to build relationships and ask the right questions.

Diplomacy, however, operates by different rules, particularly when it comes to freedom of public expression. This limitation is offset, according to Romania’s new prime minister, by the satisfaction that comes from serving the public interest and making a tangible difference to people’s lives.

Niculescu, 55, began his career as a radio journalist in 1992 and went on to become editor-in-chief of Radio France Internationale, RFI, while also contributing regularly to several French media outlets.

In 2016, he made the transition to diplomacy as Romania’s ambassador to France. He returned to Bucharest in 2022 to coordinate the country’s bid to join the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development, OECD, and last week became prime minister.

World.title: Serbian Students’ Mass Support ‘Forced Vucic to Concede’ Election
World.content:
In a park next to the presidency building in central Belgrade, the campsite known as Caciland had become a symbol of the impunity enjoyed by the ruling Serbian Progressive Party, SNS. Fenced off with metal barriers for more than a year and guarded by police, it occupied public land but served as a gathering place for SNS supporters.

Just after polls closed in Sunday’s elections, that changed, as Serbian citizens began celebrating in the streets across the country. Dancing and singing, supporters of the opposition Student List symbolically brought an end to the SNS’s 14-year rule by entering the tent camp and taking back the park for the public.

The results of the elections have electrified the country and brought a sigh of relief from political observers who feared the polls might have been severely rigged to put the SNS back into power, backed up by the muscle of the security forces. Jelena Loncar, an associate professor at Belgrade University’s Faculty of Political Sciences, told BIRN that the election results show that “Serbia is not moving towards a closed authoritarian regime.”

World.title: Czech Govt Faces Backlash Over Rushed Public Media Funding Reform
World.content:
Despite the cold and rainy weather that descended over the Czech capital, thousands of protesters filled Prague’s Old Town Square on Sunday afternoon, heeding the call of the Million Moments for Democracy movement with banners reading “Resign!”, “Hands off public media!”, “Shame!”, “We’ve had enough!”, and more colourful and explicit drawings and captions.

Other smaller demonstrations took place throughout the weekend across Czechia, including Brno, Liberec and Ceske Budejovice, hastily organised protests that testified to a sudden mood shift in society as fears of a government media grab intensify.

One of the governing coalition’s top campaign promises, the long-debated yet long-delayed reform to abolish license fees and fund both Czech TV (CT) and Czech Radio (CRo) directly from the state budget, appeared to have stalled in recent months.

But on Friday, the ruling three-party coalition of ANO, the ultraconservative Motorists for Themselves and the far-right Freedom and Direct Democracy (SPD) party abruptly pushed through a priority reading of the bill.

This led to a swift and immediate response from citizens. Hundreds of protesters gathered on Malostranske Square in central Prague, and dozens were even blocked by the police from entering the lower house of parliament later that evening.

After a fast-track procedure that limited speaking time and set a fixed voting deadline, government MPs eventually approved the draft at around 04:30 in the early hours of Saturday morning, sending the bill to a second reading following hours of heated debate that saw personal attacks and vulgarities fly from both sides of the aisle.

According to the proposal, CT should receive an annual 5.7 billion crowns (234 million euros) from the state budget in 2027 (a billion crowns less than its 2026 license fee revenues), while CRo should also see its funding cut by 400 million crowns to a little over 2 billion crowns.

No ‘nationalisation’, Babis vows

Repeating the mantra pushed for the past year, government officials dismissed any concerns about the independence or the future of the public service broadcasters. “I reject the idea that changing the financing of public media is an attack on democracy or the end of the independence of public media,” insisted Culture Minister Oto Klempir, arguing that many other European countries fund their public broadcasters in a similar way.

A long-time critic of the public service media’s coverage and management, Prime Minister Andrej Babis accused the opposition of “lying, inciting hatred and dividing society”, while drawing a feeble comparison with protesters’ attempt to enter the Chamber of Deputies in Prague last Friday with the Capitol riots in Washington DC in January 2021.

He did, however, try to strike a reassuring tone as well. “Their funding will be guaranteed by law as a mandatory expenditure and linked to inflation,” he vowed. “No government will be able to arbitrarily cut [funding] based on whether it likes or dislikes a broadcast.”

This, however, did little to assuage widespread concerns that the government’s reform could put the two public service broadcasters under greater political control.

Warning that the reform threatens their editorial independence, undermines the stability of their funding and could lead to the nationalisation of both entities, staffers at CT and CRo have declared a day-long strike for November 3. “We ask everyone who is not indifferent to the fate of CT and CRo to make their position known publicly and loudly,” stated the Verejnopravne initiative, which is backed by about 3,200 of the 4,200 employees at the two broadcasters.

Addressing both the content of the bill and the fast-track legislative push, criticism has come from all corners, including the Czech Journalists’ Syndicate, the European Broadcasting Union, the European Federation of Journalists, Reporters Without Borders, over a dozen other domestic and international media freedom groups, as well as President Petr Pavel – whose signature would be needed for the bill to come into force.

“I repeat that the media must have clear guarantees of independence in every respect, both in terms of content and funding,” Pavel said, additionally calling on politicians from both sides of the aisle to take it down a notch and work to deescalate tensions.

Experts also weighed in on the issue. “The way the rules of procedure [in the lower house of parliament] were handled in this case bears the features of a power grab, in which we can see inspiration from the rhetoric and tactics of leaders like Donald Trump and Viktor Orban,” argued political scientist Eva Klusova from the Czech Academy of Sciences.

Hypothesising that the reform could be a way for the government to cover up their earlier setback at this month’s recent municipal and senatorial elections, media expert Martina Urbanikova highlighted that the funding for public service media isn’t included in the 2027 state budget, and that the legislative agenda made it uncertain the reform could take effect from January.

But in the wake of Sunday’s street protests, Prime Minister Babis vowed not to back down, adding on Monday that specific provisions were still under consideration, including the option to allow for voluntary license fee payments.

Meanwhile, Million Moments for Democracy called for another mass demonstration, set to take place on Prague’s Letna plain on November 15, two days before commemorations marking the start of the 1989 Velvet Revolution.

World.title: Kosovo Woman Murdered Hours After Reporting Domestic Violence to Police
World.content:
The Basic Prosecution in Peja/Pec. Photo: Peja Basic Prosecution.

Arlinda Zekaj was murdered on Sunday evening in the village of Vitomirica, near Peja/Pec, shortly after returning from the police station where she reported domestic violence. Three days beforehand, she had asked the local prosecution to intervene to save her life.

“I hope the day never comes when you and the responsible institutions are forced to account for your actions only after my life has been taken,” Zekaj had written on October 22 in a letter to Lumturije Vucetaj, chief prosecutor of the Peja Basic Prosecution office. The letter called for urgent action against officials she accused of failing to protect her from domestic violence.

Three days later she was murdered with an axe, allegedly by her brother-in-law, who remains at large.

Zekaj is the seventh woman to be murdered by a family member in 2026 in Kosovo.

Kosovo police announced that they received a domestic violence report at around 7 p.m. on Sunday after which the police interviewed Zekaj and arrested her ex-husband for domestic violence. He was “placed in 48-hour detention. The victim was then taken to her home in the village of Vitomirica voluntarily,” the police statement reads.

“At around 9:10 pm, we were notified that she had been found dead”, the statement continues.

On Monday morning, Zekaj’s lawyer Adelina Shala contradicted the police statement, writing on Facebook that “it wasn’t the victim’s will” to return home. On Sunday evening, Shala accused Kosovo authorities of failing to protect her client, writing that “the state killed Arlinda”.

The prosecutor’s office in Peja/Pec stated in a late night press release that Vucetaj had ordered Zekaj’s letter to be registered for examination by the competent prosecutor, including “an assessment of potential criminal liability for abuse of official position or authority”.

Kosovo’s Chief State Prosecutor requested a detailed report and review on Monday to determine “whether there were institutional or individual failures” and how the victim’s letter was handled.

Kosovo President Justina Shiroka Pula called for “an urgent, comprehensive and impartial investigation. It must be clarified whether all necessary measures were taken to assess the risk and protect her.”

The Collective for Feminist Thought and Action, an activist group, called for a nationwide protest on Wednesday, “as an act of revolt and a final call to protect women’s lives”.

The Kosovo Women’s Network (KWN) said that “the case is particularly concerning given the challenges [Zekaj] had faced regarding custody and contact with her child, as well as the concerns raised about the institutional handling of her case”.

There have been a number of recent murders of women in Kosovo by family members.

On October 9, Nafije Bogujevci and her brother Egzon Bogujevci were shot dead. Nafije’s husband later turned himself in to the police. In late August, two women were allegedly killed by their husbands within days. The first victim was 25 years old and pregnant, the second aged 80. The first was shot, the second beaten to death.

On the last Friday in August, dozens of people marched through Pristina to demand justice for the victims of femicide and to call on authorities to treat gender-based violence in Kosovo as a national emergency.

World.title: Calls for Protest Are Spreading Across Zagreb
World.content:
October the 28th, 2026 – Calls for a protest are currently spreading across Zagreb, with the organisers insisting that there are no political parties involved.

Posters have begun appearing across Zagreb calling on the public to a protest named “Voice of Change/Glas Promjene”, announced for Saturday the 21st of November, at 10:00 on Ban Josip Jelačić Square. Behind the call stands the civic initiative “Time for Change/Vrijeme za Promjenu”, which, via social media, is inviting people to gather against corruption, abuse of power and institutional irresponsibility.

Index reports that the posters highlight the message “All of Croatia, one voice”, and the organisers say they want to bring together people who are dissatisfied with the standard of living, the political situation and the work of institutions. “Want change? Then don’t be the person who doesn’t come to Ban Josip Jelačić Square at 10:00 on the 21st of November,” one of the posts calling for the protest states.

“no more empty promises”

The organisers point to the rising cost of living, the increasingly difficult independence of young people and the feeling that wages are not keeping up with prices. “Basic life needs are becoming a luxury, young people cannot afford to leave their parents’ home for something of their own, wages are getting lower, while the quality of life and prices demand more and more,” they state in a post.

The organisers answered several questions about the goals of the protest. “The protest is directed against corruption, abuse of power and the lack of institutional accountability. We demand transparent management of public money, equal laws for everyone, accountability of those who hold public office and concrete systemic changes, not just empty promises,” they said. They emphasised that the initiative is not connected to any political party and that its goal is not to replace one set of politicians with another. “The initiative is not tied to any political party, nor is the goal to replace one politicians with others, but to demand a system in which institutions work in the interest of citizens,” they stated.

They added that they want to shape the concrete demands together with citizens so that they are clear, achievable and measurable.

is the protest against hdz or just corruption asa vague term?

One of the questions put to the organisers was whether the protest is directed against HDZ. “The protest is directed against corruption, abuse of power and the lack of institutional accountability, regardless of who is in power. That includes the actions of the HDZ when they are the subject of such criticism,” they replied. In a separate post they further emphasised that the protest is not organised in the name of any political party and that they do not belong to any political option. “This is a civic initiative for all people who have had enough of corruption, lack of transparency, institutional irresponsibility and an uncertain future for us and our children,” they said.

serbian protests were mentioned

The organisers also commented on the protests in Serbia, answering the question of whether the situation there prompted them to organise a gathering in Croatia. “The situation in Serbia has certainly shown how important civic unity and persistence are, but the motivation is much broader than that,” they stated. They added that their goal is to encourage citizens of different political views to act together. “The goal is for all of us, regardless of political views, to become active and together build a better future. Change begins when we stop just watching and decide to participate,” they said.

they want to see protests across croatia

Although a protest in Zagreb has so far been announced, the organisers are also thinking about gatherings in other Croatian cities. When asked whether the protest would have a greater impact if all citizens gathered in one city, they replied that for the start it is more important to enable people to participate in their own communities. “I think that for the start it is important to enable people to gather in their own cities because not everyone has the possibility to travel to another location,” they stated. They added that, depending on the turnout and organisation, one large joint gathering could later be held. “And when we see the turnout and the strength of the organisation in each city, we can make one large joint gathering that will send an even stronger message. Step by step, city by city,” they said.

who is actually behind this initiative?

Calls for the protest are spreading via social media, among other things through the Instagram profile @vrijemezapromjene and the TikTok profile @glas.promjene. One of the posters also lists the TikTok profile @ala_secera as a contact for joining the Zagreb group. The organisers emphasise that all citizens can participate in the protest, regardless of age or occupation, including students, high-school graduates, employed people and pensioners. It is not yet known who the people behind the initiative are, how many of them are involved in the organisation, or whether the protest has been reported to the police. Details of the gathering programme have also not been published. The protest is, once again, announced for the 21st of November at 10:00 on Ban Josip Jelačić Square in central Zagreb.

World.title: Why Did Over 100,000 Croatian Landlords Turn Their Backs on Protesters?
World.content:
October the 28th, 2026 – Over 100,000 Croatian landlords who rent out their properties to tourists turned their backs on protesters fighting for their rights in Zagreb, but why?

The recent protest by private landlords held at Zrinjevac in Zagreb once again opened key questions about representation, expertise and the future of private accommodation in Croatia. Morski reports that although the organisers’ communication channels were burning with announcements of a mass turnout and a blockade of the capital, digital engagement analytics and sociological parameters indicated in advance the modest reach of the gathering. Despite the protest platform on social media gathering around 15,000 followers, the rate of active interaction at the peak of the campaign barely reached 10 percent. When these figures are run through the usual conversion rates to physical turnout, the final outcome on Zrinjevac brought only a few hundred people, a number comparable to a larger group of mushroom pickers rather than a serious national protest.

This modest turnout confronted the organisers with the relentless mathematical reality. Application of the sociological model of the Law of Dispersion of the Passive Majority clearly shows that in moments of major legislative upheavals the vast majority of affected actors consciously choose passivity and distance themselves from reactive groups. In this case, support from as many as 105,000 Croatian private landlords was absent from the public uproar. The silent majority, which avoids street activism, thereby sent a clear message that it rejects street pressure and demands institutional strength, expertise and well-founded arguments.

a hidden internal division…

The relatively weak turnout is also a direct consequence of a completely failed communication model. The use of populist rhetoric permeated with expressions about “serfs”, “cash machines” and accusations of a “witch hunt”, along with bizarre political constructions about secret coalitions and open threats of electoral votes from the podium, disqualified the organisers from serious professional dialogue. Serious professional associations do not negotiate with the authorities through street blackmail, but with exact indicators, legal analyses and constructive proposals.

Additionally, the protest revealed a deep, though publicly unspoken, socio-economic stratification within the sector itself. Namely, around 43,000 high-category facilities with 4 and 5 stars, in which significant funds have been invested, attract guests of higher purchasing power and naturally no longer share the same interests with the rest of the base that persists with the basic 3-star model. Nevertheless, owners of higher-quality accommodation, for pragmatic reasons and the desire to preserve good-neighbourly relations in local communities, choose complete passivity, leaving the protest margins to the loudest groups.

are amendments making landlords kick the can down the road?

On the other hand, uncertainty on the ground has been further heightened by the fact that the Government and the Ministry of Tourism and Sport (MINTS) have, through months of administrative silence, delayed precise clarifications of the new legislative amendments and the announced re-categorisation. This created information vacuum has served as fuel for the spread of panic, although it is clear that the state does not want to wipe out private accommodation, but to introduce necessary regulatory order and balance the interests of landlords with the remaining 90 percent of people. It is also expected that expert teams will take a sharper approach towards non-commercial accommodation which, under the guise of hosting, often represents a source of unfair competition.

Despite the tensions, the financial contribution of private landlords to Croatian tourism remains extremely significant. On the basis of around 600,000 registered beds, landlords through the fixed lump-sum tourist membership fee of €5.97 per bed generate around €3.58 million annually, while through the lump-sum tourist tax, with a conservative average of €50 per bed, they pay an additional €30 million. As such, more than €33.5 million of original money flows into the budgets and the system of tourist boards every year.

a constructive proposal…

Instead of directing these funds into ineffective general promotion or spending from the general state budget, a real and sustainable alternative offers the redirection of part of this earmarked pool into a National Programme of Targeted Vouchers for Apartment Transition. Modelled on successful European practices, such as Italian regional micro-grants in Tuscany and Apulia or the French Gîtes de France network, this model would directly help raise the quality of accommodation on the ground. The proposed vouchers would not be distributed in cash nor would they be intended for high-category 4- and 5-star facilities that already operate well. They would be used exclusively for co-financing the costs of interior modernisation and the purchase of equipment in 3-star facilities that demonstrably move into a higher category. Functioning as closed instruments intended for payment of works to registered domestic craftsmen and companies and for the purchase of equipment in Croatian shops, these millions would return directly into the entire Croatian economy, turning fiscal contributions into a driving force of sustainable market evolution.

World.title: Hungary Bins Orbán and Serbia Bins Vučić, Is Croatia Next?
World.content:
October the 28th, 2026 – Hungary toppled Viktor Orbán after 18 years in power, and now Serbia has binned Aleksandar Vučić, many are now asking the question of whether or not a big change for Croatia is next.

After almost 14 years of political dominance, Aleksandar Vučić just suffered a staggering electoral defeat in Serbia. Only a few months earlier, Viktor Orbán was toppled from power in Hungary after 16 years. Can Croatia, where the HDZ has been in power continuously since 2016, be next? Vedran Salvia reports for Index that although it is abundantly clear that Plenković’s government has not built an authoritarian system of the kind established by Orbán and Vučić, all three countries share long-term dominance by a single political option that has over time developed a strong network of influence in state institutions and the public sector.

Croatia is thus marked by strong clientelism, party-based appointments, corruption and seriously eroded institutions. During the ten years of Plenković’s rule, the HDZ has not attempted to confront this way of running the state, but has further strengthened it. A party membership card and connections still all too often count for more than knowledge and ability, and the consequences of such a system are felt in almost all parts of society.

both hungary and serbia seek to forge new paths

Interestingly, neither Orbán nor Vučić was defeated by the traditional opposition parties. In Hungary this was achieved by Péter Magyar, a former man of Orbán’s system, who with his party Tisza gathered a broad circle of voters dissatisfied with long-term rule. Among them were also people who had previously supported Orbán’s Fidesz. In Serbia, the situation was somewhat different. Vučić was defeated by the Student List, which emerged from the protests after the tragedy in Novi Sad, where on the 1st of November 2024, a railway station canopy collapsed and killed 16 people. The accident opened questions of corruption and institutional responsibility, and the protests grew into a mass movement against Vučić’s government.

75% of people think croatia is heading in the wrong direction

In Croatia, there is no shortage of dissatisfaction with the government. According to the latest CRO Demoskop, conducted from 6 to 8 October, more than 75 percent of respondents believe that the country is going in the wrong direction. Only a little over 17 percent think that Croatia is going in the right direction. At the same time, HDZ, although recording a drop in popularity, remains the strongest individual party with 25 percent support. The SDP is at a little under 20 percent, Možemo at almost 14 percent, and Most has approached 10 percent.

Interestingly, both HDZ and SDP are declining at the same time, while Možemo is growing. In other words, dissatisfaction with those in power is not automatically translating into growth for the largest opposition party, and this is one of the biggest differences between Croatia and the two neighbouring countries. In Hungary, Tisza managed to become the main political alternative to Orbán. In Serbia, the students almost completely pushed aside the traditional opposition and turned into a movement that can win power on its own.

Croatia does not have such a political force. It has several opposition parties, some of which govern important cities and have significant voter support, but none has so far managed to gather such a broad circle of dissatisfied citizens. At the same time, the Croatian opposition doesn’t have an individual who, like Magyar, could attract a significant part of the ruling party’s voters. Magyar’s success was not based solely on criticism of Orbán. As a man who came from within the Fidesz system, he was able to convince even some conservative voters that a change of government does not necessarily mean abandoning their political beliefs.

electoral maths still favours hdz…

Croatian electoral mathematics are also highly important. Croatia is divided into ten territorial electoral units, in each of which 14 seats are distributed separately. Therefore it is not only the total number of votes that matters, but also their distribution. HDZ greatly benefits from a strong party organisation and stable support in numerous parts of the country.

The boundaries of the electoral units were redrawn in 2023 after the Constitutional Court repealed the previous law. The new model was adopted by an HDZ majority and drew criticism for the illogical linking of certain areas. Political scientist Goran Čular then warned for Gong: “The prime minister said that the arrangement of electoral units is a technical issue, but HDZ is doing everything to ensure that it is not just a technical issue.” Nevertheless, HDZ’s victory back in 2024 cannot be attributed solely to the electoral system. Its coalition won 61 seats, fully 19 more than the SDP coalition, and it formed the government again with the help of the Homeland Movement. The electoral system can be an additional advantage for it, but for a change of government the opposition must first and foremost win significantly broader voter support.

the clear differences between hungary, serbia and croatia

Political scientist Tihomir Cipek, a professor at the Faculty of Political Science in Zagreb, spoke about why long-term governments fell in Hungary and Serbia, while in Croatia the HDZ still does not have an equally strong opponent. Cipek emphasises that the situations in Croatia, Hungary and Serbia are different. “In Hungary, a strong movement against Orbán was formed, which Péter Magyar gathered around his new party. Something similar happened in Serbia with the Student List. There we have a broad movement that brought together very different people, from liberals open to the world and cooperation with the European Union to Serbian nationalists who accused Vučić of betraying Kosovo and Metohija. Among them are both those who support sanctions against Russia and those who oppose them. Despite major political differences, what connected them all was opposition to Vučić,” Cipek said.

why has no similar movement emerged in croatia?

He explained that a similar movement against Plenković’s government has not emerged in Croatia because the political scene is already clearly divided among the existing parties. “In Croatia, the political system is structured along party lines. The type of people who found themselves together on the Student List in Serbia are already organised in different parties here. Here you have Možemo, which is for a more open society and, for example, cooperation with the EU, and on the other side Most, which has different views on migration and the openness of society.

It’s very difficult to imagine them all uniting into one front against the government. In addition, the electoral system in Croatia must also be taken into account. Serbia is one electoral unit, while Croatia has ten, so it is important how the opposition will perform in each of them,” Cipek explained. He believes that the successes of the students and Magyar show that even long-term power is no guarantee of political survival. “That victory in Serbia shows that nothing is certain. You can be in power for a long time, build strong influence in state structures, but citizens can still remove you with their activity and energy. In Croatia it is much harder to create such a broad movement, but that does not mean that it is impossible to change the government,” Cipek concludes.

is there even any potential for governmental change in croatia?

“There is potential for a change of government because dissatisfaction is high. The key is how it will be politically articulated. If the SDP and Možemo organise well, change is possible,” Cipek says. He believes that the opposition parties have drawn lessons from earlier electoral defeats, when they ran separately or tried to form alliances that did not bring the expected result. “There is dissatisfaction, but it needs to be turned into a political programme. With clear messages, good organisation and voter mobilisation it is also possible for the Croatian opposition to win. Nothing is eternal,” Cipek concluded.

World.title: Dubrovnik Airport: The Biggest Corruption Scandal Involving EU Cash?
World.content:
October the 28th, 2026 – The mayor of Dubrovnik has referred to the situation with Dubrovnik Airport being “the biggest corruption scandal involving EU cash in Croatia”.

Dubrovnik’s Ruđer Bošković Airport had to return a total of €22 million in European Union funds due to irregularities in public procurement procedures during a major airport modernisation project. Index reports that in addition to all kinds of financial problems, it was also revealed that part of the expensive infrastructure was never put into operation. Among such projects is the aircraft fuel supply system, in which pipes of the type used for sewage systems were allegedly installed.

These are irregularities in the modernisation project for Dubrovnik Airport that was carried out from 2013 to 2017. Around €200 million was secured from EU funds for the renovation, but due to disputed public procurement procedures, part of that money had to be returned. The latest obligation of three million euros recently became due. Dubrovnik Airport director Viktor Šober explained how the irregularities financially burdened the airport’s operations. “In one part we returned it, in one case it was automatically deducted from us, so we had to take out loans ourselves or use our own funds to make up for that shortfall which occurred primarily because of problematic public procurement procedures,” Šober said.

dubrovnik’s mayor calls out the airport’s director

Dubrovnik’s HDZ mayor Mato Franković recently spoke about the problems at Dubrovnik Airport and, at a session of the parliamentary Transport Committee, called out the former airport director Roko Tolić.

“When you take the overall damage that occurred at Dubrovnik Airport, we can say that this is the biggest corruption affair involving European money in the Republic of Croatia that no one is talking about,” Franković said. Tolić ran Dubrovnik Airport for a long period, more specifically from 2009 to 2018, when he was dismissed due to irregularities in public procurement. Since 2024 he has held the position of executive director of Aerodromi Crne Gore, the company that manages the airports in Podgorica and Tivat.

Tolić was previously politically active in the HSS. From 2000 to 2001 he was deputy mayor of Dubrovnik under Vito Bogdanović as a representative of that party. In the 2021 local elections he ran for Dubrovnik-Neretva County prefect as an independent candidate with the support of the SDP and HNS, but did not make it to the second round.

the alleged installation of sewage-type piping

In addition to returning an enormous sum of EU money, Dubrovnik Airport is also facing problems due to the unfinished aircraft fuel supply system. Although the system was paid for, it has not been used for years because serious mistakes were made during design and construction.

“The problem here is incorrect design and incorrect execution of the works. Plastic and glass pipes were installed that are essentially not used for the flow of fuel. Later, when studying the technical specifications, we realised that pipes used for sewage systems were installed there,” said Marina Bukvić from Ruđer Bošković Airport. The airport management hired a German company to check whether the system could be repaired and put into operation. However, the experts concluded that additional investments of several million euros would be needed to make it functional. This means that the airport has already paid for infrastructure it cannot use, and repairing it would require new large expenditures.

“we bought something we can’t use”

Šober warns that a way to solve the problem will have to be found, and he does not rule out legal steps either. “If this is not resolved, of course that part will be problematic for us as an airport. We paid for something we cannot use. In that case we will have to look for some solutions. Whether of a legal nature or some kind of agreements, but difficult talks certainly await us on this,” Šober said. Former director Roko Tolić did not wish to comment on the accusations against him. Dnevnik.hr also contacted the European Public Prosecutor’s Office (EPPO) to check whether an investigation has been launched against those responsible for the irregularities in public procurement. They have not yet received a response.

World.title: Ryanair Directly Connects Zagreb and Warsaw Over Winter
World.content:
October the 27th, 2026 – Ryanair has directly connected Zagreb with the Polish capital of Warsaw during the winter schedule, with flights for as little as 17 euros.

The wildly popular Irish low-cost carrier Ryanair has introduced yet another brand new air route connecting Zagreb and Warsaw, specifically Warsaw-Modlin Airport. Poslovni reports that the first flight was operated as part of the winter timetable for the 2026/2027 season on October the 26th, giving passengers from Croatia another option for travelling to Poland. The new route will operate on Mondays and Saturdays, with two flights a week from Zagreb and two from Warsaw.

There are some ultra-cheap tickets being offered on this new route, with the differences in prices show that having a certain degree of flexibility when choosing your desired travel dates can really pay off. Since prices change depending on demand and seat availability, it is always recommended to check the current offers on Ryanair’s website or on the company’s mobile app before booking.

On the occasion of launching this new route from Zagreb Airport, Ryanair’s Director of Communications Jade Kirwan highlighted the importance of expanding the offer for passengers from Croatia. “We’re very pleased that we saw off the first flight operating on the new Zagreb–Warsaw (Modlin) route, on which the first set of very many passengers who will travel with us this winter departed,” Kirwan said.

She added that the new route will give passengers a greater choice of destinations at affordable prices. “The route will operate four times a week, offering passengers from Croatia even more travel options at the most affordable prices in Europe. The entire winter timetable for 2026 is available for booking via our app and website,” she stated.

World.title: Croatian Campsites are the Most Expensive in Europe
World.content:
October the 27th, 2026 – Croatian campsites might be considered the most expensive in Europe, but the Germans still deem them the best. Here’s how much an average day costs.

For the ever-keen German campers, Germany itself is the most popular camping destination, while Croatia is the third most popular foreign destination, behind Italy and France, with the Netherlands in fifth place. Poslovni reports that Croatian campsites can expect continued strong demand from the German market throughout 2027, given that German campers give them the highest quality ratings in all of Europe, even though according to new research they are simultaneously the most expensive. This was highlighted by Uwe Frers, CEO of PiNCAMP, part of the German automobile club ADAC system.

German tourists, along with Slovenian and Austrian visitors, are the most numerous guests filling up Croatian campsites, and the German market is of particular importance for this segment, as well as for overall Croatian tourism. In a recent interview with Hina, Frers explained that ADAC’s digital tourism platform PiNCAMP also cooperates with the Dutch automobile club ANWB and the Swiss TCS.

“These auto clubs are among the largest in all of Europe, with a total of around 30 million members, many of whom are campers,” says Frers. At the recent Croatian Camping Congress, Frers presented one of their newer surveys on campers’ attitudes towards the quality and prices of campsites in 2026 and for 2027, conducted on the German and Dutch markets. For this purpose, they surveyed more than six thousand campers in two studies during the first three quarters of 2026.

around 25% of germans now go camping

The research showed that campers have positive attitudes and that demand from these two countries for Croatian campsites is growing. Demand from German campers is growing particularly strongly, for which Frers sees reasons in the rising number of camping vehicles in that country, from last year’s 1.7 million to this year’s 2 million, which is also a new record and, as he adds, “a great figure for the camping sector.” They also established that around 25 percent of Germans now go camping, which is a 19 percent increase compared to data from 2023. Frers also noted that a quarter of all camping vehicles in Europe are registered in Germany, followed by France with 19 percent, the United Kingdom with 13 percent, and the Netherlands with a 9 percent share.

interesting results for croatia and croatian camping

For Croatia specifically, he cites two interesting research results. The first is quality, which is the most important novelty, because campers gave it the best ratings. The second result is that Croatia is at the same time the most expensive camping destination. “In the past, we discussed how someone can be the most expensive and yet not the best. Now we can end such discussions, because Croatia has shown that it is the best in camping in terms of quality, so it is therefore justified that it also leads in price levels,” Frers believes.

He finds it interesting that Croatia has pursued a fairly aggressive pricing policy in recent years, but that this has now changed, because the average price increase in camping in Europe is around 8 percent, while Croatia with 7 percent is below that average. “So, being a leader in quality, while at the same time keeping price growth below the average, is the right tactic for surviving in this market,” Frers recommends. When asked about the average prices, he said that in Croatia it is €77 per day in a campsite, which is also the highest price among all countries, while the European average is around €50.

“In Europe, there are regions that are extremely cheap, as well as some very expensive ones. Croatia is clearly positioned in the luxury segment, and that position is further strengthened by its ‘leadership’ in quality, which is additionally confirmed in the research by campers stating that Croatian campsites offer good value for money,” says Frers.

However, he adds, in the research 56 percent of respondents said they had no opinion on this, which means they do not have a negative attitude either, while the remaining 44 percent are divided – half of them consider the Croatian camping offer acceptable and good, and the other half poor. “The fact that more than half of the respondents have no opinion at all I consider a good starting point for attracting new guests to Croatian campsites that should be utilised,” Frers stated.

croatia is the third most popular camping destination

For German campers, Germany itself is the most popular camping destination, while Croatia is the third most popular foreign destination, behind Italy and France, with the Netherlands in fifth place. Croatia is rated the best by the largest number of respondents (22 percent) in terms of price-quality ratio for camping, followed by Germany, Italy, Switzerland and Austria. In terms of quality, Croatia also occupies the leading position with the best average campsite rating of 3.9 stars, while the Netherlands, Luxembourg and France have 3.7 stars, Spain 3.6, and Italy 3.5. In terms of camping prices per day for 2027, Croatia leads with an average of €77, Switzerland is second with €65, followed by Italy with €64, Austria with €61 and the United Kingdom with €55.

World.title: Omiš Fire Claimed 6 Lives, Yet There’s No investigation Result Yet
World.content:
October the 27th, 2026 – The horrific Omiš fire has now tragically claimed six lives. Despite the severity of the disaster, there has still been no investigation result even after two months.

73 days have now passed since the major fire that broke out on the 13th of August in Lokva Rogoznica and spread down towards Omiš. Katarina Ergovic Arnaut reports for Index that the public still has no answer to the crucial question: how exactly this enormous fire started and who, if anyone, is responsible for it. In the meantime, the number of victims has risen to a horrendous six. Just two days ago, a 66-year-old woman who had been being treated in hospital since August for serious injuries sustained in the fire, died in hospital.

Despite the sheer scale of the tragedy, the police and the County State Attorney’s Office in Split have so far not publicly released the results of the investigation, nor have they announced whether the cause of the fire has been determined. It has also not been announced that anyone has been suspected or arrested in connection with its outbreak.

camera footage was examined and experts have been on the terrain taking samples

The investigation was launched immediately after the fire. The State Attorney’s Office (DORH) announced 71 days ago, on 15 August, that a crime scene investigation had been carried out at the place where the fire started in Lokva Rogoznica, involving the police, a fire and explosion protection inspector, and chemical-physical experts from the “Ivan Vučetić” Centre. Material samples were taken at the site where the fire broke out. Orders were also issued for the seizure of surveillance camera footage from the entire burned area, surveying of the terrain, and photographing of destroyed houses, other buildings and vehicles.

DORH stated at the time that the necessary expert examinations and other actions would be carried out in order to establish all the circumstances of the event. Over two months later, the results of these procedures have still not been presented to the public.

the fire directly affected around 1,000 hectares

According to the findings of the on-site investigation at the time, the fire broke out on the 13th of August around 20:00 in a heavily forested area next to the road in the wider Lokva Rogoznica area. Carried by strong winds, it spread quickly towards Omiš along a strip approximately 23 kilometres long and up to one and a half kilometres wide. Around 1,000 hectares of thick pine forest, grass and Dalmatian shrubs were burned. Numerous houses, business premises, plantations and vehicles were also claimed by the flames, and material damage in the multi millions was caused. Several dozen people were also injured to some extent or another in the fire.

The first victim, a seasonal worker from neighbouring Bosnia and Herzegovina, Dragana Antešević (34), tragically died during the fire itself. Later, retired firefighter Drago Lelas (79), Katica Nikolić (58), Ivana Kovačić (41), a 70-year-old man who was being treated at KBC Split, and the 66-year-old woman who died two days ago also succumbed to their injuries.

the question of responsibility

With each new victim, the importance of answering the question of how the fire started and whether anyone bears responsibility for the tragedy grows further. The question of the warning system’s response also remains open, because the SRUUK system was not activated during the fire. The system was introduced precisely so that citizens in crisis situations, such as major fires, floods, earthquakes or other immediate dangers, would receive timely warnings and instructions on how to protect themselves. The heartbroken families of the deceased and the public are therefore still waiting for the results of the investigation, as well as an answer to the question of whether all available mechanisms for warning the population were used on the night of the fire.

World.title: Karmen Turk: Why Estonia's gambling license is not attracting foreign operators
World.content:
Estonia has strengthened its regulations through economic and money laundering crises, but along with the rules, the procedural environment has also changed, no longer conforming to good practice but instead deterring international companies, attorney-at-law Karmen Turk writes.

No one is disputing that a gambling operator is required to combat money laundering. The law requires it. The question lies elsewhere: do Estonia's rules prevent money laundering, or do they primarily act as a barrier to new companies coming to Estonia? Unfortunately, experience over the past year points more towards the latter.

The recently amended Remote Gambling Tax Act has brought into focus international opportunities for financing Estonia's state budget and, in particular, sport and culture. The environment here could be attractive given the purpose of an Estonian license is simple: to bring tax revenue earned elsewhere into digitally advanced Estonia. International remote gambling operators will not be targeting Estonian players. Their customers are in other countries, around the world. An Estonian license, however, means that taxes on their activities are paid into Estonia and go towards financing our sports and culture. Every license brought into Estonia is thus a victory for Estonian culture and sports, yet without increasing gambling in Estonia. To achieve this goal, however, companies need to actually come to Estonia. But what is deterring companies today? The simple answer is: fear-driven regulation that diminishes the legal opportunities created in Estonia, because every applicant is treated primarily as a potential risk.

To explain in more detail, a gambling operating license is issued by the Tax and Customs Board (MTA), but it must first be approved by the Financial Intelligence Unit (FIU). The applicant must submit their internal anti-money laundering regulations, appoint a person who will communicate with the FIU (the so-called contact person), and submit documents concerning its owners and managers. Companies already operating must meet these requirements by January 1, 2027, at the latest. Gambling operators are now essentially treated in the same way as financial companies and cryptocurrency firms are. The purpose of stricter rules is understandable. The problem lies in how they get applied in practice.

The contact person must work in Estonia

Under current law, the contact person must be working on a permanent basis in Estonia. The FIU's training materials even state that "the entire department should be located in Estonia." In addition, the contact person must have suitable education, experience and an impeccable reputation, while the FIU must approve their appointment.

What does our regulation mean for an international company? Usually, the people responsible for its anti-money laundering controls work in the same location as its IT and payments teams would do, for example in Latvia, Italy or Malta. In order to obtain an Estonian license, however, it must find someone who works in Estonia, understands the risks of the gambling sector and passes the FIU's checks. The FIU has also indicated that one person may serve as a contact person for no more than two companies, and must have a replacement during vacation periods. In reality, consequently, one contact person is not sufficient; two experts meeting the same criteria are needed – but this is an over-regulation of the requirements. Estonia is small and there are few such specialists. This is as a result not merely a formality, but a real barrier to market entry.

Where the contact person sits says nothing about the quality of their work. The FIU's own updated guidelines do not mention location either. They require the contact person to report directly to the management board, to be competent and to have access to all the necessary information at all times. Even an entire department can serve as the contact person. None of these conditions depends on the country. On the contrary, actual knowledge and control are more effective when they are "close" to the operations themselves. According to the FIU's own data, the sector's real weakness is also the detection of suspicious transactions. In 2025, only about 14 percent of reports were related to genuine suspicions, while nearly 94 percent of all reports came from only about a tenth of all companies. This problem is solved by a good monitoring system and a skilled team, not by whether the contact person sits in Tallinn or in Rome. If a company's international team is stronger than an individual specialist who can be found in Estonia, the Estonian requirement may n fact weaken controls. This also raises a question of EU law. Companies with Estonian licenses often belong to groups managed in other EU countries and mainly serve foreign customers. The EU guarantees companies the right to operate and provide services in other member states. The European Court of Justice has allowed countries to restrict gambling, but only if the restriction has good grounds, genuinely helps achieve its objective, is applied consistently and does not go further than necessary. Estonia's location requirement is questionable in light of the last two conditions. First, it is not consistent: according to the FIU's guidelines, customers from other EU countries are considered lower risk, but a specialist working in another EU country is considered a risk. Second, less restrictive solutions exist. It would be sufficient for the contact person to be available at all times, communicate with the FIU in Estonian and ensure that the FIU has access to the data. In addition, a uniform EU anti-money laundering regulation will take effect on July 10, 2027. It is therefore appropriate to ask whether Estonia's additional requirements, which the EU does not demand, are even still necessary.

Documents must be in Estonian

The second obstacle is the language requirement. According to the experiences of companies, the FIU requires internal rules and other documents be in Estonian. It is natural that communication with the authority would take place in Estonian. However, an international company's internal rules are an everyday working tool. They are used by employees in various countries and so get written in a language that everyone understands. If a separate Estonian-language version has to be prepared for Estonia, two documents are created: one that is actually used at work and another that is shown to the authority. This contradicts the FIU's own objective, however. The FIU will check exactly whether the rules are actually being used or exist only on paper. The updated guidelines state that the rules must be understandable to employees and describe what the company actually does. In the case of customer documents, the guidelines themselves recommend avoiding translation if the original is in a comprehensible language, such as English. There is no requirement in the guidelines for internal rules to be in Estonian. The obligation to translate does nothing to help combat money laundering.

A procedure whose duration and outcome are unknown

In 2024, the Chancellor of Justice examined the FIU's licensing procedures and identified several problems. First, the FIU does not tell applicants when all their documents are in order. As a result, applicants do not know when the statutory 60-day deadline for making a decision starts. Second, in the course of an interview, an applicant may be advised to replace the contact person, an owner or a management board member, or to withdraw the application, but these interviews are not logged in the minutes. Based on the experiences of several companies from 2026, these interviews have gone on for hours, with three to four officials questioning one person all at the same time. For a company planning investments in Estonia, uncertainty of this kind is the worst possible signal. An official refusal can be challenged in court. However, if the outcome of the procedure depends on interviews that are not recorded in minutes, the company will simply choose another country where the procedure is clear and predictable.

Rules must be based on actual risks

The state fully knows what the sector's risks are. According to the national risk assessment, the money laundering risk posed by gambling operators is high because Estonian licenses are used mainly to serve foreign customers and business partners are often located abroad. The FIU focuses on the origin of funds, the use of front persons, the splitting of transactions and cryptocurrency. These are the right issues. But having the contact person live in Estonia or the rules written in Estonian does nothing to counter these risks. What is needed is good transaction monitoring, rapid information exchange and access to data for the FIU. The latter is already guaranteed by law, even when the server is located abroad.

The law itself requires proportionality: the extent of controls must correspond to the risk and be reasonable. The same should apply to the state when it decides what to require of a new market entrant. Penalties are already severe: a fine of up to €1 million can be imposed for violating the requirements for internal rules.

Estonia does not have to choose between strict anti-money laundering controls and an attractive license in order to regulate the market and generate tax revenue. But the success of controls must be measured by whether they stop suspicious money flows. Neither an office address in Tallinn nor the language of the documentation demonstrates this.

The author of this piece advises international gambling operators.

World.title: Almost 400 migrants detained in Estonia since July
World.content:
Since July, the Police and Border Guard Board (PPA) has detained 388 foreign nationals who arrived in Estonia without a legal basis after crossing the Belarusian border. Detentions in recent weeks have taken place exclusively in Tallinn.

As of Tuesday, 258 foreign nationals were being held at the detention center in Tallinn, while 148 people who entered the European Union via the Belarus-Latvia border have been handed over to Latvia.

"Each handover is essentially a logistical operation, the success of which requires verified information about the foreign nationals' routes, origins and intentions, as well as agreements between the authorities of both countries," said Indrek Aru, head of the border guard bureau at the PPA's Northern Prefecture.

Foreign nationals are transported back in groups.

Fifteen people are suspected of organizing illegal migration.

Medical attention

Detainees at the detention center have also sought medical attention due to health problems, including cold-like symptoms and skin rashes.

"Foreign nationals with high fevers were taken to West Tallinn Central Hospital, which provides healthcare services to the detention center. As of today, one foreign national remains hospitalized, and it is known that they will be able to return to the detention center in the coming days," Aru noted.

The hospital does not provide the detention center with detailed information about tests carried out or diagnoses.

"Due to personal data protection requirements, diagnoses are not disclosed to the detention center, but in the event of a health risk, the center's staff receive all the necessary information from medical professionals to immediately implement measures to limit the spread of disease, including isolation or quarantine," Aru said.

World.title: Tallinn mulling 1+1 and 2+1 lane options for Tulika tänav renovation
World.content:
Preliminary designs have been released for the renovation of Tulika tänav and the section of Paldiski maantee that intersects with it in Tallinn's Kristiine district, and the street will be rebuilt with either 1+1 or 2+1 traffic lanes.

Ahead of the renovation of Tulika tänav, which connects the Kristiine traffic junction and the Sõle intersection, Tallinn is considering two options: rebuilding the street with either 1+1 or 2+1 traffic lanes.

Both solutions will include new sidewalks, cycle paths and street greenery. A traffic study has been carried out to find a suitable solution, and the final choice will be made after assessing spatial possibilities and the needs of different modes of transport.

Tallinn Deputy Mayor Kristjan Järvan (Isamaa) said that he and Tallinn Deputy Mayor Joel Jesse (Center) prefer the 2+1 option.

"Our clear view is that this location cannot accommodate a 1+1 solution, and our firm preference is 1+2," he noted.

However, no decision has yet been made. "When making the final decision, we will naturally take residents' feedback into account," Järvan said.

The reconstruction will also include the renovation of water supply and sewerage facilities, the construction of a separate stormwater drainage system and improvements to street lighting.

Feedback on both options can be submitted until November 10.

World.title: Swedbank lays off 100 in Baltic states, warns AI could mean more cuts
World.content:
Swedbank is laying off around 100 staff in Estonia and the other Baltic states, while the bank says Artificial Intelligence (AI) could lead to further layoffs in future.

Swedbank CEO Olavi Lepp said the company is laying off employees across the entire group, meaning both in the Baltic states and in its home nation, Sweden, with redundancies to total around 500.

"Naturally, in the process, we are also offering existing employees the opportunity to retrain for other roles, but this does not suit everyone and, unfortunately, layoffs are also needed," he said.

Lepp added that Swedbank employs more than 6,000 people in the Baltic states, of whom around 100 have been laid off. The layoffs are linked to a general restructuring of work and investments in development, he went on.

Lepp explained that when the bank experienced a period of very high profitability a few years ago, it decided to invest more in IT development and data modeling, adding some of the aims have been accomplished. "Today, when profitability is at normal levels, we do not need as many people," he said, adding that when development work is not being carried out on a large scale, it makes no sense to retain employees at the same level.

Lepp said in any case there will certainly be jobs in the future that require fewer people. "Then it depends on the company's own sales and strategy what it does next: whether it reduces the number of employees or tries to increase business volumes with its existing workforce."

He added that it is currently unclear whether companies developing AI will meet investors' expectations on profitability. "The big question is that when they become profitable, meaning they start charging the proper price for their services, how much will the software licenses and tokens that we pay AI companies for then cost?"

There are currently more than 90 applications across the Swedbank group in which AI is being tested. Lepp said that so far as Estonia goes, the primary objective is to do more business with the same number of people — increasing business capacity and market share, and in some contexts reducing costs.

In implementing AI, a company needs to carry out a standard cost comparison, and if using tokens is cheaper than employing people, layoffs or retraining will probably follow. "I would say that when it comes to tasks governed by fairly formal logic, the capabilities of artificial intelligence are certainly much greater than those of humans in a great many cases," Lepp went on.

The bigger question, he added, is whether there will be customers from whom profits can be earned. "There have to be people somewhere who consume these services, and they, too, have to earn their income from somewhere," Lepp noted.

Swedbank's net profit in Estonia for the first nine months of this year came to €193 million, €2 million more than in the same period in 2025.

World.title: Estonian foreign minister briefed on Norway-Finland call with Putin
World.content:
Minister of Foreign Affairs Margus Tsahkna (Eesti 200) said he had been briefed on Tuesday's call between the leaders of Norway and Finland and Russia's President Vladimir Putin.

A statement from the Finnish president's office described the call as "a follow-up of the meeting in Oslo on October 20 and held in consultation with Ukraine."

The call was initiated by Finland and Norway, which border Russia, and its aim "was to convey messages directly regarding future negotiations to help to end the war to President Putin." The statement said it was related to the upcoming meetings in Abu Dhabi between Russia and Ukraine.

While Denmark's Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen was critical of Tuesday's call, Tsahkna said that only increased pressure on Russia will make it take peace negotiations seriously.

He added that there is currently no indication whatsoever that Russia has changed its strategic objectives or is genuinely interested in negotiations.

Only increased pressure on Russia will make it take peace negotiations seriously. Every contact with Russia must convey Europe's unity and determination to support Ukraine and maintain pressure on Russia, while making clear that Europe will not negotiate away the fundamental principles underpinning its security. Ukraine wants peace, and Estonia supports all efforts to achieve it. But there is no indication that Russia has changed its strategic objectives or is genuinely interested in negotiations. Russia's goal is not merely to seize parts of Ukraine, but to subjugate the entire country and undermine Europe's security order, founded on NATO and the EU. A just and lasting peace requires increased pressure on Russia, tighter sanctions, action against sanctions evasion, Russia's international isolation and unwavering support for Ukraine. We must show Russia through concrete action that, as long as its war continues, pressure will remain strong and Ukraine's supporters will not abandon it. — Margus Tsahkna (@Tsahkna) October 27, 2026

Putin believes that Western support for Ukraine may weaken, which is why he remains motivated to continue the war, Tsahkna said.

"As long as Putin believes that time is on his side, he will continue the war," the minister said, referencing Russia's recent attacks on Kyiv and other Ukrainian cities.

He added that it was important to Estonia that every contact with Russia conveys Europe's unity and determination to support Ukraine and maintain pressure on Russia.

"It is also important to make clear that Europe will not negotiate over the fundamental principles underpinning its security arrangements. These include the principles of sovereignty and territorial integrity, the understanding that borders cannot be changed by force, and every country's right to decide its own security arrangements," he added.

The eight Nordic and Baltic countries are some of the strongest supporters of Ukraine and often coordinate positions and release joint statements.

World.title: Estonia has run out of asphalt, says Tallinn deputy mayor
World.content:
Estonia is experiencing a shortage of asphalt as factories in Sweden and Lithuania are currently not supplying it to the country, Deputy Mayor Kristjan Järvan (Isamaa) has said

"I have to start with some sad news. Namely, Estonia has run out of asphalt," Järvan said at a Tallinn city government press conference on Tuesday.

The official said Estonia usually imports bitumen from two sources in Sweden and Lithuania.

"And for reasons still unknown, the Swedish company decided not to bring any more. It said that the ship that arrived three weeks ago would be the last this year. The next one will come in the spring. The Lithuanian company was delighted, immediately raised its prices, and then its factory broke down. This means that asphalt plants in Estonia can no longer obtain bitumen," the deputy mayor said.

Kristjan Järvan Source: Ken Mürk/ERR

"What this means nationally is that those construction companies that have their own asphalt plants probably have their own contracts covered and, as usual, any surplus asphalt is put on the open market," he added.

Tallinn is affected by the issue as the second supplementary budget set aside money for roadworks this autumn.

"Now both of the City of Tallinn's partners have said that, unfortunately, the market situation is such that asphalt is simply unavailable. And this means that we are in a situation where we can happily announce that we have asphalt for resurfacing Liivalaia. We have to take a positive view of what we have," Järvan said.

Asphalting work on Liivalaia began on Monday, and Tallinn will grant an additional two weeks for this work, the deputy mayor added.

"But this also means that we will not take the risk of milling up Viljandi maantee and Vabaõhumuuseumi tee to lay new asphalt there. We will still avoid a situation where we have streets dug up for the winter and no asphalt to put down in their place," Järvan said.

World.title: Christopher Moseley, champion of Estonian literature in English, dies
World.content:
Christopher Moseley, the Australian-born translator and language teacher who devoted his career to bringing Estonian, Latvian and Nordic literature to English-language readers, has died. He was 76.

Moseley was born in Australia and came to Britain in 1974 to study Scandinavian languages, but his interests soon moved somewhat eastwards to Finland and the Baltic states, even while the latter countries were still shackled under the Soviet occuption.

He studied Finno-Ugric languages in Finland and the UK, and his fieldwork on Livonian between 1987 and 1993 was his first direct work with a minority language. It led to his Master's thesis at the School of Slavonic and East European Studies (SSEES), part of the University College London (UCL), and later to his book Livonian (2002).

He also authored the Estonian language installment of British publisher Routledge's "Colloquial" range, and co-authored its Latvian course too.

For many years he taught Estonian language and Baltic literature at SSEES and UCL, along with evening courses in Estonian and Latvian. He also worked as a translator and journalist specializing in Baltic affairs at BBC Monitoring for nearly two decades, before becoming a freelance translator and editor.

Moseley's own translations from Estonian into English included A.H. Tammsaare's classic "Põrgupõhja uus Vanapagan", Andrus Kivirähk's "The Man Who Spoke Snakish", Indrek Hargla's "Apothecary Melchior" series, and Ilmar Taska's "Pobeda 1946". His final translation, Rein Raud's "The Sun Script", was published by Norvik Press just this year.

From 2008 Moseley was General Editor of UNESCO's Atlas of the World's Languages in Danger, which became a key reference for the world's threatened languages. He was also a dedicated member of the Foundation for Endangered Languages.

In 2018, he was one of the speakers at the opening of the University of Latvia's Livonian Institute.

The Estonian Literature Center remembered Chris as a warm and friendly person with unceasing passion for languages and literature.

World.title: Estonian media association: Meta is planning the largest theft of content
World.content:
Estonian media companies have warned US tech giant Meta's new business terms would let it use news content without consent or payment.

The companies are urging the European Commission to intervene over the terms, due originally to take effect October 30.

The Commission says Meta has postponed them to 20 November, following discussions, but the Estonian Association of Media Companies (Eesti meediaettevõtete liit) says the delay changes little.

The Estonian Association of Media Companies has appealed to policymakers and regulators over Meta's new business terms, which would require business users — including news publishers — to grant Meta permission to access their web content by automated software. Meta could then index, store, search and update that content for its business purposes, without separate permission or payment.

Meta initially sought the right to use content for AI training. After publisher protests, it removed the word "training," but the association says the remaining terms are broad enough to permit AI-related use anyway.

In the association's view the terms threaten media business models, as Meta could build competing products from journalistic content without paying for it. Publishers now face a choice: allow the use of their content, or lose a key channel for reaching readers.

Media association board member Väino Koorberg called the development potentially the largest theft of content, while in the U.S., the News/Media Alliance, representing nearly 2,000 American publishers, has written Meta founder Mark Zuckerberg, demanding the terms be withdrawn. A further four European publishers' organizations have approached the Commission with similar concerns.

Väino Koorberg. Source: Priit Mürk/ERR

"In European Union terms, Meta is a so-called major gatekeeper, on whose activities the visibility of others hinges, hence why stricter rules have been established for them," Koorberg said.

He added that Meta is also testing restrictions on link sharing on Facebook. "Only two links can be shared free of charge during a month," he said, which serves to limit the platform as a marketing channel.

The association says the situation threatens access to reliable information: more than half of people get daily news from social media, and reduced visibility for journalism could increase vulnerability to disinformation.

Koorberg said Estonia should send a clear message. "For example, state institutions can end cooperation with Meta and leave those platforms, because the change in terms also affects them," he said.

Elis Paemurd, deputy head of the European Commission Representation in Estonia, said Meta had postponed the terms to November 20 following discussions, adding that the Commission is ensuring Meta complies with EU law, including the prohibition on abuse of a dominant position.

Koorberg said the delay does not mean media have escaped. "Meta itself explains that it wants to specify and clarify how the terms should be interpreted," he said, adding that it may be a step toward neutralizing possible legal action. The association has told members to follow developments closely, and that the most extreme step would be to end all cooperation with Meta's products.

Estonian media companies have warned US tech giant Meta's new business terms would let it use news content without consent or payment.
