World.title: Month after Russia’s ban on Georgian drinks, Russian experts to inspect laboratories in Georgia: what are risks?
World.content:
Russia’s Rosselkhoznadzor to inspect Georgian laboratories

From 2 November 2026, specialists from Russia’s agricultural watchdog, Rosselkhoznadzor, will visit Georgia to inspect Georgian laboratories, the agency said in a statement.

The Russian specialists will examine Georgia’s phytosanitary certification system for fruit and other plant products intended for export to Russia. They will also inspect a laboratory that tests such products for pesticide and agrochemical residues.

Phytosanitary certification confirms that plant-based products meet the requirements of the importing country. Laboratory tests for pesticide and agrochemical residues, meanwhile, detect the presence of these chemicals in products.

According to Rosselkhoznadzor, the visit follows an invitation from Georgia’s National Food Agency. The agency said the aim was to develop a common approach to monitoring products subject to quarantine controls.

The Russian agency did not specify which laboratory its specialists would visit. It also remains unclear whether the inspection will lead to any changes in the conditions for exporting Georgian products to Russia.

The Georgian side has yet to provide official information. Georgia’s National Food Agency promised JAMnews it would clarify the details, but subsequently stopped answering calls.

Background: the context for the planned visit by Russian specialists to Georgia

The planned inspection of laboratories in Georgia coincides with Russia’s ban on imports of several Georgian-made drinks.

The restrictions cover both alcoholic and non-alcoholic beverages. They affect seven major Georgian companies, including producers of Coca-Cola and Nabeglavi water in Georgia. The companies affected by the ban account for around 75–80% of Georgia’s wine exports to Russia. Russia’s embargo on Georgian drinks came into force on 10 October.

Later, from 20 to 22 October, Rosselkhoznadzor specialists visited Tbilisi to attend a regional seminar organised by the World Organisation for Animal Health. During the visit, they also discussed bilateral co-operation with representatives of Georgia’s National Food Agency.

Following these meetings, Rosselkhoznadzor announced on 22 October that it would allow two Georgian dairy processors to access the Russian market from November. The agency also said it was ready to inspect six Georgian fish and seafood producers interested in exporting their products to Russia.

The statement also noted a 26% increase in Russian exports of live pigs to Georgia, while onion supplies had tripled. Meanwhile, Georgia’s exports to Russia of products such as blueberries, apples, plums and mandarins continue to grow.

Figs are among the products whose exports to Russia are also increasing.

According to Rosselkhoznadzor, Russia had imported 70,500 tonnes of fruit and vegetables from Georgia by 24 October 2026.

Imports increased across several product categories:

Nectarines — 17,900 tonnes, up 7.8%;

Apples — 15,300 tonnes, up 17.5%;

Blueberries — 9,500 tonnes, up 46.7%;

Plums — 6,700 tonnes, up 74.2%;

Mandarins — around 3,400 tonnes, up 59%;

Figs — more than 1,900 tonnes, up 21.2%;

Watermelons — 1,400 tonnes, up 59.5%.

What are the risks? — expert assessments

Khatia Dekanoidze, one of the leaders of the Unity – National Movement party, sees the invitation to Russian specialists as a sign that relations with Moscow are entering a new phase.

In her view, the decision raises questions about the reliability of Georgia’s own inspection systems. It also gives Russia additional leverage to exert economic pressure on the country.

“How can you invite a Russian expert to Georgia and give them the authority to inspect our products? What does this tell us? That they do not trust the food safety standards we have established ourselves. It also makes Georgia’s economy even more dependent on Russia. We know that Russia turns economic leverage into a tool of blackmail — as it demonstrated just a few weeks ago when it imposed an embargo on goods produced in Georgia.”

Teona Akubardia, a security expert, also points to risks to national security. She says Russia could selectively restrict access to its market for Georgian products and use that leverage for political purposes.

“There is a risk that Russia will be able to grant or deny access to its market at its own discretion. The state will have no means of protecting itself. With the process of integration with the West frozen, Russia will use this leverage even more actively for political purposes, seeking to bring Georgia fully under its control. This poses a threat to national security. Moreover, the Georgian Dream party is not only failing to neutralise this threat but is creating additional risks under the current circumstances.”

Russia’s Rosselkhoznadzor to inspect Georgian laboratories

World.title: Views from Abkhazia on the campaign in Turkiye to end Abkhazia’s isolation
World.content:
Türkiye and Abkhazia

A public campaign entitled “Let’s end the isolation of Abkhazia” has been underway in Türkiye since late June 2026. The main initiators are activists from the Abkhaz diaspora in Türkiye, as well as representatives of Circassian civic circles. The initiative received support from Türkiye’s Labour Party, EMEP (Emek Partisi).

Subsequently, the campaign gained the support of representatives of several Turkish opposition parties: DEM Parti (the Peoples’ Equality and Democracy Party), TİP (the Workers’ Party of Türkiye), Yeni Parti (the New Party), DEVA (the Democracy and Progress Party), Saadet Partisi (the Felicity Party), Gelecek Partisi (the Future Party), and Yeni Yol, a parliamentary group bringing together members of parliament from several parties.

On 5 August 2026, representatives of these political forces took part in a joint press conference. Their appeal called on Ankara to take the following steps:

To reconsider its policy towards Abkhazia;

To recognise Abkhaz passports as valid documents for crossing the Turkish border;

To restore direct maritime links between Türkiye and Abkhazia;

To establish direct air links;

To consider recognising Abkhazia’s independence.

Turkish MPs at a joint press conference, 5 August 2026

The campaign has received relatively limited and superficial coverage in the Abkhaz media. It could be said that the local political leadership and media have largely paid little attention to this process.

We present the comments of several local experts on this issue. The following key points emerge from their responses.

Questions for the experts and their answers:

Question: Since August, the campaign “Let’s Put an End to Abkhazia’s Isolation” has been underway in Türkiye. It aims to establish direct transport links between Abkhazia and Türkiye and to have the Abkhaz passport recognized as a valid document for entering Türkiye. In your view, how could Abkhazia help bring this initiative to fruition? Should we provide more active support to our compatriots participating in the campaign?

Respondent 1: Without a doubt, we should support them more actively, and this support should be evident at every level and across all segments of Abkhaz society.

I also believe it is extremely important to communicate the unequivocal benefits that such an outcome would bring to all residents of Abkhazia. At present, there is a sense that it is primarily ethnic Abkhaz who support this initiative. No real effort is being made to explain the prospects that would open up for all residents of Abkhazia if this issue were resolved positively.

There are apparently no such materials, or almost none – I do not know, as I have not come across any serious analytical publications—that, for example, demonstrate the prospects for economic and cultural de-isolation or the opportunities this would create for young people, including access to education and knowledge.

Broadly speaking, the Republic of Türkiye itself remains a closed subject in Abkhazia. In other words, on the one hand, we want to end Abkhazia’s isolation from Türkiye, but perhaps, in this case, it would make sense to turn the question around and ask: how much do Turkish citizens actually know about Abkhazia?

I am afraid that today Turkish citizens may know more about Abkhazia than Abkhaz citizens know about Türkiye. Perhaps I am exaggerating somewhat, but this is the essence of what I am trying to say: paradoxical as it may sound, we too must take steps to “de-isolate” Türkiye from our side, in its relationship with us.

I believe this would be an honest conversation: a process of reaching out to one another, in which we also make genuine efforts. Just as Turkish politicians, public figures, and our compatriots are working towards this from their side, we must do everything we can on our side to open Türkiye up to Abkhaz citizens. What do we actually know about Türkiye, apart from a few clichés? Very little, really. I therefore believe there is a great deal that could be done in this regard, including, incidentally, in terms of building grassroots connections and fostering early forms of cooperation – for example, with Turkish medical professionals.

Respondent 2: In any case, the state must do everything in its power, first, to overcome Abkhazia’s isolation and, second, to secure the broadest possible international recognition of its statehood. In this regard, I would not separate the citizens from the state: it was these very citizens who once determined which state they wanted to live in.

This is consistent with the principles underpinning our vision of statehood. Therefore, the state, through its authorities, should be guided by these principles as a matter of course and take every possible step in this direction on all international platforms.

Respondent 3: I believe Abkhazia could work within Abkhaz society to explain what isolation means and how ending that isolation could tangibly change people’s lives and improve the quality of life for Abkhazia’s population. It seems to me that a more detailed discussion could be held within the country, involving different groups and taking place across various media platforms and at the university. The aim would be to convey the meaning and importance of this initiative for Abkhazia—that is, the normalization of Abkhazia’s presence on the world stage.

Furthermore, in my view, the outcomes of these discussions must also be communicated to our compatriots. Simply talking about the issue and reposting content is one thing; receiving support and feedback from Abkhazia is quite another. Without such support and feedback, it is very difficult to sustain this process and expand it on a larger scale.

Question: The campaign is receiving virtually no coverage in the official Abkhaz media. What do you think might account for this?

Respondent 1: As for the campaign that our media are not covering, I think the reason is parochialism. It is becoming increasingly prevalent in our politics.

Sadly, there has been a lack of grand ideas, accompanied in recent years by persistent lamentations, particularly on the part of former President Bzhania. This tendency began earlier and continues today, but it was neither as pronounced nor as absolute as it was under him: “We are worthless; we can do nothing on our own; we are led by the hand; we do not know how to do anything; we have to look to someone else for guidance.” We spend a great deal of time looking to others for direction, and those who are always looking up to someone else never look around them. They do not merely fail to see beyond the tip of their own nose—they cannot see beyond someone else’s mouth. And that is how the whole situation unfolds.

Why should we look for a long-term perspective? Why should we think about a national strategy? Why should we concern ourselves with anything that cannot be put into our pockets or into our mouths here and now, allowing us to live comfortably and happily for the next few days, perhaps weeks, perhaps months, provided we are allowed to do so and behave ourselves?

In the case of this initiative, there is a sense that someone might decide we are not behaving properly. And in these mind games about what is right and what is wrong, unfortunately, the machine wins.

In Abkhaz politics, the “mammon” – the cult of money and material wealth – has now definitively and irreversibly gained the upper hand, not throughout the entire political landscape, but certainly within its mainstream. This is what drives the Abkhaz establishment today, and not just the establishment: many voters, too, are sending unmistakable signals to this effect. Thank goodness, not all of them, but many.

And so we are struggling to follow the prescribed course of “proper behaviour” – in other words, the path of Pavlov’s dogs. We are finding it difficult and encountering obstacles, but, with considerable effort, we are still moving along that path.

Apparently, this initiative is particularly unwelcome to people of this kind because it pulls them away from that trend. It shows that if you demonstrate willpower – even a minimal amount – and stand up to circumstances that may seem insurmountable, you can still achieve results.

Suddenly, we begin to remember something that, by today’s standards, seems almost subversive: we resisted Georgian aggression, stood our ground, and won in a way that, by today’s standards, would be extraordinary and inexplicable. In other words, it seems that today’s Abkhaz establishment does not even ask itself what decisions its members would have made under those circumstances. Sadly, today we have neither Vladislav Ardzinba nor Zurab Achba nor Yuri Voronov. We have grown smaller in stature, and our political class has diminished along with us.

Respondent 2: I think these are the usual complexes stemming from last year’s presidential election and the tone adopted during the election campaign: smear tactics and so on. At the time, people who opposed the authorities or did not belong to their camp of supporters were branded as Turkish agents.

For example, a story was vigorously promoted claiming that opposition candidate Ardzinba was the candidate of some mythical pro-Turkish forces. Everyone knew this was nothing more than the kind of lie commonly encountered in election campaigns. Nevertheless, I think the myth worked.

Now everyone is afraid of being labelled as part of pro-Turkish forces, against the backdrop of current geopolitical developments, when there is a lack of trust in all the players involved. In a situation where Russia is confronting half the world, all sorts of phobias emerge. The West is indeed probably Russia’s number-one enemy, and the European Union unconditionally supports Ukraine. But there are also regional players about whom questions are raised and towards whom a shadow of mistrust also persists.

In this context, Türkiye is also perceived as a rival, and any discussion of policies that our authorities might pursue on Turkish territory is likely to be viewed as ambiguous or open to suspicion. That is probably why our authorities are being so cautious.

Respondent 3: In my view, this is extremely important, and this point leads directly to the second question. On the one hand, of course, we need to maintain a balance. As we understand it, any expression of Abkhaz presence on the international stage invariably provokes a negative reaction from the Georgian authorities, who then use every means at their disposal, fair or otherwise, to try to obstruct it.

Consequently, this process needs to be discussed and covered in the Abkhaz media, but certain issues must be approached strategically. It would probably be worth maintaining some distance and making it clear that this is a process initiated by our compatriots, who are citizens of the Republic of Türkiye today, and that it is their own initiative. Naturally, these efforts need to be coordinated, and there must be communication with Abkhazia, their historical homeland.

At the same time, to safeguard this process, it is both possible and necessary to strike a strategic balance and, at times, wait for the right moment. As I have already said, discussions within Abkhazia about de-isolation itself and its benefits for Abkhazia could be pursued more actively. I always say that our main goal is comprehensive and all-encompassing international recognition. But to achieve that, we need a process through which we can attain short- and medium-term objectives.

At present, in my view, the de-isolation of Abkhazia is primarily humanitarian in nature. If implemented properly, it would resolve a vast number of problems: it would provide mobility and create opportunities for Abkhazia to be represented and heard.

Question: Outside Abkhazia, some commentators have suggested that the campaign may pursue political as well as humanitarian objectives. To what extent do you consider this view justified?

Respondent 1: In this case, we are seeing doubts being cast on the sincerity of the message conveyed by the initiators of the campaign to end Abkhazia’s isolation in the Republic of Türkiye. One is tempted to say that the guilty person’s hat is on fire. In other words, who, exactly, is criticizing this initiative? As the saying goes, let the one who is without sin cast the first stone.

All of this is nothing more than a political charade and an unworthy act of manipulation—something that does not deserve even the slightest attention from us. We should understand just one thing: if this initiative irritates someone deeply, if someone categorically opposes it and frantically searches for arguments to denounce, ridicule, or belittle it, that is a clear sign that the initiative is touching on someone’s political interests.

Today, just as we have throughout the past several decades, we find ourselves at the height of a political struggle for our future, for our very survival as a nation. Attempts have been made to impose a policy of erasure on us since Soviet times, and we have been resisting Georgian nationalism for many years. Today, other problematic factors are also becoming entangled with this phenomenon, against which our people have had to resist to the best of their ability.

Since 1992, this resistance has taken on an unmistakably armed character, and we stood our ground back then. Those who now criticize, ridicule, and belittle this idea of ending isolation from various directions are certainly not our friends. At the very least, I would view with considerable suspicion anyone who tries to undermine this initiative: who are they, what do they stand for, and how do they present themselves? How should we identify and characterize these individuals who stand apart from the rest, whether in the future or even now? More likely, we are dealing with a systematic approach, because certain trends point to a serious danger: the danger that many of the actors around us may find themselves facing an Abkhazia that is more sovereign—truly sovereign—and more independent.

For many people, and unfortunately not only external actors but also the various political figures who have proliferated within the country, this prospect may be hard to swallow. Yet this is an important moment that reminds us of something fundamental: if you are not afraid to act as an independent political actor, you can move mountains. And that is precisely the attitude we should adopt towards this initiative. It should strengthen our belief that we are doing everything right.

Respondent 2: There is always a political dimension behind humanitarian issues. If Turkish politicians begin examining our problem, questions directly related to politics will inevitably arise: Georgian-Abkhaz relations, the war, and the history of the conflict. In any case, it will already have become a political matter. At the same time, the more people talk about Abkhazia, the greater the interest in its history and the current situation in the country, making it increasingly difficult to describe this campaign as purely humanitarian. Politics will always be present, at least indirectly.

I do not see any risks for us. Our situation, so to speak, is at the zero stage, and any movement, however small, is a step forward. Therefore, broadly speaking, I see no risks from the Abkhaz side. Risks could probably arise if this issue became a subject of domestic political debate in Türkiye. But that would be a Turkish problem, although I do not think the Abkhaz issue is so vital to the Turkish political elite. I believe this agenda concerns primarily representatives of the Abkhaz diaspora and perhaps the Circassian and other Caucasian diasporas, but little beyond that.

On the other hand, in the current context, when the world is undergoing a new division of spheres of influence and new rules are being established, the question of Abkhazia in Türkiye itself may be viewed not only from a humanitarian perspective but also through the lens of geopolitical interests. I do not rule this out at all, given what is happening in Azerbaijan and the development of Türkiye’s relations with the republics of Central Asia and all Turkic-speaking republics, including those located within Russia itself. In this respect, Türkiye may well have interests of its own, and that is perfectly normal.

Respondent 3: This is undoubtedly a humanitarian initiative, but it may also lead to certain political developments, as there will be more direct contacts between Abkhazia and the outside world. What makes the Abkhaz situation unique is that the idea of establishing an independent Abkhaz state is supported not merely by an overwhelming majority, but by the entire population of Abkhazia.

Therefore, whether we want it or not, this idea will continue to move forward. Here, returning to the previous question, we need to safeguard the process strategically so that, by the time it naturally moves into the political sphere, the necessary foundation for discussion will already be in place.

Question: Do you see any signs of a reversal or slowdown in the repatriation process today? If so, what do you think might be causing it?

Respondent 1: To be fair, we have to acknowledge that, in previous years as well, repatriation never became a national project in which our state and society invested serious effort and resources. This was due to a combination of objective and subjective circumstances.

What I want to emphasize is that this very process of de-isolation, which I sincerely hope will prove successful – whether fully or partially – could become a turning point for repatriation. It is also another concrete reason why external actors may find this prospect so unpalatable: each of them seems to dream of seeing fewer Abkhaz people in Abkhazia. They would prefer the Abkhaz to become less numerous and, consequently, more timid; better still, they would like them to forget their very essence, their distinct identity, altogether.

This initiative could turn any underhanded scheme involving apartments and the other tempting benefits that certain external players have in store for us on its head. They all want to grab their share of the pie, but what do they agree on? That the Abkhaz themselves, quite clearly, should have no place in this equation in the twenty-first century.

I very much hope this will not happen, although lately it has become difficult to hope for anything when we look at Palestine, devastated and wiped off the face of the earth. I hope that such a full-scale, deeply entrenched genocide cannot be allowed to happen, and so we are left having to endure the situation.

In this case, then, this is a card that could become a joker. This campaign could become the joker in our deck, capable of trumping the strongest cards held by those who assumed that they would always be able to determine our intentions, our prospects, and our understanding of things – both in the immediate future and for the foreseeable future, perhaps even indefinitely. Yet suddenly, it has turned out that a grassroots initiative launched in another country by our compatriots can take on such a scale and character.

In that sense, this initiative is equivalent to full-fledged repatriation. Moreover, it is an initiative that changes the very meaning of the process. People will no longer have to view repatriation in such stark terms: that they must abandon everything, burn their bridges – at least to a considerable extent – and completely change their lives in order to move to their historical homeland.

In other words, it suddenly becomes clear that repatriation can be carried out in a much more gradual and less disruptive way. This initiative could radically transform the very concept of repatriation. I think that everyone except us has already calculated both the real threats this poses to them and the potential gains it could bring us. But why are we so poor at doing these calculations? Why do we lack proper, comprehensive research, including in the field of internal migration? For example, what demographic groups and social strata do we have? What population movements took place after the war? Who has studied these patterns? Who has examined the specific characteristics of these movements and how people’s ways of life have changed? No one has.

And if this process comes to an end – and I hope it will end successfully – it could turn everything upside down. It is a remarkable thing, but sometimes the effect can be multiplicative, I think, when you finally get off your backside and decide that you need to do something for your country, that you need to take real action. If some Abkhaz people – not all of them, but even a substantial proportion – take this step, and if that substantial group can also rally others around them, as they did before the war, during the pre-war period of 1990, 1991, and 1992, explain the situation, suppress the first signs of arrogant nationalism and chauvinism directed at the Russian-speaking population, and bring them over to their side, then the combined effect would, of course, be extraordinary.

I believe people will very quickly recognize all the benefits they stand to gain when, for example, we are able to trade fully with the Republic of Türkiye. For us today, that would be tantamount to having full-fledged access to the rest of the world.

Respondent 2: I do not think there has been any major overall reversal in repatriation. It seems to me that the issue lies in the capacity of the Abkhaz state itself. There were no large-scale waves of return to the homeland in the past, and it is unlikely that there will be any now.

When the fourth, fifth, or perhaps even sixth generation has lived outside its historical homeland, there needs to be a sufficiently compelling case for people to return. Under current conditions, this means, first, a competitive economy; second, security; and, of course, transport links.

If the initiative pursued by the activists currently working to establish maritime connections succeeds, it could at least accelerate the return of our diaspora to Abkhazia, even if only by a small step. If, however, there were substantial flows of returnees and those flows were being obstructed, then it would be reasonable to speak of deliberate action by the authorities.

But when, by and large, no such flows have existed, it is difficult even to suggest that the authorities are holding anything back. People may think whatever they like privately, but when there are no substantial flows of returnees in the first place, there is simply no visible evidence of any efforts to obstruct them.

Respondent 3: In my view, repatriation is a declared goal of our society, at least in name. But, like many other issues, it has not received the thorough discussion it deserves. There are very successful examples of members of the Abkhaz diaspora—Abkhaz people who lived outside Abkhazia – returning to their historical homeland after 100 to 150 years and becoming fully integrated into our society. Today, Abkhazia is their only homeland. It is a wonderful process.

Unfortunately, there are other examples as well, and our society lacks a clear, unified position on the matter. The absence of integration initiatives is also a factor: we have not created spaces that would allow repatriates to interact normally with ordinary citizens. In my view, there are universal, unwritten principles shared by all Abkhaz people, wherever in the world they may live. These often transcend religious differences and cultural particularities, which may be the first factors influencing how the local population perceives repatriates.

Furthermore, there need to be ongoing support programmes – not simply programmes that provide housing, but ones that enable repatriates to achieve financial stability. It is crucial that people feel they have opportunities to develop and build a future. Abkhazia should not be a place to which someone flees when they encounter problems; it should be a place they actively choose to move to. In my view, this is one of the most important considerations when we plan repatriation and discuss it. Such approaches should probably be applied to the development of our society as a whole.

The terminology, place names and views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial position of this website

World.title: Chinese visitor numbers to Georgia rise by 23% in nine months, setting a record
Iran offers education to Azerbaijani girls in hijabs, Baku calls it interference
World.content:
Iran offers education to Azerbaijani girls

Azerbaijan and Iran have exchanged fresh accusations amid public discontent in parts of Azerbaijani society over new secular school uniform rules that have effectively banned the wearing of hijabs in schools.

Iran has offered to enrol Azerbaijani girls wearing hijabs in Iranian schools and universities. In response, Azerbaijan’s Ministry of Science and Education said the remarks were inappropriate and amounted to an attempt to interfere in the country’s education policy.

The ministry also pointed out that there were no schools or universities in Iran offering education in Azerbaijani, despite the fact that, according to the ministry, around 40 million ethnic Azerbaijanis live in Iran.

“For decades, they have been deprived of the opportunity to receive education in their native language,” Azerbaijan’s Education Ministry said.

Invitation to study extended to schoolchildren

On 22 October, Iran’s Minister of Science, Research and Technology, Hossein Simaei-Sarraf, published a video address inviting Azerbaijani girls to study at Iranian universities. He addressed his appeal to girls who, he said, were being forced to give up wearing hijabs in order to receive an education in Azerbaijan.

On 25 October, Iran’s First Vice-President Mohammad Reza Aref joined the initiative. He called on the ministers of health and education, as well as the head of Islamic Azad University, to make arrangements for admitting schoolchildren and university students from Azerbaijan. The offer, initially limited to higher education, was thus extended to schoolchildren.

However, the specific admission conditions remain unclear. It is not known which educational institutions would accept the students, what language classes would be taught in, who would cover the costs or how accommodation for underage students and their parents would be arranged.

Baku reminds Tehran of Azerbaijani-language education issue

On 26 October, Azerbaijan’s Ministry of Science and Education responded to the Iranian minister’s statement. The ministry described interference in Azerbaijan’s education policy as unacceptable and urged Iranian officials to “deal with their own country’s problems”.

Baku’s main criticism concerns the lack of opportunities to receive education in Azerbaijani in Iran. According to the ministry, there are no schools teaching in Azerbaijani in the country, nor is the language used as a medium of instruction at universities. Baku maintains that ethnic Azerbaijanis living in Iran have been deprived of the opportunity to receive education in their native language for decades.

In response to the neighbouring country’s statements about protecting Azerbaijani girls’ right to education, Baku has raised the issue of the language rights of ethnic Azerbaijanis living in Iran.

A separate practical question concerns the language in which the invited schoolchildren would be taught. While studying abroad in a foreign language is possible, it may require language training and support with adaptation. The Iranian proposal does not specify how the necessary arrangements would be made.

How did dispute over wearing hijabs in Azerbaijan begin?

A new wave of controversy began after Azerbaijan’s Cabinet of Ministers amended school uniform regulations on 21 September. Under the decree, the use of “additional items of clothing that undermine the uniformity of school uniforms and contradict the principle of secular education” is prohibited. Although the hijab is not explicitly mentioned in the document, complaints subsequently emerged that schoolgirls wearing headscarves were being barred from attending classes.

Protests took place at several schools in Baku and other parts of Azerbaijan, involving students and parents. Some students refused to attend classes in solidarity with their classmates who wear hijabs.

Police intervened during the protests. On 12 October, the Interior Ministry reported that 37 people had been detained in connection with incidents following the introduction of the new school uniform rules. According to the ministry, those detained were suspected of disturbing public order. A criminal case was also reportedly opened.

Reports later emerged that another 200 people had been detained after taking part in a protest near the 28 May metro station in Baku. Criminal cases were also reportedly opened against some of them.

Education dispute turns into political row

Iranian officials have presented their initiative as an attempt to help girls wearing hijabs continue their education. However, the link between the offer and restrictions in Azerbaijan gives it a political dimension. Tehran is openly criticising Baku’s education policy and appealing to families dissatisfied with the restrictions.

Azerbaijan’s response also focuses primarily on the political aspect of the issue rather than the conditions for admitting students. Instead of discussing arrangements for their enrolment in Iranian educational institutions, the ministry has accused Tehran of interfering in the country’s internal affairs and highlighted the lack of opportunities for ethnic Azerbaijanis living in Iran to receive education in their native language.

However, the mutual accusations do not resolve either problem. Limited opportunities to receive education in Azerbaijani in Iran do not address complaints about schoolgirls wearing hijabs being barred from attending classes in Azerbaijan. In turn, Iran’s offer does not resolve the issue preventing these girls from continuing their education at their own schools.

World.title: ‘Foreign-controlled spy forces have been eliminated’: Pashinyan on local elections
World.content:
Pashinyan on Armenia’s 2026 local elections

“The ruling Civil Contract party, along with candidates and teams affiliated with it, secured a convincing victory in the local elections,” Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan said during a live broadcast on his Facebook page.

On 25 October, Armenia held local elections in 21 communities. Voters used a proportional representation system in 19 communities and a majoritarian system in the other two.

In five communities — Armavir, Vardenis, Garni, Akhuryan and Vayk — the ruling Civil Contract party ran unopposed.

In other words, no other political forces chose to contest the elections or take part in governing these communities.

According to preliminary results from the Central Electoral Commission, Civil Contract won in 16 communities. The Amerashkhut’yun (Solidarity) bloc secured the most votes in two others. In Stepanavan, the Gortsarar (Entrepreneur) party took the lead. Its list was headed by incumbent community leader Armen Grigoryan, who won the post in 2021 on the Civil Contract party list.

Pashinyan congratulated the candidates for community leadership positions and the ruling party’s teams as a whole on their victory. He stressed that Armenian citizens had helped deliver election results that led to the “destruction of spy opposition forces”. At the same time, he expressed concern about the outcome.

“As someone who became prime minister after the Velvet Revolution, I am far from pleased when a party wins more than 90%, 80% or 70% of the vote in some communities. However appealing such figures may seem at first glance, they evoke certain associations. They also raise questions about the opposition in Armenia. We need to assess this situation correctly. On the one hand, we must completely eradicate the spy opposition in Armenia that takes orders from abroad. On the other hand, Armenia needs an opposition that puts the interests of the state first,” the prime minister said.

Stepanavan records the highest voter turnout

Armenia’s Central Electoral Commission has released the final voter turnout figures. The Lori region community of Stepanavan recorded the highest turnout, at 68.83%.

Other communities also reported high turnout:

Yeghegnadzor (Vayots Dzor region) — 62.56%,

Tsaghkadzor (Kotayk region) — 61.78%,

Meghri (Syunik region) — 57.97%.

The lowest turnout among the 21 communities came in Fioletovo, in the Lori region, at 25.39%.

54 reports of possible violations

During the elections, the Interior Ministry’s 112 Operations Management Centre received 54 reports of possible violations. Investigators have received evidence relating to 10 incidents for preliminary investigation. These include:

one case of breaching ballot secrecy;

one case of obstructing people involved in the elections from exercising their rights or performing their duties;

seven cases of repeat voting or voting on behalf of another person;

one case of voter bribery.

Election observers also reported irregularities. The Akanates (Eyewitness) observation mission recorded 217 potential violations of the electoral process at 137 of the 407 polling stations it visited.

The observers noted crowds gathering at polling stations, risks to ballot secrecy and cases of “family voting”, in which several people enter a voting booth at the same time.

On 24 October, the day before the elections, Armenian media reported the arrests of opposition candidates and their supporters in three of the 21 communities. The Anti-Corruption Committee confirmed the arrests but did not disclose the identities of those detained, citing the interests of the preliminary investigation.

“As part of criminal proceedings launched by the Anti-Corruption Committee over alleged corruption offences linked to the electoral process, investigators are carrying out investigative and other procedural measures in several communities across Armenia,” the committee said.

“We solved one problem, but two or three new ones emerged” — prime minister’s assessment

Continuing his argument that Armenia must “eradicate” an opposition network he describes as a foreign-controlled spy network, the prime minister said: “These local elections have resolved the issue to some extent, but three new challenges have now emerged.”

He was referring in particular to the following questions:

“How can we prevent election results from creating the impression of authoritarianism or dictatorship?

How can we introduce an objective mechanism for public oversight in communities where we have secured a high level of trust?

How can we build an opposition in Armenia that puts the interests of the state first — young, intellectually capable, objective and honest — and answers solely to the will of its voters and citizens?”

Pashinyan stressed that the government must not take part in creating a new opposition, as this would lead to the emergence of a “controlled, fake opposition”.

The prime minister said independent political forces needed to become more active. He added that the government would neither help nor hinder their emergence.

“We want to see a genuine opposition emerge in Armenia — one that acts in the interests of Armenia and its people and is guided by democratic values and principles. We do not want an opposition that bribes voters or channels stolen and misappropriated funds into politics to turn the political sphere into a tool for protecting assets acquired dishonestly.”

In his view, an opposition that puts the interests of the state first could also provide “genuine and constructive oversight” of the government’s actions.

“I want to point out that in communities where the elections did not produce a strong opposition, public oversight remains an open question. I hope that civic groups and representatives of civil society will take on this role.”

Pashinyan on Armenia’s 2026 local elections

World.title: Billionaire Ivanishvili won’t testify in Georgia opposition ban case. Constitutional Court, day four
World.content:
Georgia opposition ban trial

On 26 October, Georgia’s Constitutional Court began substantive hearings on a lawsuit seeking to ban opposition parties.

The lawsuit, signed by 88 MPs from the ruling Georgian Dream party, calls for five opposition parties to be declared unconstitutional and banned: Unity – National Movement, Coalition for Change, Lelo – Strong Georgia, Gakharia for Georgia and the Federalists.

Georgian Dream argues that the parties have violated Article 23 of the constitution, which prohibits political parties whose objectives include overthrowing or forcibly changing the country’s constitutional order. One of the arguments cited in the lawsuit is the parties’ refusal to recognise the legitimacy of the current authorities. The lawsuit also accuses them of organising attempts to overthrow the government. The National Movement faces additional accusations of undermining the country’s independence and violating its territorial integrity. The party is held responsible for the August 2008 war with Russia, when it was in power. All five opposition parties reject the allegations.

The hearing began at 14:00 and continued until 19:00, with a break. The court was due to hear explanations from both sides.

On the first day, the court heard arguments from Georgian Dream and Zaza Bibilashvili, a member of Unity – National Movement.

Bibilashvili presented his party’s position for two and a half hours, and the presiding judge interrupted him several times.

The hearing will resume on 27 October at 12:00 and continue until 30 October. The court must issue its ruling by 24 June 2027.

Below is a brief account of the main developments at the 26 October hearing.

Bidzina Ivanishvili will not be called as a witness

Shortly after the substantive hearing began, the full bench of Georgia’s Constitutional Court announced its decision on a motion filed by the Gakharia for Georgia party.

The motion was partially granted. Constitutional Court judge Revaz Nadaraya said the court had agreed to admit certain types of materials as evidence in the case.



However, the party was denied the right to question politicians as witnesses, including billionaire Bidzina Ivanishvili, founder and honorary chairman of the ruling party, as well as other current and former Georgian Dream leaders.

The court also refused to question Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze, Tbilisi Mayor Kakha Kaladze, former State Security Service chief Mamuka Mdinaradze, MP Archil Talakvadze and others.

This was the 14th and final motion submitted by the opposition parties. The court had rejected the previous 13 motions concerning the questioning of witnesses.

Political statements prohibited

Judge-rapporteur Vasil Roinishvili then presented a brief overview of the lawsuit and its contents.

After his presentation, Judge Revaz Nadaraya once again reminded the parties to refrain from political statements.

Although the case concerns the assessment of political activities and parties, he said, the parties should avoid political statements and speak “with the utmost restraint and propriety, without any insults, so as not to offend the other side”.

After the introductory part, the court began hearing arguments from the parties. The claimant, Georgian Dream, was represented by MP Archil Gorduladze. The defendants are the five opposition parties. On this day, only Zaza Bibilashvili, a member of Unity – National Movement, addressed the court.

What exactly are the opposition parties accused of?

The accusations were presented by Georgian Dream MP Archil Gorduladze, who outlined the allegations against the five opposition parties. According to him:

● Unity – National Movement, Coalition for Change and the Federalists are accused of supporting attempts to overthrow the constitutional order by force.

Gorduladze argued that, during the National Movement’s rule in 2004–2012, they turned a blind eye to systematic human rights violations and acted against Georgia’s independence and territorial integrity by attempting to start a war with Russia in August 2008.

He also accused the party of denying the legitimacy of parliament and government after losing power.

● Lelo – Strong Georgia, led by Mamuka Khazaradze and Badri Japaridze, is accused of denying the legitimacy of the current elected parliament and government. Gorduladze said the party supported the idea of a parallel “technical government” in 2022 and backed attempts to overthrow the government and forcibly change the constitutional order between 2019 and 2025.

The party’s leaders are also accused of refusing to distance themselves from opposition politician Aleksandre Elisashvili, who was convicted over an attempted arson attack on a court building.

● For Georgia, led by former Prime Minister Giorgi Gakharia, is accused of refusing to distance itself from the events of 20 June 2019, when a protest was dispersed, and from the circumstances surrounding the 2021 arrest of Nika Melia, then leader of Unity – National Movement. Gorduladze also alleged that Gakharia denied the legitimacy of the elected government, supported the idea of a “technical government” and attempts to overthrow the constitutional order during protests, and backed foreign forces.

Gakharia is further accused of undermining Georgia’s territorial integrity by unilaterally ordering the establishment of a police checkpoint near the village of Chorchana in the Georgian-Ossetian conflict zone in 2019. A criminal case has been brought against him over the decision, alleging that it sharply escalated tensions in the region and resulted in Georgia losing control over additional territory.

“We have no right to turn a blind eye to these facts and leave future generations a state whose constitutional foundations remain unprotected. That is why the actions of the National Movement and its offshoots [referring to the other four parties named in the lawsuit] must be declared unconstitutional and the parties banned,” Gorduladze said.

“Are you responding to the lawsuit or criticising us?”

Zaza Bibilashvili spoke on behalf of Unity – National Movement. Shortly after he began his statement, Constitutional Court President Revaz Nadaraya interrupted him.

The judge objected to Bibilashvili’s remark that the parties had “no illusions about the outcome of the proceedings”.

Nadaraya interpreted the remark as an insult to the court.

“Are you responding to the lawsuit or criticising us? Are you challenging us, or what? To some extent, indirectly, you insulted the court by questioning our impartiality. You are showing disrespect, and there are limits to that too. Bear that in mind!” he said.

Bibilashvili: “The result will be the legitimisation of Russia’s military aggression in a Constitutional Court ruling”

Zaza Bibilashvili spoke for almost two and a half hours about Unity – National Movement after his opening remarks.

He recalled the difficult socio-economic situation in Georgia in the early 2000s, when the party came to power, and described how developed the country had become by the time Georgian Dream took office in 2012.

Bibilashvili criticised Georgian Dream’s policies and several of its decisions, which he said had harmed the country as a whole.

He also argued that “the actual aim of these proceedings is to give Russia confirmation that its military aggression against Georgia in 2008 was justified, because Georgia’s own Constitutional Court would be arguing that Georgia itself supposedly created the grounds for Russia’s aggression”.

“Some may object that this is not the court’s aim. But it is impossible to dispute that, if the claims in the lawsuit are upheld, the result will be the legitimisation of Russia’s military aggression through a ruling by Georgia’s Constitutional Court,” Bibilashvili said.

He stressed that the claimant, Georgian Dream, was deliberately conflating political and legal responsibility and failing to distinguish between the state and a political party.

Bibilashvili: “The fox brought its own tail as a witness”

Zaza Bibilashvili said the only evidence cited in the lawsuit to prove the opposition parties’ guilt was a report by a temporary parliamentary investigative commission.

According to him, the report contains so many factual and legal errors that it cannot be made public.

Bibilashvili noted that the opposition had effectively been found guilty even before the commission was established, in the explanatory note prepared for its creation.

“This means the outcome was known even before the commission was set up. It’s as if the fox brought its own tail as a witness — that is the essence of these proceedings,” Bibilashvili said.

Bibilashvili: “If the opposition is annulled, it can no longer pose an immediate threat to the state”

Zaza Bibilashvili used a football analogy to question how a championship could ban every team except one from competing.

He said that in a democratic country, banning political parties should not be a form of punishment but a means of protecting the state from an immediate threat posed by those parties. The state must demonstrate that a ban is urgently necessary.

In this case, Bibilashvili argued, the claimant had failed to prove any such necessity.

Moreover, he said, “Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze himself has stated that there is no immediate threat from the opposition and no need to ban it”.

Bibilashvili also urged the court to consider a statement Kobakhidze had made earlier: “Why ban the opposition? It has already been annulled.”

Bibilashvili to judges: “Act in a way you want to be remembered by history”

At the end of his lengthy statement, Zaza Bibilashvili said his closing remarks would be anything but conventional.

“I am not asking you to reject the lawsuit. But act in a way that you want to be remembered by history, in a way you would want your children to see you. Apply the same standards you would want those who come after you to apply to you.

“Servants of authoritarianism often hope that democratic forces will treat them according to democratic standards, rather than the standards they themselves have established. However, after 14 years of Georgian Dream rule, more and more people in Georgian society are rejecting this approach.

“They support the idea that, in future, everyone should be judged by the standards they themselves have established, both politically and legally. This would allow us to break once and for all the so-called vicious circle into which our enemy, Russia, has pushed us.”

Bibilashvili’s remarks once again angered the Constitutional Court judge.

“I told you to behave with dignity! How are we supposed to interpret your statement — as an attempt to put pressure on us?”

“What kind of pressure could I possibly exert on you?” Bibilashvili asked rhetorically.

“Stop lecturing us,” the judge replied.

Zaza Bibilashvili finished his statement at 18:30, with only 30 minutes remaining before the end of the court session. Ana Tsitlidze, another member of Unity – National Movement, was due to speak next, but said she needed more time. The court therefore decided to adjourn.

Hearings on the constitutional lawsuit will resume tomorrow, 27 October, with Tsitlidze’s statement. Proceedings will begin at 12:00, and the court has agreed to sit until 19:00. According to the presiding judge, 20 representatives of the defendant parties are due to speak.

Reactions after the hearing

● After the hearing, Georgian Dream MP Archil Gorduladze said that the National Movement had no evidence to refute the facts presented in the lawsuit:

“The National Movement representative talked about everything and nothing. He claimed that Georgia experienced a triumph of democracy in 2004–2012, and that there was no torture or inhuman treatment.”

● “We heard truly unique accusations against Lelo – Strong Georgia. Apparently, signing the charter proposed by Ex-President Salome Zourabichvili and agreeing to cooperate with Giorgi Gakharia’s party during the municipal elections constitute violations of the Constitution,” said Badri Japaridze, one of the leaders of Lelo – Strong Georgia.

📌 Maia Kopaleishvili, a member of Coalition for Change, said: “We will fully refute all of Georgian Dream’s arguments and unfounded claims. An objective observer will see that Georgian Dream’s lawsuit is political in nature. Its aim is not to uphold the constitutional order in the country, but to eliminate political parties and establish one-party rule. This, of course, contributes to the establishment of a dictatorship in the country.”

News in Georgia

World.title: Turkmenistan’s exchange quotations fall 3.1% to $100.9M
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 28. The total value of external quotations published for the October 17 trading session on SCRMET has decreased by 3.1%.

The figure is calculated by Trend based on official data published by SCRMET (The State Commodity and Raw Materials Exchange of Turkmenistan) on its website.

According to the calculations, the total value of external quotations published for the October 17 trading session has fallen to $100.9 million from $104.2 million the day earlier.

The decrease was driven by the petrochemicals sector, where the total value of external quotations has fallen to $69.9 million from $73.2 million on the session the day earlier. Trend’s calculations show that the figure has fallen by 4.5%.

At the same time, the total value of external quotations in the light industry sector has increased by 2.5% to $2.62 million.

According to Trend’s calculations, the values of the remaining two categories stood unchanged:

- Agriculture - $27 million;

- Mechanical engineering - $1.4 million.

As in the previous session, no quotations were registered for the construction materials sector.

The State Commodity and Raw Materials Exchange of Turkmenistan (SCRMET), established in 1994, is the country’s main organized marketplace for trading commodities and one of the key institutions through which Turkmenistan conducts and facilitates foreign trade. The exchange brings together domestic producers, exporters, and foreign buyers through regular trading sessions, where a range of export-oriented goods are offered and transactions are concluded. Its trading portfolio covers petrochemicals, polymers, textiles, cotton products, construction materials, machinery, and chemical goods, among other commodities.

SCRMET also plays an administrative and information role in Turkmenistan’s trade system. In addition to organizing trading sessions and registering export-import contracts, the exchange publishes official quotations based on transactions conducted on the platform. These quotations provide information on the commodities traded, their values, and the markets involved, making SCRMET data a useful indicator of the composition and direction of exchange-based trade.

Through these quotations, SCRMET provides a snapshot of the value and sectoral composition of goods offered to international buyers during each trading session, reflecting shifts in the country’s export offering and highlighting which industries dominate Turkmenistan’s exchange-based trade.

World.title: Azerbaijan’s voluntary insurance premiums rise 12.6% in nine months
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 28. The volume of voluntary insurance premiums and payouts in Azerbaijan rose by 12.6% and 30.8%, respectively, from January through September 2026.

A total of 992.87 million manat ($584 million) in the mentioned premiums was collected in the reporting period.

According to Trend’s calculations based on data from the Central Bank of Azerbaijan (CBA), this is 111 million manat ($65.29 million) more than in the same period of last year.

Voluntary insurance payouts increased by approximately 178.5 million manat ($105 million) year-on-year to 756.9 million manat ($445.2 million) during the reporting period.

Thus, for every 100 manat ($58.8) in premiums collected in Azerbaijan’s voluntary insurance market from January through September 2026, 76.2 manat ($44.8) was paid back to customers.

The country’s overall insurance market also recorded growth during the reporting period.

From January through September 2026, insurance companies operating in Azerbaijan collected a total of about 1.25 billion manat ($734.4 million) in premiums. This is 91.2 million manat ($53.6 million), or 7.9%, more than in the same period of 2025.

Total insurance payouts reached 882.7 million manat ($519.3 million), compared with approximately 683.9 million manat ($402.3 million) in the same period last year. Thus, payouts increased by 198.8 million manat ($116.9 million), or 29.1%, year-on-year.

Across the overall insurance market, approximately 70.7 manat ($41.6) out of every 100 manat ($58.8) in premiums collected was allocated to payouts.

According to the CBA’s data, PASHA Life Insurance ranked first in premium volume from January through September 2026, collecting 568.35 million manat ($334.3 million), up 7.1% year-on-year.

PASHA Insurance ranked second, with 308.9 million manat ($181.7 million) in premiums, an increase of 13.2%.

The top five also included Ateshgah Life Insurance, with approximately 83.6 million manat ($49.2 million), Ateshgah Insurance, with about 69.2 million manat ($40.7 million), and Gala Insurance, with 52.58 million manat ($30.9 million). Their year-on-year changes were 3%, 42.1%, and -17.7%, respectively.

Mega Life Insurance recorded the highest growth in premiums, collecting 22.76 million manat ($13.4 million), up 84.4%. Silk Way Insurance’s premiums increased by 47.2% to 6.6 million manat ($3.9 million).

Meanwhile, premiums collected by Azerbaijan Industry Insurance declined by 20.1% to 19.78 million manat ($11.6 million), while Gala Insurance’s premiums fell by 17.7% to 52.58 million manat ($30.9 million).

PASHA Life Insurance also ranked first in payout volume, making payments totaling 548.5 million manat ($322.7 million) in the first 9 months of this year, up 28.4% year-on-year.

PASHA Insurance ranked second, with payouts of 130.9 million manat ($77 million), an increase of 27.1%.

Ateshgah Life Insurance ranked third, with payouts of 87.8 million manat ($51.6 million), up 84.7%. Ateshgah Insurance ranked fourth, with 31.99 million manat ($18.8 million), followed by Gala Insurance with almost 18 million manat ($10.6 million).

A significant change has also been recorded at Mega Life Insurance in terms of the annual growth rate of payments. Mega Life Insurance’s payouts increased by 83.3% to nearly 7.06 million manat ($4.15 million), while Gala Life Insurance’s payouts rose by 76.4% to 3.8 million manat ($2.2 million).

In contrast, Agricultural Insurance’s payouts declined by 61.9% to 1.89 million manat ($1.1 million), while Xalq Life Insurance’s payouts decreased by 12.6% to 3.56 million manat ($2.09 million).

World.title: Azerbaijan Championships in acrobatic and aerobic gymnastics kick off in Baku (PHOTO)
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 28. The 31st Azerbaijan Championships in acrobatic gymnastics and the 10th Azerbaijan Championships in aerobic gymnastics kicked off on October 27 at the auxiliary hall of the National Gymnastics Arena in Baku.

The two-day competitions bring together gymnasts representing various sports clubs across the country, who are competing for top honors in different age categories and disciplines.

On the first day, in the balance exercise program of the acrobatic gymnastics competition, women's pairs, women's groups, and mixed pairs demonstrated their skills in the pre-youth, children’s, and junior age categories.

In aerobic gymnastics, male and female gymnasts competed in individual routines in the pre-youth, children’s, junior, and youth age categories.

At the end of the day, the winners of the individual women's competition in the youth age category of aerobic gymnastics were determined. Members of Azerbaijan’s national team delivered strong performances, claiming all three places on the podium.

Ayan Agayeva won the gold medal, Amina Mustafayeva took silver, and Aydan Malikova secured bronze.

The Azerbaijan Championships will continue on October 28.

World.title: Chronicles of Victory: October 28, 2020
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 28. The Azerbaijani Army launched a counter-offensive operation, later called the "Iron Fist", on September 27, 2020, in response to the large-scale provocation of the Armenian armed forces along the frontline.

The 44-day second Karabakh war ended with the liberation of Azerbaijan’s territories from nearly 30-year Armenian occupation and the restoration of territorial integrity.

Chronicle of the 32-nd day of the second Karabakh war:

- President of the Republic of Azerbaijan Ilham Aliyev has made post on his official Twitter account.

- President Ilham Aliyev has made a post on his official Twitter account that the Azerbaijani Army liberated several villages in Zangilan, Jabrayil and Gubadli districts from the occupiers.

- President Ilham Aliyev gave an interview to Russia's Interfax news agency.

- First Vice President of the Republic of Azerbaijan Mehriban Aliyeva shared a post on her Instagram account about Armenia's attack on civilians in Barda.

- The territory of Azerbaijan's Tartar district came under artillery fire.

- The list of destroyed military equipment of Armenia has been announced.

- Armenian troops shelled Azerbaijan's Tovuz, Gadabay, Dashkasan and Gubadli districts.

- Video footage of the destruction of Armenian military equipment and personnel has been released.

- Azerbaijan’s units destroyed the enemy, who opened fire on Azerbaijani cities and districts. The enemy's manpower was destroyed by accurate fire.
