World.title: Ramiz Mehdiyev to be stripped of state awards
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 27. Former head of the Presidential Administration of Azerbaijan Ramiz Mehdiyev will be stripped of his state awards.

According to the verdict issued by the Baku Court on Grave Crimes on October 22, 2026, a submission has been ordered to be forwarded for consideration of the question of stripping Ramiz Mehdiyev of his state awards.

Ramiz Mehdiyev was awarded the Istiglal Order in 2008, the Sharaf Order in 2013, and the Shohrat Order in 2018.

As previously reported, under the verdict issued by the Baku Court on Grave Crimes on October 22, 2026, Ramiz Mehdiyev was found guilty of committing crimes under Articles 193-1.3.2, 274, 278.1, and 311.3.3 of the Criminal Code of Azerbaijan and sentenced to 14 years in prison.

However, taking into account Ramiz Mehdiyev’s age and health condition, the court ruled that the sentence would be suspended.

World.title: Azerbaijan-Türkiye relations are strong and unbreakable – Bahçeli
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 27. The brotherly ties between Azerbaijan and Türkiye are so strong and historically significant that they transcend all political and diplomatic issues and cannot be constrained by temporary developments.

This is stated in a declaration by Devlet Bahçeli, leader of Türkiye’s Nationalist Movement Party, ahead of the upcoming Summit of the Organization of Turkic States (OTS) in Ankara and the 35th anniversary of the independence of OTS member states.

According to him, the brotherhood between Türkiye and Azerbaijan is unbreakable, rooted in the will of both nations and the history of their shared struggle, and passed down from generation to generation. “The same can be said of all brotherly states of the Turkic world,” he noted, stressing that the escalation of misunderstandings must not be allowed.

“We must not allow seeds of discord to be sown among us. No disagreement should lead to long-term estrangement. Our bonds of brotherhood are built on mutual respect and faith in a shared future. It is the duty of every member of the Turkic world to contribute to our historical closeness, avoid disagreements, and refrain from actions that could weaken our future,” the politician stated.

The MHP leader called for leaving a “strong Turkic world” to future generations.

World.title: Federal government invests $180m in rare earths mine in western Victoria
World.content:
The Australian government has conditionally invested $180 million in the controversial Donald Rare Earth and Minerals Sands Project planned for western Victoria.

Once operational, the Astron Corporation mine in Donald will be the fourth-largest rare earths mine in the world outside China and the second-largest in Australia.

Two federal government agencies, the National Reconstruction Fund Corporation and Export Finance Australia, have issued conditional approval for up to $110 million and $70 million respectively, to support the project.

The mine is a joint venture between locally registered Astron Corporation and the United States uranium giant Energy Fuels, which has already provided $183 million in funding.

A total of $360 million has now been committed to the project.

Two federal government agencies have conditionally approved a total of $180 million for the Donald Rare Earth and Mineral Sands mine. (Supplied: Astron Corporation)

From the Wimmera to the world

The mine will be located near the Wimmera farming town of Minyip, which is home to about 500 people.

The mineral sands mine has been a controversial topic for the community, with concerned farmers fighting against the loss of prime agricultural land.

They are also concerned about the way the land will be rehabilitated after mining is completed.

Astron Corporation plans to mine up to 2,700 hectares for critical minerals such as zirconium and titanium, along with rare earth elements including neodymium and praseodymium.

It also holds exploration and retention licences over an additional 40,000 hectares.

Rare earth elements are critical in the production of clean-energy technologies such as wind turbines and electric vehicles, while zirconium and titanium are used in medical devices and household items such as paint.

Trace amounts of uranium will also be extracted from the ore once it is shipped to the United States.

Astron Corporation has been approved to mine 2,700 hectares of land in western Victoria. (Supplied: Astron Corporation)

Astron Corporation managing director Tiger Brown said they were grateful for the "significant investment" from government agencies.

"The funding is a major vote of confidence in the globally significant Donald project and an important milestone on our long road to making it a reality," he said.

"It's really exciting that we'll see rare earths from the Wimmera region of Victoria not just being processed, but actually being in electric vehicles and other applications all across the Western world and beyond."

The project has a planned 52-year mine life over two phases, and has already been granted major project status in recognition of its national strategic importance.

It has been fully approved by the Victorian government.

Mr Brown said the company had to complete one more step in the approvals process before construction could begin before Christmas, with mining set to start in 2028.

Astron Corporation chief executive Tiger Brown. (Supplied: Astron Corporation )

"We're working with commercial banks to make that conditional approval a full-fledged approval with commercial lenders," he said.

The company predicts the project will contribute $205 million annually to the regional economy and create 200 construction jobs and 150 ongoing operational jobs.

Minister for Resources Madeleine King said Australia had some of the world's richest critical minerals deposits.

"Projects like this are helping us turn those resources into long-term economic and strategic opportunities," she said.

"The Donald Mineral Sands Project will position Australia as an even more reliable supplier of critical minerals to our international partners and allies."

Locals yet to be convinced

With more than 1,000 hectares of prime farmland to be excavated and at least one home rendered uninhabitable to make way for the mine, local farmers have long opposed the project.

Fourth-generation farmer Paul Trotter said about 320 hectares of his land was in the path of the mine, and he was fighting to retain it for food production.

"Mining should only occur on ground that isn't suitable for food production," he said.

"We're going to run out of food to feed the nation and the world if they keep doing this.

"There is a place for mining in the right area, but in prime agricultural land where we live, it's not."

Other farmers had doubts over promised rehabilitation of the land to a productive standard and whether local roads could withstand extra trucks moving products from the mine to a nearby freight hub.

World.title: NBA's shortest-ever player to have jersey retired
World.content:
Tyrone "Muggsy" Bogues spent his entire NBA career looking up at all other players. They'll be looking up at him now.

His name and number, anyway.

The Charlotte Hornets announced on Tuesday that the No. 1 jersey worn by Bogues — the NBA's smallest-ever player at 5-foot-3 (160 centimetres)— will be retired during a half-time ceremony when the team plays host to Milwaukee on February 11.

"How ironic is that?" Bogues said.

"After all those times that you felt like you were looking up, looking up for so many years, at people, then here comes this particular moment. And when that jersey actually goes up, it'll be like I'm the one looking down at the entire world. It's going to be a surreal moment."

Muggsy Bogues played 14 seasons in the NBA. (AP: Chris O'Meara)

Bogues will be the third player whose Hornets jersey is retired, joining Bobby Phills (13) and Dell Curry (30). He began his career with Washington, then went to Charlotte in the 1988 expansion draft and essentially has called the Carolinas home ever since.

"Charlotte embraced me with open arms," Bogues said.

"This is a place I've called home more than I've called any other place home, even growing up in the city of Baltimore. So, having this type of recognition for my family, for the organisation to look at you in this type of light, I mean, it means the world."

Bogues played in the NBA for parts of 14 seasons, spending the bulk of that time with Charlotte and having stints with Golden State, Washington and Toronto. He was the 12th selection in the 1987 draft — one spot behind Indiana taking Reggie Miller — and wound up playing more games than all but eight other members of that draft class.

He averaged 7.7 points and 7.6 assists for his career. Bogues was part of Charlotte teams that reached the 50-win mark in three consecutive seasons, plus he was part of the franchise's first post-season series victory in 1993.

"Muggsy was here from the beginning and played with a heart, toughness and competitive spirit that made him a fan favourite," Hornets co-chairmen Rick Schnall and Gabe Plotkin said in a statement on Tuesday.

"At 5-foot-3, he overcame obstacles throughout his career and proved he belonged among the best players in the world. He became a role model for generations, showing young people that their size doesn't have to limit what they can achieve."

The average NBA player during Bogues's playing career stood 6-foot-7 (200cm) and weighed 213 pounds (96kg). Bogues was 40cm shorter than that average and 35kg lighter in those years.

He has remained part of the Hornets in retirement, still often representing the team at community events and travelling the world as an NBA ambassador. And he knows he changed the game, debunking the thought that someone had to have a certain height to make the NBA.

"I was just like any kid that had a dream," Bogues said.

"I just kept believing and kept having success. And my mindset was, 'If you play against the best, and you have success against the best, you need to be included with the best.'"

AP

World.title: Private school headmaster sounds warning on ATAR decline
World.content:
The headmaster of one of Perth's most prestigious private schools has raised concerns that Year 12s may not be challenging themselves, as more WA students opt out of ATAR exams.

New data from the School Curriculum and Standards Authority (SCSA) shows fewer Year 12 students are enrolling in four or more ATAR course exams.

This fell from 38.1 per cent last year to 36.9 per cent this year.

Ten years ago, 58 per cent of Year 12s statewide completed four or more ATAR courses.

Scotch College Headmaster Alec O'Connell said he supported the different Year 12 pathways, but was concerned the decline statewide in ATAR engagement was a symptom of a bigger problem.

Alec O'Connell worries that fewer students are pushing themselves in their final year. (ABC News: Mya Kordic)

"A lot of students now have been given advanced entry to university and some of the universities, that ATAR prerequisite has dropped," he said.

" I think we've got to be careful not to encourage students to look for the path of least resistance. "

Dr O'Connell questioned how students entering university through different pathways performed once they arrived.

Students opt out of ATAR for alternative pathways to university As thousands of high school students across Australia anxiously await ATAR results, many first-year university applicants are finding other ways into their course of choice.

"Is there enough empirical proof that those pathways lead to successful completion of the courses they've chosen?" he said.

In 16 years as headmaster, Dr O'Connell said he had seen many changes to ATAR.

He was worried that not enough students were pushing themselves in their final year.

"That's more of my concern is that we want to be the best part of who we can be," he said.

"Sometimes that means … taking on challenges, which may not be easy, but the end product is a far better outcome for me personally and professionally."

Dr O'Connell says taking on challenges leads to better results. (ABC News: Mya Kordic)

Dr O'Connell said stress isn't always bad, depending on the individual and whether it's measured.

"I want to make it clear here that if it's detrimental to somebody's wellbeing, then I wouldn't recommend it," he said.

"However, on the flip side to that, I think that's used as a bit of a catch-all for somebody's stress."

'Informed choices'

Policy director at the Australian Centre for Student Equity and Success, Ian Li, said the decline was due to students "making informed choices on the pathway … they feel will lead to the best outcomes for themselves".

Professor Li said around 30 per cent of government school students take at least four ATAR subjects in year 12, compared to 40-50 per cent at independent and Catholic Schools.

Ian Li says ensuring students have access to different pathways to university is crucial. (ABC News: Mya Kordic)

"There does seem to be sort of a difference and divide by the type of school sector that they are coming from," he said.

"Then I think it becomes an issue because it suggests that the same options might not be available to all students and that's why they are making the choices that they are."

Professor Li said it was important to have different pathways to university.

Pathway changes

From 2027, the SCSA said students using a tertiary preparation endorsed program would be required to complete of at least one ATAR course in year 12.

Students who get D grade will still pass ATAR Year 12 students in Western Australia who get D grades will still be able to pass ATAR subjects and graduate from high school.

"This change followed consultation with students, principals, school systems and sector bodies, and university representatives," the authority said.

"It is intended to strengthen students' preparation for university by exposing them to the content, teaching, learning, and assessment rigour of the ATAR courses."

The SCSA's executive director, Juanita Healy, said the participation rate in the Western Australian Certificate of Education has remained relatively stable in recent years.

"While we encourage students to take up the challenge of ATAR, every student should have the opportunity to reach their potential and pursue a pathway that best aligns with their goals and aspirations," she said.

"For example, vocational education and training continues to remain popular for students seeking a practical, hands-on pathway to achieve their future career aspirations."

World.title: MusicSA chair on 'post-apocalypse' industry ahead of Good Music Month
World.content:
Australian music is in the midst of a paradox.

Original acts are pumping out excellent music with an edginess fitting of a troubled era, yet local offerings account for only 8.5 per cent of what is being streamed in the country.

APRA-AMCOS reported this month that 91 per cent of the music Australians streamed in the 2025-26 financial year was imported, with Australian music down 37.5 per cent in five years.

It has previously blamed the situation on global algorithms preferencing music from countries such as the US.

This is despite an original music scene bursting at the seams with excellent rock, indie, blues and psychedelic acts in a revival that's been underway for most of the decade in pockets across Australia.

Wollongong's Chimers play a blistering set in Adelaide during September. (891 ABC Adelaide: Malcolm Sutton)

South Australia is riding the same wave.

At small venues such as The Hotel Metropolitan, Jive, Ancient World and Memphis Slim's House of Blues, as well as at mini-festivals at locations like the Fleurieu Peninsula and Adelaide Uni Bar, young people are regularly packing rooms to see local acts they know well enough to sing along to.

A difference from golden ages like the 1990s, however, is that this scene is mostly being ignored by larger media outlets.

One needs to tune into stations like 3D Radio in Adelaide, Triple R in Melbourne or RTRFM in Perth to get a real finger on the pulse, pick up a street magazine for a gig guide, then get out the house to hear it in person.

Australian musicians fighting algorithms to be heard While this year's triple j Hottest 100 featured a significant number of Australian songs, local artists have suffered a shocking decline in online streaming figures over the past five years.

In fact, the APRA-AMCOS 25-26 Year in Review pointed out, in a major study with Monash University, that 1.6 million Australians discovered local acts via community radio, and 1.5 million then looked them up on a streaming platform.

It's into this arena that Adelaide songwriter and lawyer Adrian Tisato has entered as the new chairperson of MusicSA, the not-for-profit organisation charged with promoting, supporting and developing the state's contemporary music sector.

"We are in the post-apocalypse," he said.

"Whether the apocalypse was Napster, or the post-Napster rollout of the delivery of music to consumers through digital streaming, whether it was COVID-19 or the combination of these events, it's the metaphorical apocalypse.

"But the truth is, we're still here, making music."

An 'electric buzz'

Mr Tisato has replaced John Glenn, who retired as MusicSA chair after nearly six years.

Adrian Tisato is also the Art Gallery of SA Foundation chair. (Supplied: ATG Publicity)

He believed Adelaide was in the midst of a "very important time as a music city" — one with an "electric buzz" that was attracting young and older music lovers to intimate live venues.

"The quality of music that's happening in small venues on the streets of Adelaide, in our regions and in mini-festivals, is outstanding, on a global level," Mr Tisato said.

Much of it will be on show during Good Music Month, an open access program featuring local, national and international acts that kicks off with a street party at Hyde Street on Friday night, and runs at venues in Adelaide and across the state until November 30.

Wednesday to Friday will also see the national Regional and Remove Music Summit take place in Mount Gambier, a conference hosted by MusicSA that takes a "deep dive" into the state of music in Australia.

The not-for-profit organisation will also present the annual SA Music Awards on November 10 to "celebrate those South Australian artists who are excelling".

"The calibre of the finalists for each of our awards is extraordinary," Mr Tisato said.

A background in music

The son of Italian migrants, Mr Tisato grew up a Roman Catholic in Woodville and said his home was the meeting place for neighbours, friends and extended family, who would gather around after dinner and play Italian card games.

Adrian Tisato (far right) performs with three brothers and a friend at their sister's 40th in 1999. (Supplied: Adrian Tisato)

"They would sing Italian folk songs that had been handed down in the oral tradition, funny little melodic tunes that were sweet and poignant, sometimes containing ribald innuendo or telling tragic tales," he said.

"They'd be sitting there singing in two, three or four-part harmonies while we, as kids, would run around the house absorbing this music into our minds and bodies.

"Once I started to learn the guitar as a 15-year-old, I got involved in the church music group as a singer and guitarist."

Mr Tisato soon began songwriting and ultimately formed a trio with members from the church group. The band started playing parties and then performed in pubs and Adelaide venues.

Named Lookout Joe, the band was one of many enjoying Adelaide's vibrant live music scene throughout the 1990s.

Adrian Tisato performs at a family gathering in 1998. (Supplied: Adrian Tisato)

Like the 1970s and 1980s, it was an era, Mr Tisato said, when people didn't question whether they were going out to see live music or not.

"They were going to see a band. It was just a question of which venue or venues they were going to," he said.

Mr Tisato also founded and ran an indie record label in the 2000s, and songs he has co-written in the last decade have been licensed to US and Australian television series.

Like most Adelaide artists, however, it was necessary to pursue a day job for financial security and Mr Tisato has been a commercial lawyer for more than 30 years.

A former Adelaide Fringe deputy chairperson and People's Republic of Animation chairperson, he has been actively involved in arts governance and is the current Art Gallery of South Australia Foundation chairperson and a gallery board member.

He has also served on the boards of the South Australian Film Corporation and the Motor Accident Commission.

'Quality trumps all'

Mr Tisato wants to see Adelaide continue to present itself to the world as a "global city of art and culture" and says he will bring his passion for music, business, governance and legal skills to the role.

With so much to on offer from homegrown artists, Mr Tisato urged commentators not to get stuck on whether or not the city attracted every big act that came to Australia.

"Over the years there's been an insecurity in Adelaide about the fact that certain artists don't come to Adelaide," he said.

"We need to let go of that. I actually think it's much more important to ask ourselves whether our own artists in intimate venues are great and thriving.

"Go see them perform live. They're brilliant."

Adelaide's Zyke performs to a strong crowd at Dougstock, an annual mini-festival on the Fleurieu Peninsula. (Supplied: Doug Tapfield)

Mr Tisato points out that despite the challenges in a post-digital disruption age, "quality trumps all".

"For musicians, for songwriters, however difficult it may be to make a living from this, the opportunity remains to find a way," he said.

"It starts with being great at what you do and writing extraordinary songs and performing them to audiences, and I still believe that for those who are doing that, the future is bright."

World.title: Teen charged over Sydney house fire with 88yo woman inside
World.content:
A 17-year-old boy has been charged over a house fire that left four people hospitalised, including an 88-year-old woman, in Sydney's inner west.

Forty firefighters and 10 trucks were called to Abbotsford about 4am on Tuesday to respond to a home well alight.

An 88-year-old woman, her son and his wife were rescued and taken to hospital for smoke inhalation.

A 49-year-old man, who climbed a ladder to save the elderly woman, was also taken to hospital.

A neighbour confronted a male in a balaclava, police said. (ABC News)

Another man, who police said was a long-term renter at the home, received treatment but did not require hospitalisation.

Police said a 17-year-old boy was arrested about 11pm on Tuesday at a home in Merrylands.

He was treated for burns to his hands and legs before being taken to hospital, and remains in a stable condition.

Forty firefighters with ten trucks were called to extinguish the flames. (ABC News: Patrick Thomas)

Police said a search warrant was carried out at the home with detectives seizing "a number of items of interest".

The teenager has been charged with damaging property by fire or explosion to the value of more than $15,000.

He was also charged with being carried in conveyance taken without the consent of the owner, and obtaining property by deception.

He was refused bail and is expected to appear before Parramatta Bail Division Court on Wednesday.

World.title: WA set to become first state to legalise plug-in solar panels, batteries
World.content:
Renters and people living in apartments could save hundreds of dollars on their power bills when Western Australia becomes the first state to legalise plug-in solar panels and batteries.

WA is set to unlock access to the technology commonly known as "balcony solar", used by millions of people in Europe and the United Kingdom.

Overseas, the technology is usually attached to apartment balconies or installed in backyards, typically at a cost of up to $1,300, plus extra for a plug-in battery.

In September, Australia's energy ministers agreed to explore how to safely roll out plug-in solar across the nation.

But WA is the first state or territory to give the technology the green light, announcing the start of consultation on a safety standard for the energy-saving devices, including how to ensure they do not overload power circuits.

Plug-in solar panels are a popular choice for people who live in apartments or those who do not own their home. (Unsplash: Yuma Solar)

"For too long, the benefits of cheap solar have been out of reach for anyone who doesn't own their roof. That isn't fair," Energy and Decarbonisation Minister Amber-Jade Sanderson said.

As the name suggests, they plug into regular power points and do not require an electrician for installation.

The power generated by the panels is fed into the home network via an inverter and a standard plug, helping offset electricity used by appliances.

Households reject virtual power plants Thousands of households with batteries installed under the federal government's scheme are choosing not to sign up to be a so-called virtual power plant that sells stored energy back to the grid.

That means renters, who have no incentive to spend thousands putting solar panels on their rental's roof, can now benefit from solar energy.

And people living in apartments with a balcony or other reliable spot in the sun can also benefit.

Big savings

The state government estimated a typical plug-in solar system could save households $240 a year on their electricity bill, and up to $500 if they have a battery as well.

But industry experts believe the payback period for plug-in solar systems ranges from four to 10 years.

Solar Citizens, a community organisation that has been pushing for the legalisation of the technology, has previously said an average plug-in solar panel would save people $300-400 a year, and double that with a plug-in battery.

On top of that, renters can take the device with them when they move out.

An apartment building with plug-in solar panels on the balconies. (Supplied: AlexGo)

Ms Sanderson said WA was leading the nation on the take-up of the technology.

"Millions of European households already use these systems every day, and WA families should be able to do the same," she said.

"Western Australians are already taking up solar and batteries in record numbers, and this will ensure even more families can see the savings from the energy transition."

More than 40 per cent of homes in the South West Interconnected System, WA's main electricity grid, have solar panels.

The state government will now need to bring landlords and body corporates on board to allow plug-in solar to be hung on balconies or set up in backyards.

Plug-in solar was legalised in the UK earlier this year, and New Zealand is looking to do the same within 12 months.

Germany is a world leader in plug-in solar, with an estimated one in 10 households having a system installed.

World.title: Maya Joint makes mockery of rankings with big win in Tokyo
World.content:
Maya Joint has made a mockery of the tennis rankings with an impressive display to uproot one of the top seeds at the Pan Pacific Open event in Tokyo.

Ranked a career-high 28 in February, the Australian's ranking has dropped steadily throughout the year, and she entered this WTA 500 event ranked 94th.

However, the American-born Aussie showed the numbers can't always be trusted as she powered past sixth seed and world number 16 Sorana Cirstea of Romania.

Joint's impressive 6-3, 7-6 (7-4) victory yesterday secured her a spot in the round of 16.

It also continued her recent resurgence, after she made the final at last month's Korea Open in Seoul, where compatriot Kim Birrell claimed her first WTA title with a 6-4, 6-2 win in the final.

Joint's next opponent is Spanish world number 42 Cristina Bucsa, who beat France's Diane Parry 7-5, 6-1 yesterday.

And Joint isn't the only in-form Australian still in the main draw.

On Monday, Talia Gibson, who recently reached the Singapore final, came through an all-Australian affair over qualifier Daria Kasatkina 6-0, 7-5.

Gibson powered through the first eight games in a row but was made to work hard to hold off the former world No.8 in the second set.

Her reward is a round-of-16 clash with eight-seeded Aleandra Eala, of the Philippines.

Meanwhile, in the Guangzhou Open, Venus Williams lost 6-2, 6-2 to Austrian teenager Lilli Tagger to be 0-13 in singles this year. The 28-year age gap between Williams, 46, and Tagger, 18, is believed to be a record difference between opponents in a WTA Tour match.

Williams created no break-point chances, and Tagger took four of the 16 she had.

AAP

World.title: Queensland mayor steps down citing 'smear campaign'
World.content:
Redland City Mayor Jos Mitchell has stood down after months off the job, alleging a "personalised, coordinated" smear campaign against her.

The former police prosecutor has been off work since May and faced being pushed out at next month's council meeting.

Councillors had twice voted against Cr Mitchell's absence from meetings.

Cr Mitchell — who had been dealing with "complex health conditions" — said she was met with "concerted, ongoing resistance and attacks" since taking the post in 2022.

The independent succeeded Karen Williams, who pleaded guilty to drink driving after crashing her car into a ditch while three times over the limit in 2022.

Cr Mitchell said 70 complaints had been made against her to the local government watchdog.

"There have been threats, continuous accusations and harassment. Our family's cars have been vandalised, we've had a drone hover over our backyard and my husband and our daughter have been targeted online," Cr Mitchell said.

She said the past two-and-a-half years had had a "significant effect" on her wellbeing, and her family.

"My family has paid a heavy price for my decision to serve our community. While they have dealt with the impact with grace and dignity, no-one should have to accept it as the price of public office," she said.

Cr Mitchell, who claimed to have been targeted for threatening the "status quo", added that "there must be room for new representatives who bring new skills, new ways of working and new questions, without retaliation".

Redland City Council and Local Government Minister Ann Leahy have been contacted for comment.

World.title: Israel election 2026 LIVE updates: Exit polls project no clear winner as Netanyahu, Eisenkot set for lengthy battle to win power in nation’s first election since October 7 attacks
World.content:
The United Nations nuclear watchdog said it had not detected any efforts by Iran to rebuild nuclear facilities damaged in US and Israeli strikes over the past two years, even as Tehran continues to block inspectors’ access to most of its atomic sites.

“Since June 2025, we have not identified any activity to repair or reconstruct any of the facilities damaged in the military attacks of 2025 and 2026,” International Atomic Energy Agency director general Rafael Mariano Grossi told the UN Security Council on Tuesday (US time).

Rafael Mariano Grossi. Bloomberg

Grossi’s remarks undercut US President Donald Trump’s narrative that launching a new war against Iran in late February was necessary to halt its nuclear weapons ambitions. The president has repeatedly said he’s weighing renewed strikes on Iran after the US midterm elections.

The assessment echoes a conclusion that former US Director of National Intelligence Tulsi Gabbard included in written testimony before a congressional committee earlier this year. She wrote that Iran’s uranium enrichment program had been “obliterated” in US and Israeli strikes in June 2025, and that there “has been no efforts since then to try to rebuild their enrichment capability”.

World.title: ‘You are under arrest’: Video captures the moment Lamarre-Condon hands himself in to police
World.content:
NationalNSWLamarre-Condon trial ‘You are under arrest’: Video captures the moment Lamarre-Condon hands himself in to police Michaela Whitbourn October 28, 2026 — 9:41am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Newly released footage captures the moment accused killer Beau Lamarre-Condon handed himself in to police, four days after he allegedly murdered Sydney couple Jesse Baird and Luke Davies. “You are under arrest in respect of the murder of two people at Paddington,” Lamarre-Condon is informed by Detective Chief Inspector Glenn Brown as he enters Bondi police station on February 23, 2024. Minutes earlier, on the drive to Bondi, Lamarre-Condon had made a call to a police assistance line to report a workplace injury, claiming he had been traumatised and bullied at work. The arrest footage and call audio were released by the NSW Supreme Court on Tuesday after being played to the 15-person jury in Lamarre-Condon’s double murder trial. He has pleaded not guilty to both charges.



After handing himself in shortly after 10.30am, the then 28-year-old was met by a team of lawyers including Detective Sergeant Sasha Pinazza, who led the investigation. He is shown in the video putting his hands briefly behind his head before folding them in front of him. Loading Lamarre-Condon is standing trial over the shooting deaths of Baird, 26, a former Network Ten producer and presenter, and Davies, 29, a Qantas flight attendant, on February 19, 2024. At the time of the alleged murders he was a NSW police officer. The defence does not dispute that Baird and Davies died of gunshot wounds from the accused’s police-issued Glock pistol, but the accused’s barrister has foreshadowed he will argue that he acted in self-defence. The defence case is that Lamarre-Condon panicked after the men died and disposed of their bodies in Bungonia, near Goulburn. World.title: Why being home is the best medicine this National Children’s Week
World.content:
Sponsored LifestyleHealth & wellnessHospitals United for Sick Kids Why being home is the best medicine this National Children’s Week Advertorial for Hospitals United for Sick Kids Franki Hobson October 28, 2026 — 9:29am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. This National Children’s Week, care starts with making hospitals feel like home. For Amanda*, one of the hardest parts of her newborn son’s hospital stay was being apart from the rest of her family. While baby Oliver* received treatment for jaundice, she spent long days on the ward, missing her husband and young daughter. “There were times when I felt quite isolated,” she recalls. “Being away from my husband and daughter for extended periods was difficult, and the days often felt very long.” Relief came when Oliver was able to continue treatment at home. Through Monash Children’s Hospital At Home program in Melbourne, supported by Hospitals United for Sick Kids, eligible newborns with jaundice can receive phototherapy at home, with daily nursing reviews and round-the-clock clinical support. This meant Oliver’s dad could share his care, friends could visit and Amanda could be there for both her children.



“Time seemed to move very slowly in hospital,” Amanda says. “Once we got home, life became busy and the days passed much more quickly.” Across Australia, children spend more than 780,000 nights in hospital each year¹, and further research suggests 90 per cent experience homesickness². For around half, it’s severe enough to affect their wellbeing and recovery. Helping sick kids get that homely feeling back is Hospitals United’s mission. Its FY26 Impact Report, released this Children’s Week, shows how the projects it funds are making hospital feel more like home, reducing time away and bringing hospital-grade care closer to families. Early detection of cerebral palsy for Ali, 15 months In Perth, toddler Ali Hadi loves cars, story time and being outdoors.



Ali has cerebral palsy affecting all four limbs, particularly his left side. He can lift his head, but isn’t yet able to roll, sit independently or grasp a toy. His mum, Farah, works physiotherapy and stretching into his play. Identified as high-risk from birth, he began therapy at Perth Children’s Hospital almost immediately. “Intervening as early as possible came into our life at the perfect time, pretty much as soon as Ali was born, before even seeing the true impact of CP on his life,” Farah says. That opportunity isn’t available to every child. In regional WA, distance from specialist services can delay diagnosis and treatment. Hospitals United is helping fund CONNECT-CP, which trains local clinicians and uses video assessments to identify babies at risk earlier, so more children can start early intervention therapy – bringing care closer to home and improving long-term quality of life – without long trips to hospital. Needle phobia support for Jack, 11 Jack had always been terrified of needles. Then he was diagnosed with type 1 diabetes, a condition requiring lifelong insulin treatment.



At The Prince Charles Hospital’s emergency department in Brisbane, staff attempted to insert a cannula. Jack was so distressed that several people were needed to restrain him. The hospital’s child life therapist took a different approach. She listened to his fears, explained the procedure in language he understood and helped him regain a sense of control. Jack managed the procedure calmly, without restraint. “She was so respectful to him, and she gave him confidence and control,” says his mum, Emma. “It also gave me hope that things would be OK as we started our journey with type 1 diabetes.” After funding Queensland’s first Child Life Therapy pilot program at the Prince Charles Hospital in 2022, Hospitals United’s funding has since helped extend child life therapy to Caboolture Hospital, where therapists have supported 1500 young patients since July 2025. Helping sick kids get home



These are three of the many family stories behind Hospitals United’s latest milestone: more than 1.3 million sick kids and their families helped since 2019. Australia’s only national alliance of children’s hospitals and foundations has raised $15 million and funded 100 projects through eight hospital partner networks nationwide that support 30 hospitals in metros, regional and rural areas. Other initiatives include therapy dogs comforting children in Canberra Hospital, Precision Dosing of Anticancer Therapy Program at The Children’s Hospital at Westmead and virtual specialist consultations for rural families with John Hunter Children’s Hospital. “1.3 million sick kids helped, each one a child who got better care and a family who felt less alone. That’s national support for little locals, powered by community, corporate purpose and everyday Australians,” says Hospitals United general manager Ann Billington. Hospitals United’s product-for-purpose model gives Australians a simple way to give back with their daily shopping by choosing products that support that give back. Funds raised via national partnerships with leading Australian brands such as Coles, Lowes, Duracell, Arnott’s, Mars Snacking, Simplot and Magnum are channelled into locally prioritised projects that help sick kids in every community



Coles has been a long-standing supporter of Hospitals United. Together with its customers, team members and supplier partners, more than $13.8 million have been raised nationally since 2019, making a lasting difference for sick kids and their families. “We’re incredibly proud that together with our customers, team members and supplier partners, we’ve raised a record $2.39 million this year for sick and injured children and their families. This achievement shows what’s possible when communities come together to make a real difference,” says Coles Group CEO Leah Weckert. For families like Oliver’s, Ali’s and Jack’s, that support means more time together, earlier treatment and less fear in hospital. This National Children’s Week, visit hospitalsunitedforsickkids.org to donate or learn more. Or simply add Coles Mum’s Sause for Pasta or Pizza to your Coles basket. With 50 cents from every sale going to Hospitals United for Sick Kids, every dollar makes a difference in helping sick kids and their families. *Names have been changed to protect privacy. World.content:
Sponsored Eating outGuzman y Gomez GYG’s newest filling beefs up the menu Advertorial for Guzman y Gomez Tim McDonald October 28, 2026 Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Most of us assume professional butchers cooking at home reach for the priciest cut in the cooler. And why wouldn’t they? They’re the kings of cut, the masters of meat. But if you ask them, most will say their meat of choice isn’t the one with the most dollar signs but with the most character. It’s that philosophy that led Guzman y Gomez (GYG) to launch its first new filling in five years: BBQ Beef Rib. GYG director of culinary, Nate Appleman, was instrumental in developing the restaurant’s new filling. The James Beard Award-winning chef trained as a butcher in Italy, which informed his choice of cut. “As a butcher, you learn that the hard-working cuts have the most flavour,” Appleman says. “Short rib is the cut a butcher takes home, and you’d normally find it on a restaurant menu. But while most ribs are on the fatty side, our cut has just enough marbling to keep it juicy and tender.” Juicy, tender and rich with smoky flavour: the brand new BBQ Beef Rib packs a flavourful punch. Filling high expectations



The journey began two years ago when Appleman set out to find a new cut of beef to add to the GYG menu. For a brand that waited five years to add a filling, the bar was set high, and Appleman knew he had to meet the rigorous standards of GYG founder and co-CEO Steven Marks. Restaurant reviews, news and the hottest openings served to your inbox. Sign up “We haven’t added a filling in five years because it had to be just right,” says Marks. “We started GYG 20 years ago to reinvent fast food, and this is the next chapter.” Appleman agrees. “We don’t change the menu lightly. Anything new has to clear a very high bar on taste, craveability and whether it works on our line – beef rib had to prove all three.” GYG director of culinary Nate Appleman. The payoff, he says, is a rich, slow-cooked beef with a charred crust and crisp edges, something entirely new for GYG guests. “One bite, and we knew it was the one,” he adds. “Deep, rich and juicy beef like this belongs in everything on our menu.”



Appleman’s choice was neither random nor hasty. It happens to carry a personal sentiment for him. “Beef rib is deeply Mexican to me,” he says. “Tacos de costilla are one of my favourite things to eat when I’m in Mexico. Since moving to Australia, I’ve learned that beef is king here, so it felt like the right filling at the right time.” Salt first, then fire The 100 per cent Australian beef is seasons in simplicity, allowing its authentic flavour to speak for itself. “We start with nothing but salt, because the beef is good enough to stand on its own,” says Appleman. “Then we build it up for five hours low and slow until it’s tender and then put into a hot pan in our restaurants for a golden, crisp-edged crust with Chipotle BBQ Sauce on top for a rich, smoky finish.” BBQ Beef Rib is a filling, not a one-off dish, so it goes in everything on the lunch and dinner menu. “It’s rich and juicy enough to hold its own against guac, salsa and cheese, so it works in a burrito, a bowl, a taco, a quesadilla or a Caesar,” says Appleman. He says Chipotle BBQ Sauce comes standard on the rib, but it’s your call. With the sauce or straight up, the rib holds up both ways. “That’s the great thing about GYG’s menu, it’s customisable so you can have your favourites exactly how you want them.” The chef’s own pick is the Cali Burrito, where tender BBQ Beef Rib and Chipotle BBQ Sauce intermingle with GYG’s chipotle seasoned fries, fresh guacamole and pico. “Since moving to Australia, I’ve become a BBQ Sauce convert,” he jokes. “I put it on my bacon and egg roll most mornings, so pairing it with the rib was a natural choice.”



Appleman says launching the new filling at such scale says a lot about GYG’s bold and ambitious trajectory: more innovation, more flavour and still fresh, clean food made to order. “Stay tuned, you’re going to love what’s coming!” BBQ Beef Rib is on the menu now across all GYG restaurants nationally, on the GYG App and through Uber Eats. Visit gyg.com.au for more information

World.title: Lightning blasts holes at Brisbane Airport, runway closed for hours
World.content:
NationalQueenslandWeather Lightning blasts holes at Brisbane Airport, runway closed for hours Courtney Kruk October 28, 2026 — 9:19am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. A lightning strike blasted holes in a runway at Brisbane Airport on Tuesday afternoon, forcing emergency repairs and closing the runway for more than eight hours. Footage shared by the airport shows the strike hit the western runway about 3.11pm, leaving a scattering of holes – some roughly palm-sized – across a section of bitumen. A lightning strike blasted holes through sections of Brisbane Airport’s western runway on Tuesday afternoon. Brisbane Airport Brisbane Airport spokesperson Peter Doherty said engineers were immediately deployed to assess the runway, which was closed for emergency repairs. “The lightning hit the centre of the runway, creating damage,” Doherty said.



“[Engineers] had to cut out the affected areas and re-asphalt them. “They spent the evening working on it and had it restored at 11.52pm.” He said lightning was common around the airport but such damage to a runway was rare. Brisbane Airport senior asset civil engineer Fraser Stevens surveying the impact of the lightning strike. Brisbane Airport “I spoke to the guy who looks after the runway. He’s been there 27 years and he hadn’t seen something like [what we saw] yesterday.”



While the strike and broader storm activity caused delays, no flights were cancelled on Tuesday, and the airport was operating as usual on Wednesday. Related Article Updated

Weather Former councillor and One Nation candidate found dead in floodwater “There are two runways two kilometres apart: one was out of action, the other [eastern runway] kept going through that time,” Doherty said. “We’ve done some numbers and there was an average 48-minute delay through that period in the afternoon, with storm activity around. “It’s business as usual today.”



Severe storms began moving through parts of south-east Queensland from about 1pm on Tuesday, with areas of the Gold Coast and Ipswich hit by large hail stones. Other regions copped heavy bursts of rain and damaging winds. Loading “The wind gusts at our weather station verified damaging winds … [which caused] a bit of tree damage,” said senior meteorologist David Crock, from the Bureau of Meteorology. “And we had the right conditions for storms to get strong enough for large, or giant hail, which is over five centimetres in diameter.”



Tuesday’s storms lasted until about 5pm, Crock said. No storms are expected in Brisbane on Wednesday. “It’s more likely to be rain moving through the west of Brisbane, and then beyond tomorrow, it will be a bit cooler,” Crock said. Thursday and Friday were expected to be drier than the start of the week, though rain was likely to return at the weekend. World.title: Noah Wyle named People magazine’s ‘sexiest man alive’: ‘Not in a million years’
World.content:
CultureTV & radioCelebrity life Noah Wyle named People magazine’s ‘sexiest man alive’: ‘Not in a million years’ Chris Hook October 28, 2026 — 8:14am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Noah Wyle, star of the hit HBO Max medical drama The Pitt, has been crowned People magazine’s 2026 “sexiest man alive”. The magazine noted that it had featured Wyle in its 1996 “Sexy Men of ER” edition during his time on The Pitt’s predecessor medical drama, but that was alongside co-stars George Clooney, Eriq La Salle and Anthony Edwards. Wyle played Dr John Carter in ER, from its debut in 1994 until 2006. His co-star Clooney, the outlet noted, had gone on to claim the “sexiest man” crown twice – in 1997 and 2006 – but somehow the magazine had let Wyle “get away”. The 55-year-old said it “sounded like a prank” when he heard the news, adding: “Not in a million years did I think that this would be an honour bestowed on me.”



Noah Wyle as Dr Michael “Robby” Robinavitch in season two of The Pitt. HBO Max “I hope this changes everything. I hope it’s just wine and roses, milk and honey from here on out,” he told the outlet. “No, I don’t, but I am going to take a lot of ribbing from friends and family for sure.” Asked what he thought his friend Clooney would make of his honour, Wyle told People: “I think he’ll be amused and feel, hopefully, like a proud papa, that I’ve come of gray-haired age.” His family had mixed feelings, however. Wyle revealed his wife, Sara Wells, was positive about the news because she thinks he is “a good guy and that the kind of person that I am and the kind of father I am, the kind of husband I am, is worth promoting”. Noah Wyle with his wife, Sara Wells, at this year’s Emmy Awards. Getty



More specifically he noted, she was “very pleased that this reflects well on her taste”. Wyle’s three children – Owen, 24, Auden, 21, and 11-year-old daughter Frances – had different views on the matter, he said. His son noted it would “make my life so much harder now” because of the haters, while his older daughter Auden was “was just like, ‘No way, no way’.” Wyle has won two Emmys for best actor in drama for his portrayal of Dr Michael “Robby” Robinavitch in The Pitt, which covers one long shift at a Pittsburgh trauma centre over a season’s worth of episodes. Earlier this yea, he told this masthead the strength of the drama was in the way it flipped the perspective, looking at the patient’s injuries from a doctor’s perspective, an almost documentary-style device. Other medical dramas, such as ER, tended to focus on the doctors looking down at their patients.



“The biggest difference, stylistically, is everything,” Wyle told this masthead’s culture editor at large Michael Idato earlier this year. “There are no lights on our set, there are no C-stands [the grip stands used to support lights, reflectors, backdrops and other equipment], there are no camera tracks, none of the traditional filmmaking tools.” Wyle follows last year’s winner, Wicked star Jonathan Bailey, 2024 winner John Krasinski and 2023 titleholder Patrick Dempsey, who also came to fame playing a doctor on ER. The “sexiest man alive” title dates from a 1985 People interview with Mel Gibson, with the phrase used for a cover line pointing to the piece, and has since become an annual mainstay for the magazine. The United Nations nuclear watchdog said it had not detected any efforts by Iran to rebuild nuclear facilities damaged in US and Israeli strikes over the past two years, even as Tehran continues to block inspectors’ access to most of its atomic sites.

“Since June 2025, we have not identified any activity to repair or reconstruct any of the facilities damaged in the military attacks of 2025 and 2026,” International Atomic Energy Agency director general Rafael Mariano Grossi told the UN Security Council on Tuesday (US time).

Rafael Mariano Grossi. Bloomberg

Grossi’s remarks undercut US President Donald Trump’s narrative that launching a new war against Iran in late February was necessary to halt its nuclear weapons ambitions. The president has repeatedly said he’s weighing renewed strikes on Iran after the US midterm elections.

The assessment echoes a conclusion that former US Director of National Intelligence Tulsi Gabbard included in written testimony before a congressional committee earlier this year. She wrote that Iran’s uranium enrichment program had been “obliterated” in US and Israeli strikes in June 2025, and that there “has been no efforts since then to try to rebuild their enrichment capability”.

The hospital’s child life therapist took a different approach. She listened to his fears, explained the procedure in language he understood and helped him regain a sense of control. Jack managed the procedure calmly, without restraint. “She was so respectful to him, and she gave him confidence and control,” says his mum, Emma. “It also gave me hope that things would be OK as we started our journey with type 1 diabetes.” After funding Queensland’s first Child Life Therapy pilot program at the Prince Charles Hospital in 2022, Hospitals United’s funding has since helped extend child life therapy to Caboolture Hospital, where therapists have supported 1500 young patients since July 2025. Helping sick kids get home



These are three of the many family stories behind Hospitals United’s latest milestone: more than 1.3 million sick kids and their families helped since 2019. Australia’s only national alliance of children’s hospitals and foundations has raised $15 million and funded 100 projects through eight hospital partner networks nationwide that support 30 hospitals in metros, regional and rural areas. Other initiatives include therapy dogs comforting children in Canberra Hospital, Precision Dosing of Anticancer Therapy Program at The Children’s Hospital at Westmead and virtual specialist consultations for rural families with John Hunter Children’s Hospital. “1.3 million sick kids helped, each one a child who got better care and a family who felt less alone. That’s national support for little locals, powered by community, corporate purpose and everyday Australians,” says Hospitals United general manager Ann Billington. Hospitals United’s product-for-purpose model gives Australians a simple way to give back with their daily shopping by choosing products that support that give back. Funds raised via national partnerships with leading Australian brands such as Coles, Lowes, Duracell, Arnott’s, Mars Snacking, Simplot and Magnum are channelled into locally prioritised projects that help sick kids in every community



Coles has been a long-standing supporter of Hospitals United. Together with its customers, team members and supplier partners, more than $13.8 million have been raised nationally since 2019, making a lasting difference for sick kids and their families. “We’re incredibly proud that together with our customers, team members and supplier partners, we’ve raised a record $2.39 million this year for sick and injured children and their families. This achievement shows what’s possible when communities come together to make a real difference,” says Coles Group CEO Leah Weckert. For families like Oliver’s, Ali’s and Jack’s, that support means more time together, earlier treatment and less fear in hospital. This National Children’s Week, visit hospitalsunitedforsickkids.org to donate or learn more. Or simply add Coles Mum’s Sause for Pasta or Pizza to your Coles basket. World.title: GYG’s newest filling beefs up the menu
World.content:
Sponsored Eating outGuzman y Gomez GYG’s newest filling beefs up the menu Advertorial for Guzman y Gomez Tim McDonald October 28, 2026 Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Most of us assume professional butchers cooking at home reach for the priciest cut in the cooler. And why wouldn’t they? They’re the kings of cut, the masters of meat. But if you ask them, most will say their meat of choice isn’t the one with the most dollar signs but with the most character. It’s that philosophy that led Guzman y Gomez (GYG) to launch its first new filling in five years: BBQ Beef Rib. GYG director of culinary, Nate Appleman, was instrumental in developing the restaurant’s new filling. The James Beard Award-winning chef trained as a butcher in Italy, which informed his choice of cut. “As a butcher, you learn that the hard-working cuts have the most flavour,” Appleman says. “Short rib is the cut a butcher takes home, and you’d normally find it on a restaurant menu. But while most ribs are on the fatty side, our cut has just enough marbling to keep it juicy and tender.” Juicy, tender and rich with smoky flavour: the brand new BBQ Beef Rib packs a flavourful punch. Filling high expectations



The journey began two years ago when Appleman set out to find a new cut of beef to add to the GYG menu. For a brand that waited five years to add a filling, the bar was set high, and Appleman knew he had to meet the rigorous standards of GYG founder and co-CEO Steven Marks. Restaurant reviews, news and the hottest openings served to your inbox. Sign up “We haven’t added a filling in five years because it had to be just right,” says Marks. “We started GYG 20 years ago to reinvent fast food, and this is the next chapter.” Appleman agrees. “We don’t change the menu lightly. Anything new has to clear a very high bar on taste, craveability and whether it works on our line – beef rib had to prove all three.” GYG director of culinary Nate Appleman. The payoff, he says, is a rich, slow-cooked beef with a charred crust and crisp edges, something entirely new for GYG guests. “One bite, and we knew it was the one,” he adds. “Deep, rich and juicy beef like this belongs in everything on our menu.”



Appleman’s choice was neither random nor hasty. It happens to carry a personal sentiment for him. “Beef rib is deeply Mexican to me,” he says. “Tacos de costilla are one of my favourite things to eat when I’m in Mexico. Since moving to Australia, I’ve learned that beef is king here, so it felt like the right filling at the right time.” Salt first, then fire The 100 per cent Australian beef is seasons in simplicity, allowing its authentic flavour to speak for itself. “We start with nothing but salt, because the beef is good enough to stand on its own,” says Appleman. “Then we build it up for five hours low and slow until it’s tender and then put into a hot pan in our restaurants for a golden, crisp-edged crust with Chipotle BBQ Sauce on top for a rich, smoky finish.” BBQ Beef Rib is a filling, not a one-off dish, so it goes in everything on the lunch and dinner menu. “It’s rich and juicy enough to hold its own against guac, salsa and cheese, so it works in a burrito, a bowl, a taco, a quesadilla or a Caesar,” says Appleman. He says Chipotle BBQ Sauce comes standard on the rib, but it’s your call. With the sauce or straight up, the rib holds up both ways. “That’s the great thing about GYG’s menu, it’s customisable so you can have your favourites exactly how you want them.” The chef’s own pick is the Cali Burrito, where tender BBQ Beef Rib and Chipotle BBQ Sauce intermingle with GYG’s chipotle seasoned fries, fresh guacamole and pico. “Since moving to Australia, I’ve become a BBQ Sauce convert,” he jokes. “I put it on my bacon and egg roll most mornings, so pairing it with the rib was a natural choice.”



Appleman says launching the new filling at such scale says a lot about GYG’s bold and ambitious trajectory: more innovation, more flavour and still fresh, clean food made to order. “Stay tuned, you’re going to love what’s coming!” BBQ Beef Rib is on the menu now across all GYG restaurants nationally, on the GYG App and through Uber Eats. Visit gyg.com.au for more information

World.content:
NationalQueenslandWeather Lightning blasts holes at Brisbane Airport, runway closed for hours Courtney Kruk October 28, 2026 — 9:19am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. A lightning strike blasted holes in a runway at Brisbane Airport on Tuesday afternoon, forcing emergency repairs and closing the runway for more than eight hours. Footage shared by the airport shows the strike hit the western runway about 3.11pm, leaving a scattering of holes – some roughly palm-sized – across a section of bitumen. A lightning strike blasted holes through sections of Brisbane Airport’s western runway on Tuesday afternoon. Brisbane Airport Brisbane Airport spokesperson Peter Doherty said engineers were immediately deployed to assess the runway, which was closed for emergency repairs. “The lightning hit the centre of the runway, creating damage,” Doherty said.



“[Engineers] had to cut out the affected areas and re-asphalt them. “They spent the evening working on it and had it restored at 11.52pm.” He said lightning was common around the airport but such damage to a runway was rare. Brisbane Airport senior asset civil engineer Fraser Stevens surveying the impact of the lightning strike. Brisbane Airport “I spoke to the guy who looks after the runway. He’s been there 27 years and he hadn’t seen something like [what we saw] yesterday.”



While the strike and broader storm activity caused delays, no flights were cancelled on Tuesday, and the airport was operating as usual on Wednesday. Related Article Updated

Weather Former councillor and One Nation candidate found dead in floodwater “There are two runways two kilometres apart: one was out of action, the other [eastern runway] kept going through that time,” Doherty said. “We’ve done some numbers and there was an average 48-minute delay through that period in the afternoon, with storm activity around. “It’s business as usual today.”



Severe storms began moving through parts of south-east Queensland from about 1pm on Tuesday, with areas of the Gold Coast and Ipswich hit by large hail stones. Other regions copped heavy bursts of rain and damaging winds. Loading “The wind gusts at our weather station verified damaging winds … [which caused] a bit of tree damage,” said senior meteorologist David Crock, from the Bureau of Meteorology. “And we had the right conditions for storms to get strong enough for large, or giant hail, which is over five centimetres in diameter.”



Tuesday’s storms lasted until about 5pm, Crock said. No storms are expected in Brisbane on Wednesday. “It’s more likely to be rain moving through the west of Brisbane, and then beyond tomorrow, it will be a bit cooler,” Crock said. Thursday and Friday were expected to be drier than the start of the week, though rain was likely to return at the weekend. World.title: Noah Wyle named People magazine’s ‘sexiest man alive’: ‘Not in a million years’
World.content:
CultureTV & radioCelebrity life Noah Wyle named People magazine’s ‘sexiest man alive’: ‘Not in a million years’ Chris Hook October 28, 2026 — 8:14am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Noah Wyle, star of the hit HBO Max medical drama The Pitt, has been crowned People magazine’s 2026 “sexiest man alive”. The magazine noted that it had featured Wyle in its 1996 “Sexy Men of ER” edition during his time on The Pitt’s predecessor medical drama, but that was alongside co-stars George Clooney, Eriq La Salle and Anthony Edwards. Wyle played Dr John Carter in ER, from its debut in 1994 until 2006. His co-star Clooney, the outlet noted, had gone on to claim the “sexiest man” crown twice – in 1997 and 2006 – but somehow the magazine had let Wyle “get away”. The 55-year-old said it “sounded like a prank” when he heard the news, adding: “Not in a million years did I think that this would be an honour bestowed on me.”



Noah Wyle as Dr Michael “Robby” Robinavitch in season two of The Pitt. HBO Max “I hope this changes everything. I hope it’s just wine and roses, milk and honey from here on out,” he told the outlet. “No, I don’t, but I am going to take a lot of ribbing from friends and family for sure.” Asked what he thought his friend Clooney would make of his honour, Wyle told People: “I think he’ll be amused and feel, hopefully, like a proud papa, that I’ve come of gray-haired age.” His family had mixed feelings, however. Wyle revealed his wife, Sara Wells, was positive about the news because she thinks he is “a good guy and that the kind of person that I am and the kind of father I am, the kind of husband I am, is worth promoting”. Noah Wyle with his wife, Sara Wells, at this year’s Emmy Awards. Getty



More specifically he noted, she was “very pleased that this reflects well on her taste”. Wyle’s three children – Owen, 24, Auden, 21, and 11-year-old daughter Frances – had different views on the matter, he said. His son noted it would “make my life so much harder now” because of the haters, while his older daughter Auden was “was just like, ‘No way, no way’.” Wyle has won two Emmys for best actor in drama for his portrayal of Dr Michael “Robby” Robinavitch in The Pitt, which covers one long shift at a Pittsburgh trauma centre over a season’s worth of episodes. Earlier this yea, he told this masthead the strength of the drama was in the way it flipped the perspective, looking at the patient’s injuries from a doctor’s perspective, an almost documentary-style device. Other medical dramas, such as ER, tended to focus on the doctors looking down at their patients.



“The biggest difference, stylistically, is everything,” Wyle told this masthead’s culture editor at large Michael Idato earlier this year. “There are no lights on our set, there are no C-stands [the grip stands used to support lights, reflectors, backdrops and other equipment], there are no camera tracks, none of the traditional filmmaking tools.” Wyle follows last year’s winner, Wicked star Jonathan Bailey, 2024 winner John Krasinski and 2023 titleholder Patrick Dempsey, who also came to fame playing a doctor on ER. The “sexiest man alive” title dates from a 1985 People interview with Mel Gibson, with the phrase used for a cover line pointing to the piece, and has since become an annual mainstay for the magazine. World.title: Health insurer ordered to pay customer after declining to cover ADHD diagnosis
World.content:
Southern Cross Health Insurance has been ordered to pay a customer $355 after the Disputes Tribunal found it had wrongly declined to cover a portion of his ADHD diagnosis.

The dispute arose after the man, who works as a barrister and wished to remain anonymous, sought cover for a psychiatry appointment for an ADHD assessment, in which he was seen by two doctors with different registration statuses.

The man's policy included cover up to $600 per year for consultations with a vocationally registered psychiatrist.

In order to get treatment for ADHD, he had a consultation with a doctor, who was in training to become a psychiatrist but was not yet vocationally registered, and then the report and prescriptions were signed off by their supervising doctor, Dr Han Chung Lim, who was registered.

Southern Cross argued as the doctor who did the assessment and the report was not a registered psychiatrist, the customer was only covered for a GP visit, to the amount of $45.

The tribunal accepted that point, but ruled the portion of the work done by the registered psychiatrist should also qualify for cover.

The man sought $1000.01, but ultimately the tribunal determined $400 was a reasonable amount for the qualifying portion of the consultation, and deducted the $45 Southern Cross had already paid, for a total of $355 to be paid.

In a statement, Southern Cross said: "We are currently reviewing the decision and considering our next steps, including those outlined by the Disputes Tribunal in its decision."

The barrister told RNZ he was pleased with the decision.

"It vindicates my view that Southern Cross are out of step with the needs of its customers.

"Being treated remotely, particularly post-Covid, should be embraced. In this case, seeing [the doctor], remotely, who is supervised by Dr Lim, a psychiatrist, allowed improved access, without reducing the quality of care."

World.title: Rabuka associate appointed as Fiji's new Attorney-General, third since coalition took office
World.content:
The Fijian government has appointed a close professional associate of Prime Minister Sitiveni Rabuka as the new chief legal adviser - the third since the coalition took office - in the aftermath of his acting attorney-general's explicit video saga earlier this month.

Sevuloni Valenitabua was sworn in as the government's chief law officer at the State House in Suva on Tuesday.

The government said he "brings considerable legal and regional experience, with a professional career spanning private legal practice, constitutional litigation, human rights and public legal services across Fiji and the Pacific".

Valenitabua's appointment draws attention due to his professional proximity to Rabuka. He was selected to lead a seven-member Constitutional Review Commission (CRC) earlier this year, while his son, Simione, is a wellknown Suva lawyer, who currently serves as Rabuka's personal legal counsel, representing him in several ongoing high-profile judicial review appeals.

Leaked report reveals previous health concerns

RNZ Pacific has obtained a copy of a selection panel report for Fiji's anti-corruption office chief, which Valenitabua was passed over for due to a "medical condition pertaining the heart".

According to the report, Valenitabua was considered for the position of Fiji Independent Commission Against Corruption (FICAC) commissioner in August 2024, but was passed up in favour of Barbara Malimali.

The selection panel included Acting Chief Justice Salesi Temo, Acting Chief Magistrate Josaia Waqaivolavola, and Solicitor-General Ropate Green.

"The panels were pleased that [Valenitabua] was upfront and declared that he has a medical condition pertaining the heart," the panel wrote in its final recommendation.

"The panel has been considerate of Mr Valenitabua's medical condition which may not be fit for the position as the successful candidate has to handle a challenging environment at the FICAC office," the report read.

The subsequent appointment of Malimali prompted a scandal that later sparked a multi-million-dollar Commission of Inquiry, which remains before the courts.

RNZ Pacific contacted Prime Minister Rabuka's office for comment.

Fijian Prime Minister Sitiveni Rabuka RNZ Pacific / Fiji Parliament

Attorney-General appointments

Valenitabua is the third person to be appointed to the role after Siromi Turaga resigned just days after an explicit video appeared on his Facebook profile on the eve of Fiji's 56th independence anniversary.

Turaga and Graham Leung - who was fired in May 2025 - have been the other two appointees to the role.

Filimoni Vosarogo, Rabuka's Minister for Lands, was also announced as Attorney-General to replace Turaga during a Cabinet reshuffle in October 2023, but was never sworn in following major backlash from the Fiji Law Society, which argued that he was legally disqualified from holding the position.

Rabuka subsequently rescinded the appointment.

Constitutional reform role

Valenitabua's appointment comes as Rabuka is leading a special parliamentary committee for nationwide consultations on replacing Fiji's 2013 Constitution.

Valenitabua was also the chairperson of the CRC, which was established in March to review and prepare a final report and a final draft constitution that would replace the current supreme law of the land.

Valenitabua and the Commission completed their work and formally presented the documents to Fiji's President Ratu Naiqama Lalabalavu at the end of August.

However, the government ditched the Commission's draft constitution and tabled its own version - the Constitution (Amendment) Bill 2026.

The Bill is expected to be debated for its third reading next week and Valenitabua is expected to play a key role in the process as a non-elected Attorney-General, who is entitled to attend Cabinet as a minister and sit and participate in parliament.

World.title: Three masked men storm Wellington dairy with axes, hammer to steal till, owner says
World.content:
"Never experienced anything like that before and I hope to not ever again."

Those are the words of dairy owner, Sonia, after three masked men allegedly stormed into her Wellington dairy with axes and a hammer and made off with the till.

Sonia and her husband Charlie have been running Racecourse Dairy on Ararino Street in Upper Hutt for nine years.

Police deployed spikes on State Highway One on Tuesday afternoon to catch the men who crashed in an allegedly stolen car.

The state highway was closed for three and a half hours.

Police arrested one person.

Sonia told RNZ the incident at around 5.30pm was over in a matter of minutes.

"It happened very quickly."

She said her first thought was that her customer was being attacked.

"And then I realised, oh no, they're here for us."

She said her husband pulled her out of the way, as a man jumped onto the counter and the trio grabbed the till.

"Didn't look like they wanted to take the cigarettes or anything, so just money. But there wasn't much in the till, so only got pocket change really."

After they left the shop, Sonia said she ran out to read the number plate of the car, repeating it to herself so she wouldn't forget it.

She said she called police who arrived quickly and gave her a play-by-play of the pursuit.

Sonia said she'd prepared for thieves over the years: she frequently emptied the till and kept a dog on the premises for security.

"I didn't even really go into shock or anything or realise what was, you know, kind of happening straight away."

World.title: Long Covid sufferers being denied insurance over 'mental health' exclusions - lawyer
World.content:
Audio player for " Long Covid sufferers being denied insurance pay outs " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._f0.YIZs2-J2FpwgcBcJJb29s1vXmFAWHLh_p1oUyv-l-RA/health/2201661%2Flong-covid-sufferers-being-denied-insurance-over-mental-health-exclusions-lawyer

Long Covid sufferers being denied insurance pay outs Nine To Noon Download MP3 15m

A lawyer says Long Covid sufferers are increasingly seeing their insurance claims denied using mental health exclusions.

The 2024-25 National Health Survey found more than 400,000 people reported having Long Covid symptoms, defined as ongoing symptoms that continue for more than 12 weeks after having had the virus.

Insurance lawyer Tim Gunn told Nine to Noon people were being declined income protection claims when they were unable to work.

"These people are doing the right thing from the start," he said.

"They are going through the process of applying for insurance and filling out the various insurance application forms.

"As part of that process, you're required to disclose diagnosed conditions or issues that you've experienced in the past. These are kind of pre-existing conditions."

Gunn said his clients diligently did that process and disclosed an incident of mental health in their lives, which resulted in a mental health exclusion applied to their policy.

He said the policy would run for several years before his client got Covid and Long Covid, and were then unable to work.

"(They) then go to apply for cover and find that the mental health exclusion that was applied at the start of their cover isn't a mental health exclusion.

"It is an exclusion that applies to both mental health conditions and others."

The mental health disclosure was the cause of the imposition of the exclusion, Gunn said.

He said insurance policies did not have a defined list of illnesses and there was no automatic exclusion on an income protection cover.

The exclusion was not limited to the illness that you disclosed, it was a broad and all-encompassing mental health exclusion, he said.

Gunn said insurance providers did not consider Long Covid a mental health condition.

"They are distinctly confirming that they do not believe that Long Covid is a mental health condition, but that this mental health exclusion doesn't just relate to mental health conditions," he said.

He said he had seen similar nuance applied for people who disclosed ADHD.

Unreasonable and disproportionate

Gunn said his position was that when someone disclosed a mental health condition that they had experienced in the past, it was "reasonable and proportionate to put a justifiable limit on their ability to claim into the future for that condition or conditions that were directly related to what they disclose".

"It is not proportionate and reasonable to put a blanket mental health exclusion that covers both mental health conditions and non-mental health conditions, because in effect they are saying, because the words disorders related to fatigue exist in the mental health exclusion, that they can cover claims relating to issues where the symptoms are fatigue related."

Gunn said the exclusion was a mental heath exclusion and the condition that insurance providers were excluding was a non-mental health condition and therefore was unreasonable.

He said his clients had tried to dispute it.

"There are pending reviews, but people are spending years in review processes where the insurer is accepting that they are disabled, accepting that they cannot work, accepting that they cannot work due to the profound impacts of this condition, but that the mental health exclusion was wide enough to capture this non-mental health illness," Gunn said.

Gunn said there were various legal arguments as to how you interpreted the words of a policy.

There were insurance-specific rules which related to how you interpreted the clauses, he said.

"There are various contractual arguments as to how those words should specifically be interpreted in this context," Gunn said.

"Those arguments are live and we can explore those. There are the arguments in terms of the fairness of those conditions and if they comply with the Human Rights Act in terms of the carve-out for insurers.

"On a pure contractual basis, we can argue about what the words actually say, and then we can talk about the broader fairness issues."

Insurers defend policy assessment processes

In a statement, Partners Life said it did not regard Long Covid as a mental health disorder, but recognised it as a post-infectious condition that could affect multiple body systems like fatigue, post-exertional symptoms and cognitive difficulties.

It said it had accepted claims for customers with Long Covid, including customers with exclusions for, among other things, mental health disorders.

It also said as part of its assessment process, Partners Life considered whether an individual claim sits within the policy wording conditions.
