World.title: Private radio gets cut price deal on frequencies for another 20 years
World.content:
NZME, the owner of Newstalk ZB, has been offered another 20 years of its commercial radio frequencies for $11.2 million, under a Crown deal which values the industry's spectrum at about 70 percent less than the Crown received in the previous renewal round in 2011.

Around 70 commercial broadcasters are covered by the renewal process, with formal offers sent out this week after the Crown valued the industry's radio spectrum at $29m earlier this year.

It follows a contested valuation process, with the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment (MBIE) valuing the spectrum at about $38m, versus a $27m valuation commissioned by the Radio Broadcasters Association.

Media and Communications Minister Paul Goldsmith proposed a compromise figure of $29m, which Cabinet agreed to.

The payment terms have also been sweetened for this round.

Instead of paying $11.2m up front, NZME will make payments for four five-year periods, with the applicable payment made in advance at the beginning of each period.

Notably, it can surrender individual licences during the 20-year term without having to make payments relating to future periods for those licences.

Goldsmith said in January this year following Cabinet's decision that he had taken a changing radio environment into account, when planning the approach to this spectrum renewal process.

"By making the spectrum available for 20 years, while also providing opportunities for commercial operators to relinquish their spectrum holdings at 5-yearly intervals, we will enable the broadcasting industry to make commercial decisions about its radio networks at its own pace," Goldsmith said.

NZME chief executive Michael Boggs thanked the Crown for taking industry feedback on board, saying the payment terms would allow the company to align its frequency portfolio with changing needs while reducing cash flow pressures.

NZME has six months to accept the Crown's offer, with the first payment due in 2030, ahead of the new term starting on 3 April 2031.

MediaWorks, the country's other major commercial radio operator, is also in line for a substantial discount, although it has not disclosed the terms of its personalised offer.

World.title: Agritech company Hectre opens $5 million research lab to tackle global fruit waste
World.content:
Agritech company Hectre is expanding its operations with the opening of a leading edge fruit quality research lab, which is expected to be transformative for the global industry.

Hectre's technology was set to solve one of the biggest issues in the world's billion-dollar fruit industry, by helping packhouses to decide earlier what to store, what to pack and what to ship.

"Hectre started from growers telling us what they wanted," Hectre chief executive and founder Mattie Blomfield said, adding the market was waiting for further advances in the technology.

Agriculture Minister Todd McClay officially opened the central Auckland facility, which housed the near $5 million research programme co-funded by the government and Hectre.

Hectre was developing a next-generation Arc camera, which would be able identify the internal defects of a piece of fruit.

"Understanding the internal structures of fruit being shipped allows packhouses to make smart decisions around how to store, pack and ship their product."

"Fruit will therefore reach the market in better condition, with less waste."

Waste was estimated to cost the global industry 30 percent of products to market, currently estimated at close to $2 trillion.

"The problem we're solving is gigantic," Blomfield said.

"So if we do it, then I think you will see Hectre in all of the world's largest fruit companies, capturing valuable data for their for their business."

The company's existing technology was used by customers in 22 countries.

"Most of them are using the original hardware solution, and that does very well for them for size and colour," Blomfield said.

The existing Arc camera system scanned fruit trucks as they arrived at a packhouse, which returned sizing, colour and external quality data in near-real time.

"But reading for internal defects is a much trickier problem," Blomfield said.

He said Hectre's pioneering hyperspectral technology used a super-sophisticated camera to analyse the internal structure of a range of high value fruits, such as cherries, apples, peaches, pears other stone fruits and citrus fruits.

Future crops could include blueberries and tomatoes.

The research programme was expected to have a proof-of-concept algorithm, with at least 80 percent detection accuracy by June 2027, with a rollout of product beginning early next year.

The company currently employed 40 people with a few more key roles to fill.

An Auckland-based lawyer who represents student loan borrowers with overdue debt recently helped someone get a $100,000 discount through a scheme he says not enough people know about.

A law change in April saw the Inland Revenue commissioner receive greater power to provide relief from interest on an overseas borrower's loan.

That's a step further from the commissioner's previous powers, which were to be able to cut the penalties that were added on top of interest when an overseas-based borrower was late with payment.

The department released its annual report last week showing total penalties charged to borrowers - now at $1.27 billion - are approaching the $1.4b that represents the original loans borrowed, which are overdue.

Lawyer Dave Ananth said he's easily getting 20 calls a week from overseas borrowers worried about overdue loans.

Lawyer Dave Ananth. RNZ / Liu Chen

Many of the calls are coming from people in Australia wanting to visit home, while some come from Europe or South Africa.

Ananth told Nine to Noon people are overwhelmed with their student loan debt and don't know how to deal with Inland Revenue.

"A lot of people I deal with are overwhelmed by a $20,000 loan taken 20 years ago is now $80,000 and how do I deal with it?"

That's where Ananth comes in. He explains to them there is a scheme where the IRD commissioner may grant them remission on their interest if they are willing to provide a raft of documents to support their claim.

He has managed to help student loan debtors get "quite a bit" off their total debt - sometimes up to 50 percent of the interest.

"I achieved quite a bit yesterday for someone who had quite a huge student loan and got more than $100,000 worth of remissions of penalties and interest because it was huge."

Ananth said a major condition IRD has with the scheme is that the debtor must be willing and able to settle within a month.

"If settlement is reached, you've got a 30 day window to settle."

But Ananth said he didn't believe there was enough awareness of the ability to negotiate a discount for overseas borrowers.

He said a lot of the people who contacted him had no idea they could ask for remission on their penalties and found the whole process daunting - choosing to bury their heads in the sand instead.

"We need to do more in giving that information, either from IRD themselves or going out there and getting this information across."

Ananth said he was trying to reach a compromise and "win-win" situation for both IRD and the person in debt.

"The taxpayer-funded loan gets back the money he had lent, gets back a bit of cost, gets back a bit on interest and closes the account."

IRD were approached to provide comment on Nine to Noon but declined.

World.title: Australia clawed its way back into the third Test, but big challenges await
World.content:
It was, in the final analysis, close to the perfect day of Test cricket: ebbing, flowing, intriguing, with 10 wickets falling and 329 runs-worth of enterprising batting fulfilling Les Favell's trusty old criteria for an entertaining day on the hill.

There was a six-fer for Mitchell Starc, another bundle of tantalising, shot-filled knocks from South Africa's underappreciated batting stars and a pair of remarkable sequences in which Australia took 5-29 and 4-2. Both sides will, in some ways, feel they got the better of the other for telling periods.

The nagging doubt, after day one of the third and deciding Test, is how badly Australia's chances had been damaged before a ball had even been bowled. Not sufficiently recovered from his neck injury, Steve Smith withdrew. Not sufficiently superior to his colleagues in most facets of the game a week ago, Scott Boland was dropped for Nathan Lyon.

Quick hits from Australia vs South Africa day one Here are the quick hits from day one of the third Test between Australia and South Africa.

Then there was the toss. The minute Pat Cummins won it and elected to bowl first under sunny skies, on a perfect-looking pitch — not exactly a ringing endorsement of Australia's remade top six — it was hard to stop one's mind from wandering away from Newlands and back through time in search of precedents.

The obvious destinations were Edgbaston in 2005, the scene of Ricky Ponting's ill-fated decision to bowl first in that classic nailbiter, and Brisbane three years earlier, when poor old Nasser Hussain got it even more horribly wrong.

By lunch at Cape Town, Cummins's Australians were fighting an unwelcome omen: South Africa's domineering 0-140, obtained with a procession of boundaries off the most credentialed bowling attack in world cricket, comfortably shaded both England's 1-132 at Edgbaston in '05 and Australia's 1-125 in Brisbane in '02. Was Cummins coming similarly a cropper?

Cricket history tends to write inconvenient facts out of these stories. Few remember that in the immediate aftermath of Nasser's nightmare, for instance, Australian skipper Steve Waugh admitted he probably would have bowled first, too, albeit with a caveat. "The significance of the toss is overrated," Waugh explained. "Whatever you do first, you've got to do it well."

To say Australia didn't bowl or field well in the first session of this crunch game is an understatement. The vaunted quicks misfired early. To staunch the bleeding, Lyon had to be deployed in just the 11th over. Normally apt to suffocate opponents with sharp fielding, tight lines and partnership bowling, Australia managed only two maidens in the first 25 overs.

Proteas opener Marques Ackerman, who'd never batted at the top of the order in first-class cricket until his Test debut last week, attacked the bowling like prime David Warner, clubbing 12 fours and two sixes in his run-a-ball, thrill-a-minute 95. With Aiden Markram, he raced to South Africa's first 150-run opening stand in nearly a decade.

Of particular concern for Australia was the captain's bowling performance, the tone of which was set in his first over when Markram freed his arms, swivelled into position as though the ball was travelling in slow motion and cross-batted Cummins over the fence at cow corner. Cummins would finish the day with 0-73 from 18 overs, having extracted almost nothing from the pitch he'd so liked the look of in the morning. South Africa played him as though intent on showing a competitive disrespect.

But at first, slowly, and then in two manic bursts, Australia did pull things out of the fire somewhat from their dismal early position.

Lyon, whom Ackerman had taken a particular liking to, kept his head amid the onslaught and had the left-hander stumped, later roaring back into the game at a critical juncture and sneaking one past Temba Bavuma to bowl the Proteas skipper for a duck. Australia stemmed the flow of easy runs — from 5.18 an over in the first session, down to 3.11 in the second.

Reprieved on 39 when Travis Head dropped a sitter at short cover, Markram had doubled his score but looked set for even bigger things when he fell into a trap set by Hazlewood to be caught on the fine leg boundary. Matthew Breetzke was too casual against Cooper Connolly's spin, the left-armer reviewed an LBW shout cannily to claim his first Test wicket.

In the above-mentioned half-hour of head loss, South Africa lost 3-13 and squandered its momentum. Immediately after tea, the Proteas were even more culpable for failing to resist what appeared to be a very obvious temptation: an outer ring of catchers scattered around the boundary from fine leg to deep mid-wicket and Starc banging it in short.

David Bedingham, who'd reached 50 without much trouble, was the first to fall for it, hooking recklessly to be cleverly caught on the fine leg rope by Hazlewood. Two balls later, Wiaan Mulder tried an equally daft hook and feathered an edge to Carey behind the stumps.

If South Africa is destined to win this match and with it the series — and unfortunately for Australia, there is an air of destiny about that result at the moment — perhaps the Proteas' 97-run seventh-wicket partnership will be looked back on as a critical period. Ryan Rickelton, out of form with the bat until that point, contributed a patient 42 as all-rounder Marco Jensen battered a typically confident half-century.

The latter fun, which threatened to take the game back away from Australia entirely, ended when Starc took the second new ball. Calling it a clinical demolition of the tail would undersell him: with 4-2 in the space of seven ruthlessly full and straight deliveries, the Australian paceman took his 20th Test five-wicket haul and finished with 6-72 from 16.3 overs.

Once the day's surges of chaos were done with, a comment by Cummins before play seemed worth revisiting. Boland's omission, the Australian captain claimed, was that great cliché of cricket team selection: "a good problem to have".

But is it? Perhaps Cummins was implying something else, that Australia's other selection problems — replacing three of its top-six batters with players assuredly not in the same class as Boland — are bad ones to have. Ones that may shape this game more than what happened on day one.

Which brings us to another of cricket's enduring clichés: don't judge a pitch until both teams have batted on it.

World.title: Quick hits: Starc's six balls of fury after Cummins's questionable call
World.content:
Mitch Starc produced one of the most destructive spells of his storied career and Josh Hazlewood took a special catch as the Aussies fought back from what looked to be a calamitous early call.

Here are the quick hits from day one of the third Test between Australia and South Africa in Cape Town.

1. Head's drop compounds Cummins's questionable call

It was already a horror morning for Australia.

Having sent the South Africans in to bat in what looked to be pristine conditions, Cummins was in need of quick wickets to validate what always looked to be a bizarre decision.

He didn't get them.

Instead, Proteas openers Marques Ackerman and Aiden Markram made light work of Australia's much-vaunted bowling attack, flying towards 100 at close to five runs an over.

But finally, a chance presented itself, with Markram mistiming a drive and finding Travis Head in the covers.

It was an absolute dolly, but the Australian somehow put it down, the ball slipping through his fingers and hurtling to turf.

Loading Instagram content

By lunch, the South Africans had flown to 0-140 from 27 overs, suggesting Cummins's call may well take a place among Test cricket's all-time clangers.

2. South African openers throw away tons

Ackerman went to lunch having plundered his way to a 75-ball 82.

Playing just his second Test, the southpaw made a mockery of Australia's aging attack, including taking Starc for four consecutive boundaries for the first time in the quick's Test career.

He looked odds on for a maiden Test ton — but things tightened up after the first break.

Growing increasingly impatient, he faced 18 balls for his next 13 runs before charging down the track and running past a Nathan Lyon off break.

Alex Carey broke the stumps with little fuss and Ackerman was out for 95.

Ackerman was filthy with himself after falling agonisingly short of a maiden Test ton. (Fox Cricket)

The 30-year-old was filthy with himself, throwing his head and grimacing on his way from the middle.

And not long after, Markram was following his opening partner back to the pavilion after also turning down a golden opportunity for a Test ton, having top-edged a Josh Hazlewood short ball to be caught on the boundary for 78.

Even so, it was a 158-run partnership that guaranteed a dream morning for the South Africans.

3. Hazlewood's quick thinking sends South Africa rocking

The Proteas were cruising — until they weren't.

Having lost Temba Bavuma and Matthew Breetzke before tea, South Africa's collapse continued when Josh Hazlewood took a remarkable boundary catch early in the evening session.

The big fast bowler steadied himself as a David Bedingham top edge flew his way, before contorting his body, rising high and plucking the ball from the air.

Hazlewood took a remarkable grab as Australia came roaring back after tea. (Fox Cricket)

Landing with his foot perilously close to the rope, Hazlewood was composed enough to release the ball and then complete the catch inside the field of play.

Hazlewood threw the ball back into play before completing the catch. (Fox Cricket)

And only two deliveries later, Starc had a second for the over, having Wiaan Mulder caught behind with another short ball.

Suddenly, South Africa had lost 4-29 and that explosive start was a distant memory.

Marco Jansen and Ryan Rickleton then came together to steady the ship, with a 95-run partnership, but the day's momentum swings weren't done there

4. Starc's stunning six-ball special

With twilight beginning to set in, Rickleton and Jansen looked to be cruising towards stumps.

But with Starc about to get his hands on the second new ball, the set pair would have been well aware they weren't out of the woods just yet.

And sure enough, Australia's premier spearhead proceeded to produce a devastating two-over spell.

First, he had Rickleton plumb in front to a searing swinging yorker before bowling Jansen with something similarly venomous just two balls later.

Starc produced six balls of fury to have the Proteas all out for 329. (Getty Images: Ashley Vlotman/Gallo Images)

He then castled the newly-arrived Gerald Coetzee for a golden duck with the first ball of his next over, setting up a hat-trick delivery against number 11 Kagiso Rabada.

The South African survived the initial thunderbolt, but was helpless to the second, out LBW to yet another stunning Starc special.

Starc had four wickets in the space of six deliveries and South Africa was all out for 329 as stumps were called on a ridiculous, topsy-turvy day of Test match cricket.

5. The best seats out of the house

Given the questionable decision to start the Cape Town Test on a Tuesday, there may well have been a few sick notes handed in ahead of day one at Newlands.

So, it seemed slightly unfair for the broadcast cameras to pick on the two spectators who had definitely shown up to work.

Sitting in surely the most ideally-located office block in world cricket, overlooking the oval from behind the hill, they were pictured with their eyes firmly fixed on the action unfolding below them.

These two office workers had the best seats out of the house. (Fox Cricket)

Caught out, it wasn't long before their heads were back in their work.

Nothing to see here, boss. (Fox Cricket)

Despite being a weekday, day one in Cape Town provided an engaged, colourful crowd, and undoubtedly the best of the series — both in and out of the ground.

6. Sore neck prevents Smith's Newlands return

Prior to a pulsating day in Cape Town, a dodgy neck robbed cricket fans of one of the most eagerly awaited returns in the sport's history.

How Sandpapergate rocked Australian cricket In 2018, Sandpapergate rocked Australian cricket to its very core. Here's how a febrile atmosphere colluded with a team persistently testing the limits of acceptability to change the game.

Having struggled through a couple of ginger net sessions, Steve Smith was unable to prove his fitness in the hours before play on day one, succumbing to the neck issue that had troubled him in Gqeberha.

With David Warner retired and Cameron Bancroft years out of the Test team, it meant that none of the three Sandpapergate antagonists would feature at the venue where Australian cricket was thrown into crisis eight years earlier.

Smith's late withdrawal saw Australia make four changes, with Josh Inglis, Cam Green, Lyon and Cooper Connolly all coming into the side.

Remarkably, the last time Australia made as many alterations during a single series was after that very same Cape Town Test, when Bancroft, Smith and Warner began serving their suspensions.

World.title: Loyal back to reclaim Sydney to Hobart record
World.content:
A decade after his last appearance in the Sydney to Hobart Yacht Race, Anthony Bell has unveiled a new Loyal boat to challenge for line honours in this year's race.

But it's not a new boat — it's an old one.

Bell was first to Hobart in 2011 with Investec Loyal and in 2016 with Perpetual Loyal, setting a then-race record in the latter race of one day 13 hours, 31 minutes and 20 seconds.

On Tuesday in Sydney, Bell revealed his boat for this year's edition of the bluewater classic — the race record-holder and last year's winner, Comanche.

Comanche takes out line honours in Sydney to Hobart race Master Lock Comanche claims line honours in the 80th edition of the gruelling Sydney to Hobart yacht race, with a stunning daylight hours finish.

Bell spent up big to buy the five-time line honours-winning boat, which will race on Boxing Day as Tribeca Loyal.

Bell, the owner and skipper of the supermaxi, is aiming to lift the J.H. Illingworth Challenge Cup for a third time.

He has again recruited America's Cup and Olympic gold medallist Tom Slingsby to serve as the crew's sailing master.

The three-time world sailor of the year is delighted to be working on a yacht with the quality and power of Comanche.

"It's the most powerful supermaxi there is in the world," Slingsby said in Sydney.

"There's times there where we actually try to slow the boat down because it's got so much power and the waves could be too big that you're flying off the waves too fast.

"It averages really high speeds, it loves it when it's windy, so it's an exciting boat. You wouldn't want to choose any other boats to do the home run on.

"This boat already owns the Sydney Hobart race record, but … if we get the right conditions, we can break that record by a lot."

Master Lock Comanche took line honours in Hobart last year. (Getty Images: Steve Bell)

Despite his past success with Loyal, the 2012 Olympic gold medallist admits sailing on the open seas is a long way from his comfort zone.

"I'm not an ocean racer," Slingsby declared.

"I'm more of the short-course stuff.

"It's not something that I'm good at and really want to do, but I love coming back."

A major motivation for Slingsby and the crew is the continuing partnership with the Humpty Dumpty Foundation, which raises money for life-saving infant medical equipment for Australian hospitals.

The worthy cause is why Loyal will once again take on some celebrity deckhands to boost its fundraising profile.

Former Wallaby turned Rugby Australia chief executive Phil Waugh and Sydney Roosters great Anthony Minichello are among the famous names heading south.

"I certainly don't miss the contact of playing rugby league, but the camaraderie, and everyone being laser-focused on achieving a goal, that's the stuff you do miss when you retire from professional sport," Minichello said.

This year's star-studded crew continues the tradition for Loyal to rely on some unconventional athletes taking up a new sport.

"We've had 21 people who represented Australia, won world surfing titles, gold medals, played for the Wallabies, played rugby league, and we have two TV Week Gold Logie winners as well," Bell said.

AAP

World.title: Starc's ferocious late spell helps Australia recover from horror start
World.content:
Mitchell Starc has dragged Australia back into the third Test against South Africa after a stunning spell with the second new ball.

The home side mustered 329 after being sent in by Pat Cummins, but lost its last four wickets for just two runs as Starc found swing with the new ball to blow away the tail.

Starc finished with figures of 6-72 from 16.3 overs to allow Australia to share the spoils after a pulsating day of Test cricket.

Days of Test cricket are rarely split in half, but day one at Newlands could definitively split in two as South Africa handed Australia a lifeline after throwing away a promising position.

Throughout the opening session the Proteas were absolutely cruising, a morning's play that simply couldn't have gone worse for the tourists.

Steve Smith had been ruled out before play had even started, failing a fitness test on his troublesome neck.

Travis Head dropped a sitter to reprieve Aiden Markram off the bowling of a ropable Starc.

Marques Ackerman helped put South Africa in the driver's seat early on day one, but fell five runs short of his maiden Test century. (Getty Images: Ashley Vlotman/Gallo Images)

The Proteas were scoring at over five runs per over, with openers Aiden Markram and Marques Ackerman powering their way to 0-158 not long after lunch.

Pat Cummins's decision to bowl first on a placid deck looked misguided.

But Nathan Lyon, preferred to Scott Boland in one of four changes made by the Aussies, made the breakthrough that precipitated a collapse of epic proportions.

Ackerman advanced down the pitch and was beaten by Lyon, with Alex Carey completing a regulation stumping.

Nathan Lyon (centre) picked up two first innings wickets on his return to the Test side. (Getty Images: Ashley Vlotman/Gallo Images)

The collapse was not immediate, with Markham and David Bedingham combining for a 45-run partnership.

But Markram (75) was dismissed hooking Josh Hazlewood, superbly caught by Starc on the backward square leg boundary which started the South African's slide.

Skipper Temba Bavuma was bowled by Lyon for a two-ball duck, with Matthew Breetzke trapped LBW by Cooper Connolly for 2 as the Proteas lost 3-13 in the space of seven overs.

Starc then struck twice in the space of a single over, Bedingham (50) hooking to Hazlewood on the boundary before Wiaan Mulder (0) walked without waiting for a decision just two balls later after edging a hook to Carey.

Marco Jansen again threatened to take the Test away from Australia before his innings was ended by a searing Starc yorker. (Getty Images: Ashley Vlotman)

That left South Africa 6-232 just after tea and reeling.

South Africa's hero from Gqeberha, Marco Jansen, once again proved to be a thorn in Australia's side, and notched the fourth half-century of the innings in a valuable 95-run stand with Ryan Rickelton (42).

Jansen and Rickelton saw South Africa safely to the second new ball, but then ran head first into a rampant Starc, who wiped out the final four wickets in the space of six lethal deliveries.

Follow the live blog below for a recap of all the day one action as it happened.

World.title: Walsh back at fullback in Kangaroos team to face Cook Islands
World.content:
Reece Walsh appears to be the frontrunner to wear the number one jersey for the Rugby League World Cup knockout stages after being named to start against the Cook Islands.

The Brisbane game-breaker opened Australia's campaign against New Zealand before veteran James Tedesco had his turn in their win over Fiji.

Both were among their team's best players, giving Kangaroos coach Kevin Walters a selection headache.

Despite his impressive showing that included three try assists, it appears Sydney Roosters premiership captain Tedesco may have paid the price for the Kangaroos' below-par showing in their 36-22 win over Fiji last Sunday.

He has been named on the bench, with Walters turning back to Walsh for his side's final pool game.

With the unbeaten hosts needing to stiffen their defence across the park, Tom Dearden has won the race to partner Cameron Munster in a third halves pairing, with Sam Walker relegated to the reserves.

Walker has been in the headlines since the Fiji match, with his Roosters outfit withdrawing their contract offer.

Walters has recalled rested forwards including skipper Isaah Yeo and his battle-hardened Penrith teammate Liam Martin, who will line up in the second row alongside Jacob Preston, who came off the bench against Fiji.

After coming off the bench against Fiji, who made easy metres through the middle in a gallant defeat, Pat Carrigan and Tino Fa'asuamaleaui are back in the starting pack.

David Fifita and Keaon Koloamatangi have been demoted for the clash in Townsville.

Centre Bradman Best did enough in his first Kangaroos match to keep his spot ahead of Latrell Mitchell.

Ethan Strange, who replaced the injured Mitchell Moses in the squad, is set to make his Test debut after being named on the six-man bench in the number 14 jumper.

Kangaroos team (1-13):

1: Reece Walsh; 2: Jack Bostock; 3: Kotoni Staggs; 4: Bradman Best; 5: Tom Trbojevic; 6: Cameron Munster; 7: Tom Dearden; 8: Patrick Carrigan; 9: Harry Grantr; 10: Tino Fa'asuamaleauai; 11: Jacob Preston; 12: Liam Martin; 13: Isaah Yeo (C)

Reserves:

14: Ethan Strange; 15: Keaon Koloamatangi; 16: Cameron Murray; 17: Reuben Cotter; 18: Lindsay Smith; 19: James Tedesco; 20: Sam Walker; 21: Latrell Mitchell; 22: David Fifita; 23: Blayke Brailey

Robinson ruled out of tournament for Jillaroos

Julia Robinson scored one of Australia's 15 tries against England, but the Jillaroo will miss the rest of the tournament with a dislocated wrist. (Getty Images: Janelle St Pierre)

The Jillaroos also named their team for their next game at the Rugby League World Cup, with star centre Julia Robinson ruled out of the tournament.

Robinson dislocated her wrist in Saturday's 78-0 win over England. Scans ruled out a fracture, but confirmed ligament damage.

The Jillaroos will face Wales in Sydney on Sunday. Robinson was replaced in the extended squad by Canberra's Sheridan Gallagher.

Jess Sergis comes into the centres, while Jesse Southwell was named at five-eighth alongside Tarryn Aiken. Makenzie Weale and Sariah Paki move from the bench into the starting forward pack.

World.title: Tasmania Devils' inaugural VFL captain axed after pub incident
World.content:
The Tasmania Devils have axed VFL captain Robbie Fox, following an incident at a Hobart pub, the ABC understands.

Fox, 33, is understood to have been removed from the Granada Tavern, in Hobart's northern suburbs, after becoming drunk and disorderly at the venue two weeks ago.

It's understood Fox was abusive toward some staff at the venue, and at one point a bottle was thrown.

The Granada Tavern was contacted but declined to comment.

The ABC understands Fox was removed from the Granada Tavern following an incident two weeks ago. (ABC News: Owain Stia-James)

The incident has contributed to the Devils parting ways with their inaugural skipper, opting not to offer him a fresh contract for the 2027 season.

In a statement, Devils VFL boss Aaron Pidgeon said "the club's expectations regarding player behaviour, and adherence to our standards" were part of the decision not to offer him a new deal.

Fox is also employed by the Devils as the club's strategic projects and impact lead, and it's understood he will remain in the role.

Robbie Fox is a former Sydney Swans AFL player. (Facebook: Tasmania Football Club)

The veteran defender, who hails from Burnie, was recruited to the Devils after playing 105 games with the Sydney Swans, including the 2022 and 2024 AFL Grand Finals.

In an injury-affected season, he played 13 games this year for Tasmania in the VFL, leading the club to a top four finish and a home semi-final.

World.title: Music mogul Jay-Z picks himself to perform at next Super Bowl
World.content:
Jay-Z, the American music mogul behind Empire State of Mind, 99 Problems and entertainment company Roc Nation, that helps produce Super Bowl half-time shows, will himself be next year's featured performer at the NFL showpiece in California.

The NFL, Apple Music and Roc Nation announced Jay-Z will headline the 2027 Super Bowl half-time festivities on February 14 at SoFi Stadium in Inglewood, California.

Jay-Z attending a NFL game between Washington Commanders and the Dallas Cowboys at Northwest Stadium. (Reuters: Peter Casey-Imagn Images)

NFL Commissioner Roger Goodell said he had one request when the league first reached an agreement with Roc Nation: that Jay-Z take the stage himself "whenever the moment felt right to him".

"From Reasonable Doubt to standing on the Super Bowl half-time stage, this has been a journey," Jay-Z said in a statement.

"Thirty years of music, work, and culture on the world's biggest stage.

"This run continues to be a dream come true."

After days of speculation, Jay-Z is set to return to the stadium where he closed his celebration of the 30th anniversary of Reasonable Doubt, the mogul's 1996 debut album.

The concerts included three sold-out shows at Yankee Stadium and sold-out performances in London and Paris ahead of a stop at SoFi Stadium over the weekend.

Jay-Z's Roc Nation has partnered with the NFL since 2019 to advise on and help produce the league's entertainment presentations, including the Super Bowl half-time show.

At the time, Jay-Z said he told Mr Goodell: "If this is about me performing at the Super Bowl, then we can just end this conversation now."

Inside SoFi Stadium at Inglewood, California, ahead of the Super Bowl 2022. (Getty Images: Gregory Shamus)

Seven years later, Jay-Z is ready to perform after all.

Jay-Z, born Shawn Carter, has won 25 Grammy Awards and received 89 nominations, the second-most in history behind his wife, Beyoncé — who has performed at two Super Bowls.

His catalogue also includes the albums The Blueprint and The Black Album, and hit songs such as Hard Knock Life (Ghetto Anthem), 99 Problems and Empire State of Mind, his collaboration with Alicia Keys.

NFL half-time entertainment The NFL announces the Jonas Brothers will be the half-time entertainment when Melbourne hosts the Rams and 49ers to launch the season in September.

Last year, Reasonable Doubt was inducted into the Grammy Hall of Fame.

His recent concerts brought out a rotating cast of guests.

At SoFi Stadium, his daughter Blue Ivy played piano on The Story of O.J. and Dead Presidents, while Scarface, John Legend and DJ Khaled joined him on opening night. Dr. Dre, Snoop Dogg and Too $hort appeared during Saturday's finale.

Earlier in the run, Beyoncé, Rihanna, Eminem and Nas were among the guests at Yankee Stadium.

Bad Bunny and Lady Gaga perform during this year's Super Bowl half-time show at Levi's Stadium in Santa Clara, California. (Photo by Kevin C. Cox/Getty Images)

Jay-Z has built a career as an executive and entrepreneur. The Brooklyn rapper co-founded Roc-A-Fella Records and founded Roc Nation in 2008, building it into an entertainment company that works with artists and athletes.

He became the first rapper inducted into the Songwriters Hall of Fame in 2017 and joined the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame in 2021.

He is also a four-time Emmy winner.

Kendrick Lamar performs during the 2025 Super Bowl half-time show at Caesars Superdome in New Orleans, Louisiana. (Getty Images: Patrick Smith)

Roc Nation will executive produce the half-time show, with Hamish Hamilton directing.

The half-time show has collected Emmys in recent years. Bad Bunny's performance in February won a record seven, including best live variety special, while Kendrick Lamar's show last year won for music direction.

AP

World.title: AFL abandons Opening Round for season 2027
World.content:
The AFL has abandoned the Opening Round fixture from the past two seasons, with all 18 clubs now set to play in Round One in 2027.

The previous seasons saw the four teams based in New South Wales and Queensland play home games, while this year's draw also included one game at the MCG.

The split fixture meant each of the teams that played in the Opening Round — also referred to as round zero — subsequently had an early season bye.

Marcus Bontempelli of the Bulldogs during Opening Round in 2026 in Brisbane. (Getty Images: AFL Photos/Russell Freeman)

Critics say the fixturing caused distortions in the draw, giving an advantage to the teams that played in Opening Round.

"We have listened to feedback and are pleased to be able to deliver a Round One for all our 18 clubs and fans as we bring back a traditional nine-game opening weekend across the country," AFL chief Andrew Dillon said in a statement.

Andrew Dillon announced the codes in-principle agreement to a new Illicit Drugs Policy in March. (Getty Images: Quinn Rooney)

Former premiership coach with West Coast and Collingwood and now ABC analyst, Mick Malthouse, said Opening Round compromised the fixture.

"We don't need it and it's a blessing now that we don't have it," he told ABC Sport.

"Let me say that 'zero round' was appropriately named.

"It had zero impact on the public; in fact, I'll go in the reverse and say it had a completely negative impact."

Malthouse said the early season byes caused by the Opening Round meant the ladder was not meaningful until all teams had played the same number of games, which in the season just passed did not happen until the end of Round 4.

"All round zero did was compromise the ability of sides to be ready for the next game," Malthouse said.

Mick Malthouse said Opening Round compromised the AFL draw. (Getty Images: Mark Dadswell)

"If you've got a game tucked under your belt, you're ready; you're miles in front of the next side.

"And don't worry about the results of those games; it's more important about the long-term effect on players.

The president of the AFL Fans' Association, Ron Issko, welcomed the move to reinstate a full Round One.

"Credit to the AFL for listening," he told ABC Sport.

"When you start a season after waiting six months for the season to start and not all teams are playing, it's sort of like a soft launch.

"It just didn't have that energy.

"We're a national competition and what's better than having all teams playing on Round One."

The AFL's move to highlight games in NSW and Queensland was seen as a response to the National Rugby League's move to stage that competition's opening games in Las Vegas.

Opening Round was seen as a response to the NRL starting its season in Las Vegas, in the United States. (AAP: Supplied/NRL Photos)

"We've looked over the border and so seeing that there's games played in Las Vegas, [said] 'Wow, if that's the way they operate, let us do something similar,'" Malthouse said.

"Forget about what's happening over the border and in fact embrace what's over the border and applaud them," he said.

Round One of the 2027 season will be played from March 17-21, with matches in NSW, Western Australia, South Australia and Victoria.

Hawthorn will play triple-premiers Brisbane in Round One of the 2027 AFL season. (Getty Images: Steve Bell)

It has been delayed one week from the usual season start time by the test cricket 150th anniversary match between Australia and England at the MCG.

The season will kick off with a match between the Sydney Swans and Geelong at the SCG on Wednesday, March 17.

The following night, losing grand finalist Fremantle will play the Western Bulldogs at home.

Three-time reigning premiers Brisbane will play on the Friday night against Hawthorn at the MCG.
