Tech.title: A 28-Year-Old DOGE Operative Gutted USAID. HR Had No Record of Him Working There
Tech.content:
On March 18, 2025, Secretary of State Marco Rubio handed the reins of the US Agency for International Development to Jeremy Lewin, a 28-year-old graduate of Harvard Law School, former investment banker, and affiliate of Elon Musk’s so-called Department of Government Efficiency. At the time, Lewin’s appointment drew criticism because of his lack of experience in government, diplomacy, or foreign assistance. But for career staff inside the agency, the issues surrounding Lewin’s new role were much more alarming than his thin résumé.

For at least two months, USAID senior staff had no knowledge of how Lewin, who appeared at the agency one day as a policymaker on an obscure detail from the General Services Administration, could have suddenly begun wielding the powers of the agency’s top official.

Internal USAID emails reviewed by WIRED reveal that during the three-week period of March 18 to April 4, during which Lewin began canceling lifesaving aid programs and personally signed off on the termination of thousands of USAID employees, he did not sign the paperwork typically required by law to begin work at the agency, despite repeated requests. In fact, his appointment was so mysterious that USAID security was unable to issue him an ID card because they had no records of his employment.

Lewin, currently director of policy planning at the State Department, tells WIRED that prior to Rubio delegating powers to him, he was “both detailed and dual appointed to work at USAID by Secretary Rubio according to well-established authorities and with the advice of State Department and White House counsel.”

Experts, though, say that while Lewin performed the duties of a top USAID leader under the title Rubio handed to him—deputy administrator of policy and programming and chief operating officer—it isn’t clear that he had the legal authority to do so. Questions about how DOGE affiliates like Lewin stepped into top roles at many federal agencies, including USAID, remain key to dozens of active lawsuits targeting DOGE and the Trump administration over federal workforce reductions, firings, and agency dismantlings.

Lewin has said, in a declaration submitted to the court in J. Doe 4 v. U.S. DOGE Service, that he began serving at USAID as a senior adviser as well as a director for strategy and programs on January 28, 2025. On March 18, according to court filings, Rubio, in his role as USAID’s acting administrator, delegated the authority of the deputy administrator of policy and programming and chief operating officer to Lewin, and also signed a document appointing Lewin an “officer of the United States.”

According to the emails reviewed by WIRED, on March 20, two days after Rubio placed Lewin atop the USAID hierarchy, White House liaison to USAID Adam Korzeniewski notified HR to begin the process of onboarding Lewin as a senior adviser performing duties as deputy administrator. Four days later, the emails reveal, after prompting from HR, Korzeniewski provided a proposed start date—March 18—and the next day, Lewin was sent a temporary job offer.

Tech.title: UK Home Office May Face Investigation Over Use of OpenAI Tech
Tech.content:
A UK government watchdog is considering an investigation into the Home Office’s use of generative AI tools to process asylum applications, WIRED has learned. The potential probe follows lawmakers and researchers publicly questioning the tools’ accuracy and the government’s secrecy around their use.

The Independent Chief Inspector of Borders and Immigration (ICIBI), which monitors the Home Office’s management of borders, immigration, and customs, has asked digital rights nonprofit Open Rights Group (ORG) to share more information on the tools as it draws up plans for the topics it will inspect next year, campaigner Sara Alsherif tells WIRED. ORG’s findings come from a six-month investigation into the tools, which involved 11 parliamentary questions, two ministerial letters, and 10 public records requests that attempt to pry details from the Home Office, which has withheld details on the tools.

The ICIBI tells WIRED it cannot confirm what topics are under active consideration before it publishes its annual inspection priorities, but it says it is aware of concerns about the use of AI tools and pointed to its findings last year that one of the tool’s “effectiveness and reliability were varied.”

“Asylum decisions are made by trained caseworkers, with AI tools used only to assist in navigating interview records and policy information. They cannot be used in isolation and do not make decisions on claims,” a Home Office spokesperson tells WIRED in an email. “We regularly monitor the performance of these tools alongside our established quality-assurance processes, and have already committed to publishing updated evaluations on their roll out.”

The Home Office uses the Asylum Case Summarisation (ACS) and Asylum Policy Search (APS) tools, built on OpenAI’s 2023 GPT-4 large language model and Microsoft Foundry, to summarize transcripts of interviews with asylum applicants and information about their countries of origin, according to documents obtained by ORG. The immigration and law enforcement authority started piloting these tools in late 2024 as the Labour government tried to clear a backlog of around 100,000 asylum cases, while staying on top of the tens of thousands of new applications the UK receives each year. While the department has made significant progress, halving the number of people waiting on an initial decision in the year through June, the number of appeals against decisions has ballooned.

Researchers are concerned about the accuracy of the AI tools–especially to decide something as high-stakes as whether to send someone back to a country where they fear persecution. ORG found that the percentage of summaries generated by the ACS deemed not fit for use—often because they contain factual errors or misrepresentations—is significantly higher than the published 9 percent error rate calculated in the pilot evaluation. There is no quality control for the summaries produced by the APS, it also found.

Tech.title: Halloween Candy Prices Take a Scary Bite Out of Shoppers’ Budgets
Tech.content:
If you can’t afford a trip to a haunted house this spooky season, just swing by the supermarket candy aisle for a nasty scare. The price of sweets jumped over the last few years, soaring even faster than the average inflation rate, according to a recent report from the US Bureau of Labor Statistics, with higher ingredient costs as the primary villain.

October is important for candy sales, as shoppers stock up for parties, trick-or-treaters, or — let’s be honest — personal consumption.

“The biggest purchasing days are still ahead, with about 35% of Halloween seasonal sales expected this week,” a Hershey Company spokesperson told CNET.

More from CNET

Chocolate treats have become especially expensive, as a recent global cocoa shortage squeezed the market while candy companies were preparing shipments for Halloween.

But despite chilling prices, chocolate is still making its way into Halloween bags and buckets.

“Trick-or-treat participation intent is in line with last year,” the Hershey spokesperson said. “Confection remains a resilient category.”

Money monstrosity

Americans will likely spend over $13 billion on Halloween this year, the National Retail Federation reports. That’s almost twice the $6.9 billion people spent on the holiday 11 years ago, in 2015.

“Consumers continue to make Halloween a spending priority, but they are also approaching the season with affordability in mind,” Allison Zeller, a National Retail Federation vice president, said in a statement.

Candy remains the favorite purchase, with 95% of Halloween shoppers planning to snag some this year, followed by decorations, costumes and greeting cards, according to the National Retail Federation. In 2026, shoppers are expected to spend over $4 billion on Halloween candy alone.

An Oct. 20 report from research group Groundwork Collaborative broke down which candy prices have risen the most this year. The Mondelez Sour Gummy Candy variety pack, which jumped 39% in price, and Hershey seasonal Peanut Butter Cups, which saw a 23% increase, are this year’s most expensive Halloween candy compared with last season.

The squeeze doesn’t stop in the candy aisle — utility bills and other essentials are climbing, too. A Consumer Reports survey from earlier this month found that one in five American families has cut back on groceries due to rising energy costs.

“If you’ve been waiting until now to get your Halloween goodies, you’re right to do so. Halloween sales hit the high street and online two or three days before Halloween as stores try to clear stock,” says James Bricknell, CNET commerce managing editor.

“If you’re all set for this year, do what I did last year and grab a bunch of costumes and decorations the day after Halloween,” he adds. “Then, you can store them ready to go for Halloween 2027.”

Tech.title: Anthropic, Suno Sued for Unlawfully Using Songs by Madonna, Johnny Cash, Joni Mitchell
Tech.content:
The Man in Black couldn’t have imagined this. AI companies Suno and Anthropic face a combined $338 million in lawsuits for allegedly using songs and lyrics by Madonna, Johnny Cash and Joni Mitchell to train their artificial intelligence systems.

Reservoir Media Management, a music rights company, filed two separate lawsuits on Oct. 21. In one of them, Reservoir accuses Suno of scraping 1,050 copyrighted songs — including Cash’s Ring of Fire, Mitchell’s Both Sides Now and Madonna’s Papa Don’t Preach. Suno is a platform where users can generate an AI song using only a text prompt.

In the other lawsuit, Reservoir accuses Anthropic of using copyrighted lyrics from 853 songs to train its Claude family of AI models. Some of the songs mentioned in that lawsuit include Mitchell’s Big Yellow Taxi, Billy Strayhorn’s Lush Life and Evanescence‘s Bring Me to Life.

More from CNET

“We disagree with the allegations and intend to defend this case vigorously,” a representative for Anthropic told Billboard.

Representatives for Suno and Anthropic didn’t immediately respond to requests for comment.

Reservoir seeks $186.4 million in damages from Suno and $151.4 million from Anthropic. Both lawsuits accuse the companies of copyright infringement, circumventing restrictions such as logins and paywalls and stripping song credits of title, writer and publisher data.

Anthropic was also sued last week for violating copyright for reportedly using 274 Elvis Presley songs to train Claude. The company has been sued more than a dozen times for copyright infringement — most notably in a $1.5 billion settlement over allegations that it trained its AI on millions of pirated books. Suno also faces several copyright infringement lawsuits, including a second from Sony Music and Universal Music Group.

Reservoir founder and CEO Golnar Khosrowshahi told Music Business Worldwide that the AI music industry can’t be allowed to exploit songwriters’ work.

“When we believe their work has been exploited without authorization, we will hold AI platforms legally accountable to ensure those rights are upheld,” Khosrowshahi said. “We will continue to advocate for a framework that supports technological progress while protecting the creative work at the heart of our industry.”

Lawsuits are piling up

Copyright infringement — of news articles, music, books and art — has become a major issue, with several AI companies accused of ingesting mountains of data to train AI models such as Claude, OpenAI’s GPT, Google’s Gemini and Elon Musk’s Grok. There’s even a website, the AI Lawsuit Tracker, that counts 145 copyright infringement lawsuits — more than half of the overall cases against AI companies.

AI models are trained when their companies feed a vast amount of data — text, images, music, videos and software code — into their AI systems. With all that data, as well as synthetic data generated by computers, AI models can learn to generate words, images and video that may appear human-created.

In the lawsuit filed last week, Reservoir said Suno has already admitted to copying “essentially all music files of reasonable quality that are accessible on the open internet,” a statement Suno made in court during a 2024 suit brought by Universal Music Group, Sony Music Entertainment, and Warner Music Group.

This summer, a hacker cracked into Suno’s code and revealed that the company allegedly scraped music and lyrics from platforms like YouTube Music, Deezer, Genius and stock music libraries. The hack showed more than 2 million clips in a folder called “youtube_music,” as well as thousands of hours of music from the lyrics database Genius HQ, the music streaming service Deezer, and the stock music site Pond5.

In the lawsuit, Reservoir says that Suno is not truly a platform for people to create music and “was instead always meant to replace the artists whose works were being unlawfully copied by directly reaching those artists’ listeners with AI-generated substitutes which copy the originals.”

Anthropic allegedly stripped credits

Reservoir also accused Anthropic of using a text-extraction tool called Newspaper, which removes copyright notices from written material. Reservoir said Claude is partly trained on lyrics collected from Common Crawl, a web crawler that, during its crawls, inadvertently picks up lyrics from licensed sites such as Musixmatch and LyricFind.

Tech.title: Ace Combat 8 Elevates High-Voltage Dogfights With Wistful Melodrama
Tech.content:
Up in the digital skies, I sortie with my squad (sortie, that was the word), staying quiet as they sound off over comms. A stalwart lecturer, a daredevil peacenik and a stoic rocker drifted off the edges of my wings (they’ll back you up if you bring them home). We cruise ahead, lighthearted bickering layered over views of the clearest blue over blankets of puffy white. A contact hits the edge of our radar, orders come spilling in from below, and as one, we peel off to find our enemy in the air (I can almost feel the wind).

The prologue kicking off Ace Combat 8: Wings of Theve, the latest game in the fighter jet combat franchise that debuted in 1995, is riddled with voiceovers loftily espousing the aviator’s philosophy of communing with the skies. It’s a little much, I thought, as I struggled to adjust to the game’s controls. By the time I rolled credits around 25 hours later, the aircraft in my hangar were extensions of my digital body. I was up in the clouds alongside my nameless pilot and their squadmates.

As my first Ace Combat game, it’s unclear to me how much Wings of Theve retains and how much it innovates on its predecessors. That fresh perspective, and especially my inexperience with flight simulator games of all stripes, makes my wholehearted embrace of Ace Combat 8 all the more special. If you’ve been waiting to dive into a game flying jets around a fictional warzone, Wings of Theve could enchant you as it has me.

More from CNET

That’s partially a credit to the controls and gameplay, but it’s the earnest melodrama established in the game’s intro that builds and builds over each mission. Plucked from the ocean by the crew of an old aircraft carrier serving as the last hope of an invaded nation, you’re thrown into the sky in a ridealong with a legendary pilot. Targeted by an enemy ace, you go down, but get fished out of the water alone – with the pilot’s soul riding along with you, issuing wise parentheticals about the new squad you’re assigned to lead, about war, about flying itself.

In stakes, in setting, in characters, in echoed themes, in bombastic set pieces and midmission moments your attention is pointedly drawn to, the word that comes to mind when describing Ace Combat 8 is anime. (That’s a compliment.) Characters speak their minds in hushed whispers or loud barks, but always from beliefs welling in their chests. These missives come crackling over the radio, amplifying high-tension jet combat between metal machines with a spotlight on the humans at the controls.

Missions span attacking land, air and sea targets.

Those big beliefs slam head-on into massive enemy vehicles, land- or airborne colossi bristling with weapons, another staple from anime skilfully deployed to ratchet up the challenge and spectacle. It should be silly to send your quartet of jets against land battleships (literal naval vessels footed with rows of tank treads), but their menacing blister of guns cracks the sky open with explosions, a sinful interruption to the sublime act of flight and a lethal threat to your squadmates. AC8 sells spectacle well.

From tightly paced missions to downtime on the carrier to character subplots to corporate intrigue to geopolitical strife, Ace Combat 8 dances between tightropes. It wastes little time, but lets conversations and weighty moments linger for players to absorb (again, anime, complimentary). It feels trimmed, honed down to just the hits.

That breezy pace makes the game’s more blatantly militaristic aspects easier to endure or enjoy, depending on how much you embrace the hawkish nature of a fighter pilot sim putting you in the cockpits of real-world weapons of war.



Screenshot by David Lumb/CNET

Resisting, or giving in, to the military fantasy

In the same vein as the adage that there are no antiwar films (and that combat in media is inherently promotional), military flight simulation games glorify warfare. Spotlighting the heroism of soldiers and the romance of fighter aces clashing in the sky unquestionably tilts these games into the “war is cool” genre of war stories. And by lavishing its fighter jets with flattering panning shots in cinematics and postmission recap footage, Ace Combat 8 shifts the tone toward war-machine worship.

It’s the stories your squaddies tell that reel the game back toward humanism. The stunt pilot wunderkind, Tasha, balances her loyalty to the squad with her desire never to shoot anyone down — just lure them right into your crosshairs. Coster and The Professor, your other squadmates, protect each other and risk everything for the people on the Endurance, the aging aircraft carrier serving as your home base. And that pilot riding shotgun in your mind, who was known for avoiding getting any kills, speaks of keeping the team alive and the glory of flight. Nobody loves fighting.

Your wingman, Coster, playing a lament on his guitar — for fallen comrades, for the war, for loss itself. Screenshot by David Lumb/CNET

Nobody besides the player, of course. I grew up awed by American war machines with a parent working at a defense contractor (developing rockets, not bombs), so it’s tough not to love sitting in the cockpits of jets I’ve admired most of my life. Shooting down enemy after enemy in Ace Combat 8 with an impressive range of ordnance is a delight. There’s an undeniable glee in raining destruction on justified foes, especially the big armored behemoths on land or in the sky.

But the older I got, the more my war media matured to stories exploring the human cost, and I found Ace Combat 8 to be similarly more than a power fantasy. Striving to liberate your home country and subjugate the enemy to sue for peace, clashing with enemy aces in combat and ideology, destroying metal colossi — that makes AC8 feel like a stealth Gundam game. Yoshiyuki Tomino’s anime about giant mecha battling over the course of a horrific war, anchored around an ace and the carrier ship they call home alongside a crew with their own dramas, feels like an inspiration. While I still enjoyed the glee of blowing enemies out of the sky in AC8, the characters, like in Gundam, were quick to remind me that they just wanted to go home.

Ace Combat 8 has its own modern touches. A corporate bigwig taking it upon himself to be the Endurance’s social media coordinator manipulates images to make it seem like the ship’s dwindling air wing is far larger, then sends them into the world. Ace Combat series brand director Kazutoki Kono told me at a preview for the game in June that public image is just one of the player’s challenges: “On a much larger scale, I think social media and misinformation is another challenge that teams have to overcome nowadays.”

In the game, we see a character turn a shot of a handful of planes into a full wing, intentionally spreading propaganda. Hope that doesn’t backfire… Screenshot by David Lumb/CNET

Without spoilers, the game engages with the dangers of spreading misinformation, chief among them the titular Wings of Theve itself — a title the player’s nameless pilot inherits from the dead legend who takes up residence in their head. Is the pilot really an ace if their record is constantly exaggerated, even if it’s done to boost the flagging morale of the scattered remnants of a nation? That’s squared against the realities of your squadmates and the very real danger they all fly into.

That question of authenticity is reflected in the choices made by Kono and the rest of the Project Aces team, who developed Ace Combat 8. Fans of its 2019 predecessor, Ace Combat 7, disliked fighting the hordes of unmanned drones in that game — “they actually enjoyed the man-on-man dogfight experience with the radio chatter and the heated discussions and conversations,” Kono told me in a chat last December. It’s clear how much they focused on pilot discussions in AC8 to uplift the humans at the controls, and it’s fitting that the team sought out real-life fighter pilots to improve the realism of their game.

Screenshot by David Lumb/CNET

By the end of Ace Combat 8, I felt pushed to my limits, hurling my jet through high-G turns to eke out the barest edge during tense dogfights and screaming across the sky to support my squaddies. Yet it’s always against a beautiful tableau of blue firmament and white cloud, an endless aerial landscape I felt awed to behold in mission after mission.

At the end of it all, when I fired my last missile, my aching hands finally relaxed. Together with my squad, I looked out at the sky, the site of so much conflict over a dramatic 30 missions. As the enemy wreckage drifted earthward, the sun glinted off our cockpits and the space between clouds cleared, ready for the bold aviator who can’t get enough of the blue yonder.

Ace Combat 8: Wings of Theve is out now for PC, Xbox Series X and S, and PlayStation 5.

Tech.title: Apple Creator Studio Brings MotionVFX and AI Assistants to Subscribers
Tech.content:
Apple really is “Pro and Tell“-ing us a lot of news this week. On Tuesday, the company announced that its suite of creative software, Apple Creator Studio, will receive a bevy of AI-powered updates. That’s in addition to the new iMac, MacBook Pros and new OLED iPad Mini that the company also announced this week.

Final Cut Pro, Apple’s professional-grade video editor, is getting built-in MotionVFX. That should bring more visual and graphic effects tools to content editors on Mac. Logic Pro is getting a new beta AI assistant (powered by AI models built by Apple and OpenAI) for music editors in the US, along with a redesigned browser that uses Apple’s new Liquid Glass aesthetic. Pixelmator Pro is getting a kind of generative fill tool that uses AI to resize and fill in the gaps in new images; it sounds like it may be similar to Photoshop’s popular generative fill.

In Apple’s business software, expect to see new AI assistants in Keynote, Pages and Numbers. These are likely similar to how Google has integrated Gemini into its software over the past few years (and hopefully less annoying). The updated software will be available as “a free update for existing subscribers” in November.

More from CNET

The Apple news has been fast and furious this fall. The Cupertino-based company dropped the new iPhone 18 Pro lineup, along with its first folding phone, the iPhone Duo. Then it refreshed its entire smart home lineup, complete with a new HomeView device. We’re expecting even more Apple hardware news to drop on Wednesday, the in-person day of its Pro and Tell event that experts say could bring another long-awaited Apple first: a touchscreen MacBook. CNET is tracking all the Apple shenanigans this week and testing the new iPhone Duo — by folding it over 75,000 times and counting.

You can buy individual, lifetime (or “universal” as Apple calls it) subscriptions to each of Apple’s creative software. But these new features are coming only to Apple Creator Studio subscribers, who have access to multiple programs and pay a higher price tag as a result. Apple Creator Studio subscriptions start at $13 per month, and if you do buy a new MacBook, you get a free three-month trial.

Tech.title: Ford’s Most Affordable EV Will Offer Built-in Bidirectional Home Charging
Tech.content:
Ford’s upcoming Fathom electric truck — expected to arrive early next year — is reasonably priced at $28,350, especially given that the average transaction price for a new EV is closer to $55,000. But the added bonus is a feature that could save you money, and literally save your bacon.

The automaker’s “clean sheet” reboot of its EV ambitions will be offered with bidirectional charging, which allows the truck to send power from its battery back to the house it’s plugged into. That could keep the lights on and the fridge running during an extended power outage.

Historically, true bidirectional power has been a premium feature on more expensive electric cars and has required additional, costly home hardware. Ford says it’s bringing costs down by building the tech into what will be its cheapest EV yet and making it more accessible to a wider range of homeowners.

So far, Ford hasn’t revealed much of the electric truck beyond the name and camouflaged prototypes.

Ford Fathom and Universal EV Platform

The upcoming Fathom will be based on what Ford calls its Universal EV Platform, designed with the aid of its 2023 acquisition, startup Auto Motive Power, with bidirectional power on the plate from the start.

The hardware required to invert the battery’s DC energy to an estimated 10 kW of AC home power will be built into the truck, so it won’t require a separate wall-mounted inverter box. Ford says the Fathom’s system will meet all applicable UL 1741 requirements and IEEE 1547 standards to ensure the vehicle is safely connected to the grid.

As for the actual hardware you plug into your car, all signs point to the Fathom using the NACS plug type pioneered by Tesla and now widely adopted by new EVs in North America.

In terms of the communication standard — the one that governs how AC power is routed from the slim wall box to the car’s onboard charger — that’ll be via SAE J3068, a software protocol developed for high-power, heavy-duty AC charging.

By moving the DC-to-AC inverter into the Fathom’s hardware, Ford says it can reduce the total cost of home bidirectional power. Ford

Not totally hardware-free

Ford says that bringing the power-routing hardware directly into the vehicle reduces the cost of Fathom’s wall charger, making it easier for homeowners who need multiple chargers, whether for a multi-EV household, a second home or a detached garage. In other words, you pay for the advanced bidirectional technology once (built into the vehicle’s price) rather than buying it multiple times for each wall outlet you want to install around your property.

However, while Fathom’s Universal EV Platform eliminates the need for a wall inverter box, it doesn’t completely bypass the need for additional hardware to make your home ready to accept bidirectional power.

Say you wanted to take advantage of the Home Power Management feature to draw energy into the Fathom’s battery when power is cheapest, and then use that energy to offset peak-hour usage when power is most expensive. You’ll have to install at least the Ford Home Power Station in your home, at an additional cost.

The automaker hasn’t specified pricing, but says that it’s working to reduce costs and expects this component alone to cost half as much as the first-generation Ford Home Energy system, which debuted at around $1,300. That could put the new system at roughly $650.

The Ford Fathom will be available for preorder in 2027. Ford

For full-featured Ford Home Backup Power, which lets the EV supply power to the house during a power outage, you’ll need both Ford’s Home Power Station and Home Backup Power Panel, each a separate purchase. Here again, Ford expects to price its second-generation hardware “at least 60% lower” than the equivalent first-gen package, which cost roughly $5,000. So expect a ballpark of $2,000 for that extra peace of mind that your fridge won’t spoil when the lights go out.

That’s just the cost of the equipment itself. Your installation costs will depend on where you live and your specific house. Still, making the hardware less expensive for your home and vehicle is a step in the right direction. And considering the rising cost of energy (both electricity and fuel), this setup may pay for itself relatively quickly.

Tech.title: Last Week’s Critical PHP Warning Was the Tip of the Web Vulnerability Iceberg
Tech.content:
For the past week, software engineers around the globe have been scrambling to update the backend of websites after a team using an OpenAI model discovered two major vulnerabilities in PHP, a critical piece of web software.

PHP, open-source scripting software that underpins as many as 70% of websites worldwide, can become outdated when website owners don’t update to newer versions of the software, making them vulnerable to attacks. Shortly after alerts were issued about the new vulnerabilities, new versions of PHP were issued, and site operators were urged to update. Some government websites went dark in Europe as these updates were applied, but for much of the web, it’s been left to individual website owners to apply the fixes.

But will they?

More from CNET

No law compels them to do so, although if a website suffers a data breach, the owner could be liable to customers or clients. And for web surfers, it’s not obvious what PHP version a site is running without running terminal commands or using an online PHP checker.

Given that some websites are no longer actively managed — I own a website that was latent and hadn’t had a PHP update or updates of its WordPress software in years, for instance — the PHP story has shown that the web’s aging architecture is proving to be insecure due to neglect and dwindling resources to keep it safe.

PHP security shortages

One of the most shocking revelations that has come out of the last week’s race to get websites updated and safe is that an organization tasked with making sure security flaws in PHP are addressed is itself on shaky ground.

Reuters reported that the PHP Foundation, a nonprofit formed in 2021 to work with researchers and cybersecurity companies to ensure a crisis like this wouldn’t happen, has only one full-time staff member and lacks the resources to expand.

The Foundation’s Executive Director Elizabeth Barron told Reuters that she’s the sole staff member and works with about 14 part-time contractors and unpaid board members. As AI-generated threats increase, there’s twice as much demand to change PHP code to address them as in the past. “Yet the number of contributors hasn’t doubled,” Barron said. While companies and governments rely on PHP, “It is clear PHP is severely underfunded,” she said.

A representative for PHP Foundation did not immediately return a request for comment.

Website operators may be unaware there’s a problem

Nearly all small businesses have some sort of web presence, whether it’s a social media account, a Google listing or a website they own. But small business owners, a survey from Network Solutions found, may not be addressing the PHP issue because they don’t know it affects them.

The report, based on a survey of 121 small business owners with their own websites, found 45% of them had never heard of PHP and 71% didn’t know if their websites use it. A large majority of 71% of these site owners hadn’t heard about the recent PHP flaws.

Rick Radinger, principal systems architect for Network Solutions Group, said that the survey showed awareness and knowledge gaps, but that in addition to not knowing about the current PHP problem, they may not think it’s their responsibility to act on a fix. “An owner might know about the warning but could assume their hosting provider will handle it,” Radinger said. “Others might need additional help but aren’t sure who to contact or next steps.”

Some of the mobilization about the PHP alerts included updates from large web infrastructure companies like Cloudflare and web hosts such as GoDaddy. In a blog post, Cloudflare said it deployed new web application firewall protections to detect and fend off attacks. GoDaddy made updates to its managed hosting and Windows hosting services that didn’t require website owners to take extra steps, but said that domain customers who manage their own sites or run virtual private servers may need to update PHP themselves.

In addition to its security updates, Cloudflare has also introduced a PHP Capture the Flag contest as part of its Bug Bounty Program on HackerOne. “We’ve put a deliberately vulnerable PHP installation behind our (firewall), and we’re inviting security researchers on HackerOne to try to bypass the protections and capture a flag,” Cloudflare said in its blog post. Cash prizes range from $100 to $10,000.

Frustration for web users

For those who don’t own a website, the PHP vulnerabilities aren’t something you can protect against by updating your passwords; it’s up to websites to stay updated to protect their visitors.

“For users, it is frustrating that they can’t fix this, as it is an issue with the site’s server, not the browser,” Radinger said. “Simply updating your browser doesn’t address the issue, and a site being up and running normally does not mean the site has been fixed.”

The usual advice applies more than ever: Be careful about clicking on unfamiliar website links, don’t share sensitive information with websites you don’t trust and be especially cautious about links that will download software to your device.

The PHP crisis is a good wake-up call about what’s happening to the World Wide Web as it approaches its fourth decade of operation. This latest security scramble is just one of the threats websites face (AI-generated breaches are a huge one). But many of the dangers to come may stem from aging digital architecture; PHP is just one of myriad tools websites use, including JavaScript, SQL databases, content management systems (like WordPress or Wix), and the software that the servers themselves run. If those aren’t regularly monitored, managed and updated across the web, you can expect a lot more vulnerabilities to emerge in the years to come.

Tech.title: Live Now! Watch Us Fold the iPhone Duo Thousands of Times
Tech.content:
The iPhone Duo wowed us as Apple’s first foldable phone, but it’s time to test out how its first-gen hinge holds up. We’re now testing the $1,999 iPhone Duo using our custom-made folding machine, the Fold-a-Phone, which has been diligently opening and closing the phone since we bought the Duo on Friday.

Learn more: The iPhone Duo Just Passed 75,000 in Our Fold-a-Phone Testing Machine. Can It Beat the Galaxy Z Fold 8?

CNET is livestreaming our iPhone Duo long-term folding test on our YouTube channel, which you can watch embedded here. Our robust in-house machine will open and close the foldable around 20,000 times per day to simulate years of wear and tear on the hinge. You’ll be able to watch this testing on a livestream from our CNET Labs location in Louisville, Kentucky.

More from CNET

Our iPhone Duo folding test is ongoing, with our Fold-A-Phone machine running since Friday. Faith Chihil/CNET

The livestream won’t just be for watching a phone open and close — you’ll also be able to chat with CNET editors who will be available to answer your iPhone Duo questions live in the chat. Will Apple’s first foldable live up to the likes of the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 and Google Pixel 11 Pro Fold? Will its neat opening animation remain slick over thousands of folds? Join us and find out.

This long-term test will join our iPhone Duo review, which provides a snapshot of what it’s like to be among the first to use Apple’s first foldable phone. If you’re sold on it, check out the best iPhone Duo deals. And if you want to compare even further, you can check out our roundup of the best foldable phones currently available if you want help deciding between the Duo and other folding and flip-style phones from Samsung, Motorola and Google.

Tech.title: How CNET Makes Money: Content Labeling and Revenue Sources Explained
Tech.content:
At CNET, we don’t charge a subscription fee. All of our excellent, independent journalism is available free of charge for everyone. We pursue a variety of revenue sources to support our work, including selling space on our site to advertisers, licensing our content to partners and more.

We adhere to the strict standards of editorial integrity that have earned your trust throughout our 35-year history. In the spirit of transparency, here’s a guide to how we identify sources of revenue related to our content.

Key principles

CNET writers and editors follow a few core tenets that guide how we label our work. These are non-negotiable and spelled out below.

More from CNET

Independence: Editorial coverage, including stories, videos, product reviews, recommendations, and advice, is determined solely by our editorial organization for the benefit of the audience, without any advertising, marketing, or other business considerations.

Editorial coverage, including stories, videos, product reviews, recommendations, and advice, is determined solely by our editorial organization for the benefit of the audience, without any advertising, marketing, or other business considerations. Transparency: Disclosures are always clear, conspicuous and unambiguous to ensure that our audience understands when content is paid for by an advertiser, when independent content is made possible by an advertiser or when CNET earns a commission.

Disclosures are always clear, conspicuous and unambiguous to ensure that our audience understands when content is paid for by an advertiser, when independent content is made possible by an advertiser or when CNET earns a commission. Clear distinction: We maintain a clear boundary between independent editorial content and paid or branded content. When independent editorial content is made possible by a partner, we tell you.

Revenue sources and disclosures

The list below covers revenue sources disclosed on our site and platforms using specific language.

Affiliate links

CNET prides itself on independent, expert reviews and recommendations. Our writers and editors use their years of experience, along with lab-based testing, to recommend the best products and services available to our audience, along with the best deals on those products. We may earn a commission when you buy a product or service through a link on our platforms (e.g., in product reviews, “best lists,” or writing about deals). Not every product or service included on a best list or review will include buying links or buttons.

Disclosure: We include a prominent disclosure before or in sight of the first link. Standard disclosure language includes: “If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission.”

‘Made Possible By’

CNET creates content using an organic process of ideation, collaboration and response to tech industry trends. Partners and advertisers can choose to support editorial production within a category or package in order to increase the breadth and depth of CNET’s independent, human-authored journalism.

In these cases, partners and advertisers do not have editorial control or pre-publishing approval, nor can they mandate inclusion of specific products or information not already chosen or planned by the editorial team. At no point do advertisers view this content before it is published. Advertisers or partners may provide support to broad topics, specific categories of coverage, or story types.

Disclosure: If a brand chooses to support our content on our site or on social media, we include a clear, visible disclosure near the content or pieces of content in a category with language explaining that the content was made possible by a partner.

Sponsored best list and gift guide placements, also known as Featured Deals

Some sponsors would like their product or service to be included in our best lists and gift guides, which gather our editors’ expert recommendations into lists. If the sponsor’s product is already independently recommended by our journalists, sponsors may pay a fee to be featured higher in that list or in a more visible spot. Such cases will be clearly labeled with a disclosure.

If the sponsor’s product is not already recommended by our journalists but aligns with our standards, sponsored placements sold by business teams appear outside the list itself on the same page. These are clearly labeled with a disclosure to prevent implication of editorial endorsement.

Disclosure: These entries are clearly marked as “sponsored,” “featured partner” or “featured deal,” and a “What is This?” icon displays our editorial ethics disclaimer.

Partner offers

CNET rigorously evaluates which deals bring the most value to our readers. Sometimes an advertiser will pay to have a deal considered by the editorial team. Our team vets these deals and chooses to write about them only if they meet our standards for a good value. Writers and editors evaluating these deals do not know that partners have submitted deals through this program.

Disclosure: These articles are marked “Partner Offer” and include an on-page disclosure: “An advertiser paid for editorial consideration of this deal. Our editorial experts vetted the deal based on our independent expertise. Because we determined that the deal will save money for our readers, we wrote the content.”

Paid content (branded content, custom content, native advertising)

Brand X, CNET Group’s in-house paid content studio, creates work on behalf of advertisers. It publishes content that is informed by the brand or advertiser and delivered in a tone that aligns with CNET Group brands and audience interests. Advertisers pay a premium for creative control over production, product inclusion, point of view, visual design and final prepublishing approval.

Disclosure: We clearly label any paid content using FTC-compliant terms, including “,” “Ad Content,” “Sponsored Ad,” or “Special Advertising Content from [Brand].” The standard on-page disclosure is: “This is ad content, written and produced by CNET BrandX in collaboration with the sponsor. If you buy a product featured here, we may earn a commission.” We always include a Brand X byline.
